pillars.engagement_stem: You are more likely to contribute your time, effort and identity into a group

GrpProsp.name: Group Prospects
GrpProsp.description: How far you feel the group, as it now stands, can pull off the venture it has taken on and not yet finished: a game, project, season or campaign. It is confidence in the capability the venture will run on, not luck, not your own prospects (Payoff), not whether each will do their part (Dependability) and not a general sense that the group is strong. The culture's face sets where that capability is looked for.
GrpProsp.footnote: A group with goals is formally defined as a team, but the term group is preferred as it removes the implication of a wider organisation and hierarchy.

anchors.10: You feel sure the group, as it stands, can pull off what it has set itself; the venture looks well within its reach.
anchors.1: You feel sure the group, as it stands, cannot pull off what it has set itself; the venture looks beyond it.

GrpProsp.effect_on_other_pillars: GrpProsp's impact on other Pillars is based upon your present assessment of the average group attribute. In other words, the goal still remains to be achieved.
GrpProsp.engagement: That is likely to succeed in goals that you believe are worth pursing, or you would not have joined the group in the first place, and that has agreed goals, or otherwise random changes to the group's direction will move outside the model's ability to predict.
GrpProsp.out_of_scope: Random changes to the group's direction without agreed goals.

pre_language.core: A felt sense, before any words, that this band can bring off what it is setting out to do: chimpanzee males who hear strangers chorus and advance together when their party holds three or more males, and stay silent or hold back when it holds fewer (Wilson et al. 2001); and the chimpanzee who picks as partner the one who has made a joint task work before (Melis et al. 2006). Intimates read it from her bearing as the venture starts: settled and forward-leaning, in step with the others, or hesitant and watchful, eyes on the others rather than the task.

GrpProsp.status: Tightened by the literature 3 Nov 2026 (docs/model-edits/tighten/); provisional
GrpProsp.gloss: Felt confidence the group can pull this off

excluded: Generalised group potency: 'overarching group efficiency' and the generic ability to coordinate on any venture ('hunting ANY animal').
Process efficacy: confidence in the group's coordination, communication and cooperation as such ('ability to coordinate effectively').
Outcome forecast ('will achieve'), including fortune: a probability that the goal comes about, from whatever cause.
The rule that achieved goals drop out and 'may not continue to influence your engagement'.
Personal objectives within the group.

era.why: Chimpanzees weigh their party's strength before joining an intergroup contest (Wilson, Hauser and Wrangham 2001), and early humans' joint foraging needed a felt sense that the group could bring the hunt off; no talk is needed for that confidence.

E.label: Capability spread across the members
E.description: How far you feel the group, as it now stands, can pull off the venture it has agreed to take on and not yet finished. It is confidence in the group's capability for that venture, spread across its members, their skill included, and including the skill of whoever the band looks to for this venture for the day. Whether that member lords it over you is Parity's ground, and whether the others look to you is Esteem's. It is not luck, not your own prospects (Payoff), not whether each will do their part (Dependability), and not a general sense that the group is strong.

anchors.10: You feel sure the group, as it stands, can pull off what it has set itself; the venture looks well within its reach.
anchors.1: You feel sure the group, as it stands, cannot pull off what it has set itself; the venture looks beyond it.

E.subtitle: Can the group pull this off?
E.summary: Team Confidence in its egalitarian face is how far you feel the group, as it stands, can finish the venture it has agreed to take on. It rests on capability spread across the members, including whoever the band follows for the day. It is not luck, your own Payoff, or Dependability.
E.summary_status: generated from the face's description, not canon; checked faithful

H.label: Confidence in those who steer
H.description: How far you feel those at the top of the order, yourself included if you are there, can steer the group through the venture it has taken on and not yet finished: read the ground, choose the course, set each member to the part that suits them and right the course when it goes wrong. It reads their competence to direct this venture only, with the hands they have: whether the skill below is fit for the venture is read here as part of their steering, so a crew they have kept on a venture beyond it lowers this reading. A shortfall they could not have avoided or remedied, such as fixed capacity or an outside shock, lowers it less than one they chose or failed to correct. It is not whether they deal evenly with you, hearing you, holding you to the same rules and serving no favourites first (Parity), not the deference you draw for what you bring (Esteem), not your rung in the order (Rank), not what staying will bring you (Payoff), and not whether those below will carry their parts (Dependability). A well-meaning leader out of their depth rates low; a hard one who knows the way rates high.

anchors.10: You feel sure those at the top know the way through what the group has taken on; you follow their lead without second-guessing it, and if you are among them you feel the course is in safe hands.
anchors.1: You feel sure those at the top cannot steer the group through what it has taken on; each call they make looks like the wrong one, and if you are among them you feel the course slipping out of your hands.

pre_language.core: A felt sense, before any words, that the ones in front know where to take the band: the troop's readiness to rise and follow when the lead animal moves off, as subordinate chacma baboons followed the dominant male's foraging moves even at a cost to themselves (King et al. 2008), against hanging back, lagging or drifting off when the lead's moves have come to nothing. Read with care: in King's study following depended on the followers' social bonds with the leader, so it rests on ties as well as on any reading of where he leads; and in olive baboons movement is settled among many initiators and the dominant is not simply followed (Strandburg-Peshkin et al. 2015). Following a single leader is therefore one primate pattern among several, and the model borrows it for ranked orders only. Intimates read it from how she meets a call from the top: moving with it at once, eyes on the task, or a pause, a glance at the others and a slow, half-hearted start; and, if she is at the front herself, from a sure, unhurried move off against a false start and a look back.

H.subtitle: Confidence in those who steer
H.summary: Team Confidence in its hierarchical face is how far you feel those at the top can steer the group through its unfinished venture: reading the ground, choosing the course, placing members and correcting mistakes. It judges only their competence to direct. It is not Parity, Esteem, Rank, Payoff or Dependability.
H.summary_status: generated from the face's description, not canon; checked faithful

sources.source: Dirks, K. T. (2000). Trust in leadership and team performance: Evidence from NCAA basketball. Journal of Applied Psychology, 85(6), 1004-1012.
sources.claim: In men's college basketball teams, players' trust in the coach both resulted from and predicted team performance. Grounds the hierarchical face as a reading of the top that bears on the venture; the trust measure is broader than competence, so only its competence part is taken.
sources.verified: yes, at abstract level; sample details not checked against full text

sources.source: Dirks, K. T., and Ferrin, D. L. (2002). Trust in leadership: Meta-analytic findings and implications for research and practice. Journal of Applied Psychology, 87(4), 611-628.
sources.claim: Meta-analysis (k = 106) of trust in leadership with outcomes, antecedents and correlates; direct leaders are a particularly important referent; links with attitudes such as commitment are stronger than with performance (reported in the authors' earlier conference version). Trust there mixes competence with good faith, so the face takes it as light support and leaves good faith to Levelling and Reciprocity.
sources.verified: partly; abstract and conference summary seen, correlation tables not seen

sources.source: Chen, G., and Bliese, P. D. (2002). The role of different levels of leadership in predicting self- and collective efficacy: Evidence for discontinuity. Journal of Applied Psychology, 87(3), 549-556.
sources.claim: In 2,585 soldiers from 86 combat units, leadership climate at the higher organisational level was the strongest predictor of collective efficacy. Grounds placing a ranked group's confidence in its capability on how its upper leadership is read.

sources.source: Meindl, J. R., Ehrlich, S. B., and Dukerich, J. M. (1985). The romance of leadership. Administrative Science Quarterly, 30(1), 78-102.
sources.claim: People over-attribute organisational outcomes to leadership, more so the more extreme the outcome. Grounds reading the venture's fortunes through those at the top, and warns that the face is inflated or sunk by results after the fact.
sources.verified: partly; bibliographic record and secondary summaries seen, abstract not seen

sources.source: Fiske, A. P. (1992). The four elementary forms of sociality: Framework for a unified theory of social relations. Psychological Review, 99(4), 689-723.
sources.claim: Authority ranking is one of four elementary relational models: people are ordered linearly, those above hold authority and privilege, and those below are owed guidance and protection. Grounds the hierarchical face's location of steering in those at the top.
sources.verified: partly; the four models and linear ordering confirmed, the guidance-and-protection detail from secondary summaries only

sources.source: King, A. J., Douglas, C. M. S., Huchard, E., Isaac, N. J. B., and Cowlishaw, G. (2008). Dominance and affiliation mediate despotism in a social primate. Current Biology, 18(23), 1833-1838.
sources.claim: Chacma baboon group foraging decisions were led by the dominant male, who gained most from them; subordinates followed despite consensus costs, and his closest grooming partners followed most closely. Pre-language form of the hierarchical face.

sources.source: Strandburg-Peshkin, A., Farine, D. R., Couzin, I. D., and Crofoot, M. C. (2015). Shared decision-making drives collective movement in wild baboons. Science, 348(6241), 1358-1361.
sources.claim: In GPS-tracked wild olive baboons, movement direction was settled among multiple initiators and dominant individuals were not simply followed. Bounds the pre-language form to despotic orders.

sources.source: Kruglanski, A. W., and Webster, D. M. (1991). Group members' reactions to opinion deviates and conformists at varying degrees of proximity to decision deadline and of environmental noise. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 61(2), 212-225.
sources.claim: In freely interacting groups, a deviate was rejected more when dissent came close to the group's decision deadline, attributed to heightened need for collective closure. Supports the retained mechanism of X:GrpProsp->NormExp.
sources.verified: yes for the first experiment, at abstract level; the other three experiments not checked

edits.why: Hierarchical face only. Its clause 'not their good faith or whether they push you about (Levelling)' sends leaders' good faith to Levelling, which claims only force or fear and taking more than one's due and makes it stick. Good intent as such belongs to no perception, and the face's own closing line already rules it out ('A well-meaning leader out of their depth rates low'). The fix points the Levelling clause at Levelling's actual ground and leaves good faith excluded by that closing line. The general definition, the egalitarian face and all anchors agree with OwnProsp, OutResp, Status, Prestige and Levelling boundary clauses and fit the collective-efficacy literature (Bandura 1997) and, for the hierarchical face, work tying confidence in the venture to confidence in its leaders (e.g. leader efficacy, Hannah et al. 2008; unchecked here). No change there.

problems.detail: The checker found that following depended on social bonds or affiliation with the dominant male, not grooming partners by name. Say social bonds.

problems.where: faces.H.pre_language.core: 'so the form belongs to despotic orders'
problems.detail: Neither baboon paper sets that bound (checker: not in source for Strandburg-Peshkin et al. 2015). Two troops of two species show that single-leader following is one primate pattern among others. Restricting the form to ranked orders is a modelling choice and should say so.

logic_status.common_sense: The exclusions (not luck, not Payoff, not Dependability, not general group strength) and 'yourself included if you are there' are definitional boundaries, safe because they only partition the model's own perceptions. The intimate signs (forward-leaning and in step against hesitant and watchful; moving at once against a pause and a glance) are ordinary observation of confidence. 'A well-meaning leader out of their depth rates low; a hard one who knows the way rates high' follows from defining the H face as competence only. The H face's location of confidence in the top rests on Dirks 2000 (supports) and Chen and Bliese 2002 (supports), with Meindl et al. 1985 (partly) as the caution; the E face's capability spread across members rests on Melis et al. 2006 (supports) and leaders who lead by being followed on von Rueden et al. 2014 (supports).

dimensions.setting: narrow (organisational, sport and lab teams; largely WEIRD)

evidence.why: Team efficacy and potency are member surveys about the group, so the two independent meta-analyses are direct evidence, and they agree on a moderate correlation; but neither is confirmed as bias-corrected and the causal direction is contested. Provisional for now; if the Stajkovic et al. full text shows the effect survives a bias test, the reading-tracks-capability step could be regraded substantiated with the reciprocity boundary.
evidence.boundary: The link with performance runs both ways and depends on level: past results feed confidence, and within teams across games the sign can reverse (Myers et al. 2004, to be confirmed); manipulated confidence shifts effort more reliably than performance. The primate evidence is an analogous precursor from one chimpanzee community, and single-leader following is one pattern among several (shared following in olive baboons). The separation from Payoff, Dependability and general strength rests on construct definition.

shared_note.why_shared: Both faces read one level: how far you feel the group, as it now stands, can pull off the venture it has taken on and not yet finished. Whether you look to the members at large or to those who steer, the question is the same, and it is not luck, Payoff or Dependability.
shared_note.differences: The egalitarian face looks for that capability spread across the members, their skill included. The hierarchical face looks to those at the top: reading the ground, choosing the course, setting each member to a suitable part and righting the course when it goes wrong. Shortfalls they could have avoided or remedied lower it more.

OwnProsp.name: Own Prospects
OwnProsp.description: How likely you feel it is that staying in this group will get you what you yourself are after from it: the place, play, pay, skill, advancement or mate you joined for. It is a forecast of what the group will deliver to you, not your own ability, not your present rung in the order (Rank), not the deference you draw now for what you bring (Esteem), not whether the others want you among them now (Belonging), not the group's own venture (Team Confidence), not whether help you give comes back (Reciprocity), not whether anyone takes more than their due or tilts a share-out against you now (Parity), and not a tally of what it has given so far. Each of these can feed the forecast without being it.

anchors.10: You are sure that staying will bring you what you came for; the group's dealings with you keep opening the way to it.
anchors.1: You are sure that staying will bring you nothing you came for; whatever you do here, the way to it stays shut.

OwnProsp.effect_on_other_pillars: You respond to your current assessment of goal achievement likelihood.
OwnProsp.engagement: Where you feel that you are likely to achieve your personal goals, whether or not they are part of the group goals (Team Confidence) or indeed, conflict with them. Presumably if personal and group goals are in conflict, you would prefer to have low levels of Team Confidence however such a condition is out of scope for the model as it indicates deception and potentially sabotage, which is a cognitive rather than an unconscious drive (as the Pillars are contended to be).
OwnProsp.out_of_scope: Personal goals deliberately in conflict with group goals (deception, sabotage).

excluded: Own ability: self-efficacy or perceived competence, the 'can I do it' reading.

Comparison with outside alternatives: what she could get elsewhere.

problems.where: pre_language.core: 'Its animal form is the forager's reading that a patch is still worth working, and the primate's reading that staying in this troop will or will not yield what staying costs.'
problems.detail: Two empirical claims about animal decision-making (patch-leaving, as in the marginal value theorem; primate dispersal decisions) with no cited or checked source. Calling them 'its animal form' asserts homology on top. Drop the sentence, or cite and check (for example Charnov 1976 and a primate dispersal study) and present them as analogues.

logic_status.common_sense: The whole definition rests on common sense: no source is cited, and the one sorted theory (Wageman 1995) concerns reward interdependence and effort, not this reading. Defining Payoff as a felt forecast of what staying will bring you, with boundaries against Rank, Team Confidence, Reciprocity and a running tally, is a definitional partition and safe. The intimate signs (settling in and working at one's own aims against drifting to the edge, looking outward and leaving) are ordinary observation of whether someone expects a place to pay off.

dimensions.setting: broad (field employees across countries, close relationships, wild primates)

evidence.why: Several fields point the same way, but through neighbouring constructs (alternatives, embeddedness, expectancy, romantic commitment, primate dispersal costs); the investment model is analogous and the forager and primate material is indirect or unread, so the consilience on the step itself is some rather than strong. No source is replicated or bias-corrected, so provisional.
evidence.boundary: Effects are modest and the forecast predicts staying and choice more than performance. Much of the organisational evidence measures satisfaction, commitment or support, which Payoff excludes, so the discriminant line rests on definition. The failed registered replication of commitment priming (Cheung et al. 2016) concerns a neighbouring manipulation and does not bear on the forecast-to-stay step.

Status.name: Status
Status.description: Your felt rung in the group's settled order of precedence: how far you go first, take the first turn and the first share as a matter of course, and how far you go after others and take what is left. All recognise the order, so it is not fought out each time. A single call taken or refused moves it little; it shifts as such acts settle into what all take for granted. The precedence attaches to your place, however you came by it: an office, seniority, the backing of kin or allies, an old contest no one reopens, or credit for what you bring that has settled, over time, into a place others take for granted. It is distinct from the live deference you draw for what you bring now (Esteem), and once settled it does not need present fear to hold it day to day (Parity), though an old contest or the backing of allies may stand behind it.

anchors.10: You go first as a matter of course: the first turn, the first share and the best seat are yours without a word said, and no one in the group stands above you.
anchors.1: You go last as a matter of course: you wait your turn and take your share and seat after everyone else, without a word said, and no one in the group stands below you.

Status.effect_on_other_pillars: Your perception of your status can change due to slight changes to a formal remit, or the willingness people are to be compelled. If they do not respect your authority, you would feel lower status, and influence your behaviour.
Status.engagement: Where you feel that you possess formal power within a group, enabling you to utilise the group to achieve your own vision, which aligns the group with your identity. This is why new leaders often revoke measures taken by the preceding.

pre_language.core: Her felt rung in an order all recognise: the others let her pass, eat and settle first and greet her with the calm signals of submission, or she passes, eats and settles after them and greets them so, and neither side has to fight it out each time. Intimates read it from who passes first when paths cross, who eats first, who takes the best spot, and who greets whom.

edits.by: Ben approved (9.03 am)
edits.was: This Pillar is the seniority you have been awarded within the group. This is the formal power you have to compel others and make decisions on behalf of the group. A small group may not have a rank structure, but it may formally attribute power unequally. Such power is distinct from that gained informally, or Popularity. Yet both may be the product of common consent, such as voting. The difference is the formalisation of the power, rather than being informal and thus needing to be negotiated.
edits.now: This Pillar is your felt place in the group's settled order of rank: how far others defer to you, give way to you and accept your decisions on behalf of the group. The rank may be conferred formally (an office, a title, a vote) or settled informally over time; what matters is that all recognise it and it need not be renegotiated each time. Deference here goes to your place, whatever others think of your skill.
edits.reason: Status covers rank settled formally or informally (H-to-E panel: formal conferred power has no chimpanzee counterpart, while the wordless core is a settled rank order); the Popularity cross-reference dropped and the boundary drawn against IncResp, which the status literature tends to merge with rank.

edits.by: Ben approved, 5 Nov 2026, 11.22 am (comparative psychologist's critique, docs/v3/sc-critique/)
edits.why: The present wording confuses the origin of precedence with its basis. Places are often won by skill or contribution, and in primates through kin and allies or through old contests. What makes precedence Status is that it has settled onto the place and is not fought out or held by fear now. The proposed wording from the brief is closer to the literature, but it needs 'present' fear (settled orders often began in force) and the kin and contest origins, or 'however you came by it' is undercut.

problems.where: description: 'and it is not held in place by present fear (Parity)'
problems.detail: The pre-language form is primate dominance with submission signals, which Henrich and Gil-White 2001 class as rank based on force or the threat of force. Chapais found rank held among peers when subordinates could not form coalitions, so it rests on their inability to challenge it. De Waal's formalisation supports only that day-to-day fighting falls away. The flat denial goes beyond these sources; say that a settled rank does not need present fear day to day.

problems.where: pre_language.core: 'Read with care: beliefs about the bodily signs of rank outrun the measured signs.'
problems.detail: No cited or sorted source. The literature on beliefs about nonverbal signs of the vertical dimension (for example Hall, Coats and LeBeau 2005) may back it but is not cited or checked. Drop it, or cite and check.

logic_status.common_sense: Office and seniority as routes to a settled place are ordinary features of human groups and need no source. Intimate signs (who passes first, eats first, takes the best spot) are ordinary observation of priority of access. The rest has backing: settled order not fought out each time from de Waal 1986 (partly, formalisation) and Magee and Galinsky 2008 (supports, self-reinforcing hierarchy); kin and ally backing from Chapais (partly; the citation should name the specific 1988 paper); credit settling into place from Willer 2009 (partly) with Magee and Galinsky; Rank kept apart from Esteem from Henrich and Gil-White 2001 (supports).

dimensions.setting: narrow (mostly Western student and survey samples; some forager and primate field data)

evidence.why: Lab and forager data support the separation from Esteem and primate formal dominance supports settled precedence, but the primate and ethnographic material is analogous and the psychological sources mostly measure esteem-type or society-wide status. Direct tests of a felt in-group rung come from one unreplicated programme, so provisional.
evidence.boundary: In strongly levelling groups the rung is held low and flat by coalition (Boehm 1993), and status did not predict in-camp integration among Hadza men. Effects of felt rank on wellbeing are small and partly self-report method variance.

NormExp.name: Normative Expression (norm guarding)
NormExp.description: How strongly it strikes you as wrong when another member breaks from the group's settled ways in a way the group would condemn, in act or by openly pressing to change them. The settled ways are read from what members actually do as well as from what they say should be done: where most members have stopped keeping a way, a breach of it jars less, however firmly the way is still spoken of; where most keep it, a lone breach jars most. That softening holds for the group's conventions, how things are done here. A breach that wrongs a member, taking from her, hurting her or leaving her to carry what was the breacher's to carry, jars whatever most members now do and whoever commits it. Your reading can still run stricter than what the others privately hold, since members often take a way that is openly kept to be more widely endorsed than it privately is (pluralistic ignorance: Prentice and Miller 1993). A sense of being out of step with the others can follow from such a misreading, and in that study it went with alienation from the university; it is not part of this reading, and it bears on Belonging only through how you then read the others' treatment of you. The reading starts from the breach, as felt indignation, not from any prior dislike of the person. Intimates read it from the start the breach gives you, the muttering or the open word, and not only from whether you pull the member up. An objection, a rebuke or mockery are anger's forms: they look for the member to mend their ways and be taken back. Where the breach repeats or reads as bad character, the indignation hardens into contempt for the member, and a cold shoulder or shutting them out are its forms, and they last. The reading's level does not set the form; the form sets how long the response bites and whether it ends in reconciliation or exclusion. Whether the bristle comes out as an open rebuke, a word behind the member's back or nothing at all depends on your power and on what you stand to lose with the member (Molho et al. 2020); a low member who bristles and keeps quiet still reads high. Your own conformity and your openness to ideas are not part of it. Among equals the group's ways include its levelling ways: not presuming on success or boasting, not keeping back what should be shared, and pulling your weight; a breach of these stirs the same bristle, which among equals most often comes out as ribbing and complaint (Boehm 1999; Wiessner 2005), though here too the form depends on your power and what you stand to lose. Whether such a member lords it over you yourself is Parity's ground. NormExp.effect_on_other_pillars: NormExp has a delayed impact because it is assumed that your suppression or welcoming of ideas has already occurred. As with DivsExp, there is no assumption that any opinion has been acted on (although the scenario may play out that way).
NormExp.engagement: Where you feel that you can manage (minimise unwelcome or surprising) change, by using your power to reduce any propensity for others to suggest change. While high Rule-Keeping undermines Psychological Safety for others, it makes you personally feel safer.

pre_language.core: The bristle at one of the band doing a thing the wrong way. Its sign is the move to pull them up: a protest cry, a shove, a cold shoulder or exclusion. In one small theft experiment, captive chimpanzees retaliated for their own losses but did not punish theft from others (Riedl et al. 2012); the era rests on that one study and is provisional. Intimates read it from how she meets another's departure: with indignation, shown in a start, a mutter or a rebuke, or with a shrug. Forager bands such as the Ju/'hoansi turn a like bristle, by criticism and mockery, on upstarts and stingy members (Wiessner 2005); in this model that egalitarian form is carried by Safety->Parity and stands here only as the contrast. The face here is the guarding of a ranked group's settled ways.

excluded: Endorsing and defending the status quo yourself: expressing support for the group's settled ways and resisting change as such
Unwillingness to hear other members' suggestions (closed-mindedness; the old 1-anchor's 'listening intently')

Feeling safer for enforcing (the 'and feeling safer for it' in the wordless version)

problems.detail: Abrams et al. 2000 (partly) and the subjective group dynamics work show that anti-norm deviants are derogated while pro-norm deviants at the same distance are treated better and often liked. 'Any departure' covers pro-norm deviance too, which this literature contradicts. Ben's exception of 5 Nov 2026 already records the point and keeps the definition unchanged pending games, so this fix needs his approval.

problems.where: pre_language.core: 'Two and three year olds already protest a puppet's wrong move (Rakoczy et al. 2008)'
problems.detail: Rakoczy et al. 2008 is neither cited nor checked. As commonly reported, explicit protest was clear at three and weaker at two, so 'two and three year olds' may also overreach. Drop it until it has been added and checked.

problems.where: pre_language.core: 'chimpanzees retaliate for their own losses but do not police third-party breaches (Riedl et al. 2012)'
problems.detail: Riedl et al. tested 13 captive chimpanzees in one theft paradigm, and the checker notes critics who limit the result to that set-up. 'Do not police' is a general species claim and also sits badly with reports of chimpanzees intervening in others' conflicts. Restate it as the experimental finding.

problems.where: pre_language.core: 'Ju/'hoansi pull up breaches by criticism and mockery (Wiessner 2005)' together with 'Forager bands show the same bristle turned on upstarts and stingy members; in this model that egalitarian form is carried by Safety->Parity. The face here is the guarding of a ranked group's settled ways.'
problems.detail: Wiessner's Ju/'hoansi sanctions fall mostly on stinginess and self-aggrandisement in an egalitarian band, the very form the text then assigns to Safety->Parity. It is cited as an example of this HCP's bristle and as a case of the form placed elsewhere. Keep it only as the egalitarian contrast.

logic_status.common_sense: The boundaries (felt indignation at the breach rather than dislike of the person; your own conformity and openness to ideas excluded) partition the model's own perceptions and are safe. Low-anchor behaviour (letting it pass) is the plain opposite of the high anchor. Pulling breaches up by objection, mockery and exclusion rests on Wiessner 2005 (supports) and Henrich et al. 2006 (supports, costly punishment in 15 societies).

NormExp.exceptions[0]: Exception noted (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 12.04 pm): reactions to deviance depend on its direction as well as its size. A member who falls short of the group's ways draws the jar this Pillar reads; one who goes beyond them in the group's own direction is often liked (the black sheep effect, subjective group dynamics: Marques, Abrams and colleagues). The definition was narrowed to departures the group would condemn on the facilitator's advice of 5 Nov 2026, 4.40 pm; the exception is kept for games and review.

dimensions.setting: broad (lab, lab-in-field in 15 societies, 57-country preregistered survey, forager ethnography, children)

evidence.why: Six independent fields converge on the core step that members condemn and pull up a third party's breach of group ways, with a large preregistered cross-national survey and the replicated black sheep effect; the contest over costly altruistic punishment touches the expression, not the felt reading, and becomes a boundary. Substantiated on strong consilience with adjacent evidence, while the descriptive-norm discount and the anger-versus-contempt form rule remain provisional sub-claims.
evidence.boundary: Felt indignation need not become costly punishment: disinterested third parties punish little (Pedersen et al. 2018), and small face-to-face societies show little costly third-party punishment (Henrich et al. 2010; Marlowe et al. 2008), so cheap forms (talk, mockery, withdrawal) are the expected expression. The chimpanzee era claim rests on one small captive study. Culture-level tightness is a contested construct and should not be mapped onto a member's level.
evidence.caveat: The evidence measures sanctioning in economic games, judged appropriateness of responses, protest by children and sanction forms in ethnography, not a member's felt indignation as such. Reading these as a felt indignation that varies by member is the model's framing.

NormExp.framework: Evidence boundaries. The descriptive-norm discount (a breach of a way most members have stopped keeping jars less) is common sense, pending the full text of Bicchieri, Dimant and Xiao (2021), whose snippets suggest punishment tracks perceived wrongness more than commonness; if confirmed, the clause becomes a Tier 2 item. The felt bristle need not become costly punishment: cheap forms such as talk, mockery and withdrawal are what to expect, especially in small groups (Pedersen et al. 2018; Henrich et al. 2010; Wiessner 2005). The split between anger's forms and contempt's forms rests on Schachter-type lab work and ethnography, not a tested moderator. The Homo sapiens era rests on one small chimpanzee study (Riedl et al. 2012). Tightness-looseness is a culture-level measure with contested rankings and does not set a member's level.

OutResp.name: Outgoing Respect
OutResp.description: How far you feel the other members can be counted on to do their part in the shared work: each carries through what they take on and keeps their word about it, so you leave work in their hands without checking that they are doing it. The reliance may rest on their own will or on knowing that a part let drop gets pulled up by the group or its rules; either can raise it. It is reliability, not skill (Team Confidence), not whether a slip or weak spot you show would be used against you (Safety), and not your indignation at a member who lets a part drop (Rule-Keeping); that answers the breach, while this reads what you expect of them next. A part let drop likely moves it further than a part carried through. Parts you have seen carried through or dropped move it directly and outweigh any card that reads it from your own fondness, confidence in the group, acceptance or investment; those cards bite only on parts not yet done or whose outcome you cannot see.

anchors.10: You leave any part of the work with any member and never check whether they are doing it; what they take on gets done and what they promise about it holds.
anchors.1: You check up on and chase others' work and redo what they skimp, expecting them to shirk, cut corners or go back on their word.

OutResp.effect_on_other_pillars: OutResp's impact on other Pillars is based upon your present assessment of the average group attribute.
OutResp.engagement: With competent and trustworthy people because you like being associated with 'winners', you admire and wish to model yourself off them, and they can help you to improve.

pre_language.core: Whether she can turn her back on them at a shared task. One who counts on her fellows leaves the watch, the carry or the young in their hands and goes about her own business without looking back; one who does not keeps glancing over, hovers at their work or takes it over herself. Intimates read it from how often she looks back, checks and takes over. The mechanism is trust calibrated to a partner's record of carrying a joint task, the kind of partner assessment the interdependence account places early in human cooperation (Tomasello et al. 2012). What sets this Pillar apart from Reciprocity is what the record is of: the partner's share of a joint task, not a favour returned to her. It is her reading of them; whether they turn their backs on her is a different thing and not read here.

OutResp.status: Tightened by the literature 3 Nov 2026 (docs/model-edits/tighten/); provisional
OutResp.gloss: Others do their part and keep their word

excluded: Competence (the ability facet; others' skill for their roles)
Benevolence (others' good will toward you in particular)
Warmth or sociability (friendliness, likeability)
Her own dependability as the others see it (felt trust: being counted on to deliver)

problems.where: pre_language.core: 'The mechanism, trust calibrated to a partner's record, is the one chimpanzees show when they adjust trust to partners who have come through before (Engelmann et al. 2015)'
problems.detail: Engelmann et al. 2015 is neither cited nor checked, and 'is the one chimpanzees show' asserts shared mechanism. Melis et al. 2006, the checked chimpanzee partner-choice source, picks partners for effectiveness, which this Pillar assigns to Team Confidence, so it cannot stand in. Ground the mechanism in Tomasello et al. 2012 (partly) as partner assessment, and drop the chimpanzee claim until it is checked.

problems.where: description: 'It is reliability, not skill (Team Confidence): a willing but clumsy member rates high.' against 'so you leave work in their hands without checking' and anchors.10: 'what they take on gets done'
problems.detail: You do check on a clumsy member's work, and clumsy work may not get done, so the example clashes with the definition and the top anchor. Make the example about carrying through, with quality left to Team Confidence.

logic_status.common_sense: No source is cited; the sorted sources carry the core. Reliability-based trust as distinct from care-based trust is McAllister 1995 (supports), and separating integrity or reliability from ability is Mayer et al. 1995 and Colquitt et al. 2007 (partly). Partner assessment in joint work is Tomasello et al. 2012 (partly). The behavioural signs (leaving work unchecked against checking, chasing and redoing it; leaving the watch or the young in others' hands against looking back) are ordinary observation of trust in others' follow-through. The boundaries against Reciprocity, Parity and Repute partition the model's own perceptions. Keeping this as one's reading of others, and never their reading of oneself, matches the project's OutResp definition.

dimensions.replication: some (two independent team-trust meta-analyses and a trustworthiness meta-analysis agree; none confirmed bias-corrected)
dimensions.directness: direct for the reading (member surveys of intrateam trust); adjacent for the link to leaving work unchecked
dimensions.consilience: strong (organisational behaviour, social psychology, developmental science, primatology, anthropology)

evidence.why: Two independent team-trust meta-analyses built on member surveys, the separation of integrity from ability, and convergence across five fields carry the reading on strong consilience, and no failed replication or published null was found. The weak spots (correlational data, mixed trust and control findings, an unsearched asymmetry) bound the mechanism and leave the core intact.
evidence.boundary: A low reading can show as taking a part over (social compensation, Karau and Williams 1993) as well as withdrawing or checking. The clause that rules or group cover can raise reliance has mixed support: trust and control are found both to substitute and to complement, and anticipated monitoring can lower later trust-like behaviour.
evidence.caveat: The trust meta-analyses link members' trust in teammates to team performance; no study found measures how far that reading lowers a member's checking or raises delegation, so the step to leaving work unchecked is the model's framing, supported by the documentation moderator in Breuer et al. (2016).

OutResp.framework: Evidence boundaries. 'A part let drop likely moves it further than a part carried through' is common sense, pending a search of the trust-asymmetry literature. Evidence on whether group or rule cover raises reliance is mixed, and anticipated monitoring can lower later trust-like behaviour, so cover can raise it but need not. A low reading can show as taking a part over (social compensation) as well as checking or withdrawing. The team-trust meta-analyses are correlational and do not show that reliance causes less checking. The separation from Rule-Keeping and Safety has not been tested.

Levelling.name: Levelling
Levelling.status: Tightened by the literature 3 Nov 2026 (docs/model-edits/tighten/); provisional
Levelling.description: How far you feel no one in the group sets themselves over you unfairly: by force or fear, by taking more than their due and keeping it, by tilting how shares, turns and chances are handed out, who gets a hearing, or how a quarrel is settled, towards themselves or their favourites, or by treating you with contempt, as if above you. The culture's face sets where that threat is looked for: among equals, a would-be boss; in a ranked group, partial or overbearing dealing from those above.

anchors.10: No one in the group makes you comply by force or threat, takes more than their due and keeps it, or tilts a share-out, a hearing or the settling of a quarrel against you; you take your portion and go about your business without watching anyone warily.
anchors.1: One or a few in the group make you comply through force or fear, take more than their due and keep it, or decide and divide in favour of their own while you are passed over or go unheard; you watch them warily or resent them, and mostly let them have their way, because objecting gets you nowhere or draws their anger.

pre_language.core: Freedom from a bully she must appease. The free animal moves, feeds and takes her share in the strongest member's presence without flinching or a glance at that member's mood; the coerced one tracks that member's moods, freezes on approach and does whatever heads off an attack. Intimates read it from whether she watches one particular member warily and shrinks or placates when that member comes near, while staying easy with everyone else, and whether, at a share-out, she is handed her portion in turn or watches the one dividing it feed his friends first and pass her by. The root is dominance, the coalitions that check it and the option to leave (Boehm 1999), not primate inequity aversion.

Levelling.descent: from rank perception, through coalitions of subordinates checking dominants. The capacity to read dominance is turned to levelling it (theory).
Levelling.gloss: No member bends you by force or fear

excluded: Coercion of the others: no one's will runs over the rest (witnessed or group-wide dominance)
Expectation that the others would stand with you against anyone who tried to push you about (coalitional check)
Leader's way rests on the others' going along, never imposed (consent-based legitimacy of leadership)
Appeal to a uniformly egalitarian ancestral band as the ground of the reading

edits.why: Model B has no perception that registers unequal shares or stolen credit, which is the other half of Boehm's egalitarian ethos and the best-known primate fairness finding, and arises often in everyday group life. Evidence on inequity aversion is contested, so the card effects that rely on it should be moderate.

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)

problems.where: description: 'Where the group has spoken ways of deciding, being heard and having those ways applied to you as to anyone is the later, spoken form of the same reading.'
problems.detail: Grocke et al. 2018 (supports) found children protested less only after they had agreed to a decision; being given a say and then overridden raised protest. 'Being heard' alone is partly contradicted by that result. Lind et al. 1990 (partly) supports a voice effect, but only on fairness judgements. 'The later, spoken form of the same reading' is a developmental or evolutionary claim with no source. Narrow it to having a say that counts, and drop 'later form'.

logic_status.common_sense: The felt side of coercion (watching one member warily, freezing on approach, placating to head off anger, moving freely in the strongest member's presence) is ordinary observation of fear of a particular person. A respected leader, or the group pulling up a breach together, leaving Parity high follows from Boehm 1993 (supports): followers level would-be dominants, not leadership as such. Grabbing that sticks rests on Peterson 1993 (supports). An even-handed share-out that leaves you less still leaving Parity high rests on Grocke et al. 2015 (supports). Bundling coercion, distributive grabs and tilted procedure into one reading is a modelling choice; Colquitt et al. 2001 shows the justice dimensions are distinct but intercorrelated, which does not contradict a single felt reading of 'someone sets themselves over me'. The logic leans on no animal inequity aversion, so the contested capuchin and chimpanzee results (Wynne 2004, Engelmann et al. 2017, Ritov et al. 2024) do not bear against it.

pre_language.core: Freedom from a bully she must appease. The free animal moves, feeds and takes her share in the strongest member's presence without flinching or a glance at that member's mood; the coerced one tracks that member's moods, freezes on approach and does whatever heads off an attack. Intimates read it from whether she watches one particular member warily and shrinks or placates when that member comes near, while staying easy with everyone else, and whether, at a share-out, she is handed her portion in turn or watches the one dividing it feed his friends first and pass her by.

H.label: Even hands from those above
H.description: How far you feel those above you in the order, and the order's own ways of deciding, deal evenly with you: they hear you before deciding what touches you, hold you to the same rules as anyone at your rung, hand out shares, turns and chances without serving their favourites first, settle quarrels without a thumb on the scale, give orders only as far as the rules of your place allow, without threat or fear, and treat you with the courtesy your place is owed. It is not your rung (Rank), not whether partners repay you (Reciprocity), not whether those at the top can steer (Team Confidence), not deference for what you bring (Esteem), not the cost of showing yourself (Safety), not whether you are kept among them (Belonging) and not whether a charge against your character stands before those who count (Face), though being denied a hearing on such a charge lowers this reading. A settled order that gives you less by rank but applies its rules evenly and hears you leaves it high; a decision made over your head, a patron who serves his own first, a superior who rules by threat, contempt from above, or one above who lets a wrong done to you by another member stand when it is theirs to put right, lowers it.

anchors.10: Those above you hear you out before any call that touches you, apply the same rules to you as to anyone at your rung and hand out turns and shares with no favourite served first; you take your portion when it comes without watching the one who divides it.
anchors.1: Calls that touch you are made over your head, favourites are served before you whatever the rules say, and objecting gets you waved off or met with a threat; you watch whoever divides, settles and gives orders with a wary, aggrieved eye.

pre_language.core: Whether the one who divides and settles hands her portion in its turn and hears her out, or feeds his favourites first and waves her off. Intimates read it from whether she waits at the share-out at ease or watches the divider warily, and whether she puts her case to those above or no longer bothers. After a clash with one above her, a soft grunt or easy approach from him tells her it is over and she stays near; a hard stare sends her off. When those above break up fights without taking sides, she feeds and rests among them at ease.

H.subtitle: Even hands from those above
H.summary: Parity in its hierarchical face is how far you feel those above you, and the order's own ways of deciding, deal evenly with you. They hear you, hold you to the same rules as others at your rung, serve no favourites first, settle quarrels fairly, and give orders without threat. It is not your Rank.

dimensions.replication: some (organisational justice, ultimatum rejection and abusive supervision meta-analyses; none confirmed bias-corrected)
dimensions.directness: direct for the hierarchical face (member perceptions of fair treatment from those above); adjacent for the egalitarian face (behaviour and ethnography)
dimensions.consilience: strong (forager ethnography, behavioural economics, organisational and social psychology of justice, developmental science)

evidence.why: Four independent fields converge on resistance to unfair advantage-taking, partiality and domination, and organisational justice meta-analyses give direct member-perception evidence for the hierarchical face. The one failed strand (primate inequity aversion) bears on the era support only, and the contested legitimacy and third-party findings become boundaries.
evidence.boundary: Primate inequity aversion is not a root for the reaction: the token-exchange findings failed or are contested (Bräuer et al. 2009; Ritov et al. 2024, a meta-analysis with preregistered subsets finding no effect across 18 species), so the pre-language core rests on dominance, coalition and exit evidence. In small forager groups the wronged member acts for herself far more than bystanders do (Marlowe 2009), so the backed form should not assume third-party enforcement. The step from fair procedure to going along freely runs largely through legitimacy (Walters and Bolger 2019).
evidence.caveat: For the egalitarian face the evidence is costly rejection and punishment of unfair splits in games and ethnographic accounts of levelling; none measures a member's felt reading that no one sets themselves over her, which is the model's framing of what drives those acts.

Levelling.framework: Evidence boundaries. The era and pre-language rest on dominance, coalition and exit evidence (Boehm 1999); the Brosnan and de Waal token-exchange findings are not relied on, since a meta-analysis with preregistered subsets fails them. In small forager groups the wronged party acts for herself far more than bystanders do, so the branch where others would back you reads her own sense of possible backing and does not assume third-party enforcement. Compliance from fair procedure may run through legitimacy. Organisational justice and abusive-supervision findings are largely single-source self-report.

shared_note.why_shared: Both faces read how far you feel no one sets themselves over you unfairly: by force or fear, by taking more than their due, by tilting how shares, turns, chances, hearings or quarrels are handled towards themselves or their favourites, or by treating you with contempt. It is one felt level; only the place the threat is looked for changes.
shared_note.differences: In the egalitarian face the threat is a would-be boss among equals, who forces, grabs or tilts things their way. In the hierarchical face it is partial or overbearing dealing from those above, who should hear you, hold you to the same rules as anyone at your rung and serve no favourites first.
shared_note.status: generated from the Pillar's texts; checked faithful

DivsExp.name: Diverse Expression (felt safety)
DivsExp.description: How safe you feel to show yourself in this group: to let a slip, a mood, a need or a disagreement show, or go about things your own way, expecting no put-down, mockery or rebuff for it. It includes whether a slip, a need or a weak spot you let show would be turned against you to get ahead of you or to do you harm. It is your reading of what showing yourself will cost you, not whether you speak up; not whether a need you show gets met (Reciprocity), whether your word carries weight (Esteem) or whether you are wanted (Belonging); not whether anyone pushes you about by force or fear, whether those who decide hear you out before a call that touches you or whether anyone treats you with contempt, as if above you, whatever you show (Parity); not the verdict already held on your conduct (Repute) or being openly charged or caught out before those who count (Face); and not your own indignation at others' departures (Rule-Keeping).

anchors.10: You feel free to let slips, moods, needs and disagreements show as they come and to go about things your own way, expecting no one to pounce on them, laugh at them or turn away.
anchors.1: You feel that letting a slip, a mood, a plain need, a disagreement or a way of your own show would draw a put-down or be used against you, so you scan faces before you move and keep your reactions masked.

DivsExp.effect_on_other_pillars: DivsExp has a delayed impact because it takes time for your contribution to either heard or ignored. Again, there is no assumption that it has been or will be acted on (although the scenario may play out that way).
DivsExp.engagement: Where you feel that your ideas will be welcomed and well-received. While related to IncResp (HCP), Expression is closer to a norm of Psychological Safety than being given specific respect for one's competence. Such a norm creates a warm, less hostile environment, which is distinct from cohesion: a close, friendly group can still make challenge feel risky.

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)

problems.where: pre_language.core: "(displacement activity rises with social stress: Maestripieri et al. 1992)" and the "self-scratching" detail it backs
problems.detail: Maestripieri et al. 1992 is cited inside the logic, but no checker verdict exists for it. It is a substantive mechanism claim (self-directed behaviour indexes social anxiety). Either have it checked or drop it.

logic_status.common_sense: Mood as one of the things shown (Edmondson's construct covers mistakes, problems, asking for help and being different, not mood by name): safe, since a mood is one more thing someone might mask for fear of a put-down. The loose-versus-braced body contrast as the felt sign: safe, a familiar reading of ease and wariness. The exclusions from Esteem, Belonging, Parity, Repute, Face and Rule-Keeping are model boundaries and fit the other items' texts.

dimensions.replication: some (Frazier et al. 2017 and Marlow and Lacerenza 2025 meta-analyses; no bias correction confirmed, no registered or multi-lab test)
dimensions.directness: direct (member surveys of psychological safety count as each member's felt reading, Ben 7 Nov 2026)
dimensions.setting: narrow (organisational field, mostly cross-sectional, knowledge-work weighted)
dimensions.consilience: some (organisational behaviour only at full strength; anthropology and primatology are analogous)

evidence.why: Member-survey evidence for the felt reading is now direct and pooled in two meta-analyses, but neither is confirmed to survive bias correction and consilience rests on one field, so neither route to substantiated is met. Distinctness from trust, a load-bearing part of the definition, is contested on measurement grounds; checking Frazier et al. (2017) for bias tests and discriminant correlations could lift the grade.
evidence.boundary: The link from safety to learning and performance depends on task demands (Sanner and Bunderson 2015) and safety alone did not predict later organisational performance in a large longitudinal study (Higgins et al. 2022), so the Pillar should not be credited with uniform downstream effects. Its separation from trust and leader relations rests mainly on argument; reviews of the measures flag weak discriminant evidence.

DivsExp.framework: Evidence boundaries. The era rests on the relaxed against braced bearing among fellows; the claim that subordinate primates suppress displays near dominants is withdrawn, since the search did not support it (the bared-teeth display is a signal sent upward, not one withheld). The Pillar is the member's own reading, whereas the evidence is mostly a team-aggregate belief measured cross-sectionally. Its link to learning and performance depends on task demands and accountability (Sanner and Bunderson 2015; Higgins et al. 2022). Its separation from trust and leader support rests on conceptual argument more than discriminant tests. The exploitation clause (a weak spot turned against you) has no direct evidence yet and is common sense.

Reciprocity.name: Reciprocity
Reciprocity.status: Tightened by the literature 3 Nov 2026 (docs/model-edits/tighten/); provisional
Reciprocity.description: Your felt reading of whether help in this group comes back: what you give is returned, what you ask for is met. It holds until evidence moves it. A return that falls short of what was given or agreed moves it further, and is slower to be made good, than a return that exceeds it. It concerns the return on help, not whether others carry their part of shared work (Dependability), whether anyone takes more of a common take than their due (Parity), your indignation at a member who keeps back what should be shared (Rule-Keeping), where you stand (Rank), whether the others want you among them (Belonging) or how they judge your conduct (Repute, Face), though your good name feeds the return. The culture's face sets where the return is looked for.

anchors.10: What you give comes back and what you ask for is met, as a matter of course; you count on the return without a second thought.
anchors.1: What you give is not returned and what you need goes unmet; you expect nothing back from anyone here.

Reciprocity.mechanics: Effects still assume help received (canon). The former IndRecip cards attach to the egalitarian Pillars and the former DirRecip cards to the hierarchical ones, so no card collides. A culture switch (HCP dominance drift, or its reverse) changes the face without resetting the level.
Reciprocity.effect_on_other_pillars: IndRecip's impact on other Pillars is based upon the assumption that assistance has been received. As such, it moves forward in time to the help having been rendered. The provision of assistance is not modelled because its impacts are less predictable. There is no Force card drawn if the character has provided assistance.

E.label: Return from the group
E.description: Help goes to whoever needs it, and the return comes from the group at large. Big windfalls often go out by demand and tolerated taking, to whoever is there, whatever their record, though that is one route among several. In some bands the care a member gets when sick or hurt, and some everyday giving, track being seen to share; in others even everyday giving goes by need, whatever the record. Whoever has a surplus is pressed to share on demand, and asking is as normal as giving. Your reading is whether, when you are in need, the group at large gives to you.

anchors.10: Whoever has gives to whoever needs; what you have put in comes back to you from any member when you are in need.
anchors.1: Giving goes into a hole: nothing comes back from anyone, those with a surplus hide it, and need goes unmet.

pre_language.core: Food handed over on demand within the band, with the return coming from whoever next has a surplus; those who hide food lose standing and are passed over. Intimates read it as a sign in her behaviour: whether she hands her surplus to anyone who asks and asks anyone who has, or holds back from both.

E.engagement: Where you feel that the norm of IndRecip is strong because the group can adapt to challenges smoothly by moving effort to where it is most urgently needed, without needing to debate or cajole, and there is joy in feeling part of collective endeavour where no one prioritises self-interest or their own immediate tasking.
E.subtitle: Return comes from the group
E.summary: Reciprocity in its egalitarian face is whether, when you are in need, the group at large gives to you. Help goes to whoever needs it, and those with a surplus are pressed to share on demand. Windfalls go out by demand whatever the record, while everyday giving and care track being seen to share.
E.summary_status: generated from the face's description, not canon; checked faithful

H.label: Return from the partner
H.description: Help flows between particular partners who return it to each other. It is conditional on a return from the same partner: in kind between equals, or across rank, as favour and protection passed down for loyalty and service passed up. Your reading is whether your partners pay you back, not where you stand (Rank), whether they do their part of the shared work (Dependability), whether those above decide evenly (Parity) or whether your character stands unchallenged before those who count (Face), though being shown up as one who leaves a favour unreturned lowers Face, and Face in turn feeds the return.

anchors.10: Every partner you help pays you back and those you ask deliver; whoever stands above you covers you and whoever stands below you backs you, each in turn.
anchors.1: Partners take and do not return; whoever stands above you leaves you uncovered and whoever stands below you will not back you; you expect no return from anyone you deal with.

pre_language.core: Grooming returned by the one groomed (Schino and Aureli 2008). Intimates read it as a sign in her behaviour: whether she keeps giving to those who gave to her and turns from those who did not.

H.engagement: Where you feel that the norm of DirRecip is strong because the group can adapt to challenges smoothly by moving effort to where it is most urgently needed, by trusting each other's word (assuming there are favours that each can do for each other); there is joy in feeling part of an endeavour where promises to return favours are always kept, and your efforts end up being recognised and returned; this version of trust is more honouring a deal, rather than being trusted to carry out tasks reliably (as per IncResp and OutResp).
H.subtitle: Return comes from your partner
H.summary: Reciprocity in its hierarchical face is whether your particular partners pay you back. Help is conditional on a return from the same partner, in kind between equals, or across rank as favour and protection passed down for loyalty and service passed up. It is not your Rank, Dependability, Parity or Face.
H.summary_status: generated from the face's description, not canon; checked faithful

pre_language.core: The felt return on sharing: grooming that is returned by those groomed (Schino and Aureli 2008), and forager food handed over on demand to whoever asks (Peterson 1993), with those who have given tending to be given to in turn (Allen-Arave, Gurven and Hill 2008). Intimates read it as a sign in her behaviour: whether she hands over on request and asks as of right, expecting the return, or hesitates, hoards and goes without rather than ask.

excluded: Her own readiness to give help (helping behaviour, positive-reciprocity disposition)
Her own readiness to seek help
Negative reciprocity (returning harm for harm)
Costs of helping and of offering (distraction from own tasks, risk of rejection)
The canon that a culture is dominated by one face and not both, and the mapping of unconditional help to egalitarian and conditional help to hierarchical cultures
Evolutionary claims: that unconditional reciprocity distinguishes human from primate collaboration, that direct reciprocity is more common in primates, and that bonobos trade sex for favours
The word unconditional for the egalitarian face
Others' reliability in shared work (doing their part, keeping their word)

Reciprocity.summary: Reciprocity is your felt reading of whether help in this group comes back: what you give is returned and what you ask for is met. It holds until evidence moves it. It concerns the return on help, not whether others carry their part of shared work (Dependability) or where you stand (Rank). The culture's face sets where the return is looked for.

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)

problems.where: faces.E.description: "It is conditional on being seen to share, not on a tally" (and the same in faces.E.summary)
problems.detail: Allen-Arave, Gurven and Hill 2008 (supports) find Ache transfers contingent on past giving between households, even among kin. Jaeggi and Gurven 2013 (supports) find reciprocity contributes to forager food sharing independently of kinship and scrounging. Neither shows a conscious tally, but both show contingency on the partner's past giving, so a flat "not on a tally" overstates it. Soften.

problems.where: pre_language.core: "forager food handed over on demand that comes back from the band's next kill (Peterson 1993)"
problems.detail: The checker rates Peterson 'partly': demand sharing and the pressure on holders are supported, but the return-from-the-group framing is the model's, and nothing about the return coming from the next kill was found. Do not hang it on Peterson.

problems.where: faces.H.pre_language.core: "support in fights traded between the same two (... Schino 2007), with asymmetric exchange across rank: tolerance and protection down, support and deference up"
problems.detail: Schino 2007 has no checker verdict, and the claim of asymmetric primate exchange across rank has no checked source. Only Schino and Aureli 2008 (grooming reciprocation) is checked.

problems.where: description: "though your name as a sharer (Repute) or as good for a return (Face) feeds the return"
problems.detail: Face is defined elsewhere (Repute, Esteem H, Safety) as an open charge or being caught out before those who count. It is not one's name as good for a return. The gloss contradicts that definition.

logic_status.common_sense: H face's exchange across rank in the description (favour and protection down, loyalty and service up): safe as common sense of patronage, though no checked source backs it. The mechanics line is design. The anchors are plain readings of the definition.

dimensions.replication: some (Schino and Aureli 2008 with an Egger test finding no bias; Jaeggi and Gurven 2013 phylogenetic meta-analysis; Greco et al. 2019 for negative return)
dimensions.directness: adjacent (contingent giving and receiving in behaviour; no study of the felt reading as a held state)
dimensions.consilience: strong (primatology, forager anthropology, organisational behaviour, behavioural economics)

evidence.why: Two meta-analyses in independent populations and four converging fields support contingent return of help, and the lab nulls in chimpanzees and one small failed paying-it-forward replication are contests well short of a failure. The asymmetry and the tolerated-taking wording lack equal support, which calls for a minor mechanism adjustment and leaves the core alone.
evidence.boundary: The shortfall asymmetry rests on negativity-bias neighbours (Baumeister et al. 2001) and holds most in one-off or weakly repeated exchange; in repeated settings with a threat of exclusion, positive reciprocity can dominate (Al-Ubaydli and Gneezy 2010). In the egalitarian face, windfalls going out by tolerated taking is one pattern among several: Hadza adults rank tolerated theft very low as a motive (Stibbard-Hawkes et al. 2022), and kinship and scrounging explain part of forager sharing.
evidence.caveat: The replicated evidence shows that help given predicts help received in primate grooming and human food sharing; no study found measures a member's felt reading of whether help comes back, so the reading as a held state is the model's framing of that contingency.

Reciprocity.framework: Evidence boundaries. Tolerated taking is one route for windfalls in the egalitarian face, not the rule; Hadza self-report ranks it very low, and the split between kin-directed and reciprocal sharing is contested. The shortfall-weighs-more asymmetry rests on negativity-bias work (Baumeister et al. 2001); one study finds positive reciprocity dominating in repeated settings with exclusion threats (Al-Ubaydli and Gneezy 2010), so the asymmetry is surest in one-shot or loosely repeated exchange. Controlled chimpanzee experiments often fail to find the contingent reciprocity that field data find.

shared_note.why_shared: Both faces read whether help in this group comes back: what you give is returned and what you ask for is met. It is one felt level that holds until evidence moves it, and a culture switch changes the face without resetting the level.
shared_note.differences: The egalitarian face looks to the group at large: help goes to whoever needs it, those with a surplus are pressed to share, and your reading is whether the group gives when you are in need. The hierarchical face looks to particular partners who return help to each other, in kind between equals or across rank.

Belonging.description: How far you feel the others want you among them: whether they make room for you and draw you in, or leave you at the edge. It is their acceptance of you, read from how they treat you, not whether they defer to you for skill or contribution (Esteem), where you stand in the order (Rank), how they judge your conduct (Repute) or whether shares, turns and hearings come to you evenly (Parity). Being left out in a way you accept as the group's ordinary practice (a meeting for another role, a turn not yours) moves it less than being left out where you would expect to be drawn in. The culture's face sets what the acceptance rests on. It is not your own fondness for them (Warmth). Having one or more mutual close friends among them is a different thing and is not read here; it is the scene state Close tie.

anchors.10: Others make room for you on sight and draw you into whatever is going on; you never doubt that you are wanted here.
anchors.1: Gatherings form without you and you are left at the edge; you doubt that anyone wants you here.

Belonging.effect_on_other_pillars: Popularity's impact on other Pillars is based upon your present assessment of the average group attribute.

E.label: Wanted as one of their own in good standing
E.description: The others want you among them as one of their own in good standing: you pull with the group as far as you are able and do not feed on it. The acceptance does not depend on how much you produce or on any place in an order, though being looked to for what you bring can draw you further in. Nor is it unconditional: a member the group has judged to shirk, cheat or feed on the others (Repute) tends to be edged out. You read it from how the group as a whole treats you, not from the judgement itself.

anchors.10: Others make room for you and draw you in as a matter of course, and have done so through good seasons and bad; you feel it would take shirking, cheating or turning on the group to change it.
anchors.1: Gatherings form without you and you are left at the edge: they treat you as a freeloader or an outsider, not as one of their own.

pre_language.core: Let into the huddle after a failed hunt as readily as after a good one, so long as she still pulls with the band; the one who shirks, cheats or feeds on the others tends to be edged out, however able.

E.engagement: Where you feel comfortable and accepted by the group members, who 'have your back' and will support you in the event of any difficulties.
E.subtitle: Wanted as one of their own
E.summary: Belonging in its egalitarian face is feeling the others want you among them as one of their own in good standing, because you pull with the group and do not feed on it. It does not depend on output or rank. It is conditional: members judged to shirk, cheat or feed on others are edged out.
E.summary_status: generated from the face's description, not canon; checked faithful

H.label: Included while you keep your place
H.description: The others keep you among them so long as you keep to what your place in the order calls for, high or low, and do not step out of line. The acceptance is real but conditional on keeping the place, not on the place itself (Rank). You read it from how they treat you while you keep it and from the standing threat of being dropped, not from whether anyone of standing has charged you with stepping out of line or whether that charge has been answered (Face).

anchors.10: You have kept your place and the others keep you among them: at every gathering a place is made for you, whether high or low, as a matter of course.
anchors.1: You have stepped out of line and been dropped, or were never given a place at all: gatherings form without you and you are kept at the edge.

pre_language.core: Kept in the group, at whatever rank she holds, for as long as she does what her place calls for; the moment she oversteps, the others turn on her or shut her out, and she feels the edge of that long before it happens.

H.subtitle: Included while you keep your place
H.summary: Belonging in its hierarchical face is being kept among the others so long as you keep to what your place in the order calls for, high or low. The acceptance is real but conditional on keeping the place, not on the place itself (Rank). Being dropped is a standing threat.
H.summary_status: generated from the face's description, not canon; checked faithful

Belonging.gloss: How far the others want you among them

pre_language.core: Being let into the huddle or kept out of it, time after time. The others shift to make a place, share, groom and turn towards her, or close ranks, turn away and leave her at the fringe, and keep doing so. Intimates read it from whether she moves freely into the middle of the group or hovers at its edge, watching for a gap.

excluded: Uniqueness and authenticity: being valued for what makes you different, and free to be yourself in the group
Mattering: being missed when absent, being important to and depended on by the others
Being valued for your contribution (perceived value, competence- or contribution-based respect)
Being 'one of us': group identification, solidarity and centrality of membership
Inclusion in decision-making, information and influence networks

elaboration_notes: Elaboration: when low Belonging comes from being shut out, the reaction may carry hostility towards those who did it. The hostility belongs in the elaboration, not on a card. When the exclusion is public and reads as a slight to her good name, the Reputation expansion carries the flare and the urge to hit back.
