logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)

problems.where: elaboration_notes[0]: "(rejected people turn aggressive towards the rejecters and towards neutral others: Twenge, Baumeister, Tice and Stucke 2001)" and "even with no one watching"
problems.detail: Twenge et al. 2001 has no checker verdict. The specific claims (aggression towards neutral others, with no one watching) are beyond common sense and need the check. Either have it checked or drop them.

problems.where: faces.E.engagement: "and where you enjoy the power of influence (informal leadership)"
problems.detail: Influence and informal leadership are Esteem's ground (deference freely given, following one's lead), and the Belonging description itself excludes deference for skill or contribution. The text is canon, so the fix needs Ben's approval.

problems.where: faces.E.description: "a member who shirks, cheats or feeds on the others is edged out"
problems.detail: The verdict on shirking or cheating is Repute's ground, and E:Repute->Belonging carries it. Belonging should read only the being edged out, or the condition is counted twice. Make clear the reading is of the treatment.

logic_status.common_sense: H face (acceptance conditional on keeping one's place, with the standing threat of being dropped): no checked source; safe as common sense of ranked groups, where overstepping draws sanction. E pre_language (let in after a failed hunt as after a good one): an illustration of the face's own definition, safe. Hostility after being shut out (elaboration): safe as plain experience, once the specific findings are dropped. Edging out of shirkers is partly backed by Apicella et al. 2012 (cooperators cluster) and is otherwise common sense.

dimensions.replication: replicated (Hartgerink et al. 2015, 120 Cyberball studies; Gerber and Wheeler 2009; Li et al. 2021 workplace ostracism; bias correction not confirmed)
dimensions.directness: direct (targets' self-reported belonging after exclusion, and member surveys of workplace ostracism and belongingness)
dimensions.setting: broad (lab across many countries, organisational field, forager ethnography), lab-weighted and mostly among strangers
dimensions.consilience: strong (social psychology, organisational behaviour, anthropology, educational field trials)

evidence.why: Several meta-analyses measure the target's own felt belonging after being left out, giving replicated direct evidence that the reading tracks treatment, and four fields converge on it. The contested findings concern self-esteem and the time course of distress, which are outside the Pillar's core and become boundaries.
evidence.boundary: The self-esteem consequence is unreliable (Blackhart et al. 2009), so the Pillar should not be defined or linked through self-esteem. Edging out of shirkers in the egalitarian face is a tendency: non-sharers are kept in some forager camps without sanction, and the direction of deviance matters more than its size. The hierarchical face's conditional acceptance has no direct test found, and workplace outcome links may run either way (Howard et al. 2020).

Belonging.framework: Evidence boundaries. The self-esteem consequence of exclusion is unreliable (Blackhart et al. 2009). The time course is unsettled. Workplace links may run either way (Howard et al. 2020). In the egalitarian face, edging out of shirkers is a tendency: some foragers keep non-sharers in camp, and the direction of a deviance matters more than its size. The hierarchical face (kept while you keep your place) has no direct test, and no study separates Belonging from Repute.

shared_note.why_shared: Both faces read how far you feel the others want you among them: whether they make room for you and draw you in, or leave you at the edge. It is their acceptance of you, read from how they treat you, and it is a single level whichever face reads it.
shared_note.differences: The egalitarian face rests acceptance on being one of their own in good standing, pulling with the group and not feeding on it. The hierarchical face rests it on keeping to what your place in the order calls for, high or low, with a standing threat of being dropped if you step out of line.

Prestige.name: Prestige
Prestige.description: How far the others defer to you freely for what you bring: they turn to you, watch and copy how you do it, bring you their problems and take your advice. It is not whether they want you among them (Belonging), your rung in the settled order (Rank) or their verdict on your conduct (Repute). The culture's face sets how far the deference reaches.

anchors.10: Whenever your kind of skill or contribution counts, the others turn to you, watch and copy how you do it, bring you their problems and take your advice.
anchors.1: No one asks you, watches you or copies you; when your kind of skill or contribution is needed they turn to someone else.

Prestige.effect_on_other_pillars: You respond to the current assessment of others' respect for you.
Prestige.engagement: Where you feel that others have a high opinion of your competence and trustworthiness: you feel valued and understood; you feel that others regard you to be a legitimate and useful member of the group; your identity as belonging to this group is consistent with others' appraisal of you.

pre_language.core: Being the one others watch, copy and seek out: eyes on her hands, bodies drawn near while she works, problems brought to her, her way of doing things taken up; as children attend to and learn from models whom others attend to. Intimates read it from who gets watched, copied and sought, and who is passed over when a task of her kind comes up. In apes the pull is not cleanly apart from rank: chimpanzees copy both higher-ranking and expert models (Kendal et al. 2015), and subordinates hide what they know while dominants watch (Drea and Wallen 1999).

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)

problems.where: pre_language.core and faces.H.pre_language.core: "as children and apes attend to and copy skilled or much-attended models"
problems.detail: Chudek et al. 2012 (supports) covers preschool children learning from models whom bystanders attend to. No checked source covers apes. Drop "and apes" (and "skilled or", which Chudek does not test).

problems.where: pre_language.core and faces.H.pre_language.core: "the giver sought as a partner ... and as the most giving members of a group are sought out and honoured"; faces.E.description "generosity"; faces.H.description "generosity included" and "though one generous act can feed both"
problems.detail: No checked source backs generosity as a ground of Esteem. The one candidate, von Rueden et al. 2014 on altruistic reputation, is rated 'not found', and Henrich and Gil-White 2001 is rated only on skill and knowledge. Generosity as sharing is also Repute's ground ('share what you have'), which blurs the boundary. Check a competitive-altruism source (for example Hardy and Van Vugt 2006) or drop generosity.

logic_status.common_sense: Being shown up as clumsy or mistaken lowers Esteem: safe, since deference that tracks skill (Henrich and Gil-White 2001, partly) falls when skill is shown wanting. Esteem fading when what you bring fades, with settled precedence passing to Rank: safe, and consistent with prestige as freely conferred. E face's 'no right to command' and 'kept modest': safe, backed in part by Lee 1969 (the provider's meat disparaged) and the prestige-dominance distinction (Henrich and Gil-White 2001; Cheng et al. 2013). The will-not-skill boundary with Repute rests on Delton et al. 2012 (partly) in the Repute item.

dimensions.replication: some (Cheng et al. 2013 partly replicated in real groups, Brand et al. 2019, details unconfirmed; no registered report, multi-lab study or bias-corrected meta-analysis of prestige bias)
dimensions.directness: direct (deference, attention and copying directed at skilled or attended-to models)
dimensions.setting: broad (lab and online WEIRD samples, North American children, Fijian villages, forager status studies, captive primates)
dimensions.consilience: strong (social psychology, cultural evolution, developmental psychology and forager anthropology converge on the step; primatology agrees by analogy)

evidence.why: Four independent fields converge directly on freely conferred deference and copying towards skilled members, which meets the consilience route to substantiated, and the Durkee versus Cheng dispute concerns dominance, not whether prestige confers influence. No source in the record was verified, so no load-bearing source can be added yet, and the grade should be confirmed once Cheng et al. 2013 and Henrich and Broesch 2011 are read in full.
evidence.boundary: Prestige pull is weaker where members can see the success itself or judge the content directly (Brand et al. 2020; published null for argument transmission, Jimenez and Mesoudi, to be confirmed). In apes, and sometimes in people, copying follows rank as well as skill, so Esteem and Rank can blur in practice. The 'fades when what you bring fades' clause, advice-taking and the separation from Repute have no direct test in the record and rest on common sense.

shared_note.why_shared: Both faces read how far the others defer to you freely for what you bring: they turn to you, watch and copy how you do it, bring you their problems and take your advice. It is one level, separate from Belonging, Rank and Repute, whichever face reads it.
shared_note.differences: In the egalitarian face you stay one of them: the deference gives you no right to command and lasts only while what you bring does. In the hierarchical face it reaches to being handed decisions and jobs that matter and having your word taken on them, though it still fades once what you bring does.
shared_note.status: generated from the Pillar's texts; checked faithful

Warmth.name: Warmth
Warmth.description: How fond you feel of the members as a whole: whether you like being with them, are drawn to their company and feel their troubles as partly yours. It is your liking for them, not their acceptance of you (Belonging), not whether help comes back (Reciprocity), not whether they can be counted on (Dependability), and not how much of yourself you put into the group (Engagement), which can be high in a group whose members you merely tolerate. It has no axis partner and one face: fondness for the members reads the same among equals and in a ranked group. Fondness for one particular friend is not read here; a mutual close tie is the scene state Close tie.

pre_language.core: Affection that crosses rank: she approaches those above with a relaxed face as well as the due signals of their place, lingers with equals and stays near those below without pressing her advantage, against contact kept to the ritual of rank and the body turned away once it is done. Intimates read it from how she greets each and how long she stays once the business of rank is over.

H.subtitle: Fondness for those around you
H.summary: Warmth, hierarchical face, is how fond you feel of the people you deal with up and down the order: peers, patrons and those below. It asks whether you like being with each of them and feel their troubles as partly yours, whatever their rank. It is not regard for their place, Belonging or Reciprocity.

Warmth.subtitle: Fondness for the group's members
Warmth.summary: Warmth is how fond you feel of the members as a whole: whether you like being with them, are drawn to their company and feel their troubles as partly yours. It is your liking for them, not their acceptance of you, not whether help comes back, not whether they can be counted on, and not how much of yourself you put in. Fondness for one particular friend is not read here.

dimensions.replication: some (social and task cohesion separate in several cohesion meta-analyses: Beal et al. 2003, Grossman et al. 2022, Filho et al. 2014; none bias-corrected)
dimensions.directness: direct (member surveys of social cohesion as liking for the team), with fondness for the whole group read through items about members
dimensions.consilience: strong (social psychology, organisational behaviour, sociology of small groups, primatology, forager ethnography)

evidence.why: Member surveys of social cohesion give direct evidence that liking for the team is a distinct reading, separable from task cohesion across several meta-analyses, and five fields converge on it. The opposing findings bear on antecedents, consequences and era payoffs, and none touches the existence or distinctness of the reading.
evidence.boundary: Warmth predicts performance weakly next to task orientation (social cohesion r about .11 against .45 for task cohesion in sport), so it should not be credited with strong performance effects. Familiarity raises liking only up to a point and not reliably for faces (Montoya et al. 2017; Chow et al. 2022). The fitness payoffs of primate affiliation are contested (Creighton et al. 2025 reanalysis of the Amboseli baboon data), and 'feel their troubles as partly yours' leans on the unresolved empathy and oneness debate.

engagement.ruling: Ben, 25 Oct 2026, 2.15 pm: singular Engagement, defined by five levels, non-negotiable in every build; threshold rule approved 1.52 and 1.56 pm
engagement.definition: How much of herself the member puts into this group: her time, her effort, her thinking and her feeling. One construct.
engagement.update: threshold: fires when the weighted Pillar level has moved 1.0 since Engagement last updated; Engagement moves 0.5 of the gap (0.25 long-standing, 0.75 newcomer); the player plays one Engagement card on the Pillar most relevant to the tipping vignette as a reflective beat. Snake (provisional, Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 9.20 pm): where Engagement stands at Committed or above (7 or more) and the update fires on a fall driven mainly by Parity, treatment she reads as unfair, Engagement drops 4 (never below 1) in place of the part-way move; tenure gives no cushion. Brockner, Tyler and Cooper-Schneider 1992: the most negative reactions came from those who had been highly committed and were treated unfairly. The size is calibration. Boundary: while she reads harsh treatment as deserved, Parity does not fall and the snake does not fire; committed members can reinterpret (Festinger, Riecken and Schachter 1956; Aronson and Mills 1959), and when the reinterpretation breaks the fall comes at once (Ebaugh 1988).

pack_weights.rule: Repute and Face each weigh 0.5 of a mean core Pillar weight in the level that feeds Engagement, counted only below their default (contribution = weight x (value minus 10)) and left out of the normalising denominator.
pack_weights.why: Weight each at 0.5 of a mean core Pillar weight, counted only below its default (contribution = w x (value minus 10)) and left out of the normalising denominator. They sit at 10 by default and at full weight would dilute the core Pillars; most of their real effect on staying already runs through E:Repute->Belonging and E:Repute->Reciprocity (Feinberg et al. 2014), so full weight would double count; yet shame tracks devaluation strongly (Sznycer et al. 2018) and ostracism effects are large (Hartgerink et al. 2015), so they must be able to help tip Engagement. With seven core Pillars, as on the egalitarian deck where Esteem joins, a six-point fall in Face moves the level about 0.43 directly (about 0.5 with six); its knock-on cards supply the rest. The weighting is a proposal. Yes, the pack needs E:Engagement->Repute and H:Engagement->Face: the reflective beat must have a card to play when a reputational scene tips Engagement.

structure_principle.text: In any group both decks' Pillars run, weighted by the culture and by her own preference for a steeper or flatter order; a deck marks where a Pillar is native, not where it is allowed. Hierarchy works best when augmented by peer relationships that carry the egalitarian readings (Heslop 2021, ICCRTS). A Pillar is shared, with a face per deck, only where its reading differs by mode.

pillars.state_rule: Pillars are semi-stable states. Cards are the felt reactions that move them: the emotion in a card passes, and the Pillar keeps the lasting shift it leaves until another card moves it (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 8.55 pm).

Close tie.description: Whether she has one or more mutual close friends among the members. A scene state, not a Pillar: the scene supplies it, and the cards that scale by a close tie, focal and interaction, read it. Friendship and acceptance by the group are distinct (Parker and Asher 1993); a mutual best friend protects against an escalating cycle of victimisation (Hodges, Boivin, Vitaro and Bukowski 1999).

forces.name: Making Fetch Happen
forces.increment_logic: When the others draw me in as one of their own, and after a knock one of them comes and sits with me, my bracing eases; I expect a slip, a mood or a disagreement of mine to be taken as coming from one of their own, and my felt safety to show myself rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When gatherings form without me and no one comes to me after a knock, I expect a slip or a disagreement of mine to be met as an outsider's would be, with a rebuff, and I mask myself and brace: my felt safety to show myself falls.
forces.explanation: A member who feels the others want her among them expects a slip, a mood or a disagreement of hers to be borne as one of their own's; one left at the edge expects it to be held against her. Developmental evidence carries the decrement best. Reading hostile intent into ambiguous acts goes with aggression across 41 studies, most strongly in samples selected for peer rejection (Orobio de Castro et al. 2002, a meta-analysis), which suggests a member at the edge reads the same acts as more threatening; the step from that reading to her felt safety to show herself is the model's. Children excluded by their own group, in a ball-tossing game, show more anxiety than those excluded by outsiders (Watson-Jones, Whitehouse and Legare 2016). Children who anxiously expect rejection over-read an ambiguous slight (Downey et al. 1998). The largest stress hormone responses in the laboratory, and the slowest recovery, come where the self may be judged by others and the outcome is out of one's control (Dickerson and Kemeny 2004, a meta-analysis of 208 studies); a member at the edge has least control over how she is judged. People who feel socially isolated are held to grow more watchful for social threat (Cacioppo and Hawkley 2009), though attention tests of that account are mixed, so it is secondary here. Others also regulate a member's feeling directly: people turn to others to change their own feeling (Zaki and Williams 2013), and holding a husband's hand damped neural threat responses, more so the better the marriage (Coan, Schaefer and Davidson 2006; 16 married women, so carrying it from spouse to group is the model's step). That regulation is another's act on her and belongs to the scene; the comfort after a knock enters the lines only as a sign she reads that she is wanted, and the card carries her expectation of how what she shows will be met. In chimpanzees, consolation by a valued partner lowered victims' stress behaviour in one group (Fraser, Stahl and Aureli 2008) but not in another (Koski and Sterck 2007), so the primate route stays secondary. Felt safety in teams is a shared reading that interpersonal risk is acceptable (Edmondson 1999). The link also runs the other way, since concealing oneself lowers felt belonging (Newheiser and Barreto 2014); that direction is not this card's. The excluded child's anxiety also comes with more faithful copying of the group's ways, an attempt to get back in; that is her own conformity, outside this card. Distinct from Among friends (E:Warmth->DivsExp), which reads her own fondness for the members; this card reads their acceptance of her. Play the decrement at full size and keep the increment smaller.

pre_language.increment: When others seek her out and play with her, she lets her moods and fumbles show without watching faces.
pre_language.decrement: When others leave her at the edge, she watches faces, masks her reactions and braces for a snap.

logic_status.common_sense: A member who is wanted expects her slips to be borne as one of their own, and one left at the edge expects a rebuff. Frazier et al. 2017 only partly supports supportive relations as an antecedent of psychological safety (leader relations, with peers unverified), so this step rests mainly on common sense. That is safe because it is the plain meaning of being treated as an insider, and the explanation already says felt safety is a reading of interpersonal risk (Edmondson 1999). evidence.why: The three fields that converge (exclusion harms belonging, team psychological safety, social buffering) each test a neighbouring link, and no study tests whether feeling drawn in raises a member's felt safety to show herself; the replicated meta-analyses (Hartgerink 2015, Frazier 2017) are analogous or have no confirmed bias correction and do not test inclusion as an antecedent. The only sources verified in the record either already sit in the item (Fraser 2008) or run the arrow the other way (Newheiser and Barreto 2014), so none is load-bearing for this direction.

forces.name: Friends at my back
forces.increment_logic: When I feel the others want me among them, I sense they would close round me if anyone tried to push me about, grab more than their due or tilt a share-out against me; such a move looks bound to be checked before it sticks, and my sense that no one can lord it over me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When gatherings form without me and no one seeks me out, I feel I would stand alone if someone pushed me about, grabbed or tilted a share-out against me; such a move looks able to stick, I keep away or let it pass, and my sense that no one can lord it over me falls.
forces.explanation: Felt protection from domination rests on expected coalitional support, and being bonded into the group is the felt basis of that expectation; an isolated member is exposed. The reading that numbers at one's back decide who gets their way is made early and needs no words: infants of 9 to 12 months expect the agent with the larger group to prevail in a conflict (Pun, Birch and Baron 2016), and a later report that they expect this only when the allies can see the conflict (Pun et al. 2022) awaits checking. Both are expectations about third parties' groups by size; the step from being wanted among them to expecting their backing remains the model's. Among foragers, followers acting together check a would-be dominant (Boehm 1993), so a member who feels wanted among them expects that check to include her. In children, having a mutual best friend protected against an escalating cycle of peer victimisation, and victimisation predicted rising problems only among those without one (Hodges, Boivin, Vitaro and Bukowski 1999, a longitudinal study of children); the human protective outcome thus runs through at least one mutual close tie, while the infant work bears on the expectation at group level. Scale the card by the scene state Close tie: where Belonging is high but Close tie is none, play the increment small; where Belonging is low and Close tie is none, play the decrement at full size. In primates, grooming partners are more likely to back each other in fights (Seyfarth and Cheney 1984; across species, Schino 2007, a meta-analysis), a neighbouring route from bond to backing that is consilient but not direct. Emotion research adds the felt side: people who see their group as strong feel more anger at an opposing group and more wish to move against it, with anger carrying the effect of strength on that wish (Mackie, Devos and Smith 2000, between groups, so carrying it to backing within one group is the model's step). That a member without backing meets the push with fear instead is the common-sense mirror. Backing also sets the form her reaction takes, anger she can voice or wariness, but Parity's E face counts both forms alike; the reading moves with whether the push, grab or tilt can stick, and the form shows in play and in which cards bite. Exposure lowers Parity only where someone is pushing, grabbing or tilting a share-out: where no member is doing so, there is nothing to be backed against, so set both lines small or nil.

forces.summary: Feeling wanted by the others lifts Parity, because you expect them to close round you if someone pushed, grabbed or tilted a share-out against you, so such a move would be checked. Left at the edge, you expect to stand alone, and Parity falls. The card applies only where someone is pushing, grabbing or tilting a share-out; otherwise both lines are small or nil.

logic_status.common_sense: The step from expected backing to the member's felt sense that no one can lord it over her, and the line "an isolated member is exposed". Both are safe because a felt reading follows expected support, and the sources supply the support itself. Literature: rank and file combining against would-be dominants (Boehm 1993, partly); grooming bonds exchanged for agonistic support (Seyfarth 1977, supports; Schino and Aureli 2008, partly). The elaboration says that exclusion may bring hostility towards neutral others, withheld from one who treats her warmly. That matches Twenge et al. 2001 (supports), and "may" is the right strength given the contested replication record. One caveat that is not a failure: Seyfarth's model concerns grooming up the hierarchy for support from dominants, so in a deck E card it backs the coalitional support step, not an egalitarian setting as such.

evidence.why: No study tests whether felt belonging raises a member's sense that no one can lord it over her. The replicated work (primate grooming for support, exclusion and aggression meta-analyses) concerns neighbouring constructs, and every source in the record is searched rather than verified, so none can be added as load-bearing.
evidence.boundary: The effect needs someone actively pushing, grabbing or tilting a share-out; with none present both lines are small or nil. Expected backing is one route to Parity among several: the forager record also names leaving the group and sharing norms (Boehm 1993; Thomson et al. 2025, both searched only).

forces.name: One of us, so it comes back
forces.increment_logic: When the others draw me in as one of their own, I feel surer that what I put in will come back from the group and that what I need will be met: my sense that help comes back to me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When gatherings form without me and I am left at the edge, I feel that what I give goes into a hole and that my needs would go unmet: my sense that help comes back to me falls.
forces.explanation: In the return-from-the-group face, big windfalls reach whoever is there by demand and tolerated taking, but the smaller, everyday giving and the care a member gets when sick or hurt go more readily to those the others count as their own. Being wanted as one of their own in good standing is the felt sign that she is among those this giving reaches, so her need will be met; being left at the edge is the sign that she stands outside its reach and will be passed over. Her name as a sharer is a separate route (Bad Name, Empty Hands). The expectation is present before language: 17-month-olds expect help among members of the same group and treat help across groups as optional (Jin and Baillargeon 2017), and when goods are too few for all, toddlers expect ingroup support to override fairness (Bian, Sloane and Baillargeon 2018, seen in summary only). People expect generalised returns from their own group and not from outsiders (bounded generalised reciprocity: Yamagishi and Kiyonari 2000). All of this contrasts the ingroup with outsiders; carrying it from group membership to graded acceptance within one group is an extension, so keep the step modest, and keep it smaller still where the help in question is a windfall shared out on demand. The card does not scale by a close tie.

pre_language.decrement: When others leave her at the edge, she hangs back from the food and holds what she has close, expecting nothing to come her way, and her sense that giving comes back sinks.

logic_status.common_sense: Carrying bounded generalised reciprocity over from group membership to graded acceptance within one group, so that a member left at the edge is treated as partly outside the group's giving. The explanation states that this is an extension and asks for a modest step. It is safe at that strength because being left out is the plain in-group sign of being treated as an outsider. Literature: people expect generalised returns from their own group (Yamagishi and Kiyonari 2000, supports; Balliet, Wu and De Dreu 2014, supports). Need-based giving within the face is the model's definition of that face, not a claim about the world.

evidence.why: Balliet et al. 2014 is a replicated meta-analysis on the same link at group level, but its bias correction is unconfirmed and it tests ingroup versus outsider giving, not a member's graded acceptance raising her expected return, which is the card's core step. The expectation route of bounded generalised reciprocity is itself contested (Yamagishi and Kiyonari 2000 and its follow-ups, Horita and Hamada 2024), so the core step cannot be substantiated.
evidence.boundary: The replicated evidence contrasts ingroup with outsiders, and the effect is small (d about 0.14 to 0.32); graded acceptance within one group is an extension with modest increments. Large windfalls are shared out on demand or by tolerated taking and so depend less on being one of us than everyday giving does (forager network and tolerated-theft work, searched only).

forces.name: Open or masked
forces.explanation: Whether feeling safe to show myself draws me closer to the others depends on what I would be showing them. Circumstance one: what shows is ordinary, play, laughter, moods, owned slips and disagreements aired for the group's sake. HIGH: I let them show, I join the joking and the play, and I sense I am being taken as one of their own, so my Belonging rises. LOW: braced and masked, I stay out of the play and sense I come across as aloof, someone they would leave at the edge of the talk, so my Belonging falls. Circumstance two: what I have to show is mostly a run of needs, complaints and pleas for reassurance, pressed on the others more often than they can comfortably carry. HIGH: I go on letting them show and sense I am wearing on them, so my Belonging falls. LOW: braced and masked, I keep those needs to myself; I sense nothing new laid on them, but also that masking keeps me from them, so my Belonging holds or slips a little. Someone already wanted among them can feel surer of being borne with longer, and needs she cannot help she can expect to be borne as one of their own. Whether they judge her to be feeding on them is Repute's ground, carried by Can't Look Them in the Eye. How the others in fact receive her (shared laughter drawing closeness, Kurtz and Algoe 2015; masking lowering a partner's rapport, Butler et al. 2003; disclosure drawing liking, Collins and Miller 1994; reassurance seeking going with rejection, a small and mostly concurrent effect of r about .14, Starr and Davila 2008) belongs to the scene. Most of these studies measure how partners receive the one who masks or discloses, which is scene ground; none measures her own felt belonging. Suppression's social cost also varies with context (Pauw et al. 2022, where one moderator did not replicate). That she reads her own play or masking, and her own pressing of needs, as drawing her in or setting her apart rests on common sense; laughter's homologues in great-ape play vocalisations (Davila Ross, Owren and Zimmermann 2009) suggest how basic the felt pull of shared play is. Both arms of circumstance two rest on common sense and are untested. The high arm, that pressing needs leaves her feeling she wears on them, borrows only the small adjacent effect above. The low arm allows a small fall because concealment can lower the concealer's own belonging (Newheiser and Barreto 2014, a concealed stigmatised identity), so masking likely costs something even here. Keep both circumstances modest.

pre_language.explanation: When she does her share alongside the others, showing her moods and fumbles freely draws them to her, while going still and masked leaves her on the edge. When the others have begun to turn from her constant wants and complaints, showing more of them makes them turn further away, while keeping them hidden lets them come back to her and make room for her again.

reactive_test.reason: Both directions are others' felt reactions to what she shows, read by her as warmth or coldness, with no worked-out plan involved.

forces.subtitle: Showing yourself can draw you in or wear on others
forces.summary: Whether feeling safe to show herself draws a member closer depends on what she shows. Ordinary play, moods and owned slips let her be taken as one of their own, and masking leaves her at the edge. A run of needs and pleas for reassurance pressed on the others can leave her feeling she wears on them. Both effects are modest.

problems.where: framework: "excessive reassurance seeking draws rejection (Coyne; Joiner and colleagues)"
problems.detail: The cited Joiner link resolves to Joiner et al. 2001 on how specific reassurance seeking is to depression. The checker rated it not in source. The claim is backed only by the sorted Starr and Davila 2008 meta-analysis (partly: r = .14, a small effect, in depression-linked dyads). Cite that instead and state the effect as small.

problems.where: explanation, circumstance two LOW: "braced and masked, I keep those needs to myself; with nothing new to carry, they stop edging away and let me back into the talk, so my Belonging rises."
problems.detail: No source shows that holding needs back reverses rejection. Starr and Davila show only that reassurance seeking goes with rejection. Butler et al. 2003 (supports) show that masked expression lowers a partner's rapport, which cuts against Belonging rising when she masks. Being let back into the talk within minutes is also a slow repair effect, outside a card's timescale. Make this branch hold Belonging steady. If the rulebook needs a direction for every discretionary branch, drop circumstance two LOW and let circumstance one govern.

problems.where: explanation, circumstance two HIGH: "they edge away, so my Belonging falls"
problems.detail: The rejection effect is small (r = .14). Say they edge away a little so the step stays modest.

logic_status.common_sense: "Someone already wanted among them is borne with longer, and needs she cannot help are borne as one of their own": safe as ordinary experience, and in line with the will-versus-skill line in Delton et al. 2012 (checked for Face, not cited here). The step in circumstance two from heavy needs to being read as feeding on them is the model's reading of the reassurance-seeking literature.

evidence.why: Circumstance one has a direct experiment for its masking arm and adjacent pooled support from suppression and disclosure research, but none of it is replicated at the core step or confirmed as bias-corrected, and most studies measure the partner's reception rather than the member's own belonging. Circumstance two rests on common sense and a small concurrent effect, so the card stays provisional.
evidence.boundary: The evidence for masking lowering belonging comes from concealing a stigmatised identity, not ordinary moods or play. In circumstance two, masking may still lower belonging (Newheiser and Barreto 2014) rather than leave it unchanged; no test of that arm was found.

forces.name: Mistakes in the open
forces.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a slip or a disagreement show, I sense that troubles with the venture come out where the group can deal with them, and I feel surer it can pull the venture off.
forces.decrement_logic: When I brace and mask myself, I sense that slips and doubts are being hidden around me as well as by me, and I feel less sure the group can pull the venture off.
forces.explanation: Psychological safety supports team learning behaviour, through which teams take up problems and correct course; in Edmondson's (1999) teams it worked on performance through that learning behaviour. Edmondson measured safety as a belief the team shares, so the evidence is team-level shared safety. A member's own felt safety is one sign of whether that climate holds around her, so it carries into her confidence in the group's capability; that step rests on common sense. Edmondson also found team efficacy unrelated to learning behaviour once safety was controlled, so her data do not show a path from safety to confidence in capability. The link from safety to performance depends on the task, and is stronger for complex work (Sanner and Bunderson 2015, as summarised). Direction may run both ways: confidence and performance are held to feed each other over time (efficacy-performance spirals, Lindsley, Brass and Thomas 1995, a theory piece); the longitudinal study once cited for this is unidentified, a gap. Her sense that others hide their slips too is an inference from her own masking and rests on common sense, since no source tests it. Keep the step modest. Boundary: the rise needs a group that takes problems up; where she has seen raised problems ignored, play it nil. How the others in fact respond to a problem raised belongs to the interaction card, which the scene stages. Framework: team psychological safety and learning (Edmondson 1999); common sense for the step to her own confidence.

pre_language.increment: When she is loose among them and her fumbles on the shared venture draw help rather than jeers, she sees fumbles mended as they happen and goes at the venture with confidence.
pre_language.decrement: When she is braced and hides her fumbles, she sees others hide theirs too, and the venture feels shakier to her.

reactive_test.reason: The felt climate drives the reading, but the step from her own safety to the group's capacity to correct itself can slide towards reasoning about group process.

problems.where: explanation: "Psychological safety lets errors and disagreements surface early, which is how teams learn and correct course"
problems.detail: The checker rated Edmondson 1999 partly. Safety driving learning behaviour and performance is supported, but errors surfacing early is not confirmed from that source. The error evidence sits in Edmondson 1996, which was searched but not checked. Restate the claim at what the checked source shows, or check the 1996 study and cite it.

logic_status.common_sense: A member's own felt safety is one sign of the climate around her. If she feels unsafe she reads the climate as unsafe, and so expects others to hide too; this follows from Edmondson's shared-belief definition, and the explanation keeps that step modest. Safety carrying into confidence that the group can pull the venture off is also common sense. No source links psychological safety to felt team confidence. The step is safe only as a modest one, because Edmondson 1999 keeps team efficacy distinct from safety.

evidence.why: The member-survey safety literature is direct for the felt reading of safety, but no study found tests safety as a predictor of a member's confidence that the group can pull the venture off, and Edmondson's own data do not show a safety to efficacy path. Only one field converges and Frazier et al. 2017 has no confirmed bias correction or confirmed efficacy outcome, so the card is provisional.
evidence.boundary: The safety to performance link depends on task complexity (Sanner and Bunderson 2015, as summarised), and the literature is mostly cross-sectional, so confidence may feed back to safety (potency and effectiveness look reciprocal in one longitudinal study). The evidence comes from organisational work teams.

forces.name: Free to scoff, free of bullies
forces.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a disagreement show, I feel free to speak up or scoff at anyone who starts to push me about, help themselves to more than their due, or tilt a share-out or a turn towards themselves or their favourites, and such a move looks less able to pass unanswered: my sense of Parity rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I brace and mask myself, I let a pushy member's demands, grabs and favouritism pass without a murmur and take what is handed to me, and I feel myself made to go along: my sense of Parity falls.
forces.explanation: The everyday tools of levelling are ridicule, criticism and open objection (Wiessner 2005; Boehm 1993); those studies show the tools biting when used collectively, and that collective check belongs to the scene. A member who feels safe to let a disagreement show feels free to use these tools against a pushy member, and so reads such a move as less likely to pass unanswered; both steps, including the link from felt freedom to speak to her reading of Parity, rest on common sense, since the safety in question is safety to object. The decrement has developmental support for its direction: across 18 longitudinal studies, internalising problems, close to the anxious, withdrawn masking of the decrement, predicted later peer victimisation as well as following from it (Reijntjes et al. 2010, a meta-analysis). Being leant on is others' act and belongs to the scene; the finding means her reading that a pushy move will pass unanswered tracks what tends to happen to a braced, masked member. Felt freedom to object differs from expecting the objection to succeed: objecting can bring retaliation, and bystander work suggests safety from those with power matters more than safety among peers (MacCurtain et al. 2018, not yet checked). Expected backing is carried by E:Belonging->Levelling, so keep this card modest. The indignation that prompts the objection is Rule-Keeping's ground (Ribbing the big shot); this card carries only her felt freedom to voice it. Both lines need someone pushing, grabbing or tilting a share-out: where no member is doing so, there is no move to scoff at and masking leaves nothing to let pass, so set both lines small or nil. The favouritism limb rests on the finding that a rigged procedure draws more objection than an unequal outcome alone: preschoolers protest an unequal split more when a rigged procedure produced it than when a fair one did (Grocke, Rossano and Tomasello 2015).

pre_language.increment: When she is loose among the others, she bristles, mocks or protests when a swaggering member pushes at her, and goes about her business beside him without a glance at his mood.
pre_language.decrement: When she is braced, she goes still and gives way when a swaggering member pushes at her, and watches his mood.

reactive_test.reason: Bristling or going still before a dominant is a reflexive emotional reaction found well before language.

forces.framework: Common sense on felt freedom to object; procedural fairness in children (Grocke et al. 2015). Collective levelling sanctions (Boehm 1993; Wiessner 2005) belong to the scene.

timing.typical: 2 to 10 seconds after a push or grab
timing.why: She either bristles or swallows her objection the moment someone pushes her or grabs, and her felt freedom from domination moves with that reflex.

era.why: Bristling, scoffing displays and coalitional resistance to bullies have non-verbal analogues in primates; Boehm's ridicule is the spoken form.

forces.subtitle: Feeling free to object protects fairness
forces.summary: A member who feels safe to let a disagreement show feels free to speak up or scoff at anyone pushing her about, grabbing more than their due or tilting a share-out, so such a move looks less able to pass unanswered and her sense of Parity rises. When she braces and masks herself, she lets these moves pass and her sense of Parity falls. Both lines need someone pushing, so they are set small where no one is.

critique_was.name: Free to scoff, free of bullies
critique_was.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a disagreement show, I bristle or scoff at anyone who starts to push me about or help themselves to more than their due, and I feel no one here could make me do, drop or give up anything, or keep more than their due, without an argument from me: my sense of Parity rises.
critique_was.decrement_logic: When I brace and mask myself, I let a pushy member's demands and grabs pass without a murmur and do what he wants, and I feel I am being made to comply: my sense of Parity falls.
critique_was.explanation: The everyday tools of levelling are ridicule, criticism and open objection (Boehm). A member who feels safe to show herself uses them on reflex against anyone who pushes her or grabs, and since others tend to join such sanctions, force and grabbing get less grip on her; one who is braced swallows her objection, gives way and feels the force.
critique_was.framework: Reverse dominance hierarchy (levelling sanctions: ridicule, criticism)

timing.typical: 2 to 10 seconds after a push or grab
timing.why: She either bristles or swallows her objection the moment someone pushes her or grabs, and her felt freedom from domination moves with that reflex.

problems.where: explanation: 'A member who feels safe to show herself uses them on reflex;'
problems.detail: No cited source shows that felt safety leads to reflexive use of levelling sanctions. Boehm and Wiessner describe the sanctions and their collective force, but not their link to a member's felt safety. The link holds as common sense only if it is stated as freedom to object, without 'on reflex'.

problems.where: explanation: 'they work because they are collective: Ju/'hoansi put-downs of big-shot behaviour escalate across the camp ... (Wiessner 2005; Boehm 1993)'
problems.detail: Wiessner (supports) shows escalation from put-downs to harsh criticism and withheld sharing, but the checker did not see 'across the camp'. Boehm (partly) supports collective checking of would-be dominants, and the checker could not see his sanctions list, so he should not be cited for the Ju/'hoansi detail. 'Because' claims a causal account that the sources support only as 'when they are collective'.

logic_status.common_sense: That a member who feels safe to let disagreement show will use open objection against a pushy member. This is safe because the safety in question (DivsExp) is safety to show disagreement, so using it to object is close to its definition. The decrement (a masked member lets grabs pass and feels made to go along) is also common sense.

evidence.why: Each half has distant support from three fields (ridicule and criticism as levelling in forager ethnography, children objecting to rigged procedures and selfish splits, safety and voice in organisations), but nothing tests the chain from a member's felt safety to her reading of Parity. All sources in the record are searched rather than verified, so none is added as load-bearing.
evidence.boundary: Both lines need a member who is pushing, grabbing or tilting; with none present the effect is small or nil. Felt freedom to object is not the same as expecting the objection to work: objecting can bring retaliation, and bystander work suggests safety from those with power matters more than safety among peers (MacCurtain et al. 2018, searched only).

forces.name: Need shown, need met
forces.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a need show, I can ask plainly for what I need, and a plain ask here looks likely to be answered: my sense that what I need here will be met rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I brace and keep my needs masked, I can only hint at them, and help I have not asked for looks unlikely to come: my sense that what I need here will be met falls.
forces.explanation: Felt safety lets a member ask plainly for what she needs, and a need she can ask for looks like one the group will meet. A braced member can only hint, and help she has not asked for looks unlikely to come. Both steps are her own reading and rest on common sense; the link from hinting to expecting less help is untested, a gap. Whether help then arrives belongs to the scene. People underestimate how readily others help when asked directly (Flynn and Lake 2008, not replicated as a direct replication), so a member who feels free to ask may find the return better than she feared, while one who masks her needs never learns that her estimate was too low. The underestimate holds for face-to-face asks and reverses over email (Roghanizad and Bohns 2017), and was shown among strangers; carrying it to shown needs in a standing group is an extension, so keep both lines modest, and keep the decrement small where she has no pressing need to show. Unasked, unseen support can help the receiver more than visible support (Bolger and Amarel 2007); that finding bears on outcomes, which belong to the scene, and leaves her forecast untouched.

pre_language.increment: When she is loose among them, she whimpers or reaches when hungry or hurt, is given to, and her sense that giving comes back grows.
pre_language.decrement: When she is braced, she hides her hunger or hurt, is given nothing, and her sense that giving comes back sinks.

reactive_test.reason: Showing or hiding a need and feeling it met or unmet are immediate reactions with a plain pre-language form.

Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Decrement line: a need she never shows has not been refused, so 'it goes unmet' does not by itself show that what she gives fails to come back. As written the line reads a non-event as evidence of non-return. Flynn and Lake (2008) back a different mechanism: people underestimate how readily others help, so a member who masks her needs never sees the help that would correct her pessimism, and her reading drifts down with nothing to hold it up. The fix rests the line on that. Flynn and Lake studied requests to strangers, so the explanation should flag the step to a group as an extension. The increment line passes. It leans on an observed outcome (the need met), which edges towards an evidence card, but it is acceptable as the immediate result of showing the need.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The decrement lowers Reciprocity on an absence of evidence (no need shown, so no help seen), but the Reciprocity definition says the reading holds until evidence moves it; a need never voiced and never met is no evidence that help fails to come back. The masked member needs a felt event that reads as non-return. The illusion of transparency (Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec 1998) supplies one: she half-shows the need, overrates how plainly it shows, and reads the others' failure to answer as a refusal.

logic_status.common_sense: That a need shown and met raises her sense of return, and that hinted needs are easily missed so nothing comes and her sense of return falls. Safe because both follow directly from help received or not received.

evidence.why: The central step relies on one research group's series on underestimated compliance among strangers, with no independent or preregistered replication, and the safety-to-asking link rests on cross-sectional, analogous psychological safety work. evidence.boundary: The ask-to-answer step holds for face-to-face, visible asks: over email requesters overestimate compliance (Roghanizad and Bohns 2017, to be checked). forces.name: Reading the welcome through my own stake
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into this group, the small signs (a nod, a seat kept, a glance my way) read to me as welcome for one of their own, and my sense that they want me among them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, the same small signs read as mere politeness and the gaps read as edging me out, as if I were an outsider, and my sense that they want me among them falls.
forces.explanation: Most belonging cues in a small group are ambiguous, and people read them in line with how they themselves stand. The sociometer gauges felt relational value from such cues (Leary and Baumeister 2000), and people who anxiously expect rejection readily perceive it in others' ambiguous behaviour, from strangers as well as romantic partners (Downey and Feldman 1996). Those works concern expectation and self-view, not investment, so the step from her own investment to that reading is a common-sense extension of findings that a perceiver's expectations and self-view shape her reading of others' regard. A person who puts much of herself into the group gives the others the benefit of the doubt. A person on her way out reads coolness into the same scene, and finds in it a felt reason for going. The card acts on small, ambiguous signs only; plain welcome or plain exclusion is read as it is. Higher need to belong went with more accurate reading of social cues (Pickett et al. 2004), which sits against a pure projection account, so keep the effect modest. Commitment, identification and perceived support overlap heavily in organisational meta-analyses, so the link may partly reflect one shared bond. The reverse path, Belonging raising Engagement, is better supported and stays a distinct card. Her own investment colours how she reads their acceptance of her as one of their own; how they judge her conduct is Repute's ground, and the card moves only her reading of the others' treatment, not the treatment itself.

pre_language.increment: Bound up in the band, she takes the others' approaches and the room made beside her as welcome. Her feeling of being wanted among them rises.
pre_language.decrement: Drifting away from the band, she reads the others' glances as indifferent and sees groups forming without her. Her feeling of being wanted among them falls.

reactive_test.reason: Mood-congruent reading of social cues is an immediate emotional inference, with a clear pre-language form in approach and edge-drifting.

evidence.why: Nothing found tests whether a member's own investment colours how she reads acceptance cues. The nearest work concerns rejection expectations and self-esteem (Downey and Feldman; Murray and colleagues), and Pickett et al. (2004) point to accuracy, not bias. forces.name: Bringing herself in, or bracing
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into this group, I bring my whole self into it, and the faces around me read as open rather than judging: I feel safer letting slips, moods, needs and disagreements show.
forces.decrement_logic: When I have withdrawn into myself and am on my way out of this group, the same faces read as watchful and ready to mock: I mask my reactions, braced for a put-down, and feel less safe to let them show.
forces.explanation: Kahn (1990) defines engagement and disengagement as two movements of the self, expressing it in the role or withdrawing and defending it, and names safety as one condition of engagement; a meta-analysis of psychological safety places engagement in its network as an outcome (Frazier et al. 2017; mostly cross-sectional studies). That established path runs from Safety to Engagement and is carried by the Engagement update rule, not by this card. This card is the feedback beat back from Engagement to Safety. No direct test of engagement raising felt safety was found, only an adjacent three-wave psychosocial safety climate study reporting a reversed engagement to climate path (gap), so the card rests on mood-congruent reading of ambiguous faces and on common sense. Investment carries enthusiasm and withdrawal carries flatness, and mood colours judgements of other people in its own direction (Forgas 1995, checked only in part), so an invested member may read the same faces as more open and a withdrawing one as more watchful. The mood route to face reading is mixed, has rival explanations and is weakest for familiar targets, such as members of her own group. Kahn's account does not itself show how a withdrawing member reads faces; that step rests on the mood route alone, and the bracing half also leans on interpretation bias in social anxiety, a neighbouring construct with likely publication bias and one contrary study. Keep the card small, smaller than Safety's evidence cards. I considered Inverse (an invested member has more to lose, so feels more exposed) but rejected it as the default, because Kahn treats self-expression and engagement as one movement; that exposure effect belongs on a scene card about how a shown disagreement is received.

critique_was.explanation: Kahn (1990) defines engagement and disengagement as two movements of the self: expressing it in the role, or withdrawing and defending it. The well-established path runs the other way (felt safety is a condition of engagement), and this feedback path is less directly tested; I rest it on Kahn's account plus mood-congruent social perception (Forgas 1995). problems.where: explanation: 'This feedback path is a proposal resting on Kahn's account: a self that is defending braces and reads neutral faces as threat, while a self that is expressing is loose and reads the same faces as open.'
problems.detail: Kahn (supports) gives the definitions and treats safety as a condition of engagement, which runs from safety to engagement. No checked source shows that a defending self reads neutral faces as threat. The perceptual mechanism in both lines therefore has no support from Kahn. Its only partial support is Forgas (partly), and the explanation demotes that route.

problems.where: explanation: 'across 136 samples, psychological safety is an antecedent of engagement (Frazier et al. 2017)'
problems.detail: The checker did not confirm the sample count or the direction (engagement as outcome or as comparison construct), and the meta-analysis is mostly cross-sectional. 'Antecedent' claims causal order the source does not establish.

logic_status.common_sense: Only a small residual: an invested, enthusiastic member feels at ease to show herself. Common sense here is not one-sided, because the explanation itself weighs an Inverse reading (more to lose, more exposed). So the card has to rest mainly on the partly checked mood route.

evidence.why: Frazier et al. (2017) replicate the correlation but treat safety as the cause, and no cross-lagged or experimental test of the card's direction was found. The mood route is mixed, so the direction rests on common sense and a thin reverse-path literature, which makes the card provisional; this falls short of Tier 1 because the pair can run as a loop.
evidence.boundary: The replicated finding is an association between safety and engagement, with safety as the established driver. The Engagement to Safety direction is a proposal, supported only by one unconfirmed longitudinal climate study. Mood-congruent reading of faces is weakest for familiar, personally relevant groups. The bracing half borrows from interpretation bias in social anxiety, a neighbouring construct with likely publication bias and a contrary 2022 null.

forces.name: Thrown in, the venture looks winnable
forces.increment_logic: When I am thrown into this group heart and effort, I feel buoyed, and what we manage feels like a sign of what we can do: I feel more sure that we, as we stand, can pull off the venture we have taken on.
forces.decrement_logic: When I have withdrawn from this group and am half out of the door, I feel flat, and the same showing looks like the limit of what we can do: I feel less sure that we, as we stand, can pull off the venture we have taken on.
forces.explanation: Engagement in this model includes her feeling, and work engagement carries vigour and enthusiasm that set it apart from job attitudes (Christian, Garza and Slaughter 2011). That standing enthusiasm or flatness, tied to her engagement and distinct from a passing mood, is what colours her reading of the group's capability for the venture still ahead: an invested member reads what the group manages as a sign of what it can do, a withdrawing one reads the same showing as its limit. The Affect Infusion Model describes how feeling colours judgements built from scratch (Forgas 1995), but predicts least infusion where the judge has a set aim in view, which a member weighing her own group's venture often has; passing mood is fast while Engagement moves only at checkpoints, and large tests of mood effects on life-satisfaction judgements found the effects small at most (Yap et al. 2017, as summarised, not yet checked; their judgement is of one's own well-being, so carrying it to judgements of a group's capability is an extension), so the card claims no moment-to-moment mood route. Salanova, Llorens and Schaufeli (2011) propose and test a gain spiral in which efficacy beliefs and engagement influence each other over time through positive affect such as enthusiasm, in students working in groups; the return path from engagement to efficacy was not confirmed in detail, and the efficacy to engagement direction is better supported, so the loop from engagement to felt prospects is a likely reading of their work and should be kept modest. Most of that evidence concerns a member's belief in her own capability; its spread to the group's capability is an extension. Shared performance feedback can raise both engagement and confidence at once, a third-variable account the card cannot rule out. Because Team Confidence also feeds Engagement, the two form a positive loop; the brake must come from Team Confidence evidence cards (setbacks, missed goals), and the increment here should be small.

forces.name: Inside the coalition
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into this group, it feels like ours to defend, and I feel ready to stand with the rest against anyone who throws their weight about; a forceful member no longer looks able to make me do or drop anything, or to take more than their due and keep it: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I have drawn back from this group but cannot readily leave it, it no longer feels worth a stand, and I would sooner keep my head down than face anyone down; a forceful member looms larger and I give way to their mood: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me falls.
forces.explanation: In forager bands, the absence of a bully rests on a levelling coalition of the rest, ready to check a would-be dominant (Boehm 1993). Boehm describes the coalition at the level of the band, and band-level levelling is uneven across groups (Thomson et al. 2025, searched only). The model takes her felt freedom from being pushed about to depend partly on her own readiness to join that check; that central step rests on common sense. Among employees, greater satisfaction and investment go with voice and loyalty, and lesser with exit and neglect (Rusbult and colleagues 1988); that work concerns responses to a declining job, so its extension to standing up to a forceful member is the model's. Readiness to face down a forceful member is also distinct from willingness to speak up (Sherf et al. 2021, searched only). When Engagement is high the group feels like hers to defend, so a forceful member feels less able to make her comply. When it is low and she cannot readily leave, nothing here seems worth a stand, and the same forcefulness feels like a threat she must appease. The link may run partly the other way, with felt Parity or efficacy raising her identification with the group. Caution, on common sense: a member with a ready and cheap way out depends less on the group and has less to lose by defying a forceful member, so set the decrement small or nil where her exit is ready. Both lines need a member who throws their weight about: where no one does, there is nothing to stand against or give way to, so set both lines near nil. Whether the others would back her is a separate matter, carried by Friends at my back (Belonging). Parity here is her own felt exposure to force, fear or a grab that sticks, and leaves aside whether she likes or rates the forceful member.

pre_language.increment: Drawn into the band, she stands among the others when a forceful member swaggers, feels them at her side and goes on with her business. Her sense that no one can push her about rises.
pre_language.decrement: Pulled to the band's edge, she watches the forceful member warily, goes still when it comes near and gives way, feeling no one at her back. Her sense that no one can push her about falls.

reactive_test.reason: Felt safety or wariness in a forceful member's presence, read through felt allies, is a pre-language reaction.

forces.framework: Reverse dominance hierarchy; coalitionary support and centrality

sources.source: Boehm, C. (1993) Egalitarian behavior and reverse dominance hierarchy. Current Anthropology 34: 227-254.
sources.claim: Subordinates acting together keep would-be dominants in check in egalitarian societies.

sources.source: de Waal, F. (1982) Chimpanzee Politics; Silk, J.B. et al. on social bonds and coalitionary support.
sources.claim: Coalitionary support goes preferentially to close affiliates.

forces.generator_note: A rival mechanism runs the other way: a more invested member may be more alert to anyone pushing about, which would lower Levelling when Engagement rises. That is vigilance more than felt subjection, so I kept Reinforce. If the designers want a Discretionary card instead, the circumstance would be whether a would-be dominant is active in the tipping scene.

edits_log: Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Duplicates E:Belonging->Levelling (Friends at my back). Both lines rest on whether others would rally to her ('no one would rally to me', 'at its edge'), and the primate evidence (support goes to close, central affiliates) is about being backed by others. That is Belonging's ground: whether others want her and draw her in. Engagement is her own investment, so the card should rest on her own readiness to stand up against a would-be dominant. The lines also leave out the half of Levelling about taking more than one's due.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The decrement omits a known counter-mechanism. Under power-dependence theory (Emerson 1962), a member with a ready exit depends less on the group and so is harder to coerce; a member on her way out may shrug off a forceful member's temper instead of appeasing it. The direction can stand, since low commitment does run to silence and neglect (Rusbult and colleagues 1988), but the explanation should bound the decrement.

Ripple round 3, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The decrement line is stated at the bottom of the Engagement scale ('on my way out'), which is exactly the case the explanation's own caution (Emerson 1962: low dependence, little power over her) says should give a small or nil decrement. A member already leaving has little reason to appease anyone. The line should describe a member who holds back but is still tied to the group.

Ripple round 7, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The revised Parity has a grabbing limb, and the increment line uses it ('take more than their due and keep it'). The closing sentence of the explanation still limits Parity to 'felt exposure to force or fear', so the explanation contradicts its own line and the revised definition. ripple_was.explanation: In forager bands, the absence of a bully rests on a levelling coalition of the rest, ready to check a would-be dominant (Boehm 1993). Feeling free of coercion therefore depends partly on feeling yourself inside that coalition. Among primates, coalitionary support goes mostly to close and central affiliates, while peripheral individuals are left exposed (de Waal; Silk). When Engagement is high she feels herself among those who would stand together, so a forceful member feels unable to make her comply. When it is low she feels like an edge member nobody would back, and the same forcefulness feels like a threat she must appease. Levelling here is her own felt exposure to force or fear, read through the coalition, not whether she likes or rates the forceful member.

timing.typical: 2 to 10 seconds, as the forceful member makes his move
timing.why: Her readiness to stand or to give way decides how exposed she feels the instant he presses, matching Boehm's on-the-spot coalitionary check.

era.why: Coalitions against a would-be dominant, and yielding when uncommitted, are primate and forager behaviours that predate language (Boehm 1993).

forces.subtitle: Invested members resist being pushed around
forces.summary: When a member puts much of herself into the group, it feels like hers to defend, so she stands ready to resist anyone throwing their weight about, and her sense of Parity rises. When she has drawn back but cannot easily leave, she keeps her head down and gives way, so her sense of Parity falls.

problems.where: explanation: 'Commitment to a group raises the will to speak up ... (Hirschman 1970; Rusbult and colleagues 1988)'
problems.detail: Hirschman 1970 appears nowhere in the checked literature. Only Rusbult and colleagues 1988 was checked, and only as partly.

problems.where: explanation: 'Commitment to a group raises the will to speak up and resist when things go wrong'
problems.detail: Rusbult and colleagues 1988 is about employees' responses to declining job satisfaction (voice, loyalty, exit, neglect). It says nothing about resisting a forceful member, and the checker notes the link to levelling is the model's own interpretation. The text presents it as an established finding.

problems.where: explanation: 'dependence is what gives others power over her (Emerson 1962)'
problems.detail: Emerson 1962 was never checked. The claim can stand only as common sense, without the citation.

problems.where: decrement_logic: 'When I have drawn back and am on my way out of this group'
problems.detail: The decrement line describes a member on her way out, but the Caution says to set the decrement small or nil exactly where exit is ready. As written, the line describes the very case the explanation says should barely move. The decrement should describe a withdrawn member who still has to stay.

problems.where: explanation: 'Feeling free of coercion therefore depends partly on her own readiness to join that check.'
problems.detail: Boehm describes how the coalition works at group level. Nothing in him supports the 'therefore' down to one member's feeling. Mark it as the model's inference.

logic_status.common_sense: The step from Boehm's collective levelling coalition to one member's felt freedom from coercion; a withdrawn member who cannot leave keeping her head down; a member with a cheap way out having less to lose from defiance.

evidence.why: Band-level ethnography, exit-voice-loyalty-neglect research and identification with collective action all point the same way, but none of them measures a member's felt parity, and the collective-action link is cross-sectional with contested direction. The fields converge only on analogous steps and no source is verified, so the card rests on common sense and stays provisional.
evidence.boundary: Both lines are near nil when no forceful member is present. The decrement is small when exit is cheap. Readiness to confront a forceful member differs from willingness to give voice, and voice and silence are largely independent (Sherf et al. 2021, to be checked). Levelling is uneven across groups, strongest in immediate-return foragers. The direction may partly run the other way, with felt parity or efficacy raising identification.

forces.name: Trusting those I am in it with
forces.increment_logic: When I am thrown into this group and putting in all I can, I take the others to be putting in as I am, and a part of theirs not yet done reads as on its way: I feel more confident that they will do what they take on.
forces.decrement_logic: When I have drawn back from this group and am doing the least I can, I take the others to be doing the same, and a part of theirs not yet done reads as likely to be let drop: I feel less confident that they will do what they take on.
forces.explanation: Projection is the checked route. In repeated public goods games, beliefs about others' contributions go with one's own contributions (Smith 2013), and conditional cooperators match what they expect of others (Fischbacher and Gächter 2010), though those authors put the decay of cooperation down mainly to preferences, so their work does not show beliefs falling with contributions. The link between beliefs and one's own contribution is partly reciprocal and endogenous (Smith 2013; Gächter and Renner 2010, both searched only), so the card claims a modest projection effect only. The step from expected contributions to a member's felt reading of whether the others will do their part is a model proposal. Engagement moves only at checkpoints, so the card claims a standing reading, not a passing one. Team trust and performance links shrink in time-lagged designs, a further reason to keep the card small. The card forms a loop with Engagement, since Engagement is fed by the perceptions; the brake is parts plainly carried through or plainly dropped, which move Dependability on their own evidence. Record first: where she has seen a member's part carried through or dropped, that record moves Dependability and this card plays small or not at all; the card governs only parts whose fate she has not yet seen. Two secondary routes remain possible, unchecked here. Affect: feeling colours judgements of other people (Forgas 1995), less so when she judges with a set aim in view, as she may when a teammate she depends on must deliver. Sampling over many plays: an engaged member keeps relying on others, so a single let-down is soon corrected, while a disengaged member stops relying on them and the last let-down stands (Denrell 2005). The card moves reliability only, leaving her reading of the group's capability to Team Confidence. One caution: members who believe a partner is not pulling their weight cut their own effort (the sucker effect, Kerr 1983). That reaction is driven by seeing the coasting, so it belongs on a Dependability evidence card.

pre_language.increment: Bound up in the band, she leaves tasks in others' hands and sees them done, and each task carried through sticks: her trust that those around her will do their part rises.
pre_language.decrement: Withdrawn from the band, she stops leaving tasks with others, and the last task dropped is what she carries away: her trust that they will do their part falls.

reactive_test.reason: Warmth-coloured trust and the lingering of the last let-down are emotional inferences from weighted evidence, with a plain pre-language form.

forces.framework: Endogenous beliefs in public goods games (Smith 2013; Fischbacher and Gächter 2010); affect infusion (Forgas 1995) and sampling bias (Denrell 2005) as secondary routes; motivation losses in groups (Kerr 1983).

timing.typical: within the task in hand, as she sees how the others are carrying their parts

era.why: Leaving a part of joint work to a partner rests on pre-linguistic joint collaboration in early humans; warmth colouring that reading needs no talk, though keeping one's word is spoken today.

forces.subtitle: Effort makes you trust others more
forces.summary: A member putting in all she can takes the others to be doing the same, so a part of theirs not yet done reads as on its way and she is more confident they will do what they take on. One who has drawn back takes them to be doing the least too, and trusts them less. It applies only to parts whose fate she has not yet seen, and it is kept small.

problems.detail: This phrase draws on the Denrell sampling route, which the explanation itself says works over many plays. Cards are felt reactions within minutes, so the line should rest on the in-the-moment mood route.
