logic_status.common_sense: Being invested in a group goes with a warmer mood towards its members, and drawing back with a cooler one. This is safe only as a modest default, because an invested member can also be frustrated.

evidence.why: Projection of one's own cooperation onto expectations of others is replicated in neighbouring forms (false consensus in Many Labs 2, prosocial expectations, conditional cooperation), but always as beliefs or behaviour in lab games, never as a member's engagement shifting her felt confidence in others. The organisational evidence is analogous, so consilience falls short of strong, no source is verified, and the card stays provisional.
evidence.boundary: Part of the link between own contribution and beliefs about others is reciprocal and endogenous (Smith 2013; Gächter and Renner 2010, to be checked). Fischbacher and Gächter (2010) support conditional cooperation, not decay led by beliefs, so they should not carry the decrement line. The step from beliefs about contributions to a felt reading of others' reliability is the model's proposal.

forces.name: One of us, so paid back
forces.explanation: In egalitarian sharing the return comes from the group. Whether putting much of myself in raises my sense that help comes back depends on whether what comes back seems to keep pace with what I feel I have put in. Circumstance one (the default), returns keep pace or are unclear. HIGH: I am pouring my time and effort into this group, I feel the others need what I bring, and what comes my way reads as the group looking after one it relies on: my sense that help here comes back to me rises. LOW: I am pulling out, I know I have held back and given the others less reason to look after me, and I expect to be passed over when I am in need: my sense that help here comes back to me falls. Circumstance two, I have been putting in heavily and the everyday help and care coming back look ordinary. HIGH: the more I have put in, the more my own share looms in memory and the others' fades, so an ordinary return reads as short: my sense that help here comes back to me falls. LOW: having put in little, a little back is what I expected, and the card adds nothing. Circumstance one rests on the interdependence accounts: when members depend on one another, each has a direct stake in a partner's welfare and helps that partner (Roberts 2005; Tomasello and colleagues 2012). Both are theoretical evolutionary accounts, and their extension to a member's felt Engagement in a present-day group is the model's; the reading of ambiguous cues and the expectation of being passed over rest on common sense. Circumstance two rests on egocentric credit: people overclaim their share of joint work because their own part comes to mind more readily (Ross and Sicoly 1979), and the overclaiming grows with group size, while asking members to think of others' parts one by one reduces it (Schroeder, Caruso and Epley 2016). The step from overclaimed credit to a felt shortfall in the return is a model proposal, so play circumstance two modest, larger in bigger groups. Engagement is the felt size of her stake and effort in the group. Big windfalls still reach her by demand whatever her stake, since demand sharing and tolerated scrounging do not track contribution, so the card bites on everyday giving and on the care she gets when sick or hurt. Even there, the forager literature leaves unsettled how far sharing tracks contribution (Gurven 2004, searched only), so keep circumstance one modest too. Whether the others want her among them is a separate route (One of us, so it comes back), and so is what they say of her as a sharer (Bad Name, Empty Hands). The card moves her reading of the group's return; it keeps no tally of particular debts.

pre_language.increment: Bound up in the band, she shares freely and feels the band's food and help come round to her in turn. Her sense that what she gives comes back rises.
pre_language.decrement: Loosened from the band, she keeps to herself and, when hungry, hangs back expecting nothing to be passed her way. Her sense that what she gives comes back falls.

reactive_test.reason: An inference from emotionally weighted information about her own standing among the sharers, of a kind a band-living animal could form without words; no reckoning of returns is involved.

forces.framework: Interdependence hypothesis and stakeholder theory of cooperation for circumstance one; egocentric credit bias (Ross and Sicoly 1979; Schroeder, Caruso and Epley 2016) for circumstance two.

sources.source: Tomasello, M., Melis, A.P., Tennie, C., Wyman, E. and Herrmann, E. (2012) Two key steps in the evolution of human cooperation: the interdependence hypothesis. Current Anthropology 53: 673-692.
sources.claim: Individuals who depend on one another have a direct interest in their partners' wellbeing and help them.

sources.source: Roberts, G. (2005) Cooperation through interdependence. Animal Behaviour 70: 901-908.

sources.claim: Theoretical support only: a stake in another's welfare makes helping a contributor one relies on the best move, the mechanism behind circumstance one. Supports; not load-bearing for the grade.

ripple_was.increment_logic: When this group is part of who I am, I feel myself one of us, a known sharer, and what comes my way reads as the group paying back what I put in; my sense that help here comes back to me rises.
ripple_was.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, I feel myself the one who holds back, the kind the group passes over, and when I am in need I expect nothing to come my way; my sense that help here comes back to me falls.
ripple_was.explanation: In egalitarian sharing, the return comes from the group and is contingent on being a member in good standing: households that give more receive more (Gurven 2004), and demand sharing presses those with a surplus to give to whoever counts as one of us (Peterson 1993). Engagement is the felt size of her stake and presence in the group. When it is high she feels herself a sharer the group gives to, and reads ambiguous cues of others' giving as return for what she has put in. When it is low she feels herself on the hoarder's side of the line and expects to be passed over. What moves is her reading of the group's return, not any tally of particular debts.

timing.typical: within minutes of help arriving or a need going unmet
timing.why: Her stake sets how she reads the next ambiguous cue of giving or passing over, so the reading shifts as soon as such a cue comes.

era.why: Group sharing that tracks contribution has non-verbal analogues in primate food sharing and tolerated taking, and in forager demand sharing (Gurven 2004).

forces.subtitle: Being one of us pays back
forces.summary: When a member's stake in the group is large, the group tends to look after her, so her sense that help comes back rises. When she has pulled out, she expects to be passed over, so it falls. After heavy giving, her own share can loom so large that ordinary returns feel short, and the sense falls.

problems.where: explanation: 'households that give more receive more (Gurven 2004), even where demand sharing gives every member some claim on a surplus (Peterson 1993)'
problems.detail: This is the card's core evidence, and neither Gurven 2004 nor Peterson 1993 is in the checked literature. The two sources that were checked (Tomasello and colleagues 2012; Roberts 2005) appear nowhere in the explanation.

problems.where: framework: 'Interdependence hypothesis; stakeholder theory of cooperation' against the explanation
problems.detail: The framework and the checked sources rest on stake theory: those who depend on her have a direct interest in her welfare and help her. The explanation instead argues contingent giving, where givers receive more. The cited literature backs a different mechanism from the one the text argues.

problems.where: literature use of Tomasello and colleagues 2012 and Roberts 2005
problems.detail: Both are theoretical evolutionary accounts. The checker notes that extending them to Engagement in a present-day small group is the model's step. Say so.

logic_status.common_sense: An invested member reads ambiguous cues of others' giving as return for her effort. A member who has held back expects to be passed over. Both are ordinary self-assessments of standing as a giver, and both are safe if kept modest.

evidence.why: Nothing tests the central link from a member's felt Engagement to her expected return. The interdependence sources are theory, and the overclaiming studies are single-lab and measure claimed share of work, not felt return.
evidence.boundary: Windfalls and large shares reach members by demand sharing and tolerated scrounging whatever their stake (Gurven 2004, debated), so circumstance one bites on everyday giving and care when sick or hurt, not on windfall shares. Circumstance two is modest and grows with group size; it shrinks when a member goes through others' parts one by one (Schroeder, Caruso and Epley 2016, not independently replicated).

forces.name: Circle the Wagons
forces.explanation: Whether the venture's prospects draw the others round her depends on where the trouble is seen to come from. Threats seen as external tend to strengthen group identity, and threats seen as internal can weaken it (Greenaway and Cruwys 2019, a theoretical synthesis). The card carries her own reading of how the others treat her; whether they in fact draw together or pull apart belongs to the scene. Circumstance one (the default): the trouble is seen as inside the group, or no source is named. HIGH: with the venture going well, she reads the others as easy with each other and with her and feels drawn in, so her Belonging rises (runs as Reinforce). LOW: with the venture failing, she feels the talk grow short and reads herself as left at its edge, so her Belonging falls. The stronger path may run from performance to cohesion (Mullen and Copper 1994), but the effect is small, its direction rests on a few cross-lagged studies, it comes from realised results while Team Confidence is a forecast, and it runs mainly through commitment to the task, with liking among members playing a smaller part, so keep this branch modest. In the egalitarian face acceptance holds through good seasons and bad, so keep it smallest for a member long drawn in. Being blamed herself for the failure is Repute's ground (Pointing Fingers), not this card's. Circumstance two: the trouble is seen as coming from outside (a rival group, an outside body, or a setback from outside such as lost funding or a forced change of ground), and the group still sees a fight worth making. LOW here means the venture is threatened, not yet hopeless: she feels the group closing ranks against the threat and reads herself as drawn in as one of us, so her Belonging rises (runs as Inverse). HIGH: the outside threat looks easily met, she feels the huddle loosen and her place return to its ordinary level, so her Belonging slips back down, by no more than an earlier huddle raised it; with no such rise, the step is nil. Animal findings offer analogues only, and both are correlational: green woodhoopoe groups preened each other more after conflicts with neighbouring groups, most after long ones (Radford 2008), and in wild chimpanzees oxytocin rose before and during intergroup conflict, which the authors link to in-group cohesion (Samuni et al. 2017). In people, external conflict raises cohesion only under some conditions (Stein 1976): the threat falls on the whole group, the group already has some cohesion, and a way of meeting the threat seems to exist. Physical danger and real violent conflict can lower in-group cooperation instead (Silva and Mace 2015, field experiments around sectarian riots in Belfast), so the rally branch covers setbacks to the venture and does not run where the threat is to members' safety. Where the venture looks hopeless, run circumstance one.

pre_language.explanation: Where the band huddles when things go badly and she is still half an outsider, a faltering venture has them gathering close and pulling her in among them, while a venture going well lets them drift back to leaving her on the edge. Where the band turns on whoever seems to drag, a faltering venture may leave her at the edge, while a venture going well sees them make room for her again.

reactive_test.reason: Huddling under threat and turning on a weak member are both felt group reactions she reads directly as being drawn in or edged out.

critique_was.explanation: Whether the venture's prospects draw the others round her depends on where the trouble is seen to come from. Circumstance one (the default), the trouble is seen as inside the group or no source is named. HIGH: the venture going well, the others are easy with each other and with her, make room and draw her in, so her Belonging rises (runs as Reinforce). LOW: the venture failing, heads turn to who is dragging, small cliques form, and she is left at the edge of the talk, so her Belonging falls. Circumstance two, the trouble is seen as coming from outside (a rival group, an outside body, bad luck that hit them all). LOW: the others close ranks against it and draw her in as one of us, so her Belonging rises (runs as Inverse). HIGH: with no outside pressure the huddle loosens and her place returns to its ordinary level, so her Belonging eases. Newcomers gain least from the outside-threat branch and lose most in the inside branch.

Whether the venture's prospects draw the others round her depends on where the trouble is seen to come from. Threats seen as external tend to strengthen group identity, and threats seen as internal can weaken it (Greenaway and Cruwys 2019, a theoretical synthesis). Circumstance one (the default): the trouble is seen as inside the group, or no source is named. HIGH: with the venture going well, the others are easy with each other and with her and draw her in, so her Belonging rises (runs as Reinforce). LOW: with the venture failing, the others grow short with each other and she is left at the edge of the talk, so her Belonging falls. The stronger path may run from performance to cohesion (Mullen and Copper 1994), but the effect is small, comes from results where Team Confidence is a forecast, and runs mainly through commitment to the task, with liking among members playing a smaller part, so keep this branch modest. In the egalitarian face acceptance holds through good seasons and bad, so keep it smallest for a member long drawn in. Being blamed herself for the failure is Repute's ground (Pointing Fingers), not this card's. Circumstance two: the trouble is seen as coming from outside (a rival group, an outside body, or a setback from outside such as lost funding or a forced change of ground), and the group still sees a fight worth making. LOW here means the venture is threatened, not yet hopeless: the others close ranks against the threat and draw her in as one of us, so her Belonging rises (runs as Inverse). HIGH: the outside threat looks easily met, the huddle loosens and her place returns to its ordinary level, so her Belonging slips back down, by no more than an earlier huddle raised it; with no such rise, the step is nil. External conflict raises cohesion only under some conditions (Stein 1976). On common sense the model takes those conditions to include a threat that falls on all of them and a joint effort that seems able to meet it, so where the venture looks hopeless, run circumstance one.

HIGH: the outside threat looks easily met, the huddle loosens and her place returns to its ordinary level, so her Belonging slips back down, by no more than an earlier huddle raised it; with no such rise, the step is nil. Animal findings offer analogues only, and both are correlational: green woodhoopoe groups preened each other more after conflicts with neighbouring groups, most after long ones (Radford 2008), and in wild chimpanzees oxytocin rose before and during intergroup conflict, which the authors link to in-group cohesion (Samuni et al. 2017). Physical danger and real violent conflict can lower in-group cooperation instead (Silva and Mace 2015, field experiments around sectarian riots in Belfast), so the rally branch covers setbacks to the venture and does not run where the threat is to members' safety. Where the venture looks hopeless, run circumstance one.

timing.why: In either circumstance, making room or forming cliques shows up in the same gathering in which the prospects shift.

era.why: Huddling under an outside threat and splintering under internal failure have analogues in primate intergroup encounters and redirected aggression; lost funding is a modern example of the same reaction.

forces.subtitle: Venture prospects shape felt belonging
forces.summary: Whether the venture's prospects draw her towards the others depends on where the trouble is seen to come from. By default, a venture going well leaves her easy with the others and drawn in, and a failing one leaves her at the edge. When the trouble is seen as coming from outside and a fight is still worth making, the threat can instead have the group close ranks and pull her in.

problems.where: circumstance one HIGH and LOW branches, resting on Mullen and Copper 1994
problems.detail: The checker reports that the performance-to-cohesion effect is small and comes from actual results, while GrpProsp is a forecast (partly). It also runs mainly through task commitment, with interpersonal attraction playing little part. Belonging is about being drawn in by the others, so the source backs this branch only weakly, and the text should say so. Mullen and Copper are also missing from the explanation, although they are named in the framework.

problems.where: explanation: 'small cliques form'
problems.detail: No checked source backs clique formation under failure. Greenaway and Cruwys 2019 concerns threats seen as internal, which differs from failure as such. Drop the claim.

problems.where: explanation: 'Newcomers gain least from the outside-threat branch and lose most in the inside branch.'
problems.detail: No source backs this, and it is not plain common sense either (newcomers could equally gain most from a huddle). Drop the claim.

problems.where: explanation: 'External threat binds a group only when it falls on all of them and a joint effort seems able to meet it (Stein 1976)'
problems.detail: The checker read only the abstract, which confirms that the effect is conditional and has intervening variables. The two specific conditions were not confirmed. Present them as the model's reading, resting on common sense.

problems.where: circumstance two LOW: low GrpProsp combined with 'the group still sees a fight worth making'
problems.detail: Low Team Confidence means the venture feels beyond the group, yet this branch needs a joint effort that seems able to meet the threat. The text should state that LOW here means threatened and not yet hopeless, which already hands the hopeless case to circumstance one.

problems.where: explanation: the source-of-threat split is given no citation
problems.detail: Greenaway and Cruwys 2019 (supports, as a theoretical synthesis) is the checked source for this split, but the explanation never cites it.

logic_status.common_sense: In the egalitarian face, acceptance of a long-standing member holds through good seasons and bad. An outside threat binds only when a joint effort seems able to meet it. The huddle loosens once the threat looks easily met, giving back no more than it raised. All three are safe as limits on the size of the step and never set its direction.

evidence.why: The source distinction has a theoretical synthesis and analogous animal data behind it, but no study tests Belonging after an external versus internal venture setback, and one field study runs the other way under physical conflict. The cohesion-performance meta-analyses are adjacent, small and pre-date bias correction, so neither branch reaches substantiated.
evidence.boundary: The rally branch needs the threat to fall on the group as a whole and a way of meeting it (Stein 1976; Weisel and Zultan 2021, not verified); where the danger falls on members' bodies or each fends for herself, cooperation can fall (Silva and Mace 2015). Keep the Reinforce branch modest: the cohesion-performance link is small and correlational.

forces.name: Stakes tighten or loosen
forces.increment_logic: When I feel sure the group can pull off the venture, no one is hunting for whose slip will cost us, so a slip passes without remark and I let my tiredness, moods and doubts show, expecting no one to pounce: my sense that I can show myself here without cost rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I feel the venture is beyond us, I feel heads turning to find who is dragging us down, so I mask my tiredness and keep my doubts and disagreements hidden, braced for blame: my sense that I can show myself here without cost falls.
forces.explanation: A change in the venture's prospects changes how much seems to hang on each member's showing. With the rowing crew's season looking won there is slack, no one hunts for a culprit, and a doubt about the stroke passes as a refinement. With the season looking lost, heads turn to find whose slip is costing the crew and she masks her tiredness, braced for a put-down. The card carries only that anticipated cost of showing herself, before any charge is made; a charge of shirking made openly by someone of standing is Face's ground, and the group's verdict that she does not pull her weight is Repute's, carried by Pointing Fingers. The link from failing prospects to a hunt for culprits rests on common sense; no forager or primate evidence was found for scapegoating after failure. Threat rigidity (Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981), a broad theory with thin group-level tests, points the same way but awaits a check and is not relied on, so keep the card modest. Where a group treats errors as things to learn from and fix, with no punishment, felt safety goes with learning behaviour (Edmondson 1999, one firm, cross-sectional; the construct has since been pooled in meta-analyses, mainly in the direction from safety to performance), so set the decrement small or nil there. Play the decrement small, too, where the group habitually meets setbacks by working the problem in the open; that habit bounds the card's size and does not reverse it. Where she sees the shortfall as within the group's power to put right, the decrement may also be weaker (Konig et al. 2021, searched only). Caution on the high side: in a tight-knit group whose confidence has hardened, a doubt about the plan itself can draw pressure to keep quiet. That point also rests on common sense; groupthink, often cited for it, has only partial empirical support (Esser 1998), and a meta-analysis found no overall effect of cohesion on decision quality (Mullen et al. 1994), so the effect is conditional and is not relied on. Set the increment small for disagreement in such a group. The card runs as Reinforce; no reverse effect is strong enough to make it Discretionary.

pre_language.explanation: Where the band's way is to try other ways when things go badly, a faltering venture draws them together and she shows her moods and fumbles freely, while a venture going well has them guarding what works and she keeps her fumbles hidden, bracing a little. Where the band's way is to turn on one another, a faltering venture makes her go still, watch faces and mask her reactions, while a venture going well leaves no one turning on anyone and she moves unguarded again.

reactive_test.reason: Relaxing or bracing in response to the group's mood under setback is an immediate emotional reaction.

edits_log: Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): In circumstance one HIGH, 'she keeps it to herself' describes whether she speaks up, which the DivsExp definition excludes. The fall needs to rest on what she expects showing herself to cost her.
Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 12.04 pm (social psychologist's critique, docs/v3/expert-critiques/social-psych/): The HIGH-lowers-safety branch had no support; threat, not success, narrows groups.

Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Circumstance one has no direction. Once its old high branch was dropped, DivsExp holds or rises when GrpProsp is high and rises when it is low, so the source no longer sets the movement; the group's learning climate does. That fits neither Reinforce nor Inverse, and a Discretionary card needs each circumstance to run one way or the other. Circumstance two (high raises, low lowers) is the only directional branch, and it is the one the literature supports (threat rigidity: Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981). Smallest coherent fix: retype as Reinforce on circumstance two's lines, and keep the learning-oriented group as a damper on the fall (Edmondson 1999). The claim that a failing venture raises safety in such groups lacks support and shows the climate at work rather than GrpProsp, so it is dropped. The lines below stay on felt cost and avoid whether she speaks up.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The explanation's closing sentence claims no evidence that rising confidence makes members less safe to show doubt. Groupthink theory (Janis 1972) holds that a cohesive group's illusion of invulnerability brings direct pressure on dissenters and self-censorship, though empirical support is mixed (Esser 1998). The sentence also refers to an earlier version of the card, which does not belong in the card text. The lines and type stand; the explanation needs a bounded caution instead.
Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 1.47 pm (organisational psychologist's critique and Reputation pack questions): The high-side caution rested on groupthink, whose support is thin.

Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines pass. The explanation credits Edmondson (1999) with showing that safety holds up where groups look at what to change rather than who is at fault. That study measured team psychological safety and learning behaviour, with leader coaching and context support as antecedents. It did not contrast blame and learning responses to trouble; the error-management climate work (van Dyck et al. 2005) is closer to that claim. One sentence also opens with 'This is', which the house style bars.

The card holds only as the anticipated put-down for showing herself before any charge is made, so it needs that boundary stated. The lines can stay as they are.

problems.where: explanation: 'Under threat, information narrows and control constricts (Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981)'
problems.detail: The checker gave a null verdict on all three Staw entries, so the card's only mechanism source is unchecked. Staw is also about threat narrowing information and centralising control. It says nothing directly about blame hunting or members masking themselves, so the mapping to Safety is the model's.

problems.where: explanation: '(Edmondson 1999; van Dyck et al. 2005)'
problems.detail: van Dyck and colleagues 2005 is not in the checked literature. Drop it or have it checked.

problems.where: explanation: 'felt safety and open talk about errors go together (Edmondson 1999)'
problems.detail: Edmondson is rated partly: safety predicting learning behaviour is supported, but discussing errors specifically was not confirmed, and the design is one firm, cross-sectional. As a moderator the use is fair, but it should name learning behaviour and note the design.

problems.where: explanation: 'groupthink ... has thin and partial empirical support (Esser 1998)'
problems.detail: The checker confirmed 'partial' but not 'thin' or 'few'. Esser's review suggests a sizeable literature.

logic_status.common_sense: Failing prospects start a hunt for culprits and make members mask tiredness and doubt; confident prospects give slack. Doubt about the plan in a hardened, tight-knit group draws pressure to keep quiet. Both are safe as modest everyday expectations, and the second is already marked as common sense.

evidence.why: The psychological safety meta-analyses are replicated but run from safety to performance, and nothing tests falling prospects raising anticipated blame and so lowering felt safety. Threat rigidity is contested and organisation-level, and the nearest blame-and-disclosure study is an unreviewed working paper with mixed results, none of it verified.
evidence.boundary: In a learning-oriented climate with no punishment for slips the decrement is small or nil (Edmondson 1999). With hardened confidence in a tight-knit group, the increment for disagreement about the plan is small (Mullen, Anthony, Salas and Driskell 1994, conditional). Add: where the member sees the shortfall as within the group's control, the decrement is weaker (Konig, Graf-Vlachy and Schoberl 2021, firm level, analogous).

forces.name: Failing hunts breed bosses
forces.increment_logic: When I feel sure the group can pull off the venture, I see no call for anyone to take charge by force or settle things over our heads, and if the strongest starts to drive the pace I shrug it off; I go about my business beside them without a glance at their mood: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I feel the venture is beyond us and one of us starts driving us by threat and temper and settling things without hearing us, I feel in no position to stand against them while the venture hangs in the balance, and their way looks bound to stick, so I do what they want to head off their anger: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me falls a little.
forces.explanation: The card does not run through any preference for a dominant leader: people who feel a loss of control under uncertainty favour dominant over prestigious leaders (Kakkar and Sivanathan 2017), but a preference is consent, not domination, and does not move Parity. The decrement plays only where, with the venture looking beyond the group, a member actually presses by threat or settles things over the others' heads and she does not push back. That a failing venture weakens her will to resist, so that the push looks bound to stick, is a proposal resting on common sense. Parity's E face counts fear and anger alike, so the line moves with whether the push can stick; her giving way is how that reading shows, and the fall from the push itself is played on the scene, not here. Leaders gain most authority in small-scale societies where failure of collective action threatens the group itself (Glowacki and von Rueden 2015), so keep the decrement for ventures whose failure would threaten the group, not for every setback. Where members can move to another group at little cost, they walk away from a would-be boss rather than submit (Woodburn 1982), and forager band membership is fluid (Hill et al. 2011, searched only), so the decrement applies only where leaving is costly and is small where members can readily move. On the high side, on common sense alone, members confident of success see no need for anyone to take charge, so a would-be dominant who tries to drive the pace is shrugged off. Both lines need a member who presses or starts to drive the pace: where no one does, there is nothing to shrug off or give way to, so set both lines nil. Direction that rests on force, or that settles things without a hearing, lowers a member's Parity; a respected leader simply taking the lead would not. Both lines should be small.

That a failing venture weakens her will to resist, so that the push looks bound to stick, is a proposal resting on common sense. Parity's E face counts fear and anger alike, so the line moves with whether the push can stick; her giving way is how that reading shows, and the fall from the push itself is played on the scene, not here. Leaders gain most authority in small-scale societies where failure of collective action threatens the group itself (Glowacki and von Rueden 2015), so keep the decrement for ventures whose failure would threaten the group, not for every setback. Where members can move to another group at little cost, they walk away from a would-be boss rather than submit (Woodburn 1982), and forager band membership is fluid (Hill et al. 2011, searched only), so the decrement applies only where leaving is costly and is small where members can readily move. On the high side, on common sense alone, members confident of success see no need for anyone to take charge, so a would-be dominant who tries to drive the pace is shrugged off. Direction that rests on force, or that settles things without a hearing, lowers a member's Parity; a respected leader simply taking the lead would not. Both lines should be small.

timing.typical: within the meeting, as the strongest start to drive the pace
timing.why: Her felt exposure falls once a member has begun to press by threat and temper and she finds herself appeasing him, both of which happen within the meeting.

era.why: A dominant pressing harder and meeting less resistance under stress is primate behaviour; the felt core of yielding to force predates language.

forces.subtitle: Failing ventures invite bossy members
forces.summary: When she feels sure the group can pull off the venture, no one has a call to take charge by force, and she goes about her business beside the strongest. When the venture looks beyond the group and a member starts driving the others by threat and temper, she feels unable to stand against them and gives way. The card plays only where someone actually presses, and both effects stay small.

problems.where: explanation: 'Under threat of failure, groups centralise control and accept forceful direction (threat rigidity: Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981), and would-be dominants meet less resistance.'
problems.detail: The checker gave a null verdict on every Staw entry, so this opening mechanism claim is unchecked. 'Would-be dominants meet less resistance' has no source at all.

problems.where: same sentence: 'accept forceful direction'
problems.detail: Even on the record's own summary, Staw is about centralised control and restricted information. Centralisation does not mean accepting force. Kakkar and Sivanathan cover preference for dominant leaders, and only under economic and personal uncertainty.

problems.where: decrement_logic: 'I feel the strongest start to drive the rest of us by threat and temper'
problems.detail: Kakkar and Sivanathan 2017 show followers turning towards dominant leaders. They do not show dominants becoming more forceful. The line should rest on the others looking to the strongest and no one pushing back.

problems.where: literature: Hamblin 1958
problems.detail: Rated not found, with the content never reached. The explanation does not rely on it, so nothing in the text changes, but it should not be counted as support.

logic_status.common_sense: Members confident of success see no need for anyone to take charge and shrug off a would-be dominant. Forceful direction lowers Parity where a respected leader's lead does not. Both are safe: the first is the plain converse of the dominance-preference finding, and the second follows from the definition of Parity.

evidence.why: Multi-country work shows threat raising preference for dominant leaders, but it measures leader preference under economic or intergroup threat, not a member's felt Parity after a failing venture, and the Kakkar and Sivanathan mediation is disputed. Forager evidence points to exit as the usual answer to failure, and no source here was verified, so the step stays provisional.
evidence.boundary: The decrement applies only where failure threatens the group and leaving is costly; in small groups with cheap exit, failure is met by fission or leaving more than by a boss (Glowacki and von Rueden 2015; Hill et al. 2011; Woodburn 1982 still to be located). The increment rests on common sense alone.

forces.name: Scapegoating
forces.increment_logic: When the group's venture looks well within its reach, I credit the others with carrying their parts, and I feel I can leave work in their hands without checking: my confidence that they will do their part rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When the venture looks beyond the group, my frustration looks for whose shirking or broken word is dragging it down, and I come to expect that member, and others like them, to let their parts slip: my confidence that the others will do their part falls.
forces.explanation: A venture that looks within reach casts a warm light on the others' carrying-through, so she leaves work in their hands with less checking; this step rests on common sense, so keep the increment modest. One that looks beyond the group can set her looking for a culprit, and some of the blame may land on a member's unwillingness. Blame that lands on another member's want of skill moves Team Confidence, and blame that others lay openly on her own want of skill moves her Esteem; neither belongs to this card. Members' attributions for a group's outcome shift with its success or failure, chiefly in how much each takes on herself (Forsyth and Schlenker 1977); that study does not show blame turned on fellow members, so the step to blaming another's unwillingness rests on common sense. After a group's failure, blame is reported to fall on fewer members than praise falls on after its success, across seven studies (Schein, Jackson, Frasca and Gray 2020, reported by a reviewer, not checked here), which fits the decrement's narrow search for a culprit. Schlenker and Miller (1977) is reported to show egocentric overclaiming, members taking a larger share of the group's outcome for themselves; whether members lay more of a failure on one another than on themselves awaits a reading of the paper and is not relied on. The claim that observers credit a team for success but lay its failure on individual members (Naquin and Tynan 2003) is not yet checked. Those studies concern failure already suffered; the step to a felt forecast of failure is a proposal, so keep the decrement modest. Realised team performance may not reliably move later trust (a 96-team longitudinal study found no effect, and Feitosa et al. 2020 report shrinkage of time-lagged effects; both searched only), which is a further reason to keep both lines modest. Boundary. The decrement turns on where she puts the trouble. Where she puts it down to the venture's difficulty or to something outside the group (group-serving bias, Allen et al. 2020, searched only), no member is blamed and the decrement is nil; where the failure plainly comes from luck or an outside shock that everyone can see, it is small at most. It plays at full size only where she puts the trouble down to members. This boundary rests on common sense.

pre_language.increment: When the venture is going well, she watches those carrying it with approval and leaves them to their tasks without hovering.
pre_language.decrement: When it is going badly, her frustration turns on whoever faltered: she glares at them, hovers over what they do and snatches tasks back from them.

reactive_test.reason: This is frustration-driven blame and approval, an inference from emotionally weighted information. Primates show the same pattern when they redirect aggression after a setback.

forces.name: Leaned on, left out
forces.increment_logic: When no one in the group can push me about or take what is mine, and whoever hands out shares or settles a quarrel does it even-handedly, I move among the others freely and nothing keeps me at the edge when they gather: my sense that they want me among them rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When a forceful member makes me comply through fear, I go quiet and keep out of the way at gatherings, and I take it that the others, seeing me leaned on, would as soon keep their distance from me; or when whoever hands out shares or settles a quarrel passes me over for his own and the rest let it stand, I take it that they do not much care to keep me among them: my sense that they want me among them falls.
forces.explanation: A member pushed about by force or fear draws back from the group's circle: she keeps out of the way of the one who leans on her, and so is less often among the others, and reads her own withdrawal as being less wanted. This rests on common sense about avoiding a threat. That she expects the others to keep their distance too is also common sense; whether they in fact pull away is unsettled (among children, victimisation by peers is reported to predict growing rejection, Hodges and Perry 1999, not yet checked, and the links between victimisation and rejection run both ways and vary with sex and sample), so the card stays on her own reading, what the others do belongs to the scene, and the step is kept modest. Partial dealing is a second route, since Parity covers share-outs and settlements as well as force: when whoever hands out shares or settles a quarrel passes her over and the rest let it stand, she reads it as a sign that she counts for less among them. The relational model of procedural justice holds that people read even-handed treatment by those in charge as a sign that they are valued members of the group, and partial treatment as a sign that they are not (Tyler and Lind 1992, not yet checked). Its evidence concerns identification, pride and respect, which lie close to belonging without being the same, and the effect depends on how much the member cares about her place in the group, so keep this route modest too. Where no one can lord it over her and dealing is even, nothing holds her at the edge; that removes a barrier without itself making her welcome, and the step rests on common sense only, so set the increment smaller than the decrement. Ribbing a member who gets above herself is not this card: it is Repute's ground (Tall Poppy Talk; Insulting the meat). Boundary: the withdrawal in the first limb is fear's pull. Where she meets the push with anger, as when she has backing or the wrong is a grab rather than a threat, anger moves her towards the one who leans on her rather than away, and anger tends towards later reconciliation where contempt tends towards lasting exclusion (Fischer and Roseman 2007); she is not keeping out of the way, so set the first limb small there.

pre_language.explanation: After she brings in a large kill and carries herself high, where no one can push anyone about the others run down her meat, mock and turn their backs a little, and she feels less welcome until she lowers herself; where a strong one already pushes her about and turns on her for it, the others close round her and she feels more welcome. When she has done nothing to stand out and no one can drive her off, the others close round her when a strong one tries, and she feels more welcome; when a strong one already has her cowed, she keeps out of the way, the others stay clear of her, and she feels less welcome.

reactive_test.reason: Ridicule, cooling of company and the shame of being cut down are pre-linguistic levelling sanctions; her felt loss of welcome is an emotional reaction, not a calculation.

ripple_was.increment_logic: When no one in the group can push me about or take what is mine, I move among the others freely and nothing keeps me from them; if a forceful member tries to freeze me out, the others draw me back in, and my sense that they want me among them rises.
ripple_was.decrement_logic: When a forceful member makes me comply through fear, I go quiet and keep out of the way at gatherings, the others keep their distance from the one he leans on, and the circle forms without me: my sense that they want me among them falls.
ripple_was.explanation: A member pushed about by force or fear is drawn out of the group's circle: she keeps out of the way, and the others keep clear of the one a forceful member leans on. Among children, being victimised by peers predicts growing rejection by them (Hodges and Perry 1999); carrying that to adult groups is an extension, so keep the step modest. Where no one can lord it over her, nothing holds her at the edge, and the others check a would-be dominant together, as foragers do (Boehm), so a forceful newcomer who tries to freeze her out sees her drawn back in. A member who stands out and is ribbed for getting above herself (Lee's 'insulting the meat'; Feather on tall poppies) is not pushed about by force or fear, so her Levelling stays high. The ribbing is a verdict on her conduct (Repute: Tall Poppy Talk) and leaves the egalitarian face's acceptance in place, since only shirking, cheating or feeding on the others edges a member out. When the others close round a member a forceful one is singling out, their acceptance lifts her Levelling through Friends at my back; this card adds no rise of its own for it.

forces.name: No blow to brace for
forces.increment_logic: When no one here can make me do anything by force or threat, I stop watching for a blow and let my slips, moods and disagreements show as they come: my felt safety to show myself rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When a member can make me comply through fear, I check his face before I move and keep my reactions masked, expecting any slip or disagreement of mine to draw his scorn or a put-down: my felt safety to show myself falls.
forces.explanation: In social primates, scratching and other self-directed behaviour appear in socially tense situations and track anxiety (Troisi 2002). Self-directed behaviour rises when the nearest neighbour is dominant (Castles, Whiten and Aureli 1999), and the authors read it as a measure of how secure the relationship is. That finding comes from rank alone, without coercion, so it bounds this card: the rank route is Low in the order, guarded (X:Status->DivsExp), and where the same nearby member fires both, play only one. The hearing route, a call made over her head before she could speak, is Heard before the call (X:Levelling->DivsExp); this card does not read it, and where one cue would fire both, play only one. In despotic species subordination carries the heaviest stress, though not in egalitarian ones, and the pattern turns on the style of the hierarchy, its stability and the social support open to subordinates (Sapolsky 2005), so set the decrement smaller where she has others to lean on. In people, on common sense, the same guardedness shows as masking: near someone who can hurt her, she hides whatever might set him off, and when the threat is absent she shows herself. Work on abusive supervision and fear-driven defensive silence (Kiewitz et al. 2016) is the closest human anchor; it has not yet been read at full text. Caution: the card runs through force or fear only. Where her Parity is low only because someone takes more than their due, or hands out and settles in favour of his own, with no threat behind it, she has no blow to brace for, so set the decrement small. Set it small too where she meets the threat with anger, backed by others and ready to confront him: she bristles rather than masks, so the cost of showing herself has not risen much.

problems.where: explanation: "self-directed behaviour such as scratching rises when a higher-ranking animal is close (Castles, Whiten and Aureli 1999, as cited by Model B)"
problems.detail: Castles, Whiten and Aureli 1999 was not checked. The checked source, Troisi 2002 (partly), supports scratching in socially tense situations as an index of anxiety, but the checker did not find the rank or proximity link.

problems.where: explanation: "In people the same bracing shows as masking, because the threat attaches to anything that shows"
problems.detail: No checked source links primate displacement activity to human self-masking. Edmondson 1999 (partly) supports only that team structures shape psychological safety; the checker did not confirm leader behaviour as an antecedent. The step is acceptable as common sense, but it should be labelled as such and not presented as following from the primate work.

logic_status.common_sense: In people, the guardedness near someone who can hurt you shows as masked reactions and checking his face, and it eases when the threat is gone. This is safe as common sense because the primate findings concern arousal near a threat, and hiding what might provoke a threat is the ordinary human response.

evidence.why: The closest human evidence (fear of an abusive supervisor driving defensive silence) is single-study or a low-weight conference meta-analysis, all cross-sectional self-report with the supervisor as coercer, and the primate sources are rank-only or narrative reviews. Two fields converge on the direction, but no replicated or bias-corrected test of coercive capacity on felt safety to show oneself was found, and the forager levelling evidence has not yet been searched.
evidence.boundary: The decrement is largest where the coercer harasses openly, the hierarchy is unstable and the member has little support from the others (Sapolsky 2005); it is small where Parity is low through over-taking or favouritism with no threat, or where the member meets the threat with backed anger. Rank without coercion runs through Status->DivsExp, and being heard runs through the Levelling->DivsExp hearing route; play only one where one cue fires both.

forces.name: Cowed hands
forces.increment_logic: When no one here can make me do anything by force or fear, take more than their due, or hand things out to their own, I take it that my effort and the others' will go into the venture itself rather than into watching one member's mood: my sense that the group can pull it off rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When a member makes me comply through fear, takes more than his due and keeps it, or hands out the jobs and the shares to his own, I take it that my effort and the others' will go into heading him off rather than into the venture: my sense that the group, as it stands, can pull off the venture sinks.
forces.explanation: Coercion and partiality pull attention and effort away from the task and towards the one who holds them; that the lost effort weakens the venture rests on common sense. That a member who takes more than his due and keeps it draws effort away from the venture also rests on common sense. Chimpanzee pairs low in tolerance do worse at a cooperative task than tolerant pairs (Melis, Hare and Tomasello 2006a), and an abusive supervision climate lowers group performance through collective efficacy (Priesemuth et al. 2014, a cross-sectional field study; extended here from supervisor to any member, so keep the step modest). No checked source ties partiality in handing out jobs and shares to the group's capability, so where Parity is low only through favouritism, set the decrement small. Accepted differences of role and rank are not low Parity, and this card reads only coercion, grabbing and partiality. Do not lean on hierarchy as a help to coordination: in a meta-analysis hierarchy had a small net negative effect on team performance and viability, carried by conflict, and the predicted coordination benefits were largely unsupported (Greer et al. 2018, as reported by the reviewer, details not checked here). Pressure from members to make everyone pull their weight is not coercion in this sense. The card reads only the capability left to the venture; whether each member still does their part is Bullies poison trust (E:Levelling->OutResp), and problems or know-how kept quiet travel through Safety. Contested boundary from emotion research: fear carries pessimistic forecasts and anger optimistic ones, through appraisals of certainty and control (Lerner and Keltner 2001, on judgements of risk to oneself, so carrying it to the venture is the model's step). A 2025 registered replication (searched only) did not support anger optimism for negative events, so the split is contested. The decrement fits a member who reads low Parity with fear, standing alone against force. Where she reads it with anger, either backed and ready to push back or because the wrong is a grab rather than a threat, her forecast for the venture may sag less; set the decrement small there, and treat that reduction as provisional.

pre_language.increment: When no one looms over the band, she sees them all intent on the chase or the forage, each putting in freely, and her feeling that it will come off rises.
pre_language.decrement: When one member looms and snaps, she sees the band glancing at him rather than at the quarry, hanging back and breaking off, and her feeling that it will come off sinks.

reactive_test.reason: Unease at seeing a cowed, distracted band falter is an inference from emotionally weighted information that needs no language.

ripple_was.increment_logic: When no one here can make me do anything by force or fear, or take more than their due, I see my effort and the others' go into the venture itself rather than into watching one member's mood: my sense that the group can pull it off rises.
ripple_was.decrement_logic: When a member makes me comply through fear, or takes more than their due and keeps it, I see my effort and the others' bend to heading him off or slacken because the gain goes to him, with problems left unraised: my sense that the group can pull off the venture sinks.
ripple_was.explanation: Coercion pulls attention and effort away from the task and towards appeasing the coercer. Members, herself included, do what heads off his anger rather than what the venture needs, and they keep problems and know-how to themselves. Studies of abusive and coercive leadership find lower collective efficacy and team performance under it. The card holds for coercion that serves the coercer's own power or comfort. Pressure from members to make everyone pull their weight is not coercion in this sense and can raise effort on the venture in the short run.

ripple_was.explanation: Coercion and partiality pull attention and effort away from the task and towards the one who holds them; that the lost effort weakens the venture rests on common sense. That a member who takes more than his due and keeps it draws effort away from the venture also rests on common sense. Chimpanzee pairs low in tolerance do worse at a cooperative task than tolerant pairs (Melis, Hare and Tomasello 2006a), and an abusive supervision climate lowers group performance through collective efficacy (Priesemuth et al. 2014, a cross-sectional field study; extended here from supervisor to any member, so keep the step modest). No checked source ties partiality in handing out jobs and shares to the group's capability; the evidence on favouritism is absent or mixed, and one press-reported study found it helped loosely structured teams, so where Parity is low only through favouritism, set the decrement small. Accepted differences of role and rank are not low Parity, and this card reads only coercion, grabbing and partiality. Do not lean on hierarchy as a help to coordination: in a meta-analysis hierarchy had a small net negative effect on team performance and viability, carried by conflict, and the predicted coordination benefits were largely unsupported (Greer et al. 2018, as reported by the reviewer, details not checked here). Pressure from members to make everyone pull their weight is not coercion in this sense. The card reads only the capability left to the venture; whether each member still does their part is Bullies poison trust (E:Levelling->OutResp), and problems or know-how kept quiet travel through Safety. Contested boundary from emotion research: fear carries pessimistic forecasts and anger optimistic ones, through appraisals of certainty and control (Lerner and Keltner 2001, on judgements of risk to oneself, so carrying it to the venture is the model's step). A 2025 registered replication (searched only) did not support anger optimism for negative events, so the split is contested. The decrement fits a member who reads low Parity with fear, standing alone against force. Where she reads it with anger, backed and ready to push back, her forecast for the venture may sag less; set the decrement small there, and treat that reduction as provisional.

problems.where: explanation: "Chimpanzee pairs in which one partner monopolises the food fail at a cooperative task that tolerant pairs solve (Melis, Hare and Tomasello 2006a)"
problems.detail: The checker rated this partly. The abstract supports only that tolerance constrains success and that low-tolerance pairs did worse; the claims that they fail outright and that monopolising is the mechanism come from text the checker did not read.

problems.where: decrement_logic: "or hands out the jobs and the shares to his own" and "guarding our shares"
problems.detail: No checked source ties favouritism, or the guarding of shares, to lower collective efficacy. Priesemuth et al. 2014 concerns an abusive climate and Melis concerns food monopoly. Brosnan and de Waal 2003, which the literature lists for unequal pay, is contested, and Ritov et al. 2024 found no evidence for inequity aversion in accept/reject paradigms, so it cannot carry this step.

problems.where: decrement_logic: "and our know-how kept to ourselves"
problems.detail: No checked source supports this, and it overlaps the Safety route, which the explanation reserves for problems kept quiet. Drop the claim.

problems.where: explanation (missing caveat)
problems.detail: The cited Halevy et al. 2011 and Ronay et al. 2012 (both partly) report that differentiated hierarchy can aid coordination on interdependent tasks. Read loosely as "flatter is better", the card would cut against them. It needs a sentence saying that accepted differences of role are not low Parity and that the card reads only coercion, grabbing and partiality.

logic_status.common_sense: Effort spent watching or heading off a coercer is effort lost to the venture, and its absence frees that effort. This is safe as a plain point about divided attention.

evidence.why: The coercion and grabbing decrement rests on common sense plus single adjacent studies (abusive climate to collective efficacy) and small captive ape experiments, with no replication or bias-corrected test of any link. The partiality strand has no checked support and possible counter-evidence, so it should be scaled down rather than carried at full weight.
evidence.boundary: Keep the partiality decrement small: evidence on favouritism and reward dispersion is absent or mixed, and one study known only from a press report found leader favouritism helped loosely structured teams. Accepted role and rank differences and peer pressure to pull one's weight are not low Parity. The fear versus anger split (anger leaves forecasts less pessimistic) is contested, since the 2025 registered replication of Lerner and Keltner did not support anger optimism for negative events.

forces.name: Bullies poison trust
forces.increment_logic: When no one here can make me do anything by force or fear, I take it that the others carry their parts for the work's sake rather than for one member's eye, and will keep at them whoever is watching, so I check up on them less: my confidence that they will do their part rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When a member here makes me comply through fear, I take it that the others work to please him rather than to finish their parts, and will cover themselves and let tasks drop once his eye moves on, so I start checking up on their work: my confidence that they will do their part falls.
forces.explanation: Coercion distorts how others behave: they appease, hide, protect themselves and work to the coercer's eye, and she expects all of this and reads it as unreliable. The lines carry her inference from the coercion; parts she actually sees dropped or carried move Dependability directly and are not played on this card. The central step is that compliance won by fear holds only while the one who wields it is watching, so that parts are done for his eye and dropped when it moves on, while compliance given to a respected leader is kept up whoever is watching once she is gone. It has a direct human test: 21-month-olds expected others to keep obeying a leader after she had left, but held no such expectation for a bully (Margoni, Baillargeon and Surian 2018), and a control showed the effect was not mere likeability. That is a reading of what others will do once the coercer's eye moves on, the card's own step; it is a single lab study with infants, so it counts as support until replicated. Kelman's account of compliance under surveillance gives the theory (Kelman 1958; French and Raven 1959), which awaits checking. The finding that abused subordinates hold back discretionary effort and turn to deviance (Zellars, Tepper and Duffy 2002; Mitchell and Ambrose 2007) also awaits checking; the card extends it from supervisor to any member. Hierarchy raises conflict-enabling states in teams (Greer et al. 2018), which is loose support for the decrement only. The decrement holds for coercion she reads as self-serving, a bully's fear; enforcement she sees as fair or legitimate leaves her reading of the others' dependability intact, as the leader condition in Margoni et al. shows and by analogy with the contrast between selfish and reserved sanctions in a trust game (Fehr and Rockenbach 2003, which measured trustees' returns rather than reliability at shared work), so set it nil there. Without coercion this distortion is gone and the others' carrying-through shows plainly, but shirking can persist for other reasons, so keep the increment small or nil. The card runs on force or fear only; where Parity is low only because someone grabs or hands out to their own, set it nil. The card does not scale by a close tie.

pre_language.increment: When no one bullies, she watches the others keep at their tasks and leaves them to it without hovering: her sense that they will do their part rises.
pre_language.decrement: When a bully dominates, she sees the others cringe, scramble for favour and abandon tasks as he passes, and she hovers over what they do: her sense that they will do their part falls.

reactive_test.reason: Wariness of others seen cringing and dropping tasks is an inference from emotionally weighted information, not a plan worked out in thought.

forces.framework: Surveillance-bound compliance under coercive power; withheld effort under abusive supervision (both pending checks); hierarchy and team conflict (Greer et al. 2018).

sources.source: Mayer, Davis & Schoorman, 1995, An integrative model of organizational trust
sources.claim: Trust rests on perceived ability, benevolence and integrity, each of which domination can obscure.

sources.source: Greer, de Jong, Schouten & Dannals, 2018, Why and when hierarchy impacts team effectiveness
sources.claim: Hierarchy raises conflict-enabling states in teams, which erode members' reliance on one another.

timing.typical: within the working session, once his eye has moved on
timing.why: The decrement needs her to see parts done for his eye and then dropped when he looks away, so it waits on at least one shift of his attention; the increment builds as parts are carried through in plain view.

era.why: Behaviour that holds only under a dominant's watch, and slackening once he turns away, has primate analogues; the card's word-keeping wording is a modern gloss on carrying through a part.

forces.subtitle: Bullying makes others less dependable

When a member rules by fear, I expect others to work for his eye and let tasks drop, so I check up and my confidence falls.

problems.where: explanation: "Compliance won by threat holds only while the one who wields the threat can watch (Kelman 1958; French and Raven 1959)"
problems.detail: Neither Kelman 1958 nor French and Raven 1959 was checked.

problems.where: explanation: "Under abusive leaders, subordinates also hold back discretionary effort and turn to quiet deviance (Zellars, Tepper and Duffy 2002; Mitchell and Ambrose 2007)"
problems.detail: Neither source was checked. The checked sources (Mayer et al. 1995, partly; Greer et al. 2018, partly) do not show that coercion lowers perceived dependability. The checker marks the domination-obscures-trust inference and the reliance gloss as the model's own.

problems.where: increment_logic: "I see the others do their parts in the open rather than for show, and I stop expecting them to shirk or go back on their word"
problems.detail: Removing coercion removes one distortion. It does not stop shirking, since free riding can thrive without a bully. The increment should claim only that the distortion is gone.

problems.where: framework: "Integrative model of trust (ability, integrity); hierarchy and conflict"
problems.detail: The explanation's mechanism is surveillance-bound compliance and withheld effort under coercion. The framework names neither, and Mayer et al.'s ability component belongs to skill (Esteem), not to Dependability.

logic_status.common_sense: People who are under threat work to the coercer's eye, cover themselves and let tasks drop once he is not watching, and an observer reads this as unreliability. This is safe as common sense about behaviour under surveillance, with the citations held until they are checked.

evidence.why: Large but cross-sectional organisational meta-analyses show abused members withhold effort, and one small, contested lab series shows sanctioning systems lower trust in fellow members, but no study measures a third party's read of the others' dependability under a coercer. None of the sources is yet verified at source, so none is added as load-bearing; Mulder et al. 2006 and Mackey et al. 2017 should be read and added if they hold.
evidence.boundary: The decrement holds for coercion read as self-serving; enforcement the group sees as fair or legitimate need not lower confidence in the others (Fehr and Rockenbach's own fair-sanction contrast, once checked). The increment is small or nil, since shirking has many causes besides fear of a coercer.

forces.name: No grabber, open hands
forces.increment_logic: When no one here can take what they like from me by force or threat, and no one takes more than their due and keeps it, I can share without fear that it will be seized on the way or turned into leverage over me, and I expect what I put in to go where it is needed and come back round: my reading that help comes back rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When a member can make me hand over what I have through fear, or helps himself to more than his due and gets away with it, I take it that what I put in will go to him as tribute rather than back round the group, and that the others will keep what they have out of his reach, so I expect little back from anyone: my reading that help comes back falls.
forces.explanation: Return from the group fares best where no one can seize what is shared or turn a gift into leverage. Immediate-return foragers act to prevent accumulation and domination (Woodburn 1982), and the rank and file check would-be dominants together (Boehm 1993). Demand and tolerated taking are one part of forager sharing (Peterson 1993; Blurton Jones 1984), though Hadza rankings of sharing motives suggest they are not its main driver (source not named here; awaiting check). Claims pressed among equals on whoever has a surplus are part of the return (Reciprocity) and leave Parity high; only taking beyond the group's ordinary share-out that is made to stick, most often backed by force or threat, counts as seizure here. Hiding food is also the ordinary forager answer to demand pressure among equals, with no coercer present (Peterson 1993), so only concealment from the coercer or grabber counts on this card; ordinary hiding from demand is no evidence of low Parity and does not fire it. The lines carry her expectation drawn from the coercion or grabbing; hiding or giving she actually sees moves Reciprocity directly and is not played here, and the others' answer to the grabber belongs to the interaction card of the same name (I:Levelling->Reciprocity). Sanctions run by the group or seen as fair do not lower the reading either, since peer sanctioning institutions are reported to aid cooperation in a multilab replication (source not named here; awaiting check); only seizure or threat by a coercer or an unchecked grabber counts. One strand of the decrement has experimental support: in a trust game, trustees returned less to investors who used a threat of fines than to those who held it in reserve, and sanctions read as selfish or greedy all but destroyed altruistic cooperation (Fehr and Rockenbach 2003, checked). That shows partners holding back from the one who threatens, which fits her expecting the others to keep what they have out of his reach. The effect depends on gaps in endowment (Calabuig et al. 2016) and comes from pairs of strangers, so carrying it to the expected return from a whole group is an extension. The step that giving becomes tribute rather than going back round the group rests on common sense, with the trust game as a pairwise analogue: under a coercer or a grabber who gets away with it, she expects the return from the group to dry up.

pre_language.increment: When no one in the band looms or snatches, she gives from her pile and finds others giving from theirs when she is short, and her sense that what she gives comes back rises.
pre_language.decrement: When one member snatches and threatens, what she holds out is taken and nothing comes back, the others hunch over their food, and her sense that giving brings any return sinks.

reactive_test.reason: Expecting nothing back after gifts are snatched and food is hidden is an inference from emotionally weighted information. Food-sharing primates show it.

forces.framework: Assertive egalitarianism and demand sharing in immediate-return foragers

sources.source: Woodburn, 1982, Egalitarian societies (Man)
sources.claim: Immediate-return foragers actively prevent accumulation and domination, which keeps sharing general and untallied.

sources.source: Peterson, 1993, Demand sharing: reciprocity and the pressure for generosity among foragers (American Anthropologist)
sources.claim: Much forager sharing happens on demand, an assertive practice among equals that constitutes egalitarian relations.

sources.source: Boehm, 1993, Egalitarian behavior and reverse dominance hierarchy (Current Anthropology)
sources.claim: The rank and file collectively suppress would-be dominants, the precondition for egalitarian sharing.

sources.claim: Sharing is sustained by pressure on those holding a surplus.

edits_log: 5 Nov 2026: Ben approved, 5 Nov 2026, 11.22 am (comparative psychologist's critique, docs/v3/sc-critique/): Ripple from the Levelling widening; demand sharing and inequity aversion both support it.

Ripple round 3, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Check (5), explanation only; the lines and type pass. The explanation leans on forager literature without citing it. Its sign of a coercer is also weak: foragers hide surpluses from ordinary demand sharing too (Peterson 1993), so hidden goods do not by themselves show coercion. Add the sources and mark the claim about life under a coercer as common sense.

Ripple round 4, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The increment line restates Reciprocity's top anchor ('I count on the return without a second thought') as if the mere absence of a coercer were enough for full confidence in the return. The explanation treats Levelling as a necessary condition ('survives only where no one can seize'), so a high source should only take away a block on the return. The line also gives no mechanism, while the decrement line does. Decrement line, type, boundaries and citations (Woodburn 1982; Boehm 1993; Peterson 1993) pass. Demand sharing meets what is asked for, which fits Reciprocity's 'what you ask for is met' limb.

Ripple round 5, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Decrement line: 'what I give goes to him as tribute' describes extraction under fear, which is Levelling's ground; Reciprocity reads the return on help, and the Reciprocity definition excludes taking more than one's due. The target effect should be help given and not returned, along with the others hiding what they have, so that asks go unmet. Separately, 'I expect nothing back from anyone' is the 1 anchor. One play should lower the reading, not floor it. ripple_was.explanation: Return from the group fares best where no one can seize what is shared or turn a gift into leverage. Immediate-return foragers act to prevent accumulation and domination (Woodburn 1982), and the rank and file check would-be dominants together (Boehm 1993). Demand and tolerated taking are one part of forager sharing (Peterson 1993; Blurton Jones 1984), though Hadza rankings of sharing motives suggest they are not its main driver. Claims pressed among equals on whoever has a surplus are part of the return (Reciprocity) and leave Parity high; only taking beyond the group's ordinary share-out that is made to stick, most often backed by force or threat, counts as seizure here. Hiding food is also the ordinary forager answer to demand pressure among equals, with no coercer present (Peterson 1993), so only concealment from the coercer or grabber counts on this card; ordinary hiding from demand is no evidence of low Parity and does not fire it. Sanctions run by the group or seen as fair do not lower the reading either, since peer sanctioning institutions aid cooperation in a multilab replication; only seizure or threat by a coercer or an unchecked grabber counts. One strand of the decrement has experimental support: in a trust game, trustees returned less to investors who used a threat of fines than to those who held it in reserve, and sanctions read as selfish or greedy all but destroyed altruistic cooperation (Fehr and Rockenbach 2003, checked). That shows partners holding back from the one who threatens, which fits the others keeping what they have out of his reach. The effect depends on gaps in endowment (Calabuig et al. 2016) and comes from pairs of strangers, so carrying it to the expected return from a whole group is an extension. The step that giving becomes tribute rather than going back round the group rests on common sense, with the trust game as a pairwise analogue: under a coercer or a grabber who gets away with it, she expects the return from the group to dry up.

problems.where: explanation: "in a trust game, an investor who used a threat of fines got less back than one who held it in reserve (Fehr and Rockenbach 2003)"
problems.detail: Fehr and Rockenbach 2003 was not checked.

problems.where: explanation: "Return from the group survives only where no one can seize what is shared or turn a gift into leverage."
problems.detail: "Only" claims a necessary condition that no checked source shows. Boehm 1993 (partly) supports rank-and-file suppression of dominants, but the checker did not find that this is the precondition for sharing.

problems.where: increment_logic: "nothing I share is seized on the way"; explanation's citation of Peterson 1993
problems.detail: Peterson (supports) shows forager sharing runs largely on demand, which is assertive claiming among equals (related to tolerated theft). Without a caveat, the card's line between seizing and sharing blurs: demand among equals counts as high Parity, and only a dominant's taking counts as seizure.

problems.where: explanation: "mocking, shunning or leaving anyone who hoards or bosses (Woodburn 1982; Boehm 1993)"
problems.detail: Both sources are rated partly. Prevention of accumulation and domination is supported, but the specific list of sanctions was not confirmed in text that could be read.

logic_status.common_sense: Under a coercer, giving becomes tribute, the others keep what they have out of his reach, and return from the group dries up. The card already labels this as common sense, and it is safe because it only restates what seizure means for return.

evidence.why: Two fields point the same way (sanctions read as greedy cut cooperation; foragers check dominants and accumulators to keep sharing general), but the trust-game strand is single-lab, pairwise and unreplicated and the forager strand is ethnographic and contested in its typology. No source tests a member's expected return from the group with a coercer or grabber present, which remains a gap.
evidence.boundary: Sanctions the group reads as fair, and peer-run sanctioning of free riders (Lo Iacono et al. 2023 multilab replication of Gurerk et al.), do not lower the reading; only seizure or threat by one member does. Demand claims among equals, and hiding food from that pressure, leave Parity high. Forager levelling varies with ecology, and Hadza rank tolerated theft and demand low as sharing motives, so demand sharing should not be leaned on as the mechanism.

forces.name: Don’t Dis Me Bro
forces.increment_logic: When the others carry through what they take on and keep their word, so that nothing of theirs is left for me to pick up, I read it as regard for me, as someone they would not leave in the lurch: my sense that they want me among them rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When the others drop what they take on or go back on their word and leave me to pick up their parts, I read it as not counting with them, as someone they are content to leave in the lurch: my sense that they want me among them falls.
forces.explanation: People read how much others value them from how others treat them, and being let down or betrayed is among the plainest signs of low relational value (Leary, Springer, Negel, Ansell and Evans 1998, not replicated; Leary 2001). Dependability reads whether the others carry through what they take on and keep their word. Where their parts and promises touch her, she reads reliability as regard and a dropped part that lands on her as disregard. The step from that felt regard or devaluation to her reading of whether they want her among them is common sense, since Belonging is read from how they treat her. Lab effects of rejection on mood and self-esteem are weaker than the sociometer account implies (Blackhart et al. 2009, a meta-analysis that measured mood and self-esteem, not felt acceptance). A part let drop moves Dependability further than one carried through, and the same asymmetry holds here, so keep the increment small and the decrement modest, and set the card nil where the parts carried or dropped do not touch her. Her own fondness for them is a separate route (Counted on, cared for). Others answering her trust or distrust in kind runs through their response and belongs to the scene.

pre_language.increment: When she leaves others to their tasks without hovering, they warm to her and seek her company.
pre_language.decrement: When she hovers over their work and snatches it back to redo it, they bristle, cool towards her and keep away.

reactive_test.reason: She feels wanted or unwanted by reading how the others treat her. That is an emotional reaction to their warmth or coolness.
