ripple_was.decrement_logic: When I check up on, chase and redo others' work, they read it as distrust and give less back to me: my sense that they want me among them falls.
ripple_was.explanation: Trust tends to be answered in kind. In dyads working together over time, each side's perceived trustworthiness and cooperation fed the other's in a spiral (Ferrin, Bligh and Kohles 2008), though reviews of dyadic trust warn that it is not always mutual (Korsgaard, Brower and Lester 2015). A member who leaves work in others' hands shows trust they can see, and they answer with trust and cooperation of their own. Control read as distrust lowers the controlled party's effort (Falk and Kosfeld 2006), real but usually small on replication (Ziegelmeyer, Schmelz and Ploner 2012). Neither source measures liking or inclusion. The step from how readily they work with her to her Belonging is common sense: being cooperated with is the plainest sign of being wanted. Keep the card small, and set the decrement smaller still where checking is the group's custom rather than her own choice.

ripple_was.increment_logic: When the others carry through what they take on and keep their word, so that nothing of theirs is left for me to pick up, I read it as regard for me, as someone they would not leave in the lurch: my sense that they want me among them rises a little.
ripple_was.decrement_logic: When the others drop what they take on or go back on their word and leave me to pick up their parts, I read it as not counting with them, as someone they are content to leave in the lurch: my sense that they want me among them falls.
ripple_was.explanation: People read how much others value them from how others treat them, and being let down or betrayed is among the plainest signs of low relational value (Leary, Springer, Negel, Ansell and Evans 1998; Leary 2001). Dependability reads whether the others carry through what they take on and keep their word. Where their parts and promises touch her, she reads reliability as regard and a dropped part that lands on her as disregard. The step from that felt regard or devaluation to her reading of whether they want her among them is common sense, since Belonging is read from how they treat her. A part let drop moves Dependability further than one carried through, and the same asymmetry holds here, so keep the increment small and the decrement modest, and set the card nil where the parts carried or dropped do not touch her. Her own fondness for them is a separate route (Counted on, cared for). The earlier mechanism, others answering her trust or distrust in kind (Ferrin, Bligh and Kohles 2008; Falk and Kosfeld 2006), runs through their response and belongs to the scene.

timing.why: The others must notice her checking up or her trust, respond with warmth or coolness, and she must read that response, so it takes a few exchanges.

era.why: Hovering over and redoing another's work is visible conduct, and bristling or drawing someone in are non-verbal responses; the sociometer reading of warmth predates language.

forces.summary: When the others carry through what they take on and keep their word, so that nothing is left for her to pick up, she reads it as regard for her and feels they want her among them. When they drop their parts and leave her to pick them up, she reads it as not counting with them. The card plays only where those parts touch her.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 'reviews of dyadic trust find it often, though not always, mutual (Korsgaard, Brower and Lester 2015)'
problems.detail: The checker rated Korsgaard et al. partly: the review distinguishes reciprocal, mutual and asymmetric trust and is critical of the evidence, and a citing paper reports little evidence for mutual trust. Nothing checked shows trust is 'often' mutual. The review supports only that trust is not always mutual.

problems.where: increment_logic 'they take it as a mark of trust and draw me in'; decrement_logic 'they bristle at the slight and keep me at a distance'; explanation 'they warm to her ... and they cool'
problems.detail: Ferrin et al. 2008 (partly) show trustworthiness and cooperation spiralling in dyads; Falk and Kosfeld 2006 (supports, small on replication) show control read as distrust lowers effort. Neither shows warmth, liking, drawing in or keeping at a distance. The explanation itself concedes Falk and Kosfeld do not show how far liking cools. The checked literature supports the others answering trust with trust and cooperation, and distrust with less effort; the lines should say that, with the step to Belonging left as the common-sense reading.

logic_status.common_sense: That she reads her acceptance from how readily the others work with her is common sense (and the ordinary sociometer idea, which is not cited or checked here); it is safe as a small step because being cooperated with is the plainest everyday sign of being wanted. Setting the decrement smaller where checking is the group's custom is common sense: a custom is not read as a personal slight.

evidence.why: Being let down is read as devaluation only on recall-based evidence (Leary et al. 1998), and the replicated exclusion literature tests ostracism, a neighbouring construct, rather than peers dropping their parts. The search record's reading of Blackhart et al. as fitting the small increment is the wrong way round, because their asymmetry favours acceptance moving felt worth more than rejection; this is a contest to note, not a reversal of direction.
evidence.boundary: Nil where the dropped parts do not touch the member. The decrement is expected to outweigh the increment, but this asymmetry is contested: Blackhart et al. 2009 found acceptance raised self-esteem while rejection left it no lower than neutral controls, which runs the other way for self-esteem, though Cyberball work (Hartgerink et al. 2015) shows exclusion strongly threatens the need to belong.

forces.name: Nobody hunting for cover
forces.increment_logic: When I can leave any part of the work with any of them and count on them to carry it through and keep their word, no blame is in the air over dropped parts; I stop guarding myself among them and let slips, moods and needs show as they come, expecting no one to pounce on them, laugh at them or turn away: my felt safety to show myself rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When the others drop what they take on, blame is in the air over the dropped parts, and I take it that a slip shown here will draw a sharp word or a sneer, so I mask my slips and keep my needs out of sight: my felt safety to show myself falls.
forces.explanation: Trust is the willingness to be vulnerable to others' actions (Mayer, Davis and Schoorman 1995), and team psychological safety is the shared belief that interpersonal risk is tolerated (Edmondson 1999); on common sense, felt reliance on the members is one ground of that belief. In 191 teams cognition-based trust fed affect-based trust and through it team psychological safety (Schaubroeck, Lam and Peng 2011, as reported by the reviewer and not checked here). That supported path is mediated, running from perceived reliability through affect-based trust to felt safety, and it concerns trust in the leader; the card's peer-level version, inside one member's reading, is an extension, so keep the increment moderate. Dependability reads the integrity limb, carrying parts through and keeping one's word; ability is Team Confidence's ground, and whether a slip would be turned against her is Safety's own ground. The card carries only the spill from reliability at work to Safety. Where her reliance rests mainly on rules or on knowing that a dropped part gets pulled up by the group, a pulling-up climate stays in the air, so keep the increment small. Blame contagion supports the first half of the decrement: people who watch someone blame another are more likely to blame others for their own unrelated failures (Fast and Tiedens 2010, a laboratory effect), so where parts are dropped blame is in the air. That study shows blame spreading; the further step, that she then expects a shown slip to draw a sharp word or a sneer and masks her slips, is common sense with no direct source. Keep the decrement moderate. Distinct from No blow to brace for (E:Levelling->DivsExp, fear of one coercer) and Stakes tighten or loosen (E:GrpProsp->DivsExp, the stakes of the venture).

pre_language.increment: When those around her do their share, she is loose and unguarded under their eyes when she fumbles.
pre_language.decrement: When those around her slack off, she braces when she fumbles, expecting their glares and snarls to turn on her.

reactive_test.reason: Bracing for blame among members who slack is an inference from emotionally weighted information. It needs no worked-out reasoning.

forces.framework: Integrative model of trust (Mayer et al. 1995); psychological safety (Edmondson 1999); cognition- to affect-based trust (Schaubroeck et al. 2011); blame contagion (Fast and Tiedens 2010).

problems.where: explanation, sentence 'In a group where parts are dropped, a member therefore expects her own visible slips to become someone's cover, and she masks them.'
problems.detail: Fast and Tiedens 2010 (supports) show that observing blame makes people blame others for their own unrelated failures. They do not show that dropped parts raise blame, nor that members anticipate being scapegoated and mask their slips. 'Therefore' presents the step as following from the source; it rests on common sense about shirkers shifting blame, with blame contagion only suggesting the habit spreads once started.

logic_status.common_sense: That members who drop their parts look to shift the blame for the resulting failures onto others is common sense, and fits the well-known self-serving attribution pattern (not cited or checked here). That she expects her slips to be used as cover and so masks them is common sense, flagged in the explanation as a proposal. That a group where parts are carried has less failure to account for, and so less blame about, is common sense.

evidence.why: Psychological safety surveys are direct evidence of the felt reading, but their link to peer dependability is known only from summaries of a meta-analysis whose effect size, level and bias handling are unconfirmed, and the one mediated test concerns trust in the leader. The blame strand rests on one unreplicated lab study of a neighbouring effect, and no source here is yet verified at source, so none is added as load-bearing.
evidence.boundary: The supported part is mediated: perceived reliability feeds affect-based trust, which feeds felt safety (Schaubroeck et al. 2011, for trust in the leader); the peer-level version is an extension. The increment is moderate and smaller where reliance rests on rules or on the group pulling members up. Psychological safety measures are heterogeneous (Liu et al. 2024 preprint), so no correlate should be read firmly.

forces.name: Quality Street
forces.increment_logic: When I feel the others will carry through what they take on, I count every member's skill as put to work on the venture, with none of our effort lost to chasing or redoing parts: my confidence that the group, as it stands, can pull it off rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I expect the others to shirk, cut corners or go back on their word, I count on skill that will sit idle and on effort lost to chasing and redoing their parts, so the capability left for the venture shrinks: my confidence that the group, as it stands, can pull it off falls.
forces.explanation: A joint venture depends on each part being carried through as well as on skill, so felt reliability feeds the sense of what the group, as it stands, can do. Intrateam trust is positively related to team performance across 112 studies (rho about .30), holding after past performance is controlled, and more so where tasks are interdependent (De Jong, Dirks and Gillespie 2016); team efficacy itself tracks performance more closely under high interdependence (Gully et al. 2002). The data are correlational and her forecast is a reading, so keep the card moderate, and smaller in loosely coupled groups where members can finish their work alone.

pre_language.increment: When those around her keep at their tasks and finish what they start, she settles into the shared venture confident it will come off.
pre_language.decrement: When those around her drift off and leave tasks half done, she grows uneasy about the shared venture, expecting it to fail.

reactive_test.reason: Confidence or unease about a joint venture, read from whether others keep at their parts, is an inference from emotionally weighted information.

forces.decrement_logic: When what I give goes unreturned and my needs go unmet, I have little to lose with them; after a clash I stay away and let it stand, expecting no one to draw me back, and I read their gatherings as closed to me: my Belonging falls.
forces.explanation: The lines rest on reconciliation, the better evidenced route. Primates reconcile most with partners whose relationship is valuable to them, and raising partner value experimentally raises reconciliation (Cords and Thurnheer 1993; Aureli, Cords and van Schaik 2002); friendly reunions after a clash lower the risk of renewed attack (Aureli and van Schaik 1991). That valuable relationships pattern is consistent across primates, though not uniform across species and sexes, and the evidence is dyadic. In the egalitarian face Reciprocity is her felt reading of what the group as a whole returns to her, so the step from repair with partners to her reading the whole circle as open to her is an untested extension. Scale the card to how many members are her valued partners: large in a small band where most are, small in a larger group where only one or two are. The repair route also depends on how secure her ties feel: a secure tie may need little repair, so the card moves less there. Reconciliation is commoner in tolerant than in despotic macaque species (Thierry 2000, not checked here), so the card fits deck E. Help that comes back also produces positive feeling attached to the group (Lawler 2001, affect theory of social exchange), and gratitude binds the one helped closer to the helper (Algoe 2012); those raise her fondness for them, which E:Reciprocity->Warmth carries, so they do not drive this card. On the reviewer's reading (not checked here), shared identity moderates how exchange turns into attachment, and in forager settings need met may count for more than strict return; play the card by need met where the group shares that way. The card moves her reading through her own readiness to make up or stay away; how the others actually treat her when she comes back belongs to the scene (rulebook 8.5).

pre_language.increment: When what she shares comes back and she is fed and groomed in need, she is drawn closer to the others and they to her: her feeling of being welcome among them rises.
pre_language.decrement: When she gives and nothing comes back, and she is passed over in need, she drifts to the edge of their company: her feeling of being welcome among them falls.

reactive_test.reason: Feeling welcome or passed over according to whether help comes back is an emotional reaction to how the others treat her.

forces.framework: Reconciliation with valuable partners (Cords and Thurnheer 1993; Aureli, Cords and van Schaik 2002); post-conflict reunions (Aureli and van Schaik 1991); dominance-style variation in reconciliation (Thierry 2000).

sources.source: Lawler, 2001, An affect theory of social exchange
sources.claim: Exchange generates global positive feelings that people attribute to the relation or group, building cohesion and solidarity.

sources.source: Molm, Collett & Schaefer, 2007, Building solidarity through generalized exchange: A theory of reciprocity
sources.claim: Experiments show generalised exchange produces more solidarity than reciprocal direct exchange, which beats negotiated exchange.

sources.source: Algoe, 2012, Find, remind, and bind: The functions of gratitude in everyday relationships
sources.claim: Gratitude for responsive help binds recipients closer to helpers.

sources.source: Aureli, F., Cords, M., van Schaik, C., 2002, Animal Behaviour 64: 325-343
sources.claim: Reunions are predicted especially where aggression disrupts valuable relationships; reconciliation reduces renewed aggression and post-conflict stress.

sources.source: Cords, M., Thurnheer, S., 1993, Reconciliation with valuable partners by long-tailed macaques, Ethology 93: 315-325
sources.claim: Raising partner value experimentally raised reconciliation rates.

timing.typical: 5 to 15 minutes after a clash
timing.why: The route runs through reconciliation or its absence, which in primates and people mostly happens within minutes of the conflict, and she reads her acceptance from whether the circle closes round her again.

era.why: Reconciliation weighted by relationship value, renewed tolerance and spreading coolness are shown in non-human primates.

Help that comes back also produces positive feeling attached to the group (Lawler 2001, affect theory of social exchange), and gratitude binds the one helped closer to the helper (Algoe 2012); those raise her fondness for them, which E:Reciprocity->Warmth carries, so they do not drive this card. Her Belonging moves with how they treat her when she comes back.

forces.subtitle: Help that returns binds us together
forces.summary: When what she gives comes back and her needs are met, she counts the others as people she cannot do without, goes back to make up after a clash, and feels the circle open to her, so Belonging rises. When help goes unreturned and needs go unmet, she stays away after a clash and reads their gatherings as closed to her.

problems.where: decrement_logic 'the coolness spreads to those around us, and gatherings form without me'
problems.detail: No cited or checked source shows an unmended clash spreading coolness to third parties or leading to exclusion from gatherings. The reconciliation evidence is dyadic, and the explanation says so. Drop the third-party spread.

problems.where: explanation, 'reconciliation restores tolerance and lowers renewed aggression ... (Cords and Thurnheer 1993; Aureli, Cords and van Schaik 2002)'
problems.detail: The checker rated Aureli, Cords and van Schaik 2002 partly: valuable-relationship prediction confirmed, reduced renewed aggression not seen in that paper. Cords and Thurnheer support only that raised partner value raises reconciliation. 'Restores tolerance' is checked nowhere. Reduced renewed attack is supported by Aureli and van Schaik 1991 (supports, checked under E:Reciprocity->DivsExp); cite that and drop 'restores tolerance'.

problems.where: explanation, 'gratitude draws the one helped closer to the helper (Algoe, Haidt and Gable 2008)'
problems.detail: The 2008 paper was not checked; the checked source is Algoe 2012 (partly). Cite Algoe 2012.

problems.where: framework
problems.detail: The framework names affect theory of social exchange, reciprocity and solidarity, and find-remind-and-bind, which the explanation says do not drive this card, and omits reconciliation with valuable partners, which it says does.

logic_status.common_sense: The extension from dyadic reconciliation to the group closing round her again is common sense once each member counts as worth mending with; the explanation flags it as an extension. That they take her back when she comes to make it up is common sense in a group whose members are returning her help, since that return shows they value her.

evidence.why: Step (a), relationship value raising repair, has support across primatology, social psychology and small-group sociology, but no source is replicated or bias-corrected and the primate findings are patchy by species and sex. No test of the step from dyadic repair to the member's felt Belonging was found, so the central step stays adjacent and partly common sense.
evidence.boundary: The support is dyadic: valued partners are more likely to reconcile (primates) and to forgive (humans), so the rise should scale with how many members she counts as valued partners. Where a tie is already secure, less repair may be needed (relationship security account, bonobos). Shared identity moderates how exchange turns into attachment (Buchan et al. 2002). In forager settings, need met may count for more than strict return (Agta).

forces.name: Here to Help
forces.increment_logic: When what I put in comes back and what I need is met, I take it that a need or a slip shown here will draw no put-down or rebuff, and that a clash will soon be made up; I let my moods, needs and slips show: my felt safety to show myself rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When what I give goes into a hole and my needs go unmet, I take it that a need or a slip shown here will draw a put-down or a turned back, and that a clash will stay unmended; I mask what I need and brace for a put-down: my felt safety to show myself falls.
forces.explanation: Primary route: post-conflict repair, drawn by analogy from primate work. Primate victims of aggression show more self-scratching and run a higher risk of renewed attack, and in that study friendly reunions reduced both (Aureli and van Schaik 1991); reunions happen most where the relationship is valuable (Cords and Thurnheer 1993; Aureli, Cords and van Schaik 2002). Evidence that reconciliation lowers anxiety is mixed across primate studies (capuchin, tolerant-species and olive baboon work, as reported by the reviewer and not checked here). A member whose help comes back has partners she makes up with, so a clash leaves her braced only briefly. That evidence is dyadic and holds for valued partners; scale as for E:Reciprocity->Belonging, by how many members are her valued partners. Secondary route: rewarding co-worker relations go with higher felt psychological safety (May, Gilson and Harter 2004), and high-quality relationships, measured as emotional carrying capacity, tensility and connectivity, predicted later safety (Carmeli, Brueller and Dutton 2009); both as reported by the reviewer, not checked here. Those studies test broad relationship quality and leave return of help untested, and leadership and team design are usually the stronger predictors of safety, so keep the rise at a little. Help that comes back is the everyday evidence, on common sense, that a shown need will be answered and not punished. The card takes only being braced for a put-down, since fear of force is Parity's ground (Helpers stand together, E:Reciprocity->Levelling). Overlaps E:Reciprocity->Belonging plus E:Belonging->DivsExp (Making Fetch Happen), so play this card small where both fire.

pre_language.decrement: When her need goes unmet and nothing she shared comes back, she feels unprotected, masks her moods and hides even a plain want, braced to be snapped at or turned from.

timing.typical: 2 to 10 minutes after a clash
timing.why: Post-conflict self-scratching and watchfulness fade within minutes of a friendly reunion, or persist where no reunion comes.

era.why: Post-conflict anxiety, its displacement behaviours and their relief by reunion are documented in primates.

forces.subtitle: Returned help makes showing needs safe
forces.summary: When help a member gives comes back and her needs are met, she feels safer showing her moods, needs and slips, expecting no put-down and a quick making-up after a clash. When help is not returned, she masks what she needs and braces. The evidence is indirect and the rise is small, and the card takes only being braced for a put-down.

logic_status.common_sense: The extension from dyadic reconciliation to ties with any member of a group that returns her help, flagged as an extension in the explanation. The human counterpart of post-conflict anxiety: being on edge around someone one has clashed with, fidgeting and keeping moods and disagreements out of sight while braced for a put-down, is ordinary experience; the card takes care to claim only this milder reading and leaves fear of force to Parity. Safe because the card is played small and its double route through Belonging is named.

forces.framework: Post-conflict anxiety and reconciliation (primary); co-worker support and high-quality relationships with psychological safety (secondary, pending check).

evidence.why: Two-wave and team surveys link relationship quality to psychological safety, and those member surveys are direct evidence of the felt reading, but none is replicated and none tests return of help or met needs specifically. The primate evidence is analogous and mixed, and the Frazier et al. 2017 meta-analysis was not read for a relationship effect or a bias correction.
evidence.boundary: The workplace evidence concerns broad relationship quality, and leadership, team design and climate usually predict psychological safety more strongly than co-worker relations, so the effect of returned help should stay small. The primate route (reconciliation easing post-conflict anxiety) is dyadic, depends on valued partners and is mixed across species.

forces.name: Mucking in Together
forces.increment_logic: When what I put in comes back and whoever needs help gets it, I feel the group covers its own weak spots, and my confidence that it can pull off the venture we have set ourselves rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When what I give goes into a hole and need goes unmet while others could see it, I feel those who struggle will be left to fall short, and my confidence that the group can pull off the venture falls.
forces.explanation: Where help flows to whoever needs it, members' gaps are covered by others, so the group can do more than its weakest hands alone. Backup is a core teamwork process (Marks, Mathieu and Zaccaro 2001; Porter et al. 2003), and helping goes with the quantity and quality of work-group output (Podsakoff, Ahearne and MacKenzie 1997). Those studies concern help with the work itself; Reciprocity reads the return on her own help and need, so carrying them to this card is an extension, and the card fires only where the help she sees given or withheld bears on the venture. The member-level steps are common sense: that she reads the help she sees given and returned as the group covering its weak spots, that need left unmet in plain view tells her the weak spots will stay open, and that either reading moves her felt confidence in the venture. The effect belongs to help matched to need that does not breed dependency or free riding. Backing up has costs, since helpers can neglect their own tasks and those helped can ease off later (Barnes et al. 2008), so keep the rise moderate, and smaller where the help she sees is heavy or goes to members who lean on it.

pre_language.increment: When the band shares food and help with whoever falls short, she feels them strong together, and goes to the shared hunt sure of the kill.
pre_language.decrement: When those who have hide it and the weak are left to struggle, she feels the band falling short, and goes to the shared hunt expecting it to fail.

reactive_test.reason: This is an inference from emotionally weighted information (need met or ignored) to a felt confidence or doubt about the shared venture. No plan is worked out.

logic_status.common_sense: That where help reaches whoever needs it, members' gaps are covered and the group can do more than its weakest hands, and that need left unmet in plain view leads her to expect weak spots to stay open, are common sense.

forces.framework: Backup behaviour as a teamwork process; helping and work-group performance; costs of backing up (all pending check).

evidence.why: Meta-analyses tie group-level helping to unit output and team confidence to performance, but they test behaviour and outcomes, not a member's reading of help flow changing her confidence, and bias correction was not confirmed. The step from perceived reciprocity to Team Confidence rests on common sense, and the forager insurance account is contested.
evidence.boundary: The effect applies to help that matches need and leaves the recipient able to do her own part. Heavy backing up costs the giver her own work and leads recipients to ease off (Barnes et al. 2008), and dependent helping hinders team effectiveness, so the rise should stay moderate.

forces.name: Helpers stand together
forces.increment_logic: When what I give comes back from the group as a matter of course, I count on help coming back too if anyone tries to set themselves over me, and I go about my business beside the strongest as freely as beside anyone: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When nothing I give comes back from the group, I cannot count on anyone's help if the strongest turns on me, and I grow warier of him and readier to give way: my sense that no one here can set themselves over me falls.
forces.explanation: Help repaid includes help in a quarrel. Among primates, grooming given is repaid in agonistic support, a small but reliable effect (Schino 2007, meta-analysis of 36 studies on 14 species, mean r about 0.15), and chimpanzee males gain alpha status through coalitional backing (de Waal 1982, Chimpanzee Politics). Those trades run between particular partners. Among egalitarian peoples, subordinates acting together keep a would-be dominant in check (Boehm 1993). The supported ends are therefore partner-specific support and coalitional checking of dominants. The step joining them, from help coming back from the group to counting on the group's backing against a would-be dominant, is the model's own and rests on common sense: people who repay favours as a matter of course can be expected to repay them in a quarrel too. Group-wide return does not guarantee backing, since bystanders tend to side by status or prior ties, and human evidence that friends buffer against a dominant is mixed (as reported by the reviewer, not checked here); play it moderately. Where her help comes back from the group, she counts on its backing against anyone who would set himself over her, and the fear goes out of a strong member's presence; where it does not, she stands alone. Parity's definition sets a limit: once a member actually pushes her about, grabs or tilts a share-out against her, the reading falls by the same amount whether or not she counts on backing, and backing changes only whether she meets the wrong with wariness or with anger. The card therefore reads her standing expectation of whether anyone can set himself over her, and neither softens nor deepens the fall a wrong itself brings. Where no member is pressing to set himself over others, the decrement is small: standing alone makes her warier of the strongest, but no one is yet lording it over her. The card rests on the return she can count on, not on being wanted (Friends at my back, E:Belonging->Levelling) or on her own commitment (Inside the coalition, E:Engagement->Levelling). All three carry the same expectation of backing, so where either of those also fires on the same scene, play this card small. The card reads only her expectation of backing; where a member's backing is actually given or withheld in the scene, that passes between people and belongs to I:Reciprocity->Levelling (A favour returned as backing), so play this card small on a scene where that one fires.

pre_language.increment: When the others share back with her and console her freely, she feels them as allies and feeds and moves near the strongest without a glance at their mood: her sense that no one can make her yield rises.
pre_language.decrement: When nothing passes back to her from the others, she feels unbacked, goes still when a strong one approaches and gives up her place to them: her sense that no one can make her yield falls.

reactive_test.reason: Feeling backed or alone, and fearing or not fearing a strong member, is an emotional reaction that exists before language.

problems.detail: Seyfarth and Cheney 1984 was not checked. The checked source for grooming traded for agonistic support is Schino 2007 (supports, small pooled effect, r about .15).

problems.where: explanation: 'coalitions of ordinary members are what keep a would-be dominant in check (Boehm 1999, Hierarchy in the Forest)'
problems.detail: Boehm 1999 was not checked; the checked source is Boehm 1993 (partly), which supports subordinates acting together against would-be dominants.

problems.where: explanation: 'In the egalitarian face the card rests on the wider case' and 'Among primates, support in conflicts is traded like other favours (de Waal 1982 ...)'
problems.detail: The checker found the link from generalised reciprocity to levelling is the model's own, not shown in Boehm; the text presents it as if it followed from the sources. De Waal 1982 is confirmed only for coalitional backing in gaining alpha status; constraint on dominants is unconfirmed. The extension must be marked as common sense and played moderately.

logic_status.common_sense: The step from help coming back from the group in general to counting on the group's backing against a would-be dominant. It is safe as a moderate extension because people who repay favours as a matter of course can be expected to repay help in a quarrel too, and primate data show support in conflicts is one of the currencies traded.

evidence.why: Each end is supported on its own: a replicated primate meta-analysis on favours repaid in support, and forager ethnography on ordinary members checking would-be dominants. The joining step, from group-wide return to a member's expectation of backing against domination, was not found tested in humans.
evidence.boundary: In primates, grooming is repaid in agonistic support only between particular partners, and the effect is small (r about 0.15). Human buffering against victimisation comes from friends rather than from the group at large, and it is mixed across studies. Bystanders take sides by status and by existing ties, so group-wide return does not guarantee backing.

forces.name: Good for Their Word
forces.increment_logic: When what I put in comes back from the group as a matter of course, I feel these are people who look out for more than themselves, and I leave their part of the shared work in their hands without checking and give a slip the benefit of the doubt: my sense that they can be counted on rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When what I give goes into a hole and my needs go unmet, I feel these people look after themselves first, and I start checking up on their part of the shared work, expecting them to shirk it: my sense that they can be counted on falls.
forces.explanation: The card assumes, on common sense, that trust built in one exchange carries over to other dealings with the same people. When an employer fails to deliver what it promised in exchange, employees' trust falls and their contributions fall with it, and trust, together with unmet expectations, carries that effect (Robinson 1996); across studies, breach is followed by mistrust and a sense of violation, which carry its effects onto work attitudes (Zhao et al. 2007). Those studies concern the employer, not fellow members, so the carry-over to members' carrying of their parts is an extension; keep it moderate. The breach-trust link is reported to be stronger for younger members (as reported by the reviewer, not checked here), and the carry-over may be weak between strangers and weak ties, so play the card small there. Prior trust also softens the reading of later breaches (Robinson 1996, its only source here), which the increment carries: a member whose help comes back gives others' lapses the benefit of the doubt. The decrement's checking up on their part of the shared work has no direct source; it is a gap resting on common sense, that one who expects shirking watches for it. Like the other cards that read Dependability indirectly, it bites only on parts not yet done or whose outcome she cannot see; parts she has seen carried through or dropped outweigh it.

problems.where: explanation, first sentence: 'Trust built in one exchange carries over to others with the same people.'
problems.detail: Stated as established fact with no source; Robinson 1996 and Zhao et al. 2007 concern breach and trust within one employee-employer relationship, not spillover across exchanges. It is the card's core mechanism, so it must be marked as common sense.

problems.where: explanation: 'and trust carries that effect (Robinson 1996)'
problems.detail: The checker found trust mediated the breach to contributions link together with unmet expectations, not trust alone.

logic_status.common_sense: That trust earned in exchange carries over to trust that the same people will carry their part of shared work; and that a return from the group signals people who look out for more than themselves. Safe as moderate claims because both follow from ordinary inference about character from conduct, and the explanation already limits the extension from employer to fellow members.

evidence.why: Several psychological contract meta-analyses show that unmet exchange lowers trust, but they concern the employer and draw on overlapping primary studies, so for this card they are analogous evidence. No study tests received reciprocity from fellow members shifting her sense of their dependability, and the increment rests on a single study (Robinson 1996).
evidence.boundary: Carry-over from received return to perceived dependability may be weak between strangers and weak ties. Younger members may react more strongly to unreturned giving (Bal et al. 2008). The monitoring clause has no test, so it stays common sense.

forces.name: Clinging or letting go
forces.increment_logic: When I feel myself edged out while my place here is still on trial, another member's break from the ways I am trying to be seen to keep jars me, and I catch myself muttering at it or ready to pull them up: my sense that such a breach is plainly wrong rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When I feel securely kept among them in my place, I have nothing to prove by the ways, and another member's small departure from how things are done here passes me by: my sense that such a breach is wrong falls a little.
forces.explanation: Felt inclusion sets her stake in the settled order while her place is still on trial (a newer choir member whose place rests on being seen to keep the ways). That scope and the default timing below are the facilitator's own proposals with no direct source. Feeling herself edged out, she is jarred by departures from the settled ways, so her Rule-Keeping rises a little; kept securely among them, she has nothing to prove and lets small departures from the group's conventions pass, so it falls a little. A breach that wrongs a member jars whatever her place, so the fall covers conventions only. Keep it small. Support is thin, partly contrary, and none of it measures felt indignation. Members enforce norms, even norms they privately doubt, to show that their own compliance is sincere (false enforcement: Willer, Kuwabara and Macy 2009, laboratory experiments, not replicated as far as checked), and peripheral members of a valued group are harsher towards outsiders when other members can see, while core members do not change with audience (Noel, Wann and Branscombe 1995, derogation of an outgroup, so analogous here). Both measure enforcement or derogation, and false enforcement shows enforcement running ahead of private belief, so they speak to her pulling others up more than to the bristle itself; the felt rise rests on common sense. An audience shapes whether her bristle comes out, which the scene stages, not how far the breach jars her. Against the card, in preschools dominant children report others' breaches more than other children do (Ingram and Bering 2010), so secure standing goes with more enforcement; and children excluded by their own group copy its conventions more faithfully (Watson-Jones, Whitehouse and Legare 2016), which points to reinclusion through her own conformity, outside Rule-Keeping, more than through policing others. Once the ways have long been her own, the card plays nil: a long-standing member's guarding of the ways rests on identification, which H:Engagement->NormExp (Invested, I guard our ways) already carries. Default (facilitator's proposal): play the card in a member's first months, and nil after.

pre_language.explanation: While her place is still new, slipping toward the edge sets her bristling at any new way and she snaps at whoever tries it, while being held close lets her settle and let it pass. Once the ways are long her own, being held close leaves her bristling at anyone who breaks them, while being left right out means others' new ways no longer stir her and she lets them pass.

The split into two circumstances, and the default timing below, are the facilitator's own proposals with no direct source. Circumstance one, her place is still on trial (a newer choir member whose place rests on being seen to keep the ways). HIGH: kept securely among them, she has nothing to prove and lets small departures pass, so her Rule-Keeping falls a little. LOW: feeling herself edged out, she is jarred by departures from the settled ways and quick to pull others up, so her Rule-Keeping rises a little (here the card runs as Inverse). Keep circumstance one small, and play its rise mainly where other members are watching. Support for it is thin and partly contrary. Members enforce norms, even norms they privately doubt, to show that their own compliance is sincere (false enforcement: Willer, Kuwabara and Macy 2009, laboratory experiments, not replicated as far as checked), and peripheral members of a valued group are harsher towards outsiders when other members can see, while core members do not change with audience (Noel, Wann and Branscombe 1995). Both measure enforcement or derogation, and false enforcement shows enforcement running ahead of private belief, so the pulling up can outrun felt indignation. Against it, in preschools dominant children report others' breaches more than other children do (Ingram and Bering 2010), so secure standing goes with more enforcement; and children excluded by their own group copy its conventions more faithfully (Watson-Jones, Whitehouse and Legare 2016), which points to reinclusion through her own conformity, outside Rule-Keeping, more than through policing others. Circumstance two, the ways have long been her own (a long-standing club member). HIGH: kept among them, she feels a breach of the club's ways as a breach of her own and pulls the breacher up, so her Rule-Keeping rises a little. LOW: pushed aside for good, she is no longer stung when others break ways that have stopped being hers, and lets it pass, so her Rule-Keeping falls (here the card runs as Reinforce). timing.typical: 1 to 5 seconds, at the next breach she witnesses
timing.why: Her felt place sets her stake in the ways beforehand, and the indignation (or its absence) fires as soon as a member departs from them, larger when others are watching.

era.why: NormExp is indignation at another member's break from the group's conventions; third-party enforcement of such ways has no clear primate analogue (chimpanzees do not punish third-party violations, Riedl et al. 2012) and is placed with group-minded conventional norms in modern humans (Tomasello 2016), and the card's black sheep evidence rests on a shared group identity.

forces.subtitle: An insecure place makes breaches jar
forces.summary: While a member's place is still on trial and she feels edged out, another member's break from the ways she is trying to be seen to keep jars her, and her Rule-Keeping rises a little. When she feels securely kept, she has nothing to prove and small departures pass her by, so it falls a little. Support is thin, so keep the card small and use it mainly in her first months.

logic_status.common_sense: Circumstance one (secure members let small departures pass; insecure ones police them) is an extension from Noel et al. on public outgroup negativity, already labelled a proposal; the withdrawal branch of circumstance two is own proposal. Both are safe as modest plays: a member whose place is secure has less need to show loyalty, and one pushed out for good stops caring about ways no longer hers, which fits the chronic-exclusion withdrawal Williams 2007 reports.

evidence.why: Henderson and Schnall 2021 is preregistered and replicated within the paper and supports the circumstance-one low-Belonging rise, though with strangers' moral wrongs rather than group conventions. The black sheep effect behind circumstance two is contested by a pooled null and is moderated by identification rather than felt acceptance, while the other branches rest on common sense or a narrative review.
evidence.boundary: In circumstance one, the low-Belonging rise appears mainly when the member is watched and may be display rather than felt indignation; exclusion raising moral condemnation was shown for strangers' wrongs, not for breaches of the group's own conventions. In circumstance two, the high-Belonging rise holds, if at all, only under high identification, identity threat or a shared moral norm, since a pooled file-drawer analysis found no black sheep effect overall (d = -0.01).

forces.name: Kept close, near the food
forces.increment_logic: When I am kept among them in my place, I feel within reach of the shares, mates and chances the group holds, and my sense that staying will get me what I am after rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am kept at the edge, I feel far from what the group holds and out of reach when shares, mates and chances come round, and my sense that staying will get me what I am after falls.
forces.explanation: In a ranked group, being kept close is access: to shares, partners and allies. Among primates, grooming is traded for tolerance at food (de Waal 1997, the chimpanzee's service economy); that finding concerns favours traded with a partner. Baboon work on social bonds and fitness (Silk et al. 2003; Cheney et al. 2016) is candidate primate support for closeness as access, to be cited here once verified. The step to felt inclusion as access in its own right, and from food to the shares, mates and chances of a human group, rests on common sense: what the group holds is handed out among those present and in favour. Where sharing is broad among all present, as in forager meat sharing, being kept close within the group adds little beyond being there, so the move is small. Nearness to the core goes largely with rank, so scale the move to the access that being kept close adds at her rank, kept separate from the rank itself. The card reads access through being kept close, not through rank (H:Status->OwnProsp), not through favours traded with a particular partner, such as grooming repaid with tolerance at food, which belong to H:Reciprocity->OwnProsp, and not through partial dealing by those who hand out (H:Levelling->OwnProsp): even an even-handed share-out passes by one who is not there when it is made.

pre_language.decrement: When she is pushed to the edge, she hangs back from food and partners, and her hope of getting what she is after sinks.

forces.name: Out of Sight, Not Copied
forces.increment_logic: When I am kept among them in my place, I feel what I bring is in their sight, and I expect that when my kind of skill is needed it is to me they will turn: my sense that they turn to me for it rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am kept at the edge, I feel what I bring is out of their sight, and I expect that when my kind of skill is needed they will turn to someone nearer: my sense that they turn to me for it falls.
forces.explanation: Deference for skill needs the skill to be in view. The visibility step rests on common sense, with only loose analogous support: Coussi-Korbel and Fragaszy (1995) propose, in a model built on nonhuman animals, that social spacing and coordination shape who learns from whom; it is a framework with predictions, not a test. Coelho et al. 2024 (PNAS) is candidate primate support to replace it once verified. On common sense, in a ranked group a member kept in the company feels her skill in view and expects to be looked to for it, while one kept at the edge feels it out of view and expects others to turn to someone nearer, whatever her skill. Whether they in fact watch and come to her, or pass her over, belongs to the scene (I:Belonging->Esteem). Nearness is neither necessary nor sufficient for being turned to: teams can pass over experts who are present, and members at the edge may still be turned to for knowledge only they hold. Nearness only puts what she brings in view: scale the move to what she brings the group and how visible that skill is, and set it near nil where she brings little it values.

forces.name: Kept in, deals open
forces.increment_logic: When I am kept among them, I feel the partners I help know I am there to call a favour in and that the others would see if they shorted me, and my sense that the partners I help will pay me back rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am kept at the edge, I feel I am not there to call a favour in and that fewer of the others would take note if a partner shorted me, so I expect partners to take and not return: my sense that anyone I help will pay me back falls.
forces.explanation: Exchange with a particular partner holds while defaulting would cost the partner: reciprocal cooperation is stable when future dealings are expected (Axelrod 1984), and when cooperating is not too risky for the partner (Dal Bó and Fréchette 2018, as reported by the reviewer, not checked here). Inclusion keeps her on hand to call the favour in, and among others who would see a partner short her. People give more to those seen to give (Wedekind and Milinski 2000; a partial replication, Russell, Stoilova and Dosoftei 2020, not checked here), so a partner's standing with those others rides on how they treat her. Observability raises good treatment only modestly (r about .14, as reported by the reviewer, not checked here), so keep the onlooker part small. That fewer onlookers take note when a partner shorts a member kept at the edge is the model's own step, resting on common sense; onlookers may instead make it up to an excluded member, which the scene can stage. Exclusion weakens both, so a partner can short the one at the edge, who is not there to hold them to it and is watched over by fewer who would. The felt horizon of her own staying belongs to H:Engagement->Reciprocity; this card reads only the others' inclusion of her.

forces.name: Kept close while I keep my place
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into this group, keeping to my place comes easily, and the slot they give me at each gathering reads as a real place among them; my sense that they want me among them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, the terms of my slot gall me and I hang at the margin, and I read that margin as where they have put me; my sense that they want me among them falls.
forces.explanation: In ranked groups inclusion often comes on terms: one is kept close so long as one keeps one's place. The model offers this as common sense, with no checked source. A member who has invested more accepts the terms easily and reads her slot as a real place. A member who has withdrawn finds the terms galling, drifts outward, and then reads the periphery as where she has been put. People who expect rejection are quick to see it in others' behaviour (Downey and Feldman 1996, on a disposition in close relationships). The step from her own investment to that reading is a proposal on common sense. Sociometer theory (Leary and Baumeister 2000) supplies only the reading of inclusion from others' treatment; it does not run from investment to that reading. The card needs a group that does offer real terms of inclusion to a member who keeps her place; where no such terms are on offer, her investment gives her nothing to read as a place, so set the move near nil. The reverse path, from feeling wanted to putting more in, is better supported and may carry most of this loop, so keep the card modest.

pre_language.decrement: Restless in the troop, she yields grudgingly and lingers at its edge, and she feels herself pushed out. Her feeling of being kept among them falls.

reactive_test.reason: Tolerated proximity in exchange for yielding is a primate pattern. The reading is felt inclusion or marginality. It feeds Engagement through Belonging.

forces.name: Invested, I guard our ways
forces.increment_logic: When I have put much of myself into the group, another member's break from our settled ways strikes me as an affront to what is ours, and I judge it the more harshly; my sense that such a breach is plainly wrong rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am holding back from the group, another member's departure from how things are done here barely touches me, and I let it pass; my sense that such a breach is wrong falls.
forces.explanation: Fellow members who break the group's norms are judged more harshly than outsiders who do the same (the black sheep effect: Marques, Yzerbyt and Leyens 1988). Highly identified members judge a disloyal fellow member more harshly still, at least when the group's identity is under threat (Branscombe, Wann, Noel and Coleman 1993). The effect is contested: a 2023 pooled analysis including unpublished studies found no black sheep effect overall (d = -0.01; as reported by the reviewer, not checked here), so the rise holds, if at all, under high identification, identity threat and a shared moral norm; play it moderately, and small where those are absent. Identification with the group is the tested proxy for investment here; the step from her investment to identification rests on common sense. High identifiers have also been found to follow the ingroup's salient norm more closely than low identifiers, with the difference reported to vanish under a fairness norm (Jetten, Spears and Manstead 1997); her own conformity is not Rule-Keeping, so this is context only. On common sense, as investment rises the settled ways feel more like her own, and a breach by another feels like damage to something of hers. The card holds for ways the group values and she does not judge harmful, and runs stronger when the group's identity is under threat (Branscombe). Packer's normative conflict model (Packer 2008) sets the boundary: where she sees a norm as harmful, a strongly invested member may dissent or defend the breacher, a reflective act outside this model, so the card does not fire there. Packer also separates nonconformity from disengagement from dissent. The decrement, that a member holding back has no stake in the ways, so a breach barely touches her and Rule-Keeping falls, rests on common sense with no source found. A breach that wrongs a member, taking from her, hurting her or leaving her to carry the breacher's part, jars whatever her investment (see Rule-Keeping's definition), so the decrement covers the group's conventions only; for such a breach play it small.

pre_language.decrement: Having just drawn back, she watches another try a new way and feels nothing stir; she lets it pass. Her indignation at the breach falls.

reactive_test.reason: Indignation at a breach of what feels like one's own is an emotional reaction with a pre-language form (threat, turning away).

Highly identified members judge a disloyal fellow member more harshly still, at least when the group's identity is under threat (Branscombe, Wann, Noel and Coleman 1993). High identifiers have also been found to act more in line with the ingroup's norm than low identifiers, whether that norm favours the ingroup or fairness (Jetten, Spears and Manstead 1997); her own conformity is not Rule-Keeping, so this is context only. On common sense, as investment rises the settled ways feel more like her own, and a breach by another feels like damage to something of hers. Packer's normative conflict model adds a boundary: strongly identified members may dissent when they judge a norm harmful, but that is a reflective act outside this model. Packer also separates nonconformity from disengagement from dissent; a disengaged member has no stake in the ways, so a breach leaves her unmoved and Rule-Keeping falls.

timing.typical: 1 to 5 seconds, at the next breach she witnesses after the checkpoint
timing.why: Her investment sets how much the ways feel like hers, and the jolt of indignation, or its absence, comes the instant another member breaks from them.

era.why: The target, NormExp, is indignation at breaches of group conventions, which lacks a clear primate analogue and is placed with modern human group-minded norms (Tomasello 2016); the card's evidence is social identity, so the card follows its target.

forces.subtitle: Invested members guard group ways
forces.summary: A member who has put much of herself into the group treats the settled ways as partly her own, so another member's breach strikes her as an affront and she judges it more harshly. A member who is holding back has little stake in those ways and lets a breach pass. Her Rule-Keeping moves with her investment.

problems.where: increment_logic: 'and I pull them up on the spot'
problems.detail: The black sheep and Branscombe findings concern harsher judgement, not confronting the person on the spot. Nothing checked supports sanctioning behaviour, and the target is a felt reading.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: 'and more harshly by members who identify strongly with the group (Branscombe, Wann, Noel and Coleman 1993)'
problems.detail: Rated partly. In that study the high-identifier effect appeared under threat to the group's identity, and the checker could not confirm the results beyond the hypothesis. The threat condition has been left out.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: 'Marques, Abrams and Serôdio 2001'
problems.detail: Not in the literature list; never checked.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 2: 'Members who value their membership also hold more closely to group norms themselves (Jetten, Spears and Manstead 1997; Smith and Louis)'
problems.detail: Jetten et al. was rated partly. The identification effect held only for an ingroup-favouring (differentiation) norm, not for group norms in general. Smith and Louis has no year and was never checked.

logic_status.common_sense: Two steps: as her investment rises the group's ways feel more her own, so another's breach feels like damage to something of hers; and a disengaged member is left unmoved by a breach. Both are safe as common sense. The first extends the identification findings to a short-term state. The second fits Packer's separation of disengaged nonconformity from dissent.

evidence.why: The direction has several older lab studies and a recent conceptual replication, but none is a direct or multi-lab replication, the tested construct is identification with judgments of vignette or stranger deviants, and an unconfirmed 2023 null contests the basic black sheep contrast. Consilience is limited to social and developmental psychology, so the card stays provisional with the boundaries written in.
evidence.boundary: The harsher judgment holds when the breached way is valued by the group and not judged harmful; where she sees the norm as harmful, an invested member may side with the breach (Packer 2008). The effect is stronger under threat to the group (Branscombe et al. 1993), and in workplaces highly identified observers may excuse or reintegrate a transgressor.

forces.name: Putting in, in line for my due
forces.explanation: Redrawn as Discretionary. Whether putting much of myself in raises or lowers my sense that staying will bring me what I am after depends on whether the group's dealings with me keep pace with what I put in. Circumstance one (the default), returns keep pace or are still unclear: places, shares and chances have come my way roughly in step with my effort, or nothing yet shows otherwise. HIGH: having put much in, I feel I have earned my due, and the group's dealings with me read as the way to what I came for opening up: my Payoff rises. LOW: having held back, I feel I have given them no reason to bring me on, and the way reads as closing: my Payoff falls. Circumstance two, returns are plainly flat: I have put in more and more while places, shares and chances, handed out by the group's ordinary ways, keep going to others (a share-out tilted towards favourites is Parity's ground and reaches Payoff through H:Parity->Payoff). HIGH: the more I have put in, the more the flat return reads as being taken for granted; I feel short-changed and expect more of the same however much I put in: my Payoff falls. LOW: having put in little, a flat return is no more than I looked for; the card adds nothing, and the scene alone moves my Payoff. Circumstance one is a proposal on common sense: a member's felt claim from what she has put in colours an ambiguous forecast. No direct test of it was found. Circumstance two rests on equity theory: people weigh what they get against what they put in, and under-reward relative to input brings distress and anger (Adams 1965); in social exchange, giving creates an expectation of return (Blau 1964). The step from feeling short-changed to a lower forecast of what staying brings rests on common sense, with proxy support only from work linking felt under-reward to intention to leave: a return that has stayed flat against rising input is read as what staying will go on bringing. In circumstance two part of that route runs through exhaustion from giving without return, and the exchange mechanism is weaker in cultures where identification with the group, more than exchange, binds members to it (Rockstuhl et al. 2020); set the fall smaller there. Groups do repay contribution with status and influence (Willer 2009), but that route runs through H:Engagement->Rank and H:Engagement->Esteem and on to Payoff, so this card carries only her felt claim; keep both circumstances modest. The card moves her forecast of what the group will deliver, and leaves her confidence in her own ability alone.

pre_language.increment: Her investment has just deepened; she feels herself in line for the troop's favour and looks to it to bring her what she wants. Her hope of getting what she is after rises.
pre_language.decrement: Her investment has just slackened; she feels herself out of favour and expects the troop to give her nothing. Her hope of getting what she is after falls.

reactive_test.reason: A felt sense of being owed or out of favour, drawn from emotionally weighted information about her own conduct; it must stay unbidden rather than a calculated forecast, which the lines keep.

forces.framework: Proposal (felt claim from investment); equity theory (Adams 1965); social exchange (Blau 1964); status for contribution as context (Willer 2009).

sources.source: Willer 2009, ASR 74
sources.claim: Higher contributors gained status, influence and more cooperation

sources.claim: Input without matching reward predicts later distress (pooled RR 1.49 across 8 cohorts), supporting the short-changing reaction in circumstance two, not the forecast itself.

ripple_was.increment_logic: When I have just put more of myself into the group, I feel I have earned my turn, and the group's dealings with me in that scene read as the way to what I came for opening up; my sense that staying will bring me what I am after rises.
ripple_was.decrement_logic: When I have just drawn back from the group, I feel I have given them no reason to bring me on, and their dealings with me read as the way to what I came for closing; my sense that staying will bring me what I am after falls.
ripple_was.explanation: In ranked groups, advancement, favour and reward go to those seen to commit themselves: contribution is repaid with standing and support (Willer 2009), and members who feel they have given more expect more from the group (social exchange: Blau 1964; Eisenberger et al. 1986 on felt organisational support). Her own recent investment colours an ambiguous forecast: having put in, she feels in line for her due and reads the group's treatment of her as opening the way; having held back, she feels she has forfeited her claim. What moves is her forecast of what the group will deliver, not her confidence in her own ability.

timing.why: Her felt claim colours the forecast when she reads the group's next dealings with her as the way opening or closing, which takes the run of a meeting to present itself.

forces.subtitle: Putting in, expecting a return
forces.summary: Whether putting in more lifts her Payoff depends on whether the group's dealings keep pace with her effort. Where returns keep pace or are unclear, putting in leaves her feeling she has earned her due and her Payoff rises. forces.name: Putting in, looked to
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into the group, I feel what I bring to each scene showing, and I read the others' questions and glances as turning to me for it; my sense that they defer to me for what I bring rises.

forces.explanation: Esteem, in this model, is deference freely given to those whose skill or contribution others value. Members who contribute more to the group are given more status and influence (Willer 2009); that conferral is the others' act and belongs to the scene, and here it stands only as background. That study rewards contribution as sacrifice; here only the deference for what she brings moves, and the others' verdict on whether she carries her share is Repute's (H:Engagement->Face carries the open charge). The card rests on her reading, an inference from ambiguous cues, and her own recent conduct colouring it is a step on common sense: having just put in more, she reads others' questions and glances as turning to her; having just pulled back, she reads their turning elsewhere as her contribution no longer counting. People's sense of their own status mostly tracks what others actually confer (Anderson, Srivastava, Beer, Spataro and Chatman 2006), so most of the move runs through the scene and this card adds only a small tilt to her reading. People track how much others value their relationships with them (Leary 2005), so such a reading is one she is primed to make; whether usefulness is a named part of that relational value is still to be checked against the text. The link holds only when her putting in shows as contribution to what the group values. Effort alone is not contribution, and deference may follow domain skill or other cues that her effort does not show (Brand and Mesoudi 2019), so where her effort is unseen or off what the group values, set the move near nil. Moderate confidence.

forces.name: The long shadow of staying
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into the group and mean to stay, I feel we will be around each other long enough for every favour to come back, and I read what I give my partners as sure to be repaid; my sense that help I give comes back from those I help rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am putting little of myself into the group and am half out of the door, I feel I may not be around when a favour falls due, and I read my partners as having no reason to repay one who is leaving; my sense that help I give comes back from those I help falls.
forces.explanation: Conditional exchange holds only while partners expect to meet again: the shadow of the future (Axelrod 1984). In lab games with anonymous pairs, cooperation is higher when play may continue than when the end is known, in the direction theory predicts (Dal Bó 2005). How long she means to stay is part of Engagement: a member who has put much of herself in sees herself staying, one who is gone or going does not. High Engagement lengthens the felt horizon on both sides, so she reads her partners as bound to repay one who stays; on common sense the same holds for a patron across rank. Low Engagement shortens it, and she reads herself as the one partners will stop repaying. The partner face applies: what moves is her reading of the return, not her readiness to deal.

forces.name: Guarding the ways earns a place
forces.explanation: Whether pulling up a breach leaves her feeling kept among the others depends on whether they share the bristle. Belonging reads their acceptance from how they treat her, so in each circumstance the move runs through what she then reads in their manner towards her; in a ranked group, holding to the ways the group keeps is part of keeping her place. Circumstance one, the others share the bristle: the breach falls short of what the group plainly stands for, or overshoots it in a way they resent, and they are already muttering (a member skipping the rota the rest keep). HIGH: she pulls the breacher up, reads the others' muttering as on her side and senses herself kept close as one who keeps to what her place calls for, so her Belonging rises. LOW: she lets it pass while they bristle and reads in their looks that she has been soft on the ways, so her Belonging falls. Circumstance two, the others do not share the bristle (a small departure the settled ways condemn in principle but the members present would shrug off here and now). HIGH: she pulls up a member the others think harmless, catches their looks as she does it and senses herself set apart from them as a scold, so her Belonging falls. LOW: she lets it pass as the rest do and reads nothing in their manner that sets her apart, so her Belonging holds or rises a little. In either circumstance, where HIGH has her pulling up a member well above her own place, she senses she has stepped out of line and her Belonging falls; what it does to her rung belongs to the interaction card I:NormExp->Status. Rule-Keeping reads high in a member who bristles and keeps quiet, so the card fires only on what the others can catch: where a HIGH reading shows only as a start or a mutter, play the same move smaller; where she keeps it wholly to herself, nothing in their manner answers it and the card does not fire. The card reads her own inference from the cues around her and assumes no response from the others; their actually drawing her in or edging her out belongs to the interaction card I:NormExp->Belonging. That she reads the cues this way rests on common sense. A neighbouring finding bears on circumstance two's HIGH fall: students who took a campus norm to be more widely held than it privately was felt out of step with their peers and alienated from the institution (Prentice and Miller 1993). That study concerns her own private view against a misread norm, not her pulling others up, and Rule-Keeping's definition lets such a sense of being out of step bear on Belonging only through how she then reads the others' treatment of her, so it supports the step without carrying it. The sources below bear on how others respond to deviants and punishers; they are scene context only and do not carry the card's step. Members derogate fellow members who depart from the group's norm in a direction it condemns (Abrams et al. 2000), though the black sheep base for this is contested by a reported 2023 null still to be confirmed; people seldom punish those who fail to punish, though they do reward those who punish (Kiyonari and Barclay 2008); groups can sanction those who contribute more than the norm (Herrmann, Thöni and Gächter 2008); people put down the morally motivated who seem to reproach them (Minson and Monin 2012, on an out-group minority); third-party punishers are trusted (Jordan et al. 2016), but trust is not inclusion. Responses to enforcers are mixed across games and settings, so the size of the move is uncertain. Judge the sign by the others' visible bristle, and keep the card modest. Circumstance one is the default in ranked groups with settled ways.

ripple_was.explanation: Proposal, modest weight. In ranked groups, joining in pulling up those who break the settled ways marks a member as loyal to the order and draws her in, while letting breaches pass marks her as unreliable to it and gets her held at a distance. The black sheep effect and ostracism of deviants show how breakers are treated, not how enforcers are; evidence that enforcers are rewarded is mixed: third-party punishers are trusted (Jordan et al. 2016) but not reliably liked or rewarded, and sanctions on those who fail to punish are rare in the lab (Kiyonari and Barclay 2008; Raihani and Bshary 2019). The card rests on common sense about ranked groups, where loyalty to the order is itself a ground of acceptance.

Whether pulling up a breach draws the others round her depends on whether they share the bristle. Circumstance one, the breach falls short of what the group plainly stands for and the others are already muttering (a member skipping the rota the rest keep). HIGH: she pulls the breacher up, the others close ranks with her, and her Belonging rises. LOW: she lets it pass while they bristle, they read her as soft on the ways and cool towards her, and her Belonging falls. Circumstance two, the others do not share the bristle (a small departure, or one that overshoots the group's ideal rather than falling short of it). HIGH: she pulls up a member the others think harmless or even admirable; they read her as a scold setting herself above them and edge away, so her Belonging falls. LOW: she lets it pass with the rest and stays one of them, so her Belonging holds or rises a little. Members derogate anti-norm fellow members and like pro-norm ones (Abrams et al. 2000), so siding with the group against an anti-norm breach aligns her with it. People also put down the morally motivated who seem to reproach them (Minson and Monin 2012). Third-party punishers are trusted (Jordan et al. 2016), but trust is not inclusion. Circumstance one is the default in ranked groups with settled ways.

If they do, pulling the breacher up reads as being on their side and her Belonging rises, while letting it pass reads as softness and it falls. If they do not, scolding sets her apart and it falls. logic_status.common_sense: That a member who sides with the group against a breach the others resent is drawn closer, and that one who lets it pass is cooled towards; that pulling up a member the others think harmless reads as scolding and they edge away; that pulling up a senior reads as stepping out of line; that circumstance one is the default in ranked groups with settled ways. All follow from ordinary group life and none is contradicted by the checked sources.

dimensions.replication: none (black sheep base contested by a 2023 file-drawer null)
dimensions.directness: adjacent (scene level only; the focal member's felt Belonging is untested)

evidence.why: Every source found concerns how others treat deviants and punishers, not the enforcer's own felt Belonging, so the central step is a gap. The black sheep base for the circumstance split is itself contested by an unconfirmed but sizeable null, so nothing here lifts the card above common sense.
evidence.boundary: The sign turns on whether the others visibly share the bristle: enforcing with a group that resents the breach raises Belonging, enforcing against a shrugging group lowers it, and letting it pass reverses both. Pulling up a member well above her place lowers it.

forces.name: Loyalty repaid
forces.increment_logic: When another member's breach jars me and my partners see me bristle and pull them up, I feel I have shown myself one who stands up for our ways and can be relied on, and shown those above me loyalty they owe favour for: my sense that the partners I help will pay me back rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When a breach leaves me unmoved and I let it pass while my partners look on, I feel I have given them no sign that I can be relied on, and given those above me no loyalty to repay: my sense that the partners I help will pay me back falls a little.
forces.explanation: Third-party punishers are trusted more, and in fact behave more trustworthily, than non-punishers (Jordan, Hoffman, Bloom and Rand 2016); punishment works as a signal that the punisher can be relied on. That signal has a reported direct non-replication and mixed follow-ups, and where found it is small and needs her indignation to be visible (Kupfer and Tybur 2023, citation still to be checked), so the increment fires only when her partners see her bristle, and the rise is small. Jordan et al. also found the signal weakens where helping can be shown directly, and bystanders reward third-party helpers more than third-party punishers (Raihani and Bshary 2015), so where she could have helped the wronged member instead, set the rise near nil. In small-scale settings third parties to a dispute mostly seek to restore relations rather than to punish (Wiessner 2020), so punishing may count for less there as a sign of reliability. That evidence concerns punishing unfair splits in economic games; the step to pulling up a breach of the group's settled ways rests on common sense. That the trust brings back what she gives is an inference: partners choose and keep up exchanges with those they judge reliable, so her help to them is more readily returned. Across rank, holding the line on the group's ways reads as loyalty passed up, which a patron repays with favour and protection; this step rests on common sense, with no source found. Where she pulls up a member above her own place, those above read it as stepping out of line rather than loyalty; that route belongs to the interaction card I:NormExp->Status, so set the rise near nil there. Both lines also need a breach the others condemn too (Eriksson et al. 2021): where they think it harmless, pulling up reads as scolding and letting it pass as ordinary (H:NormExp->Belonging, circumstance two), so set both moves near nil. With the Reputation expansion pack in play, the open standing she wins as one who holds the line runs through H:NormExp->Face and H:Face->Reciprocity; this card then carries only the reliance her partners take from what they saw themselves, and should be smaller still where H:NormExp->Face or X:NormExp->Repute also fires. The decrement needs her partners to have seen her let the breach pass and rests on common sense, with no source found, so the card should be modest.

pre_language.increment: When she threatens a member trying a new way, the higher-ranked one she sided with backs her in her next squabble and lets her share its food.
pre_language.decrement: When she lets a member's new way go by, the higher-ranked ones do not come to her side when she is threatened.

reactive_test.reason: Indignation at a breach and the felt sense that patrons will or will not cover her are reactions and inferences from emotionally weighted treatment, seen in primate coalitions.
