sources.claim: Bystanders reward third-party punishers over non-actors, but reward helpers more, which supports the helping boundary.

sources.source: Raihani, N. J., & Bshary, R. (2015). Third-party punishers are rewarded, but third-party helpers even more so. Evolution, 69(4), 993-1003.
sources.claim: Bystanders reward punishers over non-actors but reward helpers more; backs the boundary that the signal weakens where direct helping is available.

edits_log: 5 Nov 2026: Ben approved, 5 Nov 2026, 11.22 am (comparative psychologist's critique, docs/v3/sc-critique/): The card had no source and leaned on 'those above repay loyalty'. A checked route exists through partners' trust.

Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines pass. Explanation overstates Jordan et al.: they show punishers are entrusted with more (others send them more in a trust game), not that help punishers give is repaid. The step from being trusted to being repaid is an inference (partner choice favours those seen as reliable) and should be marked as such.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The lines, type and mechanism pass; Jordan, Hoffman, Bloom and Rand (2016) is cited correctly, including the weaker signal when helping can be observed directly. The framework field is null. Fill it.

Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The lines read the return from 'the others' as a body trusting her, which is closer to the group face (E) or to Repute than to the revised hierarchical face, where the return comes from particular partners, in kind or across rank as favour passed down for loyalty passed up. The decrement also asks her to infer lost trust from a non-reaction she gives no thought to; it holds only where her partners watch her let the breach pass. Framework is null; suggest 'Third-party punishment as a costly signal of trustworthiness (Jordan et al. 2016); patron-client exchange'.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The decrement overstates its case. Jordan et al. show that a non-punisher only lacks the signal of trustworthiness; they do not show she is read as unreliable. The explanation also leaves out that punishers can be disliked as well as trusted (Raihani and Bshary 2015), which is another reason to keep the card modest. The framework field is empty.

Ripple round 4, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines pass against both Pillars, and the Jordan et al. 2016 trust-signal mechanism agrees with the literature. The explanation leaves out a case that the sibling cards cover: when she pulls up a member above her place, those above see her stepping out of line, not loyalty, so the across-rank leg of the increment fails. H:NormExp->Belonging and H:NormExp->OwnProsp both scope this out, and this card should do the same. Fix: add the caveat to the explanation.

Ripple round 5, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Inconsistent with H:NormExp->Belonging. That card has pulling up a departure the others think harmless read as scolding, and letting it pass read as ordinary. This card raises and lowers the expected return regardless. Jordan et al. (2016) find trust for punishers of clear defection, which does not cover such cases. The fix adds that condition to the explanation; the lines and type stand.

Ripple round 8, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines, type and boundaries pass. The explanation leans on Jordan et al. 2016 without saying that their punishers were sanctioning unfair splits in economic games. NormExp covers indignation at any breach of the group's settled ways, conventions included, so the move from punishing unfairness to pulling up a breach of custom is an extrapolation, and the card should flag it as common sense the way its sibling cards do. Smallest fix: one added sentence in the explanation.

Ripple round 10, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines pass against NormExp (read through pulling up) and the revised partner face, type matches, and the moderators keep the move in one direction or near nil. The mechanism, though, runs through others' verdict that she can be relied on, which the Reciprocity definition places with Face ('good for a return') and Repute. With the Reputation pack in play, the same route already runs NormExp->Face (Flying the Flag) then Face->Reciprocity (Keeping Score), so the card partly duplicates it. Smallest fix: one sentence in the explanation limiting the card to first-hand reliance when the pack is in play. (Framework field is null; outside this schema.)

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Increment line has partners read that she 'holds to our ways', which is a reading of her own conformity; Rule-Keeping's definition excludes her own conformity, and the cited signal (Jordan, Hoffman, Bloom and Rand 2016) is that a punisher can be relied on, not that she conforms. Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The increment rises only 'a little', but the decrement falls without that limit, even though the explanation says the decrement has no source and the card should be modest. Letting a breach pass is the ordinary default: people seldom punish those who fail to punish (Kiyonari and Barclay 2008), and in Jordan et al. 2016 non-punishers are trusted less only relative to punishers. So the absence of a signal should move the expected return no more than its presence does. Smallest fix: the decrement falls a little.

ripple_was.increment_logic: When another member's breach jars me and I pull them up, the others see me as one who will not let things slide; they trust me with more and pay back what I give them: my sense that help I give comes back from those I help rises.
ripple_was.decrement_logic: When a breach leaves me unmoved and I let it pass, the others have no sign that I can be counted on, they trust me with less and are slow to repay: my sense that help I give comes back falls.
ripple_was.explanation: Third-party punishers are trusted more, and in fact behave more trustworthily, than non-punishers (Jordan, Hoffman, Bloom and Rand); punishment works as a signal that the punisher can be relied on, and that trust brings returns. The signal weakens where she can show her worth by helping directly, so the card should be modest.

forces.name: Valued service, kept place
forces.increment_logic: When the others turn to me for what I bring, watch how I do it and take my advice, I feel them keep me near because they need me, the threat of being dropped seems far off, and my sense of being kept among them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When no one asks me or copies me and they turn to someone else when my kind of skill is needed, I feel that nothing I bring holds me in and that one step out of line would see me dropped, and my sense of being kept among them falls.
forces.explanation: Groups repay valued contributors with freely conferred deference (Henrich and Gil-White 2001), and followers are held to repay a leader's valued service with prestige (Price and Van Vugt 2014, a theory review). That followers also keep close to those they learn from rests on common sense here, since the checked reading of Henrich and Gil-White did not confirm it. Under this deck's face, being kept among them rests on keeping her place, and she reads it partly from the standing threat of being dropped. A member the others turn to feels that threat recede, because the group needs what she brings; one passed over feels nothing she brings holds her in, so her keeping feels more conditional. These two steps rest on common sense, supported only by adjacent theory (service repaid with prestige) and, by analogy only, by game evidence that, where members can be expelled, expulsion falls mostly on low contributors (Cinyabuguma, Page and Putterman 2005); low contribution there is a matter of will, Repute's ground, not of skill. The link needs the group's need for her skill to be visible to her, and her own need to belong may strengthen or weaken it. Status and belonging are distinct motives (Anderson, Hildreth and Howland 2015), so esteem does not guarantee a felt place; keep the card modest. The card moves her felt security of being kept, not her place. Whether the others in fact seek her out and keep her, or drop her, passes between people and belongs to the scene (I:Prestige->Belonging); play this card small on a scene where that one fires.

logic_status.common_sense: That followers keep close to those they learn from; that a member the others turn to feels the threat of being dropped recede because the group needs her, and one passed over feels her keeping is more conditional. Felt indispensability as a source of security is plain, and nothing checked contradicts it.

dimensions.directness: adjacent (exclusion of low contributors in games; theory of conferred deference)
dimensions.consilience: some (anthropology and cultural evolution; behavioural economics)

evidence.why: No study measures whether being sought out and copied raises a member's felt security of being kept; support is limited to neighbouring steps such as low contributors being voted out in public goods games. evidence.boundary: The link holds where the group's need for her skill is visible to her, and is likely moderated by her trait need to belong (Eck et al. 2017). One lab null (2010, identity unconfirmed) found that outperforming others did not buffer ostracism distress, so esteem may not protect a member once exclusion has begun.

forces.name: Looked To, Let In
forces.increment_logic: When the others turn to me for what I bring, take my advice and hand me jobs that matter, I feel doors opening for me here, and my sense that staying will bring me what I came for rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When no one asks me or copies me and they turn to someone else, and the jobs that matter go elsewhere, I feel the way to what I came for closing, and my sense that staying will bring it falls.
forces.explanation: Under this deck's face, being deferred to includes being handed decisions and jobs that matter, and these open the way to the place, skill or advancement a member came for, so felt deference carries a forecast of what the group will deliver to her. Henrich and Gil-White (2001) hold that the prestigious receive freely conferred benefits from those who defer to them; the final step, from felt deference to her own forecast of what staying will bring, rests on common sense. The card holds where the group hands out jobs and advancement by esteem and she reads the deference as earned. It weakens in strongly egalitarian groups and where deference follows apparent more than real competence (Anderson and Kilduff 2009), since she may then doubt it will last. Whether help she gives comes back is Reciprocity's ground (H:Prestige->Reciprocity), so this card carries only the opening of the way to what she came for.

problems.where: explanation: 'Those deferred to for skill are repaid with access, allies, mates and advancement (Henrich and Gil-White 2001)'
problems.detail: The item carries no literature at all; Henrich and Gil-White 2001 is cited but was never checked, so the mechanism claim has no checked backing.

problems.where: explanation: 'repaid with access, allies, mates and advancement'
problems.detail: In Henrich and Gil-White's account learners pay deference to gain access to the skilled model, so access flows from the prestigious member to the learners rather than to her. The list of payoffs (mates, advancement) goes beyond anything checked and may misstate the source's direction of exchange.

logic_status.common_sense: That a member whom others look to and take advice from expects the group to treat her well, and so feels her prospects here improve, is everyday experience and safe as a felt forecast. The lines claim only that feeling.

evidence.why: Under option B, adjacent evidence counts towards substantiated when consilience is strong, and four independent fields converge on deference turning into access and advancement with no failed replication or published null found. The grade is fragile: no source was verified at full text and the organisational leg rests on studies with unconfirmed citations (Yuan; Li 2020; the RSOS replication URL), so the grade should fall to provisional if those checks fail.
evidence.boundary: Holds where the group allocates jobs and advancement by esteem and the deference is read as earned. Weakens in strongly egalitarian groups, where the benefits of status are muted (Hadza), and where deference follows apparent rather than real competence (Anderson and Kilduff 2009). Being sought out does not uniformly predict promotion; the effect varies with the centrality measure and with seeking versus giving advice.
evidence.caveat: Four fields (forager ethnography and evolutionary anthropology, social psychology of prestige, expectation states research, and organisational advice-network studies) show that freely conferred deference converts into influence, task opportunities, access and promotion, measured in behaviour and outcomes. forces.name: Sought-After Partner
forces.increment_logic: When the others turn to me for what I bring, I feel my help is worth a good deal to them, and my sense that the partners I help will pay me back rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When no one asks me or copies me any more, I feel my help is worth little to them, and my sense that partners will repay what I give falls.
forces.explanation: In a market for partners, exchange rates follow supply and demand, so a partner in demand can command better terms (Noe and Hammerstein 1994). Field test: when a single low-ranking vervet female could open a food box, she received more grooming relative to what she gave, and when a second provider was introduced her gain was partly lost (Fruteau, Voelkl, van Damme and Noe 2009). That is one unreplicated field test of behavioural market pricing, and moving from it to a member's expectation that partners will repay her is the model's extension. On that extension, deference for what she brings raises what she expects partners to return, and a rival with the same skill lowers it. The card holds where what she brings is scarce and the others can choose their partners; a rival offering the same skill erodes it. Being in demand may instead bring more requests and a sense of being used, so keep the rise modest. As deference fades, so does what she expects partners to give back.

pre_language.increment: When the others watch and copy her, those she grooms groom her back at length, and she feels sure of return.
pre_language.decrement: When the others turn to another to watch and copy, those she grooms move off without returning it, and she stops expecting return.

reactive_test.reason: Feeling valued or not, and expecting a return or not as a result, is a felt reading that exists before language.

problems.detail: The checker rated the source partly: it shows exchange rates set by supply and demand. 'Fuller' is a fair market reading; 'surer' (reliability of repayment) is not shown anywhere in what was checked.

problems.where: explanation: whole sentence citing Noe and Hammerstein
problems.detail: The paper models non-human animals; applying it to a human member valued for skill is the model's extension and is presented as if the source showed it.

logic_status.common_sense: That a member others turn to feels her help is valued and expects it to be returned is ordinary experience; the human application of the market model rests on this.

dimensions.replication: none for the demand-raises-returns step (grooming reciprocation in general is meta-analysed)
dimensions.directness: analogous (primate behavioural returns; human partner-choice games)
dimensions.setting: narrow (one wild vervet field experiment, 2 groups; lab games, WEIRD)

evidence.why: The step rests on biological-market theory, one unreplicated vervet field experiment and adjacent partner-choice games, while reviews find market predictions mixed in primates. No human work measures expected repayment after a rise in being sought out, so the card is provisional and needs the supply condition written in.
evidence.boundary: Holds where what she brings is scarce and the others can choose their partners; a rival with the same skill erodes the gain (Fruteau et al. 2009). Market predictions are mixed across primate tests and appear where hierarchy is steep, and being in demand may bring more requests rather than better returns.

forces.name: Trading partners keep you close
forces.increment_logic: When my partners pay me back and those I ask deliver, I feel we are worth too much to each other to lose: I sit close to them, and after a clash with one of them I go to them soon, low and friendly, expecting to be let close again: my sense of being kept among them in my place rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When partners take and do not return and what I ask for goes unmet, I feel I am worth little to them: I hang back from sitting beside them, leave a clash with one of them unmended and keep out of their way, expecting no one to draw me back: my sense of being kept among them falls.
forces.explanation: In ranked groups grooming and favours are exchanged for tolerance and support, a prediction of Seyfarth's (1977) model that later tests have mostly but not uniformly confirmed (Schino 2001); across studies the grooming-for-support effect is small (bias-corrected r = 0.15; Schino 2007). Grooming is reciprocated across primate groups (Schino and Aureli 2008), and partner value predicts reconciliation after conflict (Aureli, Cords and van Schaik 2002; Cords and Thurnheer 1993), though the valuable-partner account of reconciliation has contested cases (Silk 2002; reports from bonobos and from the Mahale chimpanzees). A partner who repays is a valuable partner: she is tolerated close day to day, and repair with her after a clash keeps a member in the troop's company. An unrepaired rift with a partner who never repaid leaves her at the edge. Reconciliation repairs one partnership; reading it as being kept among the others as a whole is an extension, resting on common sense. Boundary: the card holds partner by partner on existing ties, and carries to her felt belonging in the group only where those partners make up most of the group; play it small where they are a few among many. The card reads favours repaid by trading partners. A mutual close bond with one or two particular partners is the scene state Close tie and is read neither in Warmth nor here; where a repaid partner is also a close tie, play this card small, since a repaid partner and a bonded one are often the same member.

pre_language.increment: When her grooming is returned and partners back her, they tolerate her close by, and her feeling of being kept close grows.
pre_language.decrement: When partners take her grooming and give none back, they drift from her, and her feeling of being kept close fades.

reactive_test.reason: Feeling bound in or cut loose by partners' returns is an inference from emotionally weighted treatment, with a direct grooming analogue.

A partner who repays is a valuable partner: she is tolerated close day to day, and repair with her after a clash keeps a member in the troop's company. An unrepaired rift with a partner who never repaid leaves her at the edge. Reconciliation repairs one partnership; reading it as being kept among the others as a whole is an extension, resting on common sense. Boundary: the card holds partner by partner on existing ties, and carries to her felt belonging in the group only where those partners make up most of the group; play it small where they are a few among many. The card reads favours repaid by trading partners. Fondness for her few close partners, and their answering contact, is the interaction card I:Warmth->Belonging#2 (Close partners keep me in); where both fire on the same partner, play this card small, since a repaid partner and a bonded one are often the same member.

timing.typical: within about ten minutes of a clash
timing.why: The card works through repair after a clash. Primate reconciliation mostly happens in the first minutes after conflict (de Waal and van Roosmalen 1979, unchecked here), and whether she is let close again or left at the edge is settled in that window.

era.why: Grooming traded for tolerance, and reconciliation predicted by partner value, are documented in monkeys and apes (Seyfarth; Aureli, Cords and van Schaik).

forces.subtitle: Partners who repay keep you close
forces.summary: A partner who pays back is a valuable partner. When partners repay a member and deliver what she asks, she feels worth too much to them to lose, sits close and mends clashes, so her sense of being kept among them in her place rises. When they take and do not return, she hangs back and leaves rifts unmended, so it falls. It holds best where these partners make up most of the group.

forces.name: Power to your Elbow
forces.increment_logic: When the partners I help pay me back and those I ask deliver, I feel backed in going after what I came for, and my sense that staying will bring it to me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When partners take and do not return and those I ask do not deliver, I feel on my own in going after what I came for, and my sense that staying will bring it to me falls.
forces.explanation: In ranked primate groups grooming is predicted to be exchanged for agonistic support (Seyfarth 1977, a model that tests have mostly but not uniformly confirmed) and is traded for tolerance at food (de Waal 1997, the chimpanzee's service economy). Across species, grooming given and support received go together within pairs (Schino 2007, a meta-analysis). Carrying this to a member's expected payoff from staying in a human group rests on common sense: a member whose partners pay her back feels backed and expects staying to open the way to what she came for; one whose help is not returned stands alone and expects little from the group. Boundaries. The card runs through direct return from particular partners: macaques show strong direct reciprocity and little indirect or generalised reciprocity (source not yet given; unchecked), so help from the group at large is not read here. It also runs through perceived return, which tracks actual return only modestly (perceived and received support correlate at about r = 0.35 in a meta-analysis; Haber et al. 2007, to be checked), and the path can run the other way, with an optimistic member reading more support than she gets; keep the step modest.

logic_status.common_sense: That a member whose favours are returned feels backed and expects to get what she came for, and one whose help goes unreturned feels alone and expects little, is plain experience and safe as a felt forecast; the lines claim no more.

evidence.why: Pair-level reciprocity is well supported across primates and humans, but no study tests whether returned help raises a member's expectation that staying will bring her what she came for, so the central step is common sense with adjacent perceived-support work. forces.name: Rank draws the circle
forces.increment_logic: When I go first as a matter of course and take the first share and the best seat, I feel my place gives me slack and that a small slip would not see me dropped: my sense of being kept among them in my place rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I go last and take what is left, I feel how little slack my place gives me and that any step out of line would see me dropped: my sense of being kept among them falls a little.
forces.explanation: In ranked groups grooming tends to be directed up the order (Seyfarth 1977; tests have mostly but not uniformly confirmed it). The pattern varies across species, and grooming is also traded reciprocally (Schino 2007), which offers a competing account of why attention runs up the order: rank is one route to being drawn close among several. After a fight, low-ranking chimpanzee victims are consoled less often than high-ranking ones (Romero, Castellanos and de Waal 2010), so the comfort that keeps a member in the cluster runs up the order with the grooming. Higher status is also accorded respect and voluntary deference (Anderson, Hildreth and Howland 2015), though their status includes deference freely given, which is Esteem's ground here, so it supports this card only loosely. Under this deck's face a place is made for members high or low who keep to it, so rank does not decide inclusion outright; what moves is the felt threat of being dropped. That step from rank to felt security rests on common sense: a member who goes first feels her keeping is beyond question; one who goes last feels how little slack her place gives her, and that any step out of line would see her dropped. Status shielded its holders from punishment for low-severity deviance but became a liability for high-severity deviance (Karelaia and Keck 2013), so the slack a high rung gives covers small lapses, not serious ones. That work concerns formal leaders and observers' punishment; carrying it to the felt security of being kept among peers is a proposal. A member settled at the bottom who keeps to her place may still feel fairly secure, so the fall there is modest. Anxiety about exclusion among middle-status members (Phillips and Zuckerman 2001) cannot be carried by a card that follows a single source level and is left to play.

pre_language.decrement: When she goes last to everything, others groom her less and she feels how easily she could be left at the edge, and her feeling of being kept close fades.

reactive_test.reason: Grooming up the hierarchy is a pre-verbal pattern; the felt centrality is emotional; reaches Engagement through Belonging.

ripple_was.decrement_logic: When I go last and take what is left, I feel how little slack my place gives me and that any step out of line would see me dropped: my sense of being kept among them falls a little.
ripple_was.explanation: In ranked groups grooming tends to be directed up the order (Seyfarth 1977; tests have mostly but not uniformly confirmed it). Under this deck's face a place is made for members high or low who keep to it, so rank does not decide inclusion outright; what moves is the felt threat of being dropped. problems.detail: Checker rated Seyfarth partly: upward-directed grooming is the model's core prediction, with mixed tests. 'Approached and kept central' was not checked and is not Seyfarth's claim; 'attention and affiliation flow up the order' outruns a grooming model.

problems.where: explanation: 'though that credit is partly earned by competence and a serious breach by a high member can draw the harsher response'

logic_status.common_sense: That a member settled at the bottom who keeps to her place may still feel fairly secure, so the fall there is modest, is common sense under the hierarchical face, where a place is made for those who keep to it.

evidence.why: Primate behaviour, backed by a contested meta-analysis, shows grooming and consolation running up the order, but no human study tests the focal member's felt security of being kept. The one human sub-step (lapse slack) is a single paper about observers punishing leaders, so the card is provisional with the central step a gap.
evidence.boundary: Rank buys slack for small lapses only; for serious deviance high status becomes a liability (Karelaia and Keck 2013, observers' punishment of formal leaders). In primates grooming is also traded reciprocally and for support, and some species show no rank effect, so attention running up the order is one account among several. Middle-status anxiety remains to be checked as a possible non-monotone boundary.

forces.name: Self Interest Quo
forces.increment_logic: Secure at the top of the order, I feel a member's break from the settled ways as a break in the order that puts me first; it jars at once and I pull them up: my sense that such a breach is plainly wrong rises.
forces.decrement_logic: Low in the order, the settled ways are what keep me last, so a member breaking from them stirs less in me, though I still bristle a little: my sense that such a breach is wrong falls a little.
forces.explanation: Proposal, modest weight, resting on common sense with adjacent support. Those an order puts first have most to lose by a breach of it, so a breach of the settled ways jars them as a breach of their own place; those it holds at the bottom have less stake. The indignation is felt, not reasoned. Social dominance theory concerns attitudes to rank between social groups and is a trait measure, so it is set aside. The nearest checked support is the black sheep effect: an unlikeable ingroup member is judged more harshly than a matching outgroup member (Marques, Yzerbyt and Leyens 1988). That study compared ingroup with outgroup and did not measure identification; later work found highly identified members judging a disloyal fellow member more harshly, at least when the group's identity was under threat (Branscombe, Wann, Noel and Coleman 1993). The effect is contested: a 2023 pooled analysis including unpublished studies found no black sheep effect overall (d = -0.01; as reported by the reviewer, not checked here), a further reason for modest weight. Nothing there links it to rank, and treating a high place as one ground of identification is the model's step. Middle-status conformity (Phillips and Zuckerman 2001) concerns members' own conformity, and later work finds the pattern depends on ascribed status and reverses for actors of low ascribed status (Prato and colleagues 2019), so it bounds the slope only. Idiosyncrasy credit (Hollander 1958), the latitude a high-status member earns to deviate, likewise bounds the card only. Boundaries. Those holding high rank as a stable trait opposed norm violators rising, but the slope did not appear when rank was manipulated (Stamkou et al. 2016), so the card reads a settled place, not a passing one. The reaction also shifts with the violator's own rank and with whether that rank rests on dominance or prestige (Kakkar et al. 2020). The earlier appeal to system justification is withdrawn: the claim that the disadvantaged legitimise the order more than others did not hold across three large representative data sets (Brandt 2013). Keep the decrement small for a different reason: a low-ranked member who identifies with the group still bristles at breaches by the black sheep route, so far as that route holds. A low-ranked member welcoming a challenge to rules that keep her down is common sense with no test found; that is a gap, and the small decrement covers most of it. The stake in the order runs through the ways that set it, such as turns, shares, seats and precedence; a breach that wrongs a member, taking from her, hurting her or leaving her to carry the breacher's part, jars whatever her rung (see Rule-Keeping's definition). The card bites on conventions that uphold the order; for a breach that wrongs a member, play it small, with the decrement near nil. The card follows a single source level and cannot carry a middle peak. The insecurity of a place still on trial, whatever its rung, is carried by H:Belonging->Rule-Keeping (Clinging or letting go). Only her reaction to others' breaches moves here.

The nearest checked support is the black sheep effect: an unlikeable ingroup member is judged more harshly than a matching outgroup member (Marques, Yzerbyt and Leyens 1988). That study compared ingroup with outgroup and did not measure identification; later work found highly identified members judging a disloyal fellow member more harshly, at least when the group's identity was under threat (Branscombe, Wann, Noel and Coleman 1993). The effect is contested: a 2023 pooled analysis including unpublished studies found no black sheep effect overall (d = -0.01; as reported by the reviewer, not checked here), a further reason for modest weight. Nothing there links it to rank, and treating a high place as one ground of identification is the model's step. Middle-status conformity (Phillips and Zuckerman 2001) concerns members' own conformity, and later work finds the pattern depends on ascribed status and reverses for actors of low ascribed status (Prato and colleagues 2019), so it bounds the slope only. Idiosyncrasy credit (Hollander 1958), the latitude a high-status member earns to deviate, likewise bounds the card only. Boundaries. Those holding high rank as a stable trait opposed norm violators rising, but the slope did not appear when rank was manipulated (Stamkou et al. 2016), so the card reads a settled place, not a passing one. The reaction also shifts with the violator's own rank and with whether that rank rests on dominance or prestige (Kakkar et al. 2020). The earlier appeal to system justification is withdrawn: the claim that the disadvantaged legitimise the order more than others did not hold across three large representative data sets (Brandt 2013). Keep the decrement small for a different reason: a low-ranked member who identifies with the group still bristles at breaches by the black sheep route, so far as that route holds. A low-ranked member welcoming a challenge to rules that keep her down is common sense with no test found; that is a gap, and the small decrement covers most of it. The stake in the order runs through the ways that set it, such as turns, shares, seats and precedence; a breach that wrongs a member, taking from her, hurting her or leaving her to carry the breacher's part, jars whatever her rung (see Rule-Keeping's definition). The card bites on conventions that uphold the order; for a breach that wrongs a member, play it small, with the decrement near nil. The card follows a single source level and cannot carry a middle peak. The insecurity of a place still on trial, whatever its rung, is carried by H:Belonging->NormExp (Clinging or letting go). Only her reaction to others' breaches moves here.

forces.name: Built-in Advantage
forces.increment_logic: Going first as a matter of course, with the first turn and the first share mine without a word said, I feel the group opening the way to what I came for, and my sense that staying will bring it to me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: Going last as a matter of course, waiting my turn and taking what is left, I feel what I came for slipping past me to those ahead, and my sense that staying will bring it to me falls.
forces.explanation: Precedence is a standing claim on what the group hands out: the first turn, the first share and the best seat fall to the high-ranked before anyone else, so a member who goes first as a matter of course can expect what she came for to reach her, and one who goes last cannot. The step from going first or last to her expected payoff from staying rests on common sense about ordered access and has no direct test. Primate work on rank and priority of access to mates (Altmann 1962; Cowlishaw and Dunbar 1991) and on social queuing (Kokko and Johnstone 1999) points the same way, but none of it has been checked for this card and the card does not rely on it. In humans the link between men's status and reproductive success is modest (r = 0.19 across 33 nonindustrial societies; von Rueden and Jaeggi 2016, to be checked); its status measures mix settled rank with deference for what one brings, so it bears on this card only loosely. Precedence can follow from rank as well as signal it, so keep the step modest. Play it small where what she came for does not come by turns, shares or seats, as with skill or company. Where the order is a queue by seniority, a low place is the start of the line and staying is how one moves up; play the decrement weak for a junior who expects to rise.

pre_language.increment: High in the order, she takes first pick and others give way, and she goes after what she wants confident of getting it.
pre_language.decrement: Low in the order, she waits on others' leavings, and expects to miss out on what she wants.

reactive_test.reason: A felt forecast drawn from emotionally weighted evidence of where shares reach her; the pre-language forms are confident pursuit and resigned waiting.

forces.name: Faltering venture tightens ranks
forces.increment_logic: When I feel those at the top cannot steer us through what we have taken on, our settled ways look like all that still holds us on course, so a member breaking from them or pressing to change them where it bears on how we work through it, in a way the group would condemn, jars me at once as wrong, whether or not I say so: my indignation at breaches rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I feel those at the top know the way through what we have taken on, a member trying something different or urging a change in how we work through it, even in a way the group would condemn, looks like no danger, since the course is in hands that will right it, and I let it pass: my indignation at breaches eases.
forces.explanation: Deck H; the source is Team Confidence's hierarchical face. The card covers only breaches that bear on how the group works through the venture. The nearest small-group evidence: in freely interacting groups an opinion deviate was rejected more when the dissent came close to the group's decision deadline, which the authors put down to a heightened need for collective closure (Kruglanski and Webster 1991). That study manipulated time pressure, not doubt about the venture; reading a faltering venture as raising the same need for closure is an inference. The closure effect also depends on who deviates, including the deviate's gender (Doherty, searched, not checked). Across whole societies, histories of threat go with stronger norms and less tolerance of deviance (Gelfand et al. 2011), which points the same way but does not test a member's reaction to her group's venture, and the tightness measure it rests on has had its validity challenged. Work on threat rigidity, which describes constricted control and information under threat (Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981, a theory review of organisational evidence, not replicated as a test of this step), supports the tightening; the step from tightening to felt indignation rests on common sense. The face adds its own step, a common-sense proposal: in a ranked group the settled ways are partly the top's standing direction, so when live steering from the top looks weak, members lean harder on those ways and a departure reads as one more push off course; when steering looks sure, the top is trusted to catch a stray move, and it passes. Boundaries. The decrement covers departures that do not cross a call from the top; a member who defies the top's own direction is challenging the order, which this card does not carry, so keep the decrement small. The decrement also covers the group's conventions only: a breach that wrongs a member, taking from her, hurting her or leaving her to carry the breacher's part of the venture, jars however sure the steering looks (see Rule-Keeping's definition), so for such a breach set the decrement near nil. Where she reads the settled ways themselves as the cause of the trouble, departures can read as a needed correction; there the pull to guard the ways and the pull to welcome change offset each other, so the increment is nil (common sense; no direct test found, gap). These boundaries rest on common sense. Scale the card to who deviates as well as to the venture. The card covers the acute, felt jar of a venture slipping out of the leaders' grip, and the effect should be modest.

pre_language.increment: When the band's venture is going badly and the prize looks out of reach, she clings to the usual way of doing it and bristles at a fellow who does it differently, with a protest or a shove. Her norm guarding rises.
pre_language.decrement: When the prize looks well within the band's reach, she lets a fellow try an odd way of doing it without a second look. Her bristle at breaches subsides.

reactive_test.reason: Narrowed attention and a pull back to familiar routines under threat are unbidden and have animal analogues, but the step from that rigidity to indignation at others' departures is shown mainly at organisational and societal scale, and chimpanzees do not police third-party breaches, so the pre-language analogue is weaker than for the other two cards.

forces.note: The direction is consistent across the literatures I know, but none of them tests a member's felt indignation at a fellow's breach as a function of her confidence in the group's venture, and one search turned up only an unpublished null result on threat and the black sheep effect. Do not read this card as damping: threat rigidity is described as often dysfunctional, and later work argues it can feed further threat, so the loop through NormExp may deepen a faltering venture rather than rescue it. Threat rigidity also centralises control, which in a hierarchical culture may load onto high-Status members and lower others' Levelling; that is outside this card.

ripple_was.decrement_logic: When I feel those at the top know the way through what we have taken on, a member trying something different or urging a change looks like no danger, since the course is in hands that will right it, and I let it pass: my indignation at breaches eases.

critique_was.increment_logic: When I feel sure the group as it stands cannot pull off what it has set itself, a member doing things differently or pressing to change our ways jars me as wrong and I am quick to pull them up: my indignation at breaches rises.
critique_was.decrement_logic: When the venture looks well within our reach, a member trying something different or urging a change leaves me unmoved and I let it pass: my indignation at breaches eases.
critique_was.explanation: A felt threat to the group's venture narrows attention onto the established way of doing things and makes departures from it feel dangerous, so indignation at breaches rises; when success looks secure there is slack, and departures are tolerated. timing.typical: 1 to 3 seconds after the departure, while the venture feels shaky
timing.why: A faltering venture is the background state. The card's reaction is the jar at a departure, and that is immediate.

era.why: The NormExp end needs group-wide norms (Riedl et al. 2012; Tomasello). Its evidence also concerns opinion deviates in discussing groups (Kruglanski and Webster 1991), which needs language.

forces.subtitle: Faltering leadership tightens rule-guarding
forces.summary: When a member feels those at the top cannot steer the group through its venture, the settled ways look like all that holds it on course, so a breach of them jars her and her indignation rises. When she feels the top knows the way, a breach looks like no danger and her indignation eases. The effect should be modest.

problems.where: explanation: 'A felt threat to the venture narrows attention onto the established way of doing things and makes departures feel dangerous, while a venture in safe hands leaves slack for them.'
problems.detail: The only source for narrowing under threat is Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981, and both of its checks have a null verdict. The sentence states the mechanism as fact with no checked support.

problems.where: explanation: 'Under threat, control constricts (Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981; carried over, not rechecked here).'
problems.detail: The explanation itself admits the claim is unchecked. A null verdict cannot back a claim.

problems.where: explanation: '(problemistic search: Cyert and March), and since failure is readily laid at the leaders' door (Meindl, Ehrlich and Dukerich 1985)'
problems.detail: Neither source appears in the literature, so neither has been checked. The boundary they prop up can stand as common sense.

problems.where: explanation: 'The same holds where she is at the top herself and doubts her own steering.'
problems.detail: No source, and it is not safe as common sense. A leader who doubts her own steering may just as plausibly welcome a member's different approach. Drop the claim.

problems.where: framework
problems.detail: The framework lists threat rigidity and romance of leadership as grounds even though neither has been checked. Gelfand et al. 2011, which was checked and rated partly, is the better indirect support.

logic_status.common_sense: The step through the hierarchical face: settled ways stand in for weak live steering, and sure steering leaves slack. This is marked as a proposal and is safe as plain sense. The defiance boundary is also common sense. So is the offset boundary, where an openly failing course makes departures read as a correction.

dimensions.setting: lab only (student samples), plus one society-level correlational study

evidence.why: The general direction (threat or uncertainty about the group's footing raises intolerance of deviants) has single-study lab support and a contested society-level correlation, and nothing tests the card's own step through doubt about the top's steering. The card is common sense resting on analogous evidence, so it stays provisional with its boundaries, and nothing found opposes it enough to change the text.
evidence.boundary: Keep the existing boundaries (nil where the settled way is the top's openly failing course; the decrement excludes defiance of the top's own direction). Add that the step through doubt about the top's steering is untested: support comes from neighbouring threat and uncertainty work (closure near deadlines, derogation of deviants when the group's norm is undermined, tightness under societal threat), the tightness measure is under a validity challenge, and the closure effect is reported to depend on who deviates (Doherty, not read). Effect modest and acute.

forces.name: Shirkers sharpen the bristle
forces.increment_logic: When I can leave any part of the work with any member and see it carried through, a member who dodges a part or cuts a corner in the way we do the shared work stands out against everyone else's keeping of it; it jars me at once as plainly wrong and I pull them up with a sharp word: my indignation at breaches rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I keep having to check up on and chase what others took on, a dodged part or a cut corner in the shared work is only what most here do, and where it leaves no one in particular to carry it, it no longer strikes me as a breach worth pulling up; I let it pass: my indignation at breaches eases.
forces.explanation: The settled ways are read from what members actually do: people keep a norm, and expect it kept, when they see most others keep it, and drop it when they see most break it (Bicchieri and Xiao 2009). Free riders are punished in proportion to how far they fall below the others' contributions (Fehr and Gächter 2000), so the same dodge stands out more, and draws more anger, where the rest carry their parts; the negative emotions that appear to drive the punishment grow likewise (Fehr and Gächter 2002; the emotion evidence is questionnaire-based). Where many shirk, the threat of exclusion also fails to hold the line (Kerr et al. 2009). Unaffected observers punish breaches of a cooperation norm too, though less than those harmed (Fehr and Fischbacher 2004), and cooperators punish defectors even where punishing cannot narrow the payoff gap, so the motive reads as retaliation for unfair conduct rather than inequity (Falk, Fehr and Fischbacher 2005); for that reason anger at a coaster is Rule-Keeping's ground, and Parity does not carry it (E:OutResp->Levelling). The evidence concerns contributions to a common pool; reading it as doing one's part of the shared work is the model's step, and the card is limited to the way the shared work is done. Among equals pulling your weight is one of the levelling ways Rule-Keeping guards, so the step is short there. The shirking that lowered Dependability is not counted again here; the bristle at that shirking itself belongs to the scene. Noise: where she cannot see who dropped what, punishment goes astray and fails to hold up cooperation (Grechenig, Nicklisch and Thöni 2010), so set the increment small there. Boundary (see Rule-Keeping's domain limit): only conventions are local, and a dodge that leaves a particular member to carry it wrongs her, so prevalence does not soften the bristle at it; the decrement applies only where no one in particular is left carrying the dodge. The card was earlier Inverse, on the proposal that chasing shirkers sensitises her to the next breach; that runs against the evidence above and against Rule-Keeping's own definition, and is dropped. With X:NormExp->OutResp the card forms a Reinforce loop: a keen bristle keeps parts carried, and parts carried keep a dodge conspicuous. The loop runs down as readily as up, as contributions decay where shirking goes unchecked (Fehr and Gächter 2000, rounds without punishment); watch for runs from play to play. The public goods evidence is shared with X:Reciprocity->NormExp, read there as the ways of sharing; play both small where one scene fires both.

pre_language.increment: When the others keep leaving their end of the carry or the watch to her, she bristles sooner at any of them doing a thing the wrong way and moves to pull them up: a protest cry, a shove, a cold shoulder. Her norm guarding rises.
pre_language.decrement: When the others reliably hold their end of the shared task, she meets a fellow's odd way of doing things with a shrug and goes about her business. Her bristle at breaches subsides.

reactive_test.reason: Anger at those who leave her the work is an unbidden emotional reaction with a clear primate analogue in retaliation for one's own losses; the generalisation to third-party breaches is human-specific but already present in toddlers' protest, and the card moves felt indignation, not a planned sanctioning strategy. It bears on Engagement through NormExp.

forces.framework: Altruistic punishment (Fehr and Gächter 2000, 2002); third-party punishment (Fehr and Fischbacher 2004); retaliation motive (Falk, Fehr and Fischbacher 2005); empirical expectations (Bicchieri and Xiao 2009) and bad apples (Kerr et al. 2009) for the graded boundary; noise (Grechenig, Nicklisch and Thöni 2010); conditional cooperation (Fischbacher, Gächter and Fehr 2001) for the brake.

sources.source: Fehr and Gächter, 2002, Altruistic punishment in humans
sources.claim: Punishment expenditure rises with how far a member's contribution falls below the others'; negative emotions toward defectors appear to be the proximate mechanism.

sources.source: Fehr and Fischbacher, 2004, Third-party punishment and social norms
sources.claim: Up to about 60% of unaffected observers punish violations of a cooperation norm, at a cost to themselves; second parties punish more strongly than third parties.

sources.source: Kerr, Rumble, Park, Ouwerkerk, Parks, Gallucci and van Lange, 2009, How many bad apples does it take to spoil the whole barrel?
sources.claim: The threat of exclusion counters a few bad apples but not a majority of them. A boundary: where most shirk, sanctioning gives way to withdrawal.

sources.claim: Negative emotions towards defectors are the proximate mechanism of altruistic punishment of free riders.

sources.claim: Idiosyncrasy credit, earned by positively disposed impressions, permits deviation from group expectancies.

sources.source: Fehr, E., Gächter, S., 2002, Altruistic punishment in humans, Nature 415
sources.claim: Anger at defectors drives punishment

sources.source: Fischbacher, U., Gächter, S., Fehr, E., 2001, Are people conditionally cooperative?, Economics Letters 71
sources.claim: Contribution tracks others' contribution

sources.source: Idiosyncrasy credit (Hollander) and later tests
sources.claim: Leniency towards deviant leaders is conditional and not specified by the theory

forces.note: The evidence is strongest where shirkers are a minority. Where most members shirk, public-goods groups mostly respond by cutting their own contributions rather than sanctioning, so the rise may level off near the floor of OutResp; a cap or a saturating increment is advisable. Status and Levelling gate the outward sign: a low-ranked or cowed member may feel the bristle but pull up only those at or below her, so intimates may under-read it. This card feeds NormExp but I found no defensible return path from NormExp to OutResp (see X:NormExp->OutResp), so it does not by itself close a balancing loop.

edits_log: 5 Nov 2026: Ben approved, 5 Nov 2026, 11.22 am (comparative psychologist's critique, docs/v3/sc-critique/): The source supports anger at free riding, not a general bristle at every departure.

Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The two lines cover different breaches. The increment is about a member who cuts a corner, which is shirking and so sits on OutResp's ground (reliability). The decrement is about a member doing the shared work their own way, which is a departure from settled ways (NormExp). logic_status.common_sense: Where she has been left to chase and redo others' work, she reads a different way of doing the shared work as another dodge; among people who deliver, she lets the same departure pass. This is safe as plain sense if it is marked as the card's step and kept to the way the shared work is done. A weak increment where nearly everyone shirks is also common sense, matching the sibling card X:Reciprocity->Rule-Keeping.

evidence.why: The central step, that a shirker draws more sanction the further he falls below what the others contribute and that people read what is expected from what others do, rests on behaviour replicated across many societies and a meta-analysis (Herrmann et al. 2008, Henrich et al. 2006, Balliet et al. 2011) and on the replicated conditional-cooperation finding. The questionnaire-based emotion mechanism and the reading of pool contributions as one's part of the shared work are unreplicated single-study support and the model's step, which the card already flags, so they do not lower the grade; Kerr 2009 and Hollander are not load-bearing.

forces.name: Hoarders stir the levellers
forces.increment_logic: When whoever has gives to whoever needs and what I put in comes back from any member, a member who keeps back what should go round stands out against everyone else's giving; it strikes me at once as wrong and I am quick to pull them up: my indignation at breaches rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When what I give stops coming back and those with a surplus hide it, a member keeping back what should go round is only doing what most here now do, and where no one in particular is left in need by it, it no longer strikes me as a breach worth pulling up; I let it pass: my indignation at breaches eases.
forces.explanation: The settled ways are read from what members actually do: people keep a norm, and expect it kept, when they see most others keep it, and drop it when they see most break it (Bicchieri and Xiao 2009). Free riders are punished in proportion to how far they fall below the others' contributions (Fehr and Gächter 2000), so the same holding back stands out more, and draws more anger, where the rest give freely; the negative emotions that appear to drive the punishment grow likewise (Fehr and Gächter 2002; the emotion evidence is questionnaire-based). Reading a high return as a sign that sharing is still kept, and a low return as a sign that it has lapsed, is the model's step, and follows Reciprocity's egalitarian anchors (whoever has gives; those with a surplus hide it). The card was earlier Inverse, on the proposal that being left short sensitises her to the next departure; that ran against Rule-Keeping's definition and against X:OutResp->NormExp, which dropped the same proposal on the same evidence, and is dropped. Her own grievance at being left short is Reciprocity's ground, and the extra anger of one harmed over a bystander (Fehr and Fischbacher 2004) belongs to the scene. Boundary: where she alone is left short while the others still share among themselves, sharing still reads as the settled way, so set the decrement near nil. Boundary (see Rule-Keeping's domain limit): only conventions are local, and holding back that leaves a particular member in need wrongs her, so prevalence does not soften the bristle at it; the decrement applies only where no one in particular is left in need. About half of subjects in a one-shot public goods experiment cooperated conditionally, giving more the more others gave (Fischbacher, Gächter and Fehr 2001); that is her own conformity, not Rule-Keeping, and is context only. The felt indignation is better supported than the voiced rebuke: bystanders to unfairness feel modest anger but seldom act on it (Pedersen, McAuliffe and McCullough 2018, searched, not verified), so the pulling up is the likelier sequel, not a certain one. Enforcement also depends on settled cooperative norms and trust: where civic norms are weak, punishment can turn antisocial and fall on cooperators (Herrmann, Thöni and Gächter 2008; Balliet and Van Lange 2013; both searched, not verified). The public goods evidence is shared with X:OutResp->NormExp; here it is read as the ways of sharing and helping, there as doing one's part of the work, and each reading is the model's step. Play both small where one scene fires both. The card reads her guarding of a settled way of sharing, which is Rule-Keeping's ground; the levelling of a grabber who takes more than his due and makes it stick is Parity's ground and stays there. The felt jar may run ahead of the voiced rebuke where her Rank or Parity is low. Any era claim for third-party enforcement stays unchecked until Pedersen et al. 2018 and Riedl et al. 2012 are read in full.

pre_language.increment: When her food goes out and nothing comes back while others hide their surplus, she bristles at fellows doing things the wrong way and moves to demand, protest or turn her back; her norm guarding rises.
pre_language.decrement: When food passes freely and comes back to her from whoever next has, a fellow's odd way of doing things draws no bristle; her norm guarding falls.

reactive_test.reason: Demand sharing, protest at the stingy and coalitional mockery of the self-aggrandising have pre-language and forager analogues; the response is indignant rather than calculated; it acts on Engagement through NormExp.

forces.framework: Conditional cooperation (Fischbacher, Gächter and Fehr 2001); altruistic punishment (Fehr and Gächter 2002); empirical expectations (Bicchieri and Xiao 2009).

sources.source: Peterson, 1993, Demand sharing: reciprocity and the pressure for generosity among foragers, American Anthropologist 95: 860-874
sources.claim: Forager sharing runs largely on demands and pressure for generosity, not unsolicited giving: the egalitarian return is enforced.

sources.source: Wiessner, 2005, Norm enforcement among the Ju/'hoansi Bushmen: a case of strong reciprocity?, Human Nature 16: 115-145
sources.claim: Breaches, including stinginess, are met mainly with criticism and mockery; enforcement is common though its effect on behaviour is limited.

sources.source: Boehm, 1993, Egalitarian behavior and reverse dominance hierarchy, Current Anthropology 34: 227-254
sources.claim: Egalitarian bands keep would-be dominants and hoarders in check by ridicule, criticism and ostracism.

Where giving comes back and those with plenty share, someone who keeps back what should go round stands out and draws anger, so Rule-Keeping rises. Where giving stops coming back and surplus is hidden, holding back is only what most do, and Rule-Keeping eases, unless it leaves a particular member in need.

logic_status.common_sense: Several claims rest on common sense. When nobody shares any more, holding back is no departure, so the increment is weak. A member secure in the return can overlook an occasional lapse. A flat refusal still stands out in a high-giving group. The felt jar may run ahead of the voiced rebuke when her Rank or Parity is low. All of these are safe as plain sense about norms measured against what the group actually does.

evidence.why: The parts are replicated or supported at the adjacent level (conditional cooperation, anger at free riders that grows with their shortfall, forager criticism of stinginess), but no study tests whether being left short herself makes a member quicker to resent the next breach, and none of the sources is yet verified. It stays provisional, with the norm-dependence boundary and a softer voiced rebuke.
evidence.boundary: Keep the graded boundary that the effect shrinks as hoarding spreads, since which ways count as settled is read from what members do. forces.name: Low in the order, guarded
forces.increment_logic: When I hold a high place in a settled order, I expect an objection or a slip of mine to be let pass, with no one pouncing on it, so I let it show with less softening first: my felt safety to show myself rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When I sit low in the order, I expect a slip or an objection of mine to be pounced on while those above are watching, so I soften every objection and swallow my first reaction: my felt safety to show myself falls.
forces.explanation: A low place goes with holding back while those above watch, and a high place in a settled order with expecting slips to be let pass. Subordinate rhesus monkeys that had learned a task performed it only when apart from higher-ranking animals, with little aggression needed to suppress it (Drea and Wallen 1999); subordinate chimpanzees approach only food a dominant cannot see (Hare et al. 2000); self-directed behaviour, a measure of anxiety, rises when the nearest neighbour is dominant (Castles, Whiten and Aureli 1999). Low-ranking victims of aggression are consoled less than high-ranking ones (Romero, Castellanos and de Waal 2010), a sign that a low place draws less kindly attention; consolation itself, a need met, is Reciprocity's ground and is not played here. Reduced power goes with attention to threat and inhibited social behaviour (Keltner, Gruenfeld and Anderson 2003), a theory paper about power, so carrying it to settled rank is the model's step. In hospital teams, higher profession-based status goes with greater psychological safety, and leader inclusiveness weakens the status gap (Nembhard and Edmondson 2006; checked against the abstract only). Embarrassment works as an appeasement display (Keltner and Buswell 1997), which fits the softening in the decrement line. Keep the increment smaller than the decrement: the power literature reports approach and inhibition effects of unequal size, and the primate evidence concerns subordinates holding back, not dominants opening up. Boundaries. Where places are being contested, set the increment nil: in unstable orders dominants carry the most stress (Sapolsky 2005), and alpha male baboons have high glucocorticoids (Gesquiere et al. 2011). Scale the card to dominance style: large in steep, despotic orders and small in tolerant ones, where conflicts are milder and more often two-way (Thierry 2000, not checked here). Scale it also to power distance: the cost of speaking up from a low place is greater where hierarchy is accepted as proper (not checked here). Rank and safety stay distinct readings, since a member can be well placed in a group that punishes slips, or lowly in one that does not; an inclusive leader weakens the card. Play rule: where her Parity reading is high because those above hear her out (X:Parity->Safety), play this card's decrement small; play it at full size only where those above are known to pounce. Where E:Parity->Safety or X:Parity->Safety fires on the same nearby dominant, play only one. The same holding back shows as unseen skill on H:Rank->Esteem; do not count one act on both in a scene. This card carries the route through settled place; E:Esteem->Safety carries the weaker route through live deference for what she brings. From the comparative psychologist's synthesis build (Standing->Safety), its most-used card.

pre_language.increment: When she stands high in the band, she bares a protest openly and goes on, and no one turns on her for it. Her ease in showing herself rises.
pre_language.decrement: When she stands low, she wraps any protest in appeasing grins and crouches, checks her first flare, and flushes and averts when caught out. Her ease in showing herself falls.

forces.framework: Subordinate inhibition (Drea and Wallen 1999; Hare et al. 2000); rank and social anxiety (Castles et al. 1999); rank and consolation (Romero et al. 2010); rank, stability and stress (Sapolsky 2005; Gesquiere et al. 2011); approach/inhibition theory of power (Keltner, Gruenfeld and Anderson 2003); embarrassment as appeasement (Keltner and Buswell 1997); professional status and psychological safety (Nembhard and Edmondson 2006).

timing.typical: 1 to 5 seconds
timing.why: A low place primes the threat response at once: the urge to soften, swallow a reaction or flush when caught out comes unbidden at the moment of exposure.

era.why: Rank-linked appeasement, submission and inhibited display are plain in social primates (Gilbert; Keltner), and a settled dominance order needs no language.

forces.subtitle: Low rank makes speaking up unsafe
forces.summary: A member high in a settled order expects a slip or objection to be let pass, so she shows herself with less softening and feels a little safer. A member low in the order expects a slip to be pounced on while those above watch, so she softens objections and holds back, and her felt safety to show herself falls. The fall is the larger effect.

problems.where: explanation: 'Low rank keeps the threat system primed: appeasing, submissive and shame displays come unbidden, and each retreat is felt as a sign that showing oneself is dangerous; high rank releases them.'
problems.detail: Social rank theory (Gilbert) is not in the literature and has not been checked. Keltner and Buswell 1997 supports embarrassment as appeasement, but the checker found nothing tying it to rank. No source backs the self-perception loop ('each retreat is felt as a sign').

problems.where: explanation: 'Reduced power goes with attention to threat and inhibited behaviour (Keltner, Gruenfeld and Anderson 2003)'
problems.detail: The source is a theory paper about power, defined as control of resources and punishments. The card applies it to settled rank without saying that this is the model's step.

problems.where: explanation: 'profession-based status goes with greater psychological safety (Nembhard and Edmondson 2006)'
problems.detail: Rated partly. The direction was not confirmed from the paper, the setting is neonatal intensive care teams, and the link is moderated by leader inclusiveness, which the card leaves out.

problems.where: framework: 'Social rank theory (Gilbert); ... psychological safety and status (Kahn; ...)'
problems.detail: Gilbert and Kahn have not been checked and are not in the literature.

logic_status.common_sense: A low place leads her to expect a put-down for a slip or objection, and a high place leads her to expect it to be let pass. This is safe as plain sense and agrees in direction with the checked power and status sources. The distinction between rank and safety, and the weakening of the card under an inclusive leader, are also common sense; the second agrees with the moderation reported by Nembhard and Edmondson.

dimensions.setting: narrow (one health care field survey; captive and wild primates; lab power studies)

evidence.why: Primatology, organisational behaviour and power theory agree on the direction, but none of the sources is a replication, the one human field test uses formal professional status in one clinical setting, and no direct test of felt rank within a small group was found (a gap). The card already marks the increment as small, so the text can stand with the added power-distance boundary.
evidence.boundary: Keep the existing boundaries (nil where places are contested; larger in despotic orders, smaller in tolerant ones; an inclusive leader narrows the gap). Add power distance or culture as a scale factor, since high power distance raises the cost of speaking up. The high-place increment is weaker than the low-place decrement: the primate evidence concerns subordinates holding back, and the 2025 power meta-analysis is reported (not read) to find inhibition links smaller than approach links. Power and settled rank are different constructs, so the power literature is analogous only.

forces.name: Heard from where I sit
forces.increment_logic: When I go first as a matter of course, I expect what I put forward to be taken as good before it has shown its worth, my suggestion taken up and the result credited to me, and I feel they turn to me for what I bring: my sense that they defer to me for it rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When I go last as a matter of course, I keep my way of doing things to myself while those above are watching, so what I bring stays out of sight, I expect anything I do put forward to count for less than the same from someone higher, however good it is, and I expect the next problem to go to someone else: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring falls.
forces.explanation: Two routes. First, her expectation from her rank: status creates expectations that favour those already ahead, and hierarchies reinforce themselves through those expectations (Magee and Galinsky 2008); eminent people get more credit for comparable work (Merton 1968), though such cumulative credit is contested outside peer review. Those works describe how others judge and credit; that she, knowing her rank, infers the same deference for herself is a common-sense step, and the others' actual crediting belongs to the scene. Expectation states theory (Berger and colleagues) makes the same argument about who is listened to in task groups, but no primary source for it has been checked yet. Second, her own inhibition: subordinate rhesus monkeys that had learned a task performed it only when apart from higher-ranking animals (Drea and Wallen 1999), so what a low-ranked member brings stays out of sight. Chimpanzees copy dominant as well as knowledgeable models (Kendal et al. 2015), so rank draws the watching that Esteem reads. The reading stays on Esteem's ground; deference owed to the place itself is Rank and is not carried here. A superior who takes her credit, or decides without hearing her, is Parity's ground (H:Parity->Esteem, and I:Parity->Esteem#2 in the scene) and is not carried here either. With H:Esteem->Rank it forms a reinforcing pair. The brake is Esteem evidence, a visible failure of what she brings. Boundary, provisional: the halo is strongest where a contribution's worth is hard to judge and credit is assigned opaquely, and weakens where quality is easily seen or credit is transparent, since a plain result can be seen whoever offers it (consistent with Huber et al. 2022, searched, though that work does not test this boundary). The increment rests on that unchecked expectation, so keep it modest. The holding back is the same act that lowers Safety on X:Rank->Safety; do not count one act on both in a scene. Where the scene stages the others crediting or passing over what she puts forward, play the interaction card I:Rank->Esteem instead of this one, never both.

edits_log: Ripple round 9, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Boundary with Status. The revised Prestige definition says the deference is given, not owed to any place in the order. The increment line opens with her suggestion 'listened to before it has shown its worth', which reads as deference owed to her rung, and that is Status's ground. Expectation states theory puts the mechanism in the others' inflated judgement of what she brings, and her rank shapes that judgement. The line and the explanation should both say so, which keeps the target reading on Prestige's ground. The decrement line, the type and the literature pass.
logic check Tier 2 fix (wording), facilitator's under Ben's rule of 5 Nov 2026, 4.33 pm: explanation

comp-r2-minor: Added the inhibition route (subordinates hiding competence) to the decrement and explanation, with a double-count rule against X:Status->DivsExp. (facilitator, Tier 2 or 3, Ben's rule of 5 Nov 2026, 4.43 pm)
focal-trims: First route recast as her rank-based expectation; others' crediting moved to scene. (facilitator, Tier 2 or 3, Ben's rule of 5 Nov 2026, 4.43 pm)

evidence search, 6 Nov 2026 (facilitator, Tier 3): Labelled her inference of deference from rank as common sense, kept the increment modest, wrote in the hard-to-judge and opaque-credit boundary as provisional, and noted that Matthew-type credit is contested outside peer review.

Ripple round 8, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The decrement strays into Parity's ground. Having her contribution 'credited to someone higher' is a superior taking more than his due of credit, and being 'passed over' when she puts something forward reads as not being heard. Under the revised hierarchical faces, whether those above hear her out and deal evenly with her is Parity's ground, and Esteem's hierarchical face excludes it. Smallest fix: the decrement keeps the inhibition route and the discounting of her contribution against those higher, without credit-taking or denied hearing, and the explanation names the boundary.

Ripple round 9, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The increment line ends with 'I feel sure they turn to me for what I bring', which overreaches. The explanation calls the rank-to-deference inference a common-sense step resting on an unchecked expectation and says to keep the increment modest. Feeling sure also reads like Esteem's high anchor, as if rank alone could carry her there, when the Prestige hierarchical face says deference is given, not owed to the place. Softened to match the explanation.

Ripple round 10, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): (3, 6) The decrement line has her watch the next problem go to someone else. That stages the others' response, which a focal card must not assume; it belongs to the twin I:Status->Prestige, which shares the card's name. Make it her expectation instead. The explanation also lacks the twin rule that the other focal cards with interaction twins carry, so the two could both fire on one act. Lines otherwise sit on Rank (high and low anchors) and Esteem; the type matches; the literature is cited accurately (Magee and Galinsky 2008; Merton 1968; Drea and Wallen 1999; Kendal et al. 2015).
