problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: "Rank sets performance expectations, and expectations steer who is listened to and how contributions are judged, in a self-fulfilling way (expectation states theory)."
problems.detail: The only source given for expectation states theory is a Wikipedia entry the checker could not read (verdict: not found), and no primary work by Berger and colleagues or Correll and Ridgeway was located. The sentence carries the card's main mechanism. Magee and Galinsky (supports) back the narrower claim that status creates expectations favouring those already ahead and that hierarchies reinforce themselves, and Merton (supports) backs extra credit for the eminent. The named theory and the specific steering of who is listened to are uncited until a primary source is checked.

logic_status.common_sense: The proposal that the halo is strongest when a contribution's worth is hard to judge rests on common sense: a plain result can be judged on its face whoever offers it, so prior expectations have least room to act. It is marked as a proposal and nothing checked contradicts it. The boundary sentence (deference owed to the place is Rank, deference for what she brings is Esteem) is a model definition, not an empirical claim.

forces.framework: Self-reinforcing status expectations (Magee and Galinsky 2008); Matthew effect (Merton 1968); subordinate inhibition (Drea and Wallen 1999); rank-biased copying (Kendal et al. 2015).

evidence.why: Four independent fields (small-group sociology, meta-science of peer review, primatology, social psychology of hierarchy) converge on rank bringing credit and uptake from others, with two meta-analyses and a large preregistered experiment, which meets strong consilience on adjacent evidence. The contest found concerns cumulative advantage in funding and one unidentified small null, neither load-bearing; the bias handling of the two meta-analyses still needs confirming from full text.
evidence.boundary: The crediting halo is strongest where the worth of a contribution is hard to judge and weaker where quality is easily judged or credit is assigned transparently (the proposed moderator fits Huber et al. 2022, a hard-to-judge case, but is untested). Matthew-type cumulative advantage in research funding is weak or mixed (multi-funder replication, 2025 preprint), so the card should claim the immediate crediting step and not a compounding one. The decrement's withholding route (Drea and Wallen 1999; Amici, Call and Aureli 2009) is better supported than the increment.
evidence.caveat: The evidence measures how others treat a ranked member: expectation states meta-analyses (Driskell and Mullen 1990; Kalkhoff and Thye 2006) and a preregistered peer-review field experiment (Huber et al. 2022) show higher status brings more credit and uptake, and primate studies show subordinates withholding skill before dominants. The member's own felt sense that the others turn to her for what she brings is the model's framing of that link.

forces.name: Settling into a place
forces.increment_logic: When the others keep turning to me for what I bring, leave the first word to me, hand me decisions and leave jobs that matter in my hands, I come to take that first word as mine as a matter of course, and I feel it has become my place: my felt rung in the order rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When what I bring stops counting and my word is doubted in front of the others, with nothing that matters handed to me, I stop expecting the first word and give way: my felt rung in the order slips a little.
forces.explanation: Freely conferred deference is a route to rank (Henrich and Gil-White; Cheng et al.). Contributors are repaid with standing and influence (Willer), and perceived competence buys influence (Anderson and Kilduff). Once established, status holds itself through expectations (Magee and Galinsky). Those works describe the others conferring rank, which belongs to the scene; here she settles into the place, or lets it go, herself as the deference she reads builds up, a step resting on common sense. Respect for skill need not become rank or influence (von Rueden, Gurven and Kaplan 2008), so the increment rests on deference that shows up as decisions and jobs that matter handed to her; esteem alone, with nothing handed over, does not fire it. The rise needs the others to leave the first word to her; deference alone, with no turn ceded, moves Rank little. Across 276 samples, status in face-to-face groups fitted a micropolitics path best and competence and virtue paths only tentatively (Grosz et al. 2024, as reported by the reviewer, not checked here), as the I twin's boundary already notes. The step from live deference to a place taken for granted is slow. Proposal: each play moves Rank by a small fraction of Esteem's level, so the settling builds over many plays; make the decrement weaker than the increment, because a settled place outlasts the skill that earned it. That asymmetry rests on theory only (Magee and Galinsky 2008; expectation-states accounts of how a standing order preserves itself) and has no direct test. It applies once a place is established: in a new group's early weeks, places still move when contributions fall short, so there play the decrement at full strength. This card absorbs the older model's most-used card: being trusted with something that matters is Esteem evidence, and its settling is this card.

forces.subtitle: Deference slowly becomes rank
forces.summary: When others keep turning to a member for what she brings, leave her the first word and hand her decisions and jobs that matter, she comes to take that first word as hers and her felt rung rises. When her contribution stops counting and her word is doubted, she gives way and her rung slips a little. Settling is slow, and loss is weaker than gain.

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)
logic_status.common_sense: Two claims rest on common sense. (1) The step from live deference to a place taken for granted is slow, so each play moves Rank by a small fraction: one show of regard does not make a settled place, and the self-reinforcing persistence of status (Magee and Galinsky, supports) fits a slow build. (2) The decrement is weaker than the increment because a settled place outlasts the skill that earned it: seniority and incumbency are familiar everywhere, and the same self-reinforcement finding points the same way. Neither is contradicted by checked literature. Willer (supports) concerns contribution as the route to status, and Anderson and Kilduff (partly) shows signalled competence winning influence only in short lab tasks; the card claims no more from them than that contribution and perceived competence buy standing and influence, which is within what they show. Henrich and Gil-White and Cheng et al. (both supports) carry the core link from freely conferred deference to rank.

evidence.why: Six fields (social psychology, small-group sociology, behavioural economics, organisational behaviour, anthropology, primatology) converge on deference for what one brings becoming rank and influence, which meets strong consilience on adjacent evidence; the dominance-prestige dispute concerns dominance and does not touch this step. The only field contest (von Rueden et al. 2008) and the movement of early positions (Bendersky and Shah 2013) are written in as boundaries.
evidence.boundary: Respect for skill does not always become rank or influence (von Rueden, Gurven and Kaplan 2008, Tsimane), so the increment depends on deference shown as decisions and jobs handed over, as the line already says. The weaker decrement holds for established places; in new groups early positions move when contributions fall short (Bendersky and Shah 2013), so there the decrement may match the increment. The asymmetry has theoretical support only.
evidence.caveat: The evidence measures others' conferral and observed influence: prestige behaviour predicts peer-rated and behavioural influence (Cheng et al. 2013, with a natural-team follow-up), contributors gain status (Willer 2009), and established hierarchies are preserved by expectations. The member's own felt rung rising from the deference she receives is the model's framing of that link.

forces.name: Backed into my place
forces.increment_logic: When I am kept among them and a place is made for me as a matter of course, and a turn or a share of mine is questioned, I feel the room is with me and hold to it without a word: my felt rung in the order, shaken by the question, firms up again.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am kept at the edge and my turn or my share is questioned in front of the others, I feel no one here would speak for me, and I give way: my felt rung in the order falls a little.
forces.explanation: In macaques, kin support matters for winning rank (Chapais and Larose 1988), though keeping rank among peers need not depend on it when subordinates cannot form coalitions (same source), and grooming is traded for agonistic support (Schino 2007), in line with Seyfarth's (1977) model of grooming directed up the hierarchy for rank-related benefits. Those findings concern support from particular partners in return for service. That is the ground of H Reciprocity, where a patron covers you. This card reads the acceptance of the group as a whole and takes from the primate work, by analogy only, that whether a challenge to a place succeeds depends partly on who backs it. The card therefore fires only when a turn or share of hers is contested; it does not carry a rank held steady by acceptance alone. The human step has no direct test and is a proposal, common sense in any committee: a member kept at the edge whose turn is questioned feels no one would speak for her and gives way, while one kept among them feels the room with her and holds. The decrement's route through felt self-worth is uncertain: two 2009 meta-analyses of rejection disagree on whether exclusion lowers self-esteem (Blackhart et al. 2009; Gerber and Wheeler 2009), so the card leans on her reading that no one would back her more than on any drop in her worth. Whether the questioner in fact yields belongs to the scene. Hierarchical acceptance is held at any rung, high or low. The increment therefore only firms up a turn or share that was in doubt and never lifts her above her place; keep it smaller than the decrement. It is distinct from Esteem: the felt assent is for who she is to them, not for what she brings. Where the questioning is an open charge, by someone of standing, that she has stepped out of her place, the charge itself is Face's ground and reaches Rank through H:Face->Rank; this card then carries only whether the room backs her, and the drop in Rank is counted once in the scene.

sources.source: Schino, G., 2007, Grooming and agonistic support: a meta-analysis of primate reciprocal altruism, Behavioral Ecology 18: 115-120
sources.claim: Across 36 studies and 14 species, grooming and agonistic support are positively related (r about 0.15).

sources.source: Seyfarth, R., 1977, A model of social grooming among adult female monkeys, Journal of Theoretical Biology 65: 671-698
sources.claim: Grooming is directed up the hierarchy in exchange for rank-related benefits including support.

sources.source: Chapais, B. & Larose, F. (1988). Experimental rank reversals among peers in Macaca fuscata: rank is maintained after the removal of kin support. American Journal of Primatology 16: 31-42
sources.claim: Backing matters for acquiring rank, but peer rank held after support was removed when no challenge arose; supports the card firing only when a place is questioned (by analogy).

sources.source: Hartgerink, C. H. J., van Beest, I., Wicherts, J. M. & Williams, K. D. (2015). The ordinal effects of ostracism: a meta-analysis of 120 Cyberball studies. PLoS ONE 10(5): e0127002
sources.claim: Exclusion sharply threatens need satisfaction, grounding the low pole of the Belonging input; does not test the step to felt rank (bias handling unconfirmed).

sources.source: Chapais, B., Larose, F. (1988). Experimental rank reversals among peers in Macaca fuscata: rank is maintained after the removal of kin support. American Journal of Primatology 16: 31-42
sources.claim: Backing matters for rank when it is challenged; without challenge, rank holds after support is removed (analogy, supports the conditional framing).

sources.source: Blackhart, G. C., Nelson, B. C., Knowles, M. L., Baumeister, R. F. (2009). Rejection elicits emotional reactions but neither causes immediate distress nor lowers self-esteem. Personality and Social Psychology Review 13: 269-309
sources.claim: Contest: rejection did not lower self-esteem against neutral controls, against Gerber and Wheeler (2009).

sources.source: Chapais, B., & Larose, F. (1988). Experimental rank reversals among peers in Macaca fuscata: rank is maintained after the removal of kin support. American Journal of Primatology, 16, 31-42.
sources.claim: Supporting only (analogous) and for the boundary: kin support matters for acquiring rank, but peer rank held after support was removed because subordinates did not challenge, which fits the card's condition that it fires only when a place is questioned.

timing.typical: 2 to 10 seconds
timing.why: The challenge to her turn is met or left unmet on the spot, and she yields or holds her place as the allies move to her side or stay silent.

era.why: Coalitionary support for rank, traded for grooming, is well shown in macaques (Chapais; Schino), so the backing and the yielding have direct primate analogues.

forces.subtitle: Being backed protects your rank
forces.summary: A member kept among the group, with a place made for her, feels the room is with her when her turn or share is questioned, so her felt rung firms up again. A member kept at the edge feels no one would speak for her and gives way, so her rung falls a little. The card applies only when a turn or share is contested.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: "kin and allied support is central to acquiring rank (Chapais 1992)"
problems.detail: The checker could not identify a Chapais 1992 paper, and the cited URL points to Chapais, Girard and Primi 1991 on non-kin alliances, which does not state the claim. The paper that does support it is Chapais and Larose 1988 (supports, abstract). The citation needs to name that paper.

problems.where: explanation: "takes from the primate work only that a place in the order is held partly by who would let it stand"
problems.detail: The same Chapais and Larose 1988 abstract reports that among peers, keeping rank need not depend on kin support when subordinates cannot form coalitions, and Chapais and St-Pierre 1997 is reported (from its title) as finding kin bonds unnecessary for keeping matrilineal rank. The primate work supports support as a route to winning rank, which fits a challenge to a turn or share, and does not support rank being held by support. The word 'held' overreaches.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: "with grooming directed up the hierarchy for rank-related benefits (Seyfarth 1977; Schino and Aureli 2008)"
problems.detail: Schino and Aureli 2008 rated partly: its finding is grooming exchanged for grooming, and rank-related benefits appear only as cited background. Seyfarth 1977 alone carries the upward-grooming claim, and it is a model whose tests are mixed.

logic_status.common_sense: The human step is offered as common sense: a member kept at the edge whose turn is challenged finds no one speaking for her and gives way, while one kept among them has the challenge fail. That is safe as ordinary experience of groups and committees, and it is labelled as a proposal. The rule that the increment only firms up a turn or share already in doubt, and stays smaller than the decrement, also rests on common sense: acceptance can be held at any rung, so it defends a place rather than raising one.

dimensions.setting: narrow (captive and free-ranging primates; lab exclusion studies; one small-scale society)

evidence.why: The pieces are analogous or adjacent (exclusion threatens belonging, primate backing matters when a place is challenged, perceived support goes with challenge appraisal), and nothing tests the central step that felt belonging decides whether a questioned member holds or yields her felt rung. The card's conditional wording already matches what the evidence allows, so it stays provisional with the added contest on the self-worth route.
evidence.boundary: Keep the written boundaries (fires only when a turn or share is questioned; the increment only restores a place in doubt and never lifts her above it; primate coalition evidence by analogy only). Add that the decrement's self-worth route is contested: Blackhart et al. (2009, verified) found rejection did not lower self-esteem against neutral controls, while Gerber and Wheeler (2009, not verified) found it did. No direct human test of felt rank under challenge as a function of felt belonging was found (a gap; status characteristics and bystander-support work not yet searched).

forces.name: Friends get the rope
forces.increment_logic: When the others draw me in as one of their own, I expect them not to let one of their own down on the work we share, so I hand them parts of it without a second thought and leave them to it: my confidence that they will do their part rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am left at the edge, I expect them to feel no call to keep their word to someone who is not one of their own, so I keep the work in my own hands and check what little I hand over: my confidence that they will do their part falls.
forces.explanation: The felt shift at the cue rests on group-based trust: people extend more trust to fellow members of their own group because they expect them to treat members well (Foddy, Platow and Yamagishi 2009, not checked here). The ingroup effect in trust games is small (Romano et al. 2017; the size of about d 0.14 is not checked here) and appears to depend on reputational stakes, on membership being common knowledge and on culture (moderators reported in the meta-analysis of Balliet, Wu and De Dreu 2014 as well; neither source checked here for this card, including the claim that it is weaker in Japan). That work compares ingroup with outgroup; carrying it to graded acceptance within one group is the model's extension, and so is narrowing expected good treatment to expecting members not to let one of their own down on shared work. Being drawn in as one of their own tells her she is a member they will not leave in the lurch, so she leaves work in their hands more readily. Whether help she gives or asks for comes back is Reciprocity's ground and is not carried here. The decrement, that a member left at the edge trusts less and checks more, has no direct test and rests on the same extension. Parts she has seen carried through or dropped outweigh this card, as Dependability's definition says, so it bites only on parts not yet done or whose outcome she cannot see. Trust that rests on her own fondness for the members is carried by E:Warmth->Dependability; where both fire, play this card small. The gain for Dependability also builds across plays from sampling, a common-sense step pending a check of Fetchenhauer and Dunning 2010 and Denrell 2005: a member who trusts more sees more work carried through, while one who withholds trust sees little and has nothing to correct her last let-down. Control read as distrust lowers the other's effort (Falk and Kosfeld 2006), an effect that is real but usually small on replication (Ziegelmeyer, Schmelz and Ploner 2012); that is the others' response and belongs to the scene, so over many plays withheld trust may prove partly self-fulfilling there, not on this card. Keep the card modest.

timing.typical: within the task, as she hands out the next piece of work
timing.why: Warm or cold treatment shifts at once how readily she trusts and which memories come up, and the felt confidence settles as she decides what to hand over; the larger gain builds over many plays.

era.why: Chimpanzees extend more trust to friends in a non-verbal trust game (Engelmann and Herrmann 2016), and leaving a part of joint work to a partner has early human analogues before words are given.

forces.subtitle: Belonging breeds trust in others' work
forces.summary: When others draw a member in as one of their own, she expects them not to let her down on shared work, so she hands over parts of it freely and her confidence that they will do their part rises. Left at the edge, she expects less and keeps the work close, and that confidence falls. Parts she has seen carried through or dropped outweigh this.
forces.summary_status: generated from the source texts, not canon; checked faithful

problems.where: explanation, sentence 3: "...since withheld trust gets no feedback that could correct it (Fetchenhauer and Dunning 2010; Denrell 2005)."
problems.detail: Neither Fetchenhauer and Dunning 2010 nor Denrell 2005 appears among the cited sources, and neither has a checker's verdict. The sentence carries the card's mechanism for the gain to Dependability building across plays, so the card's main mechanism has no checked support.

problems.where: increment_logic: "the times they carried work through come to mind before the lapses"; decrement_logic: "the last let-down comes back to me as the verdict on them"
problems.detail: These are claims about memory at the cue, and no source makes them. The explanation's own account is a slower sampling effect across plays, not a recall bias within seconds, so the lines claim more than the explanation and its sources show. The fix restates them as acts she can observe.

problems.where: explanation, final sentence: "Elaboration: when the low reading comes from being shut out, her reaction may show hostility... (Twenge, Baumeister, Tice and Stucke 2001)."
problems.detail: Twenge et al. rated partly: aggression is a behaviour, and the source says nothing about one's assessment of others, which is Dependability's ground. The checker also flags the exclusion-aggression effect as contested. The sentence describes conduct rather than the target reading. Drop it from this card.

logic_status.common_sense: The carry from the chimpanzee trust game to confidence that members do their part of the work is declared as analogy; it is safe as common sense in that people drawn into a group extend more working trust to its members. The sampling argument (withheld trust gets no feedback that could correct it) is sound reasoning on its own, but it is currently attributed to sources nobody has checked; the fix recasts it as common sense pending a check.

forces.framework: Group-based trust (Foddy, Platow and Yamagishi 2009, pending check); sampling as proposal; control aversion (Falk and Kosfeld 2006).

dimensions.replication: some (ingroup favouritism in cooperation pooled by meta-analysis, bias correction not confirmed)
dimensions.setting: lab only (cross-cultural trust games; one captive chimpanzee study)

evidence.why: Replicated ingroup favouritism in cooperation and a multi-society trust game back the sign, but the pooled effect has no confirmed bias correction, it is small and contested (a null in an investment game, a weaker effect in Japan, mixed exclusion results), and it concerns category membership, not felt acceptance or handing over shared work. Provisional, with the within-group step marked as extension and the moderators written in.
evidence.boundary: The evidence is for ingroup versus outgroup category; carrying it to graded acceptance within one group is the model's extension. The effect is small in trust games (d about 0.14) and depends on reputational stakes, on the other members knowing she is one of them (Foddy, Platow and Yamagishi 2009, not verified), and on culture (weaker in Japan). The decrement side (at the edge, she keeps the work and checks) has no direct test and rests on the exclusion literature and common sense.

forces.name: Generous, so sought
forces.increment_logic: When the partners I help pay me back as a matter of course, I can afford to give freely, beyond any one partner and in the others' sight, and I feel myself one with help worth bringing their problems to: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When the partners I help do not pay me back, I stop giving beyond what I must, and I feel I have less in hand that the others would come to me for: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring falls a little.
forces.explanation: In public settings, the most generous members gain the most status, here freely given deference (Esteem), and are the most preferred partners (Hardy and Van Vugt 2006), and contributors are given influence and deference (Willer 2009). Both studies concern contributions to a common pool; the step to help given beyond her own partners in the others' sight is by analogy. Repayment only sustains the giving: a felt return makes open-handed giving affordable to her, a step resting on common sense and untested, and her felt esteem comes from the open-handed giving itself, never from being repaid. Work on helping and status ties esteem to giving more than one receives (Flynn et al. 2006). The card carries her felt reading as that giving opens or closes, a cautious proxy for what the others confer; their answering deference belongs to the scene (rulebook 8.5). The standing gain holds for visible, open-handed giving and fades when the giving reads as strategic or as a paid trade (Bliege Bird and Power 2015; a further source cited earlier as Livingston, Cohen and Halevy 2010 is not confirmed and needs checking, the nearest found being Halevy, Chou, Cohen and Livingston 2012). Each play moves her felt reading a step; the deference builds over many plays. Her name as a sharer is Repute's ground and is not carried here. The card forms a positive loop with H:Prestige->Reciprocity; the brake is a partner who stops repaying.

sources.source: Hardy, C., Van Vugt, M., 2006, Nice guys finish first: the competitive altruism hypothesis, PSPB 32: 1402-1413
sources.claim: When contributions were public, the most altruistic members gained the highest status and were most preferred as partners.

sources.source: Willer, R., 2009, American Sociological Review 74
sources.claim: Contributors receive status, influence and gifts, and those given status contribute more later.

edits_log: Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Decrement line: 'what I give is not returned' does not mark the hierarchical face, which reads the return from the partner helped, as the increment line does. 'No one now knows me as one who gives' overstates a felt reaction of minutes: a reputation for giving does not vanish at once, though the others see her give less. Increment line, type and literature (Hardy and Van Vugt on competitive altruism; Willer on contributors given deference) are fine.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The lines pass on source, target, type and boundaries, and the mechanism agrees with competitive altruism (Hardy and Van Vugt) and Willer. The explanation fails in two ways. It does not say that the chain (her giving, then others coming to know her as a giver) is a reputation that builds over many plays, although cards act within minutes. It also opens with 'This is my build's', which breaks the prose style and uses an author's first person out of keeping with the other explanations. Smallest fix is to the explanation only.

Ripple round 5, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The increment runs the rise through 'they come to know me as one who gives', which is her name as a sharer: Repute's ground (sharing what you have), as the Reciprocity definition itself marks. Prestige rises on deference for what she brings, so the line should go from visible giving to being sought and heeded without passing through a verdict on her character. The explanation says the generous gain 'status'; in Model B the deference Hardy and Van Vugt and Willer describe is Prestige, not the settled order (Status), and 'the reputation as a giver builds' carries the same Repute slip. The decrement passes.

Ripple round 11, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Explanation only. It says a felt return makes open-handed giving 'cheap', which sits badly with its own sources: competitive altruism credits giving as a costly display (Hardy and Van Vugt), and observers give less credit to giving they see as repaid or self-interested. The mechanism holds if the return makes giving affordable to her while the deference rests on the giving the others see. The explanation should also mark that giving seen as a paid trade earns less deference. Lines, type and direction pass.

Ripple round 12, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines pass against hierarchical Reciprocity and Prestige, and keep the sharer's name off the card (Repute). The explanation refers to 'Model B's terms', which is defined nowhere in the model texts, and cites Hardy and Van Vugt (2006) and Willer (2009) without years.

Ripple round 5, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The support (Hardy and Van Vugt 2006; Willer 2009) concerns contributions to a group's common pool, made in public. The increment line has her giving only to the partners she helps, and on the hierarchical face that giving is partner trade, which the explanation itself says earns less deference. Prestige's ground is contribution the group values, so the giving that earns deference has to reach past the one partner. Name the analogy in the explanation. The decrement and type pass.

Ripple round 6, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The decrement overstates. Esteem's hierarchical face rests on skill, knowledge and contribution, generosity only one part of it. Cutting back her giving thins only the generosity part, so 'they stop seeking me out, and I feel passed over' claims a loss of the whole deference. The fall should be small and limited to what her giving earned.

Ripple round 7, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The lines pass. The explanation carries a stale note about where the card came from in the older build ('carries the older build's Acceptance->Standing'). V1 origins carry no weight of their own, and the note does nothing for the mechanism. Tier 3: delete the sentence.

Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Both lines run through the others' response (they see, seek me out, bring fewer problems), so the card assumes another's response (evidence standard, Ben 6 Nov 4.37 am; rulebook 8.5). The card should carry her felt reading as her giving opens or closes, leaving the others' deference to the scene. Citations (Hardy and Van Vugt 2006; Willer 2009) are correctly described.

timing.typical: by the next occasion that day
timing.why: The return frees her to give openly at once, but her felt deference rises only when others later seek her out, which needs a fresh occasion after the giving has been seen.

forces.subtitle: Repaid help lets generosity show
forces.summary: When partners she helps pay her back, she can afford to give freely, in front of the others, and she feels she has something they would turn to her for. Without repayment she gives only what she must and her sense of being sought out dips a little. Repayment only makes the giving affordable. The felt esteem comes from the giving itself.

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)
logic_status.common_sense: Three claims rest on common sense. (1) A felt return makes open-handed giving affordable to her: help that is repaid costs less, so she can give more widely. (2) Giving the others read as a paid trade earns less deference: observers discount generosity that looks self-serving, an ordinary attribution, and it fits Hardy and Van Vugt's finding that status rewards rose with the cost of the altruism. (3) The decrement falls only a little: when repayment stops she still gives what she must, so some visible giving remains. None is contradicted by checked literature. The core link, that public generosity earns status and partner preference and that contributors receive influence and deference, rests on Hardy and Van Vugt 2006 and Willer 2009 (both supports). The card itself flags the step from common-pool contribution to help beyond her own partners as analogy.

dimensions.setting: lab only for the core link, with a few small-scale field cases

evidence.why: The observer-side link (visible generosity earns status and partner preference) rests on single lab studies and a few field cases, none independently replicated, and it is contested in part. Nothing tests the card's own step from being repaid to giving openly to feeling sought out, which stays common sense. Provisional, with no cause to remove the card.
evidence.boundary: The standing gained applies to visible, open-handed giving and fades when the giving looks strategic or like a paid trade (Bliege Bird and Power 2015; Livingston, Cohen and Halevy 2010; Hays and Blader, all not yet verified). Repayment as the enabling condition is untested, and Flynn-type work ties esteem to giving more than one receives, so repayment sustains her giving rather than adding to the esteem itself. Treat her felt sense of being sought as a cautious proxy for what observers confer, and note a later lab study (PMC8753170, unidentified) finding no added effect of partner choice beyond observation.

forces.name: Low rung, easy target
forces.increment_logic: When I hold a high place in a settled order, I feel no one would try to push me about, take my due or pass me over when things are handed out, and I go about my business beside the strongest without a glance at their mood: my sense that no one here can force me, take more than their due or hand out unfairly, and get away with it, rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I sit low in an order I have not accepted, the one who likes to push is about and no one here reins him in, I read myself as his easy target, open to losing my turns and my share beyond what the order gives him and to being passed over when he hands things out to his own; I start to watch him and do what heads off his temper: my sense that no one here can force me, take more than their due or hand out unfairly, and get away with it, falls.
forces.explanation: Rank shapes how much aggression and stress an animal receives, but direction and size depend on the society: subordination is most stressful in stable despotic orders and not in egalitarian ones, and in unstable orders the high-ranked face the most challenges (Sapolsky 2005); formalised, reconciled orders damp overt aggression (de Waal 1986). In a settled order she accepts, a low place moves Parity little, and an even-handed share-out that gives her less by rank leaves it high, as the Parity definition says; a low place in a settled, legitimate order may not lower the reading at all and can raise tolerance of unequal shares (Albrecht et al. 2012, not confirmed; needs checking, and the step rests on the Parity definition and common sense meanwhile). In well-levelled groups low rank carries less exposure (Boehm 1993). The card bites only when someone who could use her low place to push, take or pass her over is about and the group does little to check him; the decrement is her reading of her own exposure to him. In peer-victimisation studies the link runs both ways over time, low standing among peers predicting later victimisation and victimisation predicting later low standing (Hodges and Perry 1999, children; not checked here); the standing there was peer rejection, nearer Belonging than Rank, so it is adjacent support only, and the card claims no more than her reading of exposure. His actual grabs belong to the scene. Set it small in settled orders and larger in despotic ones. While places are being contested, set the increment to zero, since a high place then draws challenges instead of shielding her. Where she has accepted the order she sits low in, play the decrement nil. Limb: coercion, grab, allocation.

In a settled order she accepts, a low place moves Parity little, and an even-handed share-out that gives her less by rank leaves it high, as the Parity definition says; a low place in a settled, legitimate order may not lower the reading at all and can raise tolerance of unequal shares (Albrecht et al. 2012). In well-levelled groups low rank carries less exposure (Boehm 1993). The card bites only when someone who could use her low place to push, take or pass her over is about and the group does little to check him; the decrement is her reading of her own exposure to him. Peer-victimisation evidence is cross-sectional, and low status may follow being targeted as much as cause it, so the card claims no more than that reading. His actual grabs belong to the scene. Set it small in settled orders and larger in despotic ones. While places are being contested, set the increment to zero, since a high place then draws challenges instead of shielding her.

problems.where: increment_logic: "When I hold a high place in the order, no one tries to push me about or take my due..." and explanation: "Set it small in settled orders and larger in despotic ones."
problems.detail: Sapolsky 2005, the card's own main source (supports), says which ranks bear more stress depends on whether the hierarchy is stable: in unstable orders the high-ranked face the most challenges. The increment states without condition that a high place brings freedom from being pushed, and the explanation's scaling covers settled and despotic orders but never contested ones, where the increment should vanish.

problems.where: increment_logic, final clause: "my sense that no one here can force me or take more than their due and keep it rises"
problems.detail: The decrement names the target as no one being able to force her, take more than their due or hand out unfairly, and get away with it. The increment leaves out unfair share-outs, so the two lines describe different readings of Parity. The increment should match the decrement's wording and add the share-out face.

logic_status.common_sense: The human step, that a pusher picks the low-ranked as an easy target and that a high place shields one from being pushed in a settled order, rests on common sense about bullying and is safe as stated for settled orders. The primate sources (Sapolsky, supports; de Waal, partly, read as formalised orders damping overt aggression) back only the moderating role of the society.

evidence.why: The search scores consilience as strong, but on the central step only primatology (explicitly inconsistent), school peer studies (cross-sectional, bias handling unconfirmed) and workplace incivility (attribution unchecked) bear on low rank as exposure; the economics and ethnographic sources support the boundaries, and none is replicated or verified beyond two narrative primate reviews. The card text already makes the decrement conditional on an unchecked pusher and the increment conditional on a settled order, so the evidence calls for written boundaries, not a text change.
evidence.boundary: The decrement needs a pusher whom no one reins in: a settled, accepted low place on its own moves Parity little and can raise tolerance of unequal shares (induced-status games, unconfirmed). The effect is larger in despotic orders, small where the group levels would-be bullies (Boehm), and in unstable orders the shielding of high rank lapses because the high-ranked draw the most challenges. Low standing is partly a consequence of being targeted (cross-sectional peer studies), so the card describes her reading of exposure and not a causal rank effect.

forces.name: Ideas aired, ideas taken up
forces.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a half-formed idea show, I put forward how we might do the work better in front of the others, and I feel I have shown them something worth turning to me for: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When I brace and keep my ideas masked, what I could bring to the work in hand stays in my head, and I feel that on this matter the others have seen nothing of mine to turn to me for: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring falls a little.
forces.explanation: Felt psychological safety is taken as a precondition for letting half-formed ideas show, since an untested idea risks a slip or a disagreement shown, which is Safety's ground; the link from safety to voice is carried by Safety's evidence and is not rechecked here. The card now carries only her own felt sense of having shown, or withheld, something worth turning to her for, which rests on common sense; play it small. The evidence on status conferred for speaking up measures the others' response and belongs to the scene: speaking up raises the status colleagues confer, partly because those who speak are seen as more agentic (Weiss and Morrison 2019); promotive voice raised peer-rated status and later leader emergence, while prohibitive voice did not, and men gained from promotive voice and women did not (McClean et al. 2018); members high in trait dominance are rated more competent by peers (Anderson and Kilduff 2009). The others' taking up of what she airs is I:DivsExp->Prestige (Idea aired, idea taken up); do not count it again here. The card covers promotive voice only, ideas offered to improve the shared work; voicing alarm or criticism is not covered. Where she expects a status penalty for speaking up, as McClean et al. found for women, the felt gain is smaller or absent. The gain tracks visible contribution more than its quality (Anderson and Kilduff 2009), so the card reads that she has shown something, whatever its worth. The decrement reads only the matter in hand: deference she already draws for a skill the others have seen is not lowered by an idea kept back. Deck E: the card reads Esteem's egalitarian face, deference freely given on the matter in hand with no right to command. It forms a Reinforce loop with E:Prestige->DivsExp; the brake is a visible failure of what she puts forward (Esteem evidence).

The evidence on status conferred for speaking up measures the others' response and belongs to the scene: speaking up raises the status colleagues confer, partly because those who speak are seen as more agentic (Weiss and Morrison 2019); promotive voice raised peer-rated status and later leader emergence, while prohibitive voice did not, and men gained from promotive voice and women did not (McClean et al. 2018); members high in trait dominance are rated more competent by peers (Anderson and Kilduff 2009). The card covers promotive voice only, ideas offered to improve the shared work; voicing alarm or criticism is not covered. Where she expects a status penalty for speaking up, as McClean et al. found for women, the felt gain is smaller or absent. The gain tracks visible contribution more than its quality (Anderson and Kilduff 2009), so the card reads that she has shown something, whatever its worth. Deck E: the card reads Esteem's egalitarian face, deference freely given on the matter in hand with no right to command. It forms a Reinforce loop with E:Prestige->DivsExp; the brake is a visible failure of what she puts forward (Esteem evidence).

critique_was.name: Ideas aired, ideas taken up
critique_was.increment_logic: When I feel safe to let a half-formed idea show, I put forward how we might do the work better in front of the others; they take it up and turn to me on it: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring rises.

critique_was.explanation: Felt psychological safety is the main spur to speaking up in work teams (Edmondson 1999; Detert and Burris 2007). Speaking up raises the status colleagues confer, partly because those who speak are seen as more agentic and competent (Weiss and Morrison 2019). Promotive voice, ideas for doing things better, raised peer-rated status and later leader emergence, while prohibitive voice, raising concerns, did not; men gained from promotive voice and women did not (McClean et al. 2018). Members who act confidently are judged competent and gain influence even when their answers are no better (Anderson and Kilduff 2009). The card covers ideas offered to improve the shared work; voicing alarm or criticism is not covered and may cost her. Where the group's norms follow McClean's pattern, set it smaller for women members; the gap rests on one set of field studies, so treat it as a caution. Deck X: Safety is egalitarian, Esteem hierarchical. It forms a Reinforce loop with X:Prestige->DivsExp; the brake is a visible failure of what she puts forward (Esteem evidence).

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: 'Felt psychological safety is the main spur to speaking up in work teams (Edmondson 1999; Detert and Burris 2007).'
problems.detail: Neither Edmondson 1999 nor Detert and Burris 2007 is in the cited list, so neither was checked. 'The main spur' also overreaches: both works treat safety as one antecedent of voice (Detert and Burris centre leader openness, with safety as the mediator), and neither ranks it first.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 2: 'partly because those who speak are seen as more agentic and competent (Weiss and Morrison 2019)'
problems.detail: The checker found agency (all three studies) and communion (two studies) as mediators. Competence is not among them.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 4: 'Members who act confidently are judged competent and gain influence even when their answers are no better (Anderson and Kilduff 2009).'
problems.detail: Rated partly. The checked chain runs from trait dominance through competence-signalling behaviour to peer-rated competence; influence was read only in secondary coverage, and 'even when their answers are no better' was not confirmed. logic_status.common_sense: That ideas kept masked cannot earn deference, and that a visible failure of what she puts forward brakes the loop. Both are safe: deference for what one brings needs others to see it, and Esteem evidence is the stated brake.

evidence.why: No study measured the speaker's own felt Esteem after airing or withholding ideas; the nearest evidence is unreplicated single studies of observers' ratings, with a status-attainment meta-analysis (Grosz et al. 2024) whose bias handling is unconfirmed and which is analogous at best. The increment already names promotive ideas ('how we might do the work better'), so the boundaries belong in the explanation and the text can stand.
evidence.boundary: Promotive ideas only; prohibitive voice (alarm, criticism) is outside the card. The felt gain may be smaller or absent where the member expects a status penalty for speaking (McClean et al. 2018, gender result), and it tracks visible contribution more than its quality (Anderson and Kilduff 2009).

forces.name: No passengers
forces.increment_logic: When every member carries through what they take on, the credit and reward each draws is earned by a part they have done, so no one gets more than our reckoning gives by coasting: my sense that no one here takes more than their due and keeps it holds or rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When some members coast yet still draw the full share of credit and reward that our reckoning gives only to those who do their part, and no one makes them give it up, I see them taking more than their due and keeping it: my sense that no one here takes more than their due and keeps it falls.
forces.explanation: A coaster who draws the full share where the group's reckoning ties shares to doing one's part takes more than that reckoning gives, which is what Parity's second limb reads; the reading falls only when no one stops him and the grab sticks. The reckoning itself is early and specific to joint work: three-year-olds divide the spoils equally after collaborating but not after a windfall (Hamann et al. 2011), give a free rider less than a collaborator (Melis, Altrichter and Tomasello 2013), and keep less for themselves when they contributed less (Kanngiesser and Warneken 2012); 21-month-olds expect a reward for each who worked and not for one who did not (Sloane, Baillargeon and Premack 2012). So in shared work a member expects shares to track parts, and a coaster on a full share breaks that expectation. That breaking it lowers her felt Parity, rather than only stirring indignation, is still the model's step and rests on common sense. In public goods games cooperators punish free riders even where punishing cannot narrow the payoff gap, so their motive reads as retaliation for unfair conduct rather than inequity (Falk, Fehr and Fischbacher 2005); that anger is Rule-Keeping's ground, since pulling your weight is one of the levelling ways it guards, and X:OutResp->NormExp carries only the sensitising it leaves. Unearned pay gaps do lower output and attendance (Breza, Kaur and Shamdasani 2018), but those gaps were set by an employer, which is Parity's H face, not a coasting peer. So the card holds only where the work was joint and the group's reckoning plainly ties shares to parts, and does not fire where the band answers the coasting with ribbing and complaint as a breach of its ways, since then the grab has not stuck; one coasting scene is counted once, on this card and not also as a bare unequal share on Parity's face. Members also cut their own effort rather than carry a partner who free rides (the sucker effect: Kerr 1983), which does not move here. Where the group's reckoning gives equal shares whatever each puts in, the coaster gets what the reckoning gives and Parity is untouched; where reward tracks each member's own output, shirking costs only the shirker. High reliability removes coasting as one route to an unearned share; it says nothing of grabbing or coercion by other means. The card does not scale by a close tie. Modest; forms a Reinforce loop with E:Levelling->OutResp.

edits_log: Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Levelling's second limb reads taking more than the group's own reckoning gives and making it stick. A coaster who draws an equal share takes more than his due only where the reckoning ties shares to doing one's part; where the group shares its take equally regardless of input, as many forager bands do (tolerated scrounging), he takes exactly what the reckoning gives. The increment assumes an equity reckoning ('each share matches what each has put in') and the decrement omits 'makes it stick'. 'I feel a sucker for carrying them' strays into Reciprocity (her help unreturned) and into her own effort cut (Kerr's sucker effect proper), and indignation at the shirk is already carried by X:OutResp->NormExp. The explanation's scope clause names the wrong boundary.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines, type and scope pass. Two citations are glossed loosely. Kerr 1983 found that members cut their own effort rather than be the sucker carrying a capable free rider, and it does not report resentment as such. Blurton Jones 1984 calls the mechanism 'tolerated theft' (later writers say 'tolerated scrounging'). Fix: gloss both as the sources state them.

Ripple round 3, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Both lines pass: the source is read at the stated level, the target moves through Levelling's second limb (taking more than the reckoning gives and making it stick), the lines keep off OutResp's work ground and NormExp's indignation, the type fits, and the card does not duplicate its loop partner E:Levelling->OutResp or X:OutResp->NormExp. Two faults in the explanation. (a) It says the reading 'falls further when no one stops him', which implies it falls even when the coaster is stopped; by Levelling's definition a grab only lowers it once it sticks, as the decrement line rightly says. (b) Tolerated theft (Blurton Jones 1984) explains sharing as a holder yielding what costs too much to defend. It does not show a band reckoning that gives equal shares regardless of input, so it is a poor cite for the boundary case; widespread Ache meat sharing irrespective of who made the kill (Kaplan and Hill 1985) fits the point directly. Fehr and Gächter 2002 and Kerr 1983 are cited correctly.

Ripple round 4, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Increment line overreaches: high OutResp (members carry through and keep their word) does not show that 'no one keeps what our reckoning would not give them'; a reliable member can still grab or coerce. High OutResp only removes coasting as a route to an unearned share, so the line should say that. Decrement passes (1)-(4) and keeps to Levelling's second limb, leaving shirking itself to OutResp and indignation to NormExp. Explanation conflict: Fehr and Gaechter 2002 is a public goods game, where the pool is shared equally whatever each puts in, the very setting the card says leaves Levelling untouched. The free rider there ends ahead by keeping his own stake, and the anger itself is NormExp's ground; the explanation should say so and say what separates it from the Ache case. Kerr 1983 (sucker effect) is sound but concerns her own effort, which the card already sets aside. No duplication with other cards.

Ripple round 3, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Lines, type and boundaries pass against the revised Levelling (second limb: taking more than the group's reckoning gives and making it stick) and the revised OutResp. The explanation overstates its evidence: in a public goods game the formal rule splits the pool equally whatever each puts in, the same structure the card later uses (Ache sharing) to say Levelling is untouched. Players' sense that shares should track contribution is inferred from contributors' anger and punishment, so 'plainly bring with them' overclaims and sits awkwardly beside the Ache case. Smallest fix: state it as an inference from the anger and note the formal equal split. Also spell Gächter as in X:OutResp->NormExp.

Ripple round 4, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The increment overreaches. High OutResp removes only coasting as a route to an unearned share, and the explanation says it tells her nothing of grabbing or coercion by other means. The line still ends with her whole sense that no one takes more than their due rising at full strength. Ending it with a small rise keeps the line in step with the explanation and with the card's 'Modest' setting.

Ripple round 6, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The lines pass. The explanation cites two card ids that do not exist: 'X:Dependability->Rule-Keeping' should be X:OutResp->NormExp and 'E:Parity->Dependability' should be E:Levelling->OutResp.

forces.summary: In joint work, members expect shares to follow the parts each has done. When everyone carries through what they take on, no one gets more than their due by coasting, and Parity holds or rises a little. When coasters still draw the full share and no one stops them, members see more than the due being taken and kept, and Parity falls.

logic_status.common_sense: That under a reckoning tying shares to doing one's part, a coaster who draws a full share and keeps it is taking more than his due. Safe: it follows from the reckoning itself and from Parity's second limb, and the card limits itself to that reckoning.

forces.framework: Proposal on Parity's second limb; retaliation rather than inequity as the motive for sanctions (Falk, Fehr and Fischbacher 2005), the reason to keep it small.

evidence.why: The free-rider literature (Falk et al. 2005; Fehr and Gächter 2002; Price et al. 2002) shows anger and punishment aimed at coasters, motivated by retaliation, which matches the item's allocation of that anger to Rule-Keeping, but nothing tests whether an unsanctioned coaster lowers an observer's sense that no one takes more than their due. No source was verified this round (Kerr 1983 and Fehr and Gächter were not reopened, and the Giamattei 2025 'replicated' entry is a placeholder from a seminar listing with no findings), so the step stays common sense with adjacent support.
evidence.boundary: Fires only where the group's reckoning ties shares of credit and reward to parts done, and only while the coaster's grab sticks (no sanction, ribbing or complaint). Anger at free riders belongs to Rule-Keeping, and the sucker effect (cutting one's own effort) does not move this reading. Sanctioning of free riders is not universal: in pools with weak civic cooperation norms punishment also falls on cooperators (Herrmann et al. 2008, searched), so the decrement should be read as a member's perception and not as a prediction that the group will act.

forces.name: Credit to spend
forces.increment_logic: When the others turn to me for what I bring and take my advice, I feel a slip, a doubt or a disagreement of mine would be shrugged off as a bad day rather than met with a put-down or a laugh: my felt safety to show myself rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When no one turns to me for anything I bring, I feel I have nothing to set against a slip, and that a doubt or a disagreement of mine would sooner draw a put-down: my felt safety to show myself falls a little.
forces.explanation: Higher professional status goes with greater felt psychological safety (Nembhard and Edmondson 2006), and power releases approach and expression, while low power primes attention to threat and inhibition (Keltner, Gruenfeld and Anderson 2003). Both bear on settled place and power, which X:Status->DivsExp carries. The step to live deference is a proposal resting on common sense: a member the others turn to has something to set against a slip. Hollander's idiosyncrasy credit says members who have earned standing are allowed more latitude, but direct tests are few and weak, so it is not relied on. Work on deviance credit (Abrams et al. 2018) is a candidate neighbour once its full text confirms what it measures. The pratfall effect points the same way for a slip off the skill: a blunder made a highly competent person more liked (Aronson, Willerman and Floyd 1966), though later studies found it depends on the observer's self-esteem and sex (Helmreich, Aronson and LeFan 1970; Deaux 1972) and it measured liking, not felt safety, so it is not relied on. Standing can also raise the stakes of a slip: people react more strongly to the prospect of losing standing than to gaining it (Pettit, Yong and Spataro 2010, unchecked until located), and a loss of status hurts performance more when it comes from a high position than from a lower one (Marr and Thau 2014). Deference that fades with what she brings is a thinner cushion than a settled place, so this card should be the weaker of the two. Boundary, resting on common sense with adjacent support from the status-loss work, none of it replicated: where a slip would show up the very skill the others look to her for, high standing raises the cost of the slip and the card does not fire.

logic_status.common_sense: The step from live deference to felt safety: a member the others turn to has something to set against a slip, so a slip is more likely to be put down to a bad day. Safe because the explanation labels it a proposal, declines to rest on idiosyncrasy credit, keeps the literature on settled status and power with X:Status->DivsExp, and sets this card weaker than that one. The decrement is played as 'falls a little', within what common sense carries.

evidence.why: No source tests live deference (being turned to for what one brings) as a cause of felt safety to show doubts apart from settled rank or power; the status-and-safety field surveys carry the Status card, and the power-approach meta-analysis (Sabey et al. 2025, bias handling unconfirmed) is about power, with a contested priming line (Mayiwar and Lai 2019). None of the sources was verified this round, so nothing is added as load-bearing and the step stays a common-sense proposal.
evidence.boundary: Keep the existing boundary: the card does not fire where a slip would expose the very skill others turn to her for, since high standing raises the cost of a status loss (Marr and Thau 2014, searched) and a slip helps only those already seen as highly competent (pratfall work, contested). The cushion from live deference is thinner than the settled place carried by Status->DivsExp. Abrams et al. 2018 (deviance credit, searched) is the better-evidenced relative of idiosyncrasy credit, but it concerns others' tolerance of leaders' deviance, not the member's own felt safety.

forces.name: Good season, open hands
forces.explanation: Whether the venture's prospects open hands around me depends on where the trouble is seen to come from. Circumstance one (the default), the trouble is inside the group or has no named source. HIGH: with the venture well within our reach I am buoyed, I help whoever asks without counting and expect the same around me, so my reading that help here comes back rises. LOW: with the venture looking beyond us, I expect everyone to hunch over their own part and help asked for to be slow to come, so my reading that help here comes back falls a little. Circumstance two, the trouble comes from outside (a rival group, lost funding, a forced change of ground), it threatens the group as a whole, and a fight still looks worth making. LOW here means the venture is threatened and not yet hopeless: I expect the others to pool what they have and help to flow to whoever needs it, so my reading that help here comes back rises. HIGH: the threat looks easily met and I expect giving to slip back to its ordinary level, so my reading eases back by no more than the threat raised it. Good mood raises helping (Carlson, Charlin and Miller 1988). Mood spreads through a group by contagion, and in one lab study groups exposed to pleasant contagion showed more cooperation and less conflict than those exposed to unpleasant contagion (Barsade 2002). That Team Confidence carries such a mood is common sense, untested by these studies. The mood evidence backs the circumstance-one increment only: a bad mood does not reliably lower helping and sometimes raises it (Carlson and Miller 1987, to be checked). The circumstance-one decrement, each member guarding her own part when the venture looks beyond the group, rests on common sense: people who doubt the shared outcome turn to securing their own. Keep it weaker than the increment, since a bad mood does not reliably lower helping. Exposure to war violence raises local cooperation, and may strengthen in-group norms in particular (Bauer et al. 2016, review, checked). In the laboratory, competition between groups raised contributions within them and sharpened anger at free riders and guilt at free riding (Puurtinen and Mappes 2009), which grounds circumstance two in rivalry between groups and not only in war; carrying either finding to an everyday outside threat such as lost funding is the model's step, so play it modest. Circumstance two needs the threat to fall on the group as a whole: where members feel singled out one by one, threat can lower cooperation within the group (Weisel and Zultan, unverified, single study; likely their 2016 European Economic Review paper on the perceived target of threat, year to be checked), so run circumstance one. Where the venture looks hopeless, run circumstance one. The step from the group's mood to her felt expectation of return rests on common sense too. Matches the rally case in E:GrpProsp->Belonging. Modest; forms a loop with E:Reciprocity->GrpProsp.

Whether the venture's prospects open hands around me depends on where the trouble is seen to come from. Circumstance one (the default), the trouble is inside the group or has no named source. HIGH: with the venture well within our reach I am buoyed, I help whoever asks without counting and the others do the same around me, so my reading that help here comes back rises. LOW: with the venture looking beyond us, everyone hunches over their own part, help asked for is slow to come and mine goes unreturned, so my reading that help here comes back falls a little. Circumstance two, the trouble comes from outside (a rival group, lost funding, a forced change of ground) and a fight still looks worth making. LOW here means the venture is threatened and not yet hopeless: the others pool what they have and help flows to whoever needs it, so my reading that help here comes back rises. HIGH: the threat looks easily met and giving slips back to its ordinary level, so my reading eases back by no more than the threat raised it. Good mood raises helping (Carlson, Charlin and Miller 1988). Mood spreads through a group by contagion, and in one lab study groups exposed to pleasant contagion showed more cooperation and less conflict than those exposed to unpleasant contagion (Barsade 2002). That Team Confidence carries such a mood is common sense, untested by these studies. The mood evidence backs the circumstance-one increment only: a bad mood does not reliably lower helping and sometimes raises it (Carlson and Miller 1987, to be checked). The circumstance-one decrement, each member guarding her own part when the venture looks beyond the group, is a proposal resting on common sense: people who doubt the shared outcome turn to securing their own. Keep it weaker than the increment. Exposure to war violence raises local cooperation, and may strengthen in-group norms in particular (Bauer et al. 2016, review, checked). In the laboratory, competition between groups raised contributions within them and sharpened anger at free riders and guilt at free riding (Puurtinen and Mappes 2009), which grounds circumstance two in rivalry between groups and not only in war; carrying either finding to an everyday outside threat such as lost funding is the model's step, so play it modest. Where the venture looks hopeless, run circumstance one. The step from the group's mood to her felt return is a proposal too. Matches the rally case in E:GrpProsp->Belonging. Modest; forms a loop with E:Reciprocity->GrpProsp.

timing.typical: within the next few requests for help, 5 to 20 minutes
timing.why: Mood about the venture shifts at once, but her reading of the return moves only as she sees help offered or withheld over the next few exchanges.

era.why: Shared mood in a coalition and the readiness to share or withhold food and aid have non-verbal analogues in social primates and early human hunting groups.

forces.subtitle: Hopeful groups help each other
forces.summary: When the venture looks within reach, a member helps freely and expects help to come back. When it looks beyond the group, she expects everyone to guard their own part. If the trouble comes from outside and the fight still looks worth making, the pattern reverses and she expects the others to pool what they have. Where the venture looks hopeless, the first pattern runs.
forces.summary_status: generated from the source texts, not canon; checked faithful

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)

problems.where: explanation: 'Under threat, attention narrows and control tightens (Staw et al. 1981); the step to each member guarding her own part belongs to the proposal, since the same work finds groups under threat drawing closer, which is the rally case below.'
problems.detail: Staw, Sandelands and Dutton 1981 is not in the cited list and was not checked, so neither the threat-rigidity claim nor the 'drawing closer' claim has a checked source. The decrement line ('everyone hunches over their own part') leans on it.

problems.where: explanation: 'positive contagion brings more cooperation and less conflict, negative contagion the reverse (Barsade 2002)'
problems.detail: Rated partly. The checker confirmed the negative half only in the 2001 working paper, not the published abstract, and the study is a single lab study of short-lived groups. State the contrast between conditions, not two separate effects.

logic_status.common_sense: That confidence in the venture carries a good mood, and that a side expecting to win helps freely so help is felt to come back. Safe as a proposal: confidence about a shared venture is a pleasant state, and the mood-to-helping link is well supported.

forces.framework: Mood and helping (Carlson, Charlin and Miller 1988; Barsade 2002) for circumstance one; war and local cooperation (Bauer et al. 2016) and between-group competition (Puurtinen and Mappes 2009) for circumstance two.

evidence.why: The two candidate replicated sources, a bias-corrected 2025 PSPB meta-analysis on positive emotion and prosocial behaviour and a 2025 meta-analysis on intergroup competition and ingroup cooperation (Snijder et al., known only from a LinkedIn post), are both unread and unverified, so they cannot carry a substantiated grade yet. Even if confirmed, they test behaviour after mood induction or competition, not the felt reading of return, and the link from Team Confidence to group mood is untested common sense, so the item stays provisional with the boundaries above; read both meta-analyses before regrading.
evidence.boundary: Circumstance two holds when the outside threat is seen as aimed at the group as a whole; where members feel individually targeted, threat can lower ingroup cooperation (Weisel and Zultan 2021, searched, details unconfirmed). In circumstance one keep the decrement weak, because negative mood does not reliably lower helping (Carlson and Miller 1987, contested by Cialdini and Fultz 1990). Both circumstances are evidenced in helping and contribution behaviour; the move to a member's expectation that help comes back, and Team Confidence as the source of group mood, are the model's own steps.

forces.name: Backs to each other
forces.increment_logic: When the others draw me in as one of their own, I see us talk the work through, pass on what we know and pull the same way, and the venture looks within the reach of a side like ours: my confidence that the group, as it stands, can pull it off rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am left at the edge, I see the work run in knots that do not talk it through or pass things on, and what I could bring left out of it, and the venture looks beyond the group as it stands: my confidence that the group can pull it off falls.
forces.explanation: Cohesion is related to group performance, and all three of its components count, most for behaviour and efficiency and where work flows intensively between members (Beal et al. 2003). Nearer the target, members' felt cohesion, task cohesion above all, goes with their collective efficacy in sports teams (Paskevich et al. 1999; Kozub and McDonnell 2000; both unchecked here), though these studies are mostly cross-sectional. The card runs mainly through task cohesion, work talked through and knowledge passed on, which is why the lines speak of how the work flows; social acceptance on its own carries less. Of the model's perceptions, Warmth, her liking for the members, sits nearest the social component, interpersonal attraction; Belonging, the others' acceptance of her, is further off, so the evidence for this card is indirect. Her Belonging reads the others' acceptance of her, not how close-knit the group is, so the step from her own inclusion to the group's cohesion is a proposal: a member left at the edge sees the group as split, and sees what she brings go unused. Where she is shut out by a group that plainly works well together, the decrement is weak or nil. The link between cohesion and performance runs at least partly in reverse, from performance to cohesion (Mullen and Copper 1994, full text to be checked), so keep this card small. E:Team Confidence->Belonging is Discretionary and carries that direction only in some circumstances. It is distinct from E:Reciprocity->Team Confidence (help that comes back) and E:Dependability->Team Confidence (reliability).

problems.where: explanation, sentence 2: 'In sport teams, task cohesion early in a season predicts collective efficacy later, as well as the reverse (Heuzé, Raimbault and Fontayne 2006, to be checked).'
problems.detail: Checker verdict not found. The secondary summary of the likely source (Heuzé, Bosselut and Thomas 2007) supported only collective efficacy as an antecedent of task cohesion, so the cohesion-to-efficacy direction this card needs is at risk of contradiction. Drop the sentence.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 3: 'and the link runs mainly through commitment to the task (Mullen and Copper 1994)'
problems.detail: The checked part of Mullen and Copper is the direction of the path, not the task-commitment claim, and a later critique calls that claim premature. Beal et al. 2003 (supports), cited in the sentence before, found each cohesion component independently related to performance. The two sentences sit against each other.

logic_status.common_sense: The step from her own inclusion to her reading of the group's cohesion and of what she brings being used. Safe as labelled: she reads the group from where she sits, and the explanation weakens the decrement where she is shut out by a group that plainly works well.

evidence.why: The replicated evidence is group-level cohesion against objective performance, and the collective efficacy meta-analysis does not take cohesion or inclusion as a predictor, so no pooled source tests a member's acceptance against her confidence in the group; the one direct test (a 2010 linguistic ostracism study lowering perceived team potency) was read only in abstract and lacks authors and N. The card text already routes the step through task cohesion ('talk the work through, pass on what we know'), so the boundaries go in the explanation and the grade is provisional.
evidence.boundary: The link runs mainly through task cohesion (the work being talked through and passed on) and only weakly through social acceptance (sport meta-analysis: task r = .45, social r = .11, searched). Direction is partly reversed, since success draws members in, so the card stays small. Where a group plainly works well together while leaving her at the edge, the decrement should be small or absent.

forces.name: Rising tide
forces.increment_logic: When I feel those at the top can steer us through what we have taken on, I see what I came for riding on a venture in safe hands: a well-led side that wins has places, credit and shares to hand down, and my sense that staying will bring me what I came for rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I feel those at the top cannot steer us through what we have taken on, I see what I came for going down with a venture in the wrong hands: a badly led side has little to hand down and no name to lend me, and my sense that staying will bring me what I came for falls.
forces.explanation: Deck H; the source is Team Confidence's hierarchical face. The mechanism is kept: where members' outcomes ride on the group's, the venture's prospects are part of each member's own. Reward interdependence acts on members' effort (Wageman 1995), though that effect is itself inconsistent, and loafing falls when members value the group outcome and expect their effort to matter to it (Karau and Williams 1993). In a ranked group those prospects are read through the top, as Team Confidence's hierarchical face defines. Leadership climate predicts collective efficacy (Chen and Bliese 2002), adjacent support. Work on authority ranking (Fiske 1992) and leadership as a predictor of team performance (Dirks 2000; Dirks and Ferrin 2002) points the same way but is pending a check and is not relied on here. How fairly the top will share out what the venture yields is Parity's or Reciprocity's ground, not this card's; the card reads only how much a well- or badly-led venture will have to hand out. No study here measures a member's forecast of her own yield, so the felt step is a proposal resting on common sense: nobody expects to get ahead under leaders who are running the side aground. Where she is at the top herself, her confidence in her own steering feeds her forecast through the venture; what her rung itself brings her is H:Status->OwnProsp. Outcome interdependence is the condition: set the card small or nil where her aims do not ride on the venture (a member there for the company, or paid by her own output alone). A run of results can inflate or sink the face beyond the leaders' real grip, a step resting on common sense; the romance of leadership is not relied on for it, since replications failed or were mixed (Hammond et al. 2021; Schyns et al. 2025). The brake is Team Confidence evidence on the venture itself.

forces.name: Nothing left for me
forces.increment_logic: When no member here can make me act or hold back through fear, none takes more than his due of the shares, the credit or the say and keeps it, and none tilts a share-out or the settling of a quarrel towards his own, what I came for is mine to work towards, and my sense that staying will bring it to me rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When a member can make me comply through fear, takes more than his due of the shares, the credit or the say and keeps it, or tilts a share-out or the settling of a quarrel towards his own, I see what I came for going his way or hanging on his whim, and my sense that staying will bring me what I came for falls.
forces.explanation: Narrowed to Parity's egalitarian face: coercion, grabbing and tilting by a member among equals. The evidence on those in authority (injustice from authorities, Colquitt et al. 2001; abusive supervision and organisational justice) moves to the notes of H:Parity->Payoff on Parity's hierarchical face and is not relied on here. The coercion, grabbing and tilting limbs left here are untested proposals with no checked source, resting on common sense: where one member can take or block what the group would give, staying looks less likely to pay. Peer conduct moves Payoff less than the same conduct from an authority: in work on workplace mistreatment, coworker effects run smaller than supervisor effects (likely Hershcovis and Barling 2010, meta-analysis), and prospective studies of bullying find only a small effect over time (likely Nielsen and Einarsen 2012, meta-analysis); both named from the checker's search and not checked, and both measure attitudes and strain, not a forecast of what staying will bring, so they are adjacent support only. Set the increment small, since freedom from a coercer opens no way by itself. Play the decrement moderately, for grabbing and where Parity is low because a peer tilts a share-out or the settling of a quarrel towards his own. Deck X: the card runs from Parity's egalitarian face to Payoff, which is hierarchical. Distinct from Built-in Advantage (H:Rank->Payoff), which runs through her own place in the order.
