problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: 'Abusive supervision is linked with lower commitment and higher intent to leave (Mackey et al. 2017)'
problems.detail: The checker rated Mackey et al. 2017 'not found': the abstract was not reached and the commitment and intent-to-leave findings were not confirmed. The sentence presents it as established support.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: 'distributive and procedural injustice each predict lower commitment and outcome satisfaction (Colquitt et al. 2001)'
problems.detail: Colquitt supports the justice-outcome link in organisational samples with injustice from those in authority. The explanation already admits the extension to peers is a proposal, but leaves the coercion-through-fear strand of both lines with no checked source; it should be marked as resting on common sense.

problems.where: increment_logic: 'When no one here can make me do or drop anything by force or fear, take more than their due ... or hand things out to their own past me'
problems.detail: The clause list hangs off 'can make me', so the sentence reads as 'no one can make me take more than their due', which inverts the meaning of the grabbing and favouritism strands. Also the explanation asks for a small increment, which the line does not reflect.

logic_status.common_sense: The coercion strand (a member who can make others comply through fear puts what they came for at his whim) and the extension from authorities to any member rest on common sense. Both are safe as small, modest steps: where one member can take or block what the group would give, staying looks less likely to pay. The increment (freedom from a coercer makes what I came for mine to work towards) also rests on common sense and is safe only if kept small, as the explanation says.

evidence.why: Coworker incivility and bullying meta-analyses link peer mistreatment to lower commitment and intent to leave, but none of these was verified, they measure attitudes and exits rather than the member's expectation of getting what she came for, and the grabbing and tilting limbs have no test. The step stays a proposal backed by common sense; the existing 'rises a little' already fits the boundary, and authority-sourced evidence (abusive supervision, organisational justice) belongs with H:Levelling->OwnProsp.
evidence.boundary: Peer coercion, grabbing or tilting weighs less than the same conduct from an authority (coworker mistreatment effects on commitment and leaving are smaller than supervisor effects, and small over time in prospective studies), so the decrement is moderate and the increment small.

forces.name: Following a lead I believe in
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into this group, I follow those at the top willingly, and what they steer us to reads as a sign of what they can do: my confidence that they can bring the venture off rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, I follow half-heartedly, and each misstep from the top reads as the limit of what they can do: my confidence that they can bring the venture off falls.
forces.explanation: Hierarchical-face twin of E:Engagement->GrpProsp, on the same grounds: investment carries enthusiasm or flatness that colours judgements built from ambiguous cues (Forgas 1995), and engagement and efficacy beliefs feed each other over time (Salanova, Llorens and Schaufeli 2011), though those were members' beliefs in their own efficacy, so carrying the finding to confidence in the group's leaders is an extension. Trust in leadership is reported to run both ways with team performance (Dirks 2000), but that source is pending a check, as on H:GrpProsp->OwnProsp, and its trust takes in the leader's integrity and care, which lie nearer Parity, so it is not relied on here. Where she is among those at the top herself, her investment colours her reading of her own and her fellows' steering in the same way. The step from her own investment to confidence in those at the top rests on common sense with adjacent support only. Gap: no cross-lagged or preregistered test of follower engagement predicting rated leader competence was found. The colouring works on steering that could be read either way, so it weakens when the leaders' performance is plain: Team Confidence evidence cards (a leader's visible failure) act as the brake. Keep the size small and the time to impact short.

forces.name: Backers at my shoulder
forces.increment_logic: When the partners I help pay me back and the one above me covers me, and my turn or share is questioned, I count on them at my side and hold to it: my felt rung in the order, shaken by the question, rises back to where it stood.
forces.decrement_logic: When my partners take and do not return and the one above me no longer covers me, and my turn or share is questioned, I know no one would stand at my side, so I give way and let others go ahead of me: my felt rung in the order falls.
forces.explanation: The card reads Reciprocity's hierarchical face: return from particular partners, and favour and protection passed down from the one above in return for loyalty, as in patron and client ties (Scott 1972, to be checked; a framework, not a test). It plays only when a turn or share of hers is questioned. In primates grooming given is repaid in agonistic support (36 studies, 14 species, small effect: Schino 2007), and allied and kin support decides how macaque females acquire and hold rank (Chapais 1992). Being repaid does not by itself lift a member's standing: in exchange research status went to those who gave more than they received, while productivity went with frequent exchange (Flynn 2003), and status is the return for services that cannot be repaid in kind (Blau 1964). That giving route is Esteem's ground and is not carried here, so the increment only restores a place in doubt and never lifts her above it, and the decrement runs larger. The half from backing to her felt rung rests on common sense. H:Belonging->Status hands partner support to Reciprocity but no card carried it; this one does. Support from particular partners and a patron, not the whole room's assent (Backed into my place): on one questioned turn, play this card for named partners and a patron, that one for the room. The effect per exchange is small and runs both ways, since higher status also draws support (Redhead and von Rueden 2021, from the checker's search, unchecked), so the step is modest. The card needs backing she can see; where she reads the backing as dependence bought for the backer's own ends, it may restore her rung less or lower it (Yu and Shea 2024, unverified).

forces.subtitle: Backers at hand hold my rank
forces.summary: Reciprocity drives Rank when her turn or share is questioned. If her partners pay her back and the one above covers her, she counts on them and her felt rung returns to where it stood. If they take and do not return, she knows no one would stand with her, gives way, and her felt rung falls. The card restores a place in doubt and does not lift her above it.

ripple_was.explanation: In primates grooming given is repaid in agonistic support (36 studies, 14 species, small effect: Schino 2007), and allied and kin support decides how macaque females acquire and hold rank (Chapais 1992). forces.framework: Agonistic support repaid for grooming; patron and client exchange.

evidence.why: Reciprocity producing support is pooled and bias-corrected in primates, but that is analogous evidence and covers only the first half; the backing-to-felt-rank half rests on contested primate rank acquisition, mixed Tsimane field work and common sense. With no human test of the felt step and the direction contested, the card is provisional.
evidence.boundary: The effect is small and runs both ways (higher standing also attracts and gives support); it depends on the backing being visible, and may reverse where backing is read as dependence on a powerful contact (Yu and Shea 2024, pending a check).

forces.name: Skill shared, drawn in
forces.explanation: Whether being looked to for what I bring draws me in among the others turns on how I carry it. Circumstance one (the default), I carry it modestly: I share what I know freely and laugh along when my work is ribbed. HIGH: the others watch how I do things, bring me their problems and seek my company, and I feel a place kept for me wherever they gather, so my sense that they want me among them rises. LOW: no one watches or seeks me for anything I bring, I am the one who has to seek them out, and I read the quiet as being wanted a little less, so my sense that they want me among them falls a little. Circumstance two, I let my success show as a claim: I wait for thanks, direct others unasked or boast. HIGH: I sense the room cooling at my claim and expect them to leave a gap beside me, so my sense that they want me among them falls. LOW: I have nothing to claim, and the card adds nothing. Prestige-based influence comes with being liked, dominance-based influence does not (Cheng et al. 2013, from a secondary summary; liking falls short of belonging). Learners defer to the models they learn from to gain access to what they know (Henrich and Gil-White 2001), and skilled Agta storytellers are preferred campmates (Smith et al. 2017); that she feels sought for her company is a common-sense step from access. These ground the circumstance-one rise. The step runs through being liked and sought, which follows modest carriage, not through output or standing alone: being looked to and being included are separable, so the effect is small and conditional on how she carries it. The circumstance-one decrement and circumstance two rest on common sense with no direct source: in circumstance two she senses the cooling her claim invites. The forager levelling of a provider who presses his success (Lee 1969; Wiessner 1996) is the others' response and belongs to the scene, or to the Reputation route. Under the E face, acceptance does not rest on output, so the circumstance-one rise runs through the liking and contact that come with being sought out, and through what she shares freely, which counts as pulling with the group; skill as output adds nothing by itself. The circumstance-one decrement is small and lies in her reading, not in the group's acceptance, which still counts her one of their own: being sought less is easily felt as being wanted less, a common-sense step until a source on relational value (Leary and Baumeister 2000, unchecked) is read. A member who brings little but pulls as far as she is able stays one of their own in good standing, and the card must never edge her out on that ground alone. The others' actual seeking her out is staged by I:Esteem->Belonging (Skill shared, sought out); where both fire on one scene, play circumstance one small here so the same seeking is not counted twice. With the Reputation pack on, circumstance two runs through Insulting the meat (X:Esteem->Repute) and Repute's own card into Belonging (E:Repute->Belonging); set circumstance two nil here then, so one boast is not counted twice.

edits_log: Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Belonging's egalitarian face says acceptance does not rise or fall with output. The explanation does not square the card with that clause, and the decrement, though small, could be read as a member losing her place for lacking skill. The lines can stand if the explanation pins the rise to modest sharing, which is pulling with the group, and keeps the fall to a thinner draw with her standing as one of their own untouched. The literature is cited correctly (Cheng et al. 2013; Henrich and Gil-White 2001; Smith 2004).

Ripple round 6, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The decrement clashes with Belonging's egalitarian face, where acceptance does not rise or fall with output. As written, the group's acceptance of her thins because she brings little, even though she may still pull as far as she is able. The fix makes the fall her own felt reading: being sought less reads to her as being wanted less, while the group still counts her one of its own. Sociometer theory backs this, since people read acceptance from signs of their relational value.

Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): (1) The decrement line contradicts itself: in her own voice she says they still count her one of their own, which is the egalitarian Belonging reading itself, yet her sense of being wanted falls. A felt misreading can be carried, but she cannot both know she is still counted in and feel less wanted on the same ground; the clause belongs in the explanation. forces.subtitle: Sharing skill draws people in
forces.summary: Whether being looked to for what she brings draws her in depends on how she carries it. If she shares freely and takes ribbing well, her sense that the others want her among them rises when they seek her out, and falls a little when no one does. If she presses her success as a claim, that sense falls. The effect is small and conditional.

problems.detail: The checker could not confirm which mechanisms Smith supports; the paper weighs competing accounts and the cause is debated. It is also a gain from skill itself, which sits against the card's own claim that under the E face the rise comes from sharing and not from the skill. Drop it.

logic_status.common_sense: That access to what she knows leads others to seek her company; that modest sharing draws people while boasting repels them; that being sought less is felt as being wanted less. Each is safe as a small step, and the decrement is already set small and confined to her reading.

forces.framework: Prestige and liking (Cheng et al. 2013); prestige as access (Henrich and Gil-White 2001). Forager levelling of the successful (Lee 1969; Wiessner 1996) belongs to the scene.

evidence.why: Others like prestige-holders and choose skilled sharers as company (Cheng et al. 2013, partly replicated in established groups; Agta campmate preference), but the replication of the liking result is unconfirmed and no study measures the focal member's own sense of being wanted. The upward step has adjacent support without replication or strong consilience, and the other limbs are common sense, so the card is provisional.
evidence.boundary: The step runs through being liked and sought for what one shares, not through output or status alone (status and inclusion are separable), so it holds only when success is carried modestly and stays small.

forces.name: Eyes on skill, not on the bully
forces.increment_logic: When no one here can make us do anything by force or fear, or hand things out to their own, and nothing presses on the group from outside, I see nothing standing between what I bring and the others' notice, and where I do the work well in their sight I expect them to watch and come to me for it: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When a member makes us comply through fear or hands things out to his own, I sense the others' eyes on him and on what he will allow, not on how I do things, and what I could bring waits on his say: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring falls.
forces.explanation: Dominant and prestigious members both draw more visual attention than others (Cheng et al. 2013, eye tracking). That a dominant's hold on attention leaves less for skilled members is a common-sense step, since attention in a small group is limited; the study did not test it. Cooperation in chimpanzees depends on tolerance between partners (Melis et al. 2006a), and chimpanzees recruit the more effective of two collaborators (Melis et al. 2006b). The step to her own felt deference is a proposal: keep it modest and scale it to what she brings. The increment is weaker than the decrement and needs her skill to be visible and the group to be under no threat: under outside conflict, members lean towards dominant leaders (Laustsen and Petersen 2015, not checked here). Even without coercion, assertive members can capture attention and deference by signalling competence (Anderson and Kilduff 2009, not yet read here), and in a preregistered study prestige was unrelated to task-specific knowledge (Brand and Mesoudi 2019, from the checker's search, unchecked), so freedom from a bully does not by itself turn the others' eyes to her. The lines carry her felt reading only; the actual shift in where the others look is staged by I:Levelling->Prestige, and where both fire, play this card small.

forces.subtitle: No bully, so my skill gets noticed
forces.summary: Parity drives Esteem, my sense that the others turn to me for what I bring. When no one can force or favour, nothing stands between my work and their notice, so Esteem rises a little. When a member makes us comply through fear or hands things out to his own, the others watch him instead of me, and Esteem falls. The fall is stronger than the rise.

evidence.why: Levelled groups favour prestige over dominance and dominance loses its hold over time, but none of the supporting sources was verified, none tests the focal member's felt sense that others turn to her, and the eye-tracking result has no replication. evidence.boundary: The increment needs skill done in the others' sight and no threat on the group; even without coercion, assertive members can draw attention and deference by signalling competence (Anderson and Kilduff 2009), and prestige tracks task skill only weakly (Brand and Mesoudi, preregistered), so the rise stays small.

ripple_was.decrement_logic: When a member makes us comply through fear or hands things out to his own, everyone's eyes track him instead; my way of doing things goes unwatched and what I could bring waits on his say: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring falls.
ripple_was.explanation: Dominant and prestigious members both draw more visual attention than others (Cheng et al. 2013, eye tracking). That a dominant's hold on attention leaves less for skilled members is a common-sense step, since attention in a small group is limited; the study did not test it. Cooperation in chimpanzees depends on tolerance between partners (Melis et al. 2006a), and chimpanzees recruit the more effective of two collaborators (Melis et al. 2006b). The step to her own felt deference is a proposal: keep it modest and scale it to what she brings. The increment is weaker than the decrement and needs her skill to be visible and the group to be under no threat. Even without coercion, assertive members can capture attention and deference by signalling competence (Anderson and Kilduff 2009, not yet read here), and in a preregistered study prestige tracked task skill only weakly (Brand and Mesoudi, from the checker's search, unchecked), so freedom from a bully does not by itself turn the others' eyes to her.

forces.name: Putting in, looked to
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into this group, I bring what I can to each venture and share it freely, and I read the others' glances and questions as turning to me for it: my sense that they look to me for what I bring rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, I bring little and keep what I know to myself, and I read their turning to others as what I bring no longer counting: my sense that they look to me for what I bring falls.
forces.explanation: Egalitarian-face twin of H:Engagement->Esteem, needed because every Pillar must have an Engagement card for the reflective beat. Members who contribute to the group earn status and influence (Willer 2009, laboratory public-goods studies), and in an egalitarian society men with more exchange partners carry more influence (von Rueden et al. 2014; correlational, and kin and size also predict it there), so investment and visible contribution go together with being looked to. That investment also colours her reading of ambiguous glances and questions rests on common sense; keep the step modest. The rise needs what she brings to be visible to the others; where it goes unseen, the card adds nothing. In egalitarian settings overt status seeking can draw levelling instead of deference, and work among Hadza foragers disputes sharing as a prestige signal (from the checker's search, unchecked); where she presses her contribution as a claim, the card does not run, and the others' levelling belongs to the scene (see E:Esteem->Belonging, circumstance two). The lines carry her felt reading only; the others' actual turning to her is staged by I:Engagement->Esteem, and where both fire, play this card small.

problems.where: explanation: 'so investment and visible contribution go together'
problems.detail: Rests on the unsupported von Rueden claim. Willer 2009 (sorted, rated supports) gives the contribution-to-status link and should carry it, added to the cited list.

logic_status.common_sense: That investment colours her reading of ambiguous glances and questions as deference, and that an invested member brings and shares more. Safe as a modest step at checkpoints.

evidence.why: The behavioural link (contributors are granted status) rests on within-paper repeats in two lab programmes and correlational Tsimane fieldwork, with no independent or registered replication and nothing measuring the contributor's own reading. Two fields converge only loosely and the cue-colouring step is common sense, so the card stays provisional.
evidence.boundary: Holds where her contribution is visible to the others. In strongly egalitarian groups, giving that reads as status seeking can draw levelling rather than deference. The step from investment to reading ambiguous glances as deference is common sense, untested.

forces.name: Steering on trial
forces.increment_logic: When I am among those at the top who steer the group and feel sure we can steer it through what it has taken on, my calls come out sure, and I sense the others take my word on them and bring me the calls that matter, beyond what my place alone would draw: my sense that they defer to me for what I bring rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am among those at the top who steer the group and feel we cannot steer it through, my calls come out hesitant, and I sense the others no longer take my word on them, doing what my place requires and no more, so I am readier to give ground: my sense that they defer to me for what I bring falls.
forces.explanation: The lines move live, freely given deference for what she brings (Esteem), beyond what her place draws, not settled precedence (Rank). In a small-scale egalitarian society, leaders hold influence over collective action without formal office (von Rueden et al. 2014); the abstract ties that influence to strength, kin and exchange partners. That is live influence, the ground Esteem reads, though from an egalitarian setting, so it is adjacent support for this H card. Garfield, von Rueden and Hagen (2019) review political leadership from evolutionary anthropology, but the check did not read it, so it is not relied on here. Nearer the mechanism, members who display confidence in task groups are granted higher status, in the sense of respect and influence (Anderson et al. 2012, a status-enhancement account of overconfidence; unchecked, not relied on). No source, as checked, shows that a leader's influence tracks the group's prospects. That link is a proposal resting on common sense: the mechanism runs through the confidence or hesitancy she displays. A member at the top who doubts the group can be steered through hears the doubt in her own calls, feels the others' readiness to take her word loosen and is readier to give ground; a fall needs the doubt to show in her calls, and doubt she keeps to herself need not cost her. Where she is prototypical of the group, or the goal was a maximal one, a shortfall is judged less harshly (Giessner and van Knippenberg 2008, searched, not verified), so play the decrement weaker there. The lines carry her felt reading only; where the scene stages the others' actual following or turning away, play the interaction card I:Team Confidence->Esteem instead of this one, never both. Any challenge from another member belongs to the scene. Nil where she is not among those at the top who steer. Keep the fall modest. Settled precedence (Rank) is not moved by this card.

timing.typical: within the meeting or outing, after a hesitant call is questioned
timing.why: The fall needs a hesitant call, a challenge to the first turn and her giving ground, a sequence over minutes; the card asks for it to be slower than Esteem's.

forces.subtitle: Sure steering earns deference
forces.summary: For a member among those at the top who steer the group, confidence that the group can be steered through shows in her calls. Sure calls lead her to sense the others take her word on them, so Esteem rises a little. Hesitant calls lead her to sense they no longer do, and it falls. The link rests on common sense, and it moves Esteem, not Rank.
forces.summary_status: generated from the source texts, not canon; checked faithful

logic_status.by: logic checker (fresh Opus sessions), Ben reviews the flags (Ben, 5 Nov 2026, 4.12 pm)

problems.where: explanation, sentence 1: "Leaders in small-scale societies hold influence by results and reputation, not by office alone (von Rueden et al. 2014; Garfield, von Rueden and Hagen 2019)"
problems.detail: Neither source as checked supports 'by results and reputation'. The von Rueden et al. check (partly) confirms only that leaders exist and influence collective action in an egalitarian society; the abstract ties their influence to strength, kin and exchange partners, with reputation unconfirmed and results never mentioned. The Garfield et al. check (partly, not read) explicitly could not confirm that the group's success raises a leader's standing. The card's whole route (group prospects to the leader's standing) leans on the very link these checks fail to show.

problems.where: explanation, sentence 2: "Her own doubt about the top's steering, where she is at the top, shows in hesitant calls that others notice."
problems.detail: No source is cited for this mechanism. It holds up as common sense, but the text needs to say it is a proposal so that it does not read as following from the leadership sources.

logic_status.common_sense: That a top member's private doubt about steering the group shows in hesitant calls, that others notice and step into the first turn, and that her felt rung slips as she gives ground. Safe as common sense because it limits itself to members already at the top and to doubt that shows in their conduct, and the fall is kept modest.

evidence.why: No source tests a top member's confidence in the group's prospects against her felt rank; the status-enhancement studies concern confidence in one's own ability, their status-gain step is unreplicated, and the one registered replication covers only the status-desire to overconfidence link. The decrement rests on common sense bounded by leader-failure work, so the card is provisional; the card's mechanism through calls coming out sure or hesitant already matches the adjacent evidence.
evidence.boundary: The decrement is weaker for leaders seen as prototypical of the group and where the goal was maximal rather than minimal (Giessner and van Knippenberg 2008, unverified). The effect runs through displayed confidence or hesitancy: private doubt that is not shown need not lower standing, since confident display is rewarded even when unwarranted.

forces.name: Heard, so kept
forces.increment_logic: When those above me hear me out before deciding what touches me, hold me to the same rules as anyone at my rung and hand out turns and shares with no favourite served first, I take it that I count among them and that the place they keep for me is secure: my sense of being kept among them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When a decision that touches me is made over my head, or the one who hands out or settles things serves his own first and waves my objection aside, I take it that I am kept here on sufferance and could be dropped without a second thought: my sense of being kept among them falls.
forces.explanation: Relational model of authority: people read procedural justice as an index of their standing with the authority, through neutrality, trust in benevolence and status recognition (Tyler and Lind 1992, as summarised by Lind, Tyler and Huo 1997). In the integrative model of respect, treatment from the group conveys two separate components, status and inclusion (Huo, Binning and Molina 2010); this card carries the inclusion route only. Justice dimensions are related but each adds its own variance (Colquitt et al. 2001), and voice raises felt fairness beyond control (Lind, Kanfer and Earley 1990). Under Belonging's H face what moves is the felt threat of being dropped. Distinct from H:Belonging->Status (the room backing her turn) and H:Reciprocity->Belonging (partners who repay). Decrement larger than increment: a fair hearing is expected, and its absence is the stronger cue.

sources.claim: Justice dimensions each add incremental variance

evidence.why: The procedural justice to identity link is pooled in large meta-analyses (Colquitt et al. 2001; Chan et al. 2023), but on fairness, legitimacy and identification with police or organisations, without confirmed bias correction, and the two studies nearest felt belonging are single unverified lab studies. forces.name: Wanted, so fond
forces.increment_logic: When the others draw me in as one of their own, I read it as goodwill towards me and warm to them in turn, glad of their company: my fondness for them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When gatherings form without me, I feel the sting of it and turn cold towards those who left me out, though I may still look for company elsewhere: my fondness for them falls.
forces.explanation: Reciprocity of liking: being liked is read as benevolent intent and returned (Montoya and Insko 2008). Exclusion raises hostility, though not towards those who treat the excluded person warmly (Twenge et al. 2001), and the excluded seek reconnection with new partners but not with those who excluded them (Maner et al. 2007). In a small group the excluders are her fellow members, so the decrement holds and is aimed at those who left her out, not at members who treat her warmly; where one clique shut her out, scale it to that clique. Time course, from the temporal need-threat model of ostracism (Williams 2009): the sting is immediate and large, with an average effect above d = 1.4 across 120 Cyberball studies (Hartgerink et al. 2015); that figure concerns need threat and mood, not liking. Play that sting as her felt reaction in the scene, and size the move in Warmth to what lasts. The meta-analysis gave weak support to the temporal need-threat model, so the time course used here is the facilitator's judgement. In the reflective stage that follows, a member who sees a way back in often works to win it before she cools, so set the decrement small for a single exclusion by a group that has long counted her one of its own, and full where exclusion repeats or settles. Chronic exclusion ends in resignation and withdrawal, which reaches Engagement through the Pillar levels, not through this card.

forces.name: Benefit of the doubt from above
forces.increment_logic: When I am putting much of myself into this group, a call from above that goes against me and could be read either way reads as made by the order's own rules and in good faith: my sense that those above deal evenly with me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I am pulling out of this group, the same kind of call, one that could be read either way, reads as one more case of favourites served first, and a decision I may have had no need to be asked about reads as a sign I was never going to be heard: my sense that those above deal evenly with me falls.
forces.explanation: Reflective beat for Parity's H face. Ambiguous cues are read in line with what the reader expects (Downey and Feldman 1996, for expected rejection, used here by analogy; contested for this use). In the group engagement model fair procedure builds identification, which drives engagement (Tyler and Blader 2003; that forward path is itself contested); that path runs the other way, so this card is the return limb of a loop and rests on common sense: one who is invested gives the order the benefit of the doubt, one who is leaving finds grievances. The card acts only on calls that could be read either way. Treatment that is plainly unfair cuts the other way: members with high prior commitment show the steepest fall in commitment after unfair treatment, in employees who survived layoffs and in citizens dealing with legal authorities (Brockner, Tyler and Cooper-Schneider 1992). That fall is carried by the Engagement update rule (the drop of 4 at Committed or above), not by this card, and play scores the unfair treatment on Parity directly. A proposal; modest.

forces.name: Among friends
forces.increment_logic: When I am fond of them, I am glad to be among them, and among people I like a slip, a mood or a need of mine feels as if it would be met with ease, with no put-down or laugh: my felt safety to show myself rises.

forces.explanation: Social buffering: the presence of, or contact with, a bond partner lowered urinary glucocorticoids in wild chimpanzees across stressful events and in everyday affiliation, not only in crises (Wittig et al. 2016). Self-directed behaviour, a measure of anxiety, varies with how secure the relationship with a nearby animal is (Castles, Whiten and Aureli 1999). In wild female chimpanzees preferred associates co-fed more tolerantly and aggressed less, with proximity explaining tolerance better than grooming, and a 2024 meta-analysis links non-sexual affiliation to lower glucocorticoids and aggression to higher (Fox et al. 2024; Fiorini-Torrico et al. 2024; as reported by the reviewer, not checked here). All of this concerns particular bond partners, which is the scene state Close tie; carrying the easing of bracing to fondness for the members at large is the model's own step, so the primate work supports the card by analogy only. Human studies point the same way: high-quality relationships predicted later psychological safety (Carmeli, Brueller and Dutton 2009), and rewarding co-worker relations went with felt safety (May, Gilson and Harter 2004); those measure relationship quality, which includes the others' care, while Warmth is her own fondness. Assumed reciprocity of liking, the belief that those she likes like her back (Kenny and DePaulo 1993; Kenny 1994), stays as a secondary route. Because the evidence is partner-specific, scale the increment by Close tie: full where she has a close tie among those present, small where she has none. The scene carries the buffering towards the partner herself; this card carries only its spread to the members at large, so the two are not counted twice. Keep moderate, and the decrement smaller: a member who cares little for the others may still expect no put-down from them. Distinct from E:Belonging->Safety (comfort after a knock from those who accept her) and E:Reciprocity->Safety (support received). forces.framework: Social buffering by bond partners (Wittig et al. 2016); relationship security and self-directed behaviour (Castles, Whiten and Aureli 1999); relationship quality and psychological safety; assumed reciprocity of liking as secondary route.

evidence.why: Evidence from three fields points the same way (a psychological-safety antecedent meta-analysis, bond-partner glucocorticoid reduction in wild chimpanzees, and conditional friend buffering), but each measures support received or physiological stress, never the focal member's own fondness, so it is analogous more than adjacent. No registered or bias-corrected test of the central step was found, and the friend-buffering work is conditional, so the card is provisional with boundaries.
evidence.boundary: The easing depends on a liked member being near and responsive, or sharing the situation; friend presence alone can fail to ease, or can even raise, stress reactions (adolescent friend-buffering work, not yet verified), and in one lab study it helped only the socially anxious (Pontari 2009, not yet verified). The decrement is smaller than the increment. Direction is open in the cross-sectional work, since felt safety may also raise fondness (the loop the card already flags).

forces.name: Counted on, cared for
forces.increment_logic: When I can leave the work in their hands and they come through, I take it as goodwill towards me, stop watching them, spend easier time in their company and come to care how they fare: my fondness for them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I keep having to chase and redo what they took on, I read it as little thought for me, their company turns into watching them, and I care less how they fare: my fondness for them falls.
forces.explanation: Cognition-based trust, grounded in beliefs about others' reliability, and affect-based trust, grounded in reciprocated care, are distinct, and in managers' and professionals' ratings of peers at work the first predicted the second (McAllister 1995). In 191 teams cognition-based trust in the leader likewise fed affect-based trust (Schaubroeck, Lam and Peng 2011). The step runs largely through the goodwill that dependable work signals: benevolence is the main driver of affect-based trust (Tomlinson et al. 2020, not yet read here), and reliability and goodwill correlate strongly in how people judge others, though each adds to trust on its own (Colquitt, Scott and LePine 2007). Where she reads reliability as mere competence, with no regard for her in it, fondness moves little. Affect-based trust is mutual care, nearer Warmth than any other perception, but not the same as her one-way fondness, so keep the step modest. The decrement, resentment of those she must chase, rests on common sense. Distinct from E:Reciprocity->Warmth (gratitude for help returned) and E:Belonging->Warmth (liking returned for acceptance). It forms a Reinforce loop with E:Warmth->Dependability; the brake is parts plainly dropped, scored by play.

evidence.why: The cognition-to-affect trust path rests on single cross-sectional or multilevel field studies (McAllister 1995; Schaubroeck, Lam and Peng 2011), mostly about trust in a leader rather than fondness for peers, and a 2023 critical review finds affect-based trust poorly measured. Nothing replicated tests the step and no null was found, so the card stays provisional, with the newer finding that benevolence carries affect-based trust written in as a boundary.
evidence.boundary: Dependability raises fondness mainly when she reads it as goodwill towards her. Perceived benevolence, more than ability or reliability, drives affect-based trust (Tomlinson et al. 2020, not yet verified), and ability, benevolence and integrity correlate highly, so the reliability effect may be carried by inferred goodwill (Colquitt, Scott and LePine 2007, not yet verified). Reliability she reads as mere competence or self-interest should do little for warmth.

forces.increment_logic: When those above hear me out and weigh what I put forward by the same rules as anyone's, what I bring gets a fair showing, and I come to expect, a little more, that the next problem will come to me: my sense that they turn to me for what I bring rises a little.

forces.explanation: In the group engagement model, fair procedure from authorities shapes members' sense of respect, their standing within the group, which with pride carries identification and cooperation (Tyler and Blader 2003). The integrative model of respect splits respect conveyed by treatment into status and liking, or inclusion, and finds perceived status the stronger predictor of social engagement (Huo, Binning and Molina 2010). H:Parity->Belonging (Heard, so kept) carries the inclusion pathway but not the status pathway; that pathway maps on Esteem, deference for what she brings. Respect in those works is a felt evaluation conveyed by treatment, close to Esteem but not identical (it does not need her to be copied or sought out). The gain in felt worth reaches her expectation of being sought out only by inference, a common-sense step, so keep the card small. Boundary: the group engagement model routes these effects through identification, so the card is weaker where she values a hearing only for what it gets her, or where the group matters little to who she is. evidence.why: Social psychology and organisational justice support fair hearing raising felt respect and status recognition, but the load-bearing studies (group-value and group engagement work, Lind, Tyler and Huo 1997, Huo et al. 2010) are single, non-preregistered and not replicated, and the replicated justice meta-analyses do not measure status or being sought out. No source measures the card's outcome and no bias-corrected test of the status pathway was found, so the card is provisional with its low strength kept.
evidence.boundary: Where she values voice mainly for its effect on outcomes, the status route is weaker and an expected-outcome route competes (Hildreth, Moore and Blader 2014, not yet verified). The identity pathway is weaker where her identity motivation in the group is low. Status also moderates reactions to voice (van Prooijen et al. 2005, not yet verified), so part of the association may run from standing to reactions to procedure rather than the card's direction.

forces.name: Heard before the call
forces.increment_logic: When those above me hear me out before a call that touches me and weigh an objection of mine instead of waving it off, I expect a slip, a doubt or a disagreement shown in front of them to draw no put-down or rebuff, and I let it show: my felt safety to show myself rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When calls that touch me are made over my head and an objection gets me waved off or met with a threat from above, I expect anything I let show in front of them to draw a put-down or a rebuff, so I swallow my doubts, hide my slips and keep my face set: my felt safety to show myself falls.
forces.explanation: Leader inclusiveness, words and acts of those in charge that invite and value others' contributions, predicts psychological safety and weakens the inhibiting effect of status differences (Nembhard and Edmondson 2006, 23 neonatal units). Managerial openness was more consistently tied to improvement-oriented voice than transformational leadership, with psychological safety carrying the link (Detert and Burris 2007). Supportive supervisor relations go with higher felt safety (May, Gilson and Harter 2004), and positive leader relations are among the meta-analytic antecedents of safety (Frazier et al. 2017). The card reads Parity's hierarchical face, the hearing and even dealing of those above. Distinct from X:Status->DivsExp (her own rung) and E:Levelling->DivsExp (fear of a coercer among equals). Where this card and the rung card fire on one scene, play the rung card smaller: inclusiveness moderates the status gap. Mostly cross-sectional evidence; keep the step moderate. A cross card: Safety is an egalitarian Pillar that keeps running in a ranked group, and this card carries the hearing of those above into it.

forces.subtitle: Being heard makes speaking up safe
forces.summary: When people above hear me out before a call that touches me, and weigh my objection fairly, I expect that showing a doubt or slip in front of them will not be punished. Parity in its hierarchical face, the hearing and even dealing of those above, therefore raises my sense of Safety to show myself. Being shut out or threatened lowers it.
forces.summary_status: generated from the source texts, not canon; checked faithful

evidence.why: The association rests on member surveys of psychological safety, which count as direct, pooled in a 136-sample meta-analysis and in a 105-sample inclusive-leadership meta-analysis, with longitudinal support (Hirak et al. 2012) and no null for the main step. It is graded provisional only because no source confirms the pooled effect survives bias correction and the leader antecedent is not cleanly separated from general supervisor support. It should move to substantiated if the Frazier et al. or 105-sample full text shows a bias-corrected effect for leader inclusiveness or openness.
evidence.boundary: Hearing her out raises safety only when her objection is visibly weighed and acted on; in a randomised field experiment, assigning leaders to seek feedback did not raise team safety (Coutifaris and Grant 2022, not yet verified). Effect size may vary with how the culture treats rank (power distance; Dai et al. 2022, not yet verified). The claim that inclusiveness weakens the inhibiting effect of rank rests on one 23-unit study (Nembhard and Edmondson 2006) and is unreplicated.

forces.name: Ribbing the big shot
forces.increment_logic: When a member's grab, boast or bossing jars me as plainly wrong, I rib him for it and say so, and knowing that ribbing here tends to bring a big shot back to size, I feel no one here can set himself over us without an answer: my sense that no one here can lord it over me rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When a big-shot move leaves me unmoved, I let it pass with a shrug, and with no answer from me I expect him to keep the extra and give the next direction unchecked: my sense that no one here can lord it over me falls a little.
forces.explanation: The everyday levelling tools of foragers are third-party ribbing, criticism and complaint, which escalate only rarely (Wiessner 2005), and the rank and file check would-be dominants together (Boehm 1993); the !Kung belittle a successful hunter's meat to keep him modest before he can think himself a big man (Lee 1969). These make her expectation that ribbing checks a big shot a fair one; collective uptake and his backing off belong to the scene. The interaction card I:Rule-Keeping->Parity, which shares this card's name, carries that uptake; this card carries only her own expectation, so where the scene stages the uptake, play this card small. The step from her own ribbing to her felt sense that no one can lord it over her rests on common sense. Where she bristles but keeps quiet, for want of power or for what she stands to lose with him (Molho et al. 2020, as cited in the Rule-Keeping definition), play the increment small: a silent bristle checks no one. All 15 societies tested showed some willingness to pay to punish unequal behaviour, with its strength varying widely and tracking altruism (Henrich et al. 2006, checked), but costly third-party punishment is weaker in small societies (Marlowe et al. 2008, not checked here), so in small groups the card runs on talk and coolness, not fines or blows. Disapproval that costs the target nothing raises cooperation, though less lastingly than fines (Masclet et al. 2003, not checked here). Boundary: the effect of costless disapproval is small and fades without repeated contact or some backing (Masclet et al. 2003; Sparks, Burleigh and Barclay 2024, cited by the checker, neither checked here), so keep both lines small and stronger in a group whose members keep meeting. Both lines need a member pushing, grabbing or bossing; where no one is, set both nil. Whether they would back her is E:Belonging->Parity. Where this card and E:Safety->Parity fire on one scene, play E:Safety->Parity small. Forms a Reinforce loop through E:Parity->Reciprocity and X:Reciprocity->Rule-Keeping; it runs down as readily as up, so watch for drift from play to play.

forces.subtitle: Ribbing keeps big shots in check
forces.summary: Rule-Keeping drives Parity. A member who is jarred by a grab, boast or bossing ribs the big shot, and expects that ribbing brings him back to size, so she feels no one here can lord it over her. If a big-shot move leaves her unmoved, she expects him to keep the extra, and her sense of Parity falls. It needs someone pushing, and runs stronger where members keep meeting.
forces.summary_status: generated from the source texts, not canon; checked faithful

evidence.why: The ethnography (Boehm, Wiessner, Lee) and the experiments on costless disapproval agree on the direction, but none of it is replicated and none was read in full, so nothing verified can be load-bearing yet. The step from ribbing to the member's own felt Parity rests on common sense.
evidence.boundary: Talk alone checks a big shot only a little and the check fades without backing (Masclet et al. 2003; Sparks, Burleigh and Barclay 2024, both still to be read), so the rise needs repeated contact and some backing from the others (see E:Belonging->Levelling). Costly third-party punishment is weaker in small societies (Marlowe et al. 2008), so the card runs on ribbing and criticism, not fines or blows. The shrug line has no direct evidence beyond the absence of a sanction.

forces.name: Rope for friends
forces.increment_logic: When I am fond of them, I leave work in their hands and turn my back on it as I would with a friend, sure it will be carried through: my confidence that they will do their part rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When their company is a duty, I keep the work in my own hands and check what I hand over: my confidence that they will do their part falls.
forces.explanation: Chimpanzees chose to trust friends far more often than non-friends in a trust game, yet friends were no more likely to return food once trusted (Engelmann and Herrmann 2016, a single small study of 15 animals; no replication found). So fondness raises her readiness to rely on them, and the card carries that felt confidence, not their reliability. The decrement rests on common sense: with little fondness she holds back that readiness. What she later sees carried through, and the sampling gain from entrusting more (Denrell 2005 is cited by Model B, not checked here), belong to the scene. Boundary: friends are trusted more without proving more trustworthy, so the card never stands in for their actual reliability; confidence built on affect predicts outcomes less well than confidence built on evidence, and its measures overlap with expectations of reliability (cited by the checker, not checked here). The card bites only on parts whose outcome she has not yet seen; a seen record outweighs it (Dependability definition), and clear evidence of parts dropped sets the increment nil. Keep the card modest. Takes over the chimpanzee evidence from E:Belonging->Dependability; where both fire, play that card small. The interaction card I:Warmth->Dependability carries the same link once the scene stages the others' side; this card carries only her own readiness to rely on them, so where the scene stages that card, play this one small. It forms a Reinforce loop with E:Dependability->Warmth; the brake is parts plainly dropped, scored by play. Evidence: provisional.

forces.name: Friends don't keep count
forces.increment_logic: When I am fond of them, I give without marking it, and a return that came late, in another kind or from another member would still count with me as help come back: my sense that help here comes back to me rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I care little for them, I mark every favour I give, and each one not yet returned stands out as help that has not come back: my sense that help here comes back to me falls.
forces.explanation: Primates reciprocate over long time frames, and the proposed mechanism is emotional bookkeeping: accumulated feeling towards partners, not a tally of who gave what (Schino and Aureli 2009). Reciprocity in food sharing may run through preferring friends (Jaeggi and Gurven 2013). People in communal relationships keep less track of inputs than people in exchange relationships (Clark 1984; Clark, Mills and Corcoran 1989; neither checked here), track the other's needs more (Clark, Mills and Powell 1986, not checked here), and like a partner less when a benefit is promptly repaid (Clark and Mills 1979). These studies concern particular partners; carrying the loose bookkeeping to the members at large, so that a return from another member counts, is the model's own step and untested. Warmth therefore slows the fall in her reading when returns lag, and lets a return from anyone count. Boundaries: the loose accounting is shown with close partners and is weaker with members she barely knows, so keep the card moderate in a large group or one new to her, and let a Close tie in the scene carry the partner-level effect. Humans reciprocate more in kind than other primates do (Jaeggi and Gurven 2013, not checked here), so a return in another kind may count for less. The card moves her reading, not the return itself; help that plainly fails to come back still lowers Reciprocity through scenes. It forms a loop with E:Reciprocity->Warmth; keep both moderate. Distinct from E:Belonging->Reciprocity (their acceptance of her) and I:Warmth->Reciprocity (friends actually giving back).

evidence.why: Communal and exchange tracking work comes from one lab with no registered replication, and the perceived-return side and the group-wide step are untested. forces.name: Told, and closer
forces.increment_logic: When I feel safe to show myself, I tell them how things are with me, the good news as well as the knocks, and in the telling I find myself drawn to the ones I have told: my fondness for them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When I brace and mask myself, I keep my news and my troubles to myself and sit through their talk at arm's length, and the distance I keep settles into a coolness towards them: my fondness for them falls a little.
forces.explanation: People tell others about most of their emotional episodes, and sharing builds bonds between teller and listener (Rimé 2009, review); the card takes from this that the telling itself draws the teller closer. Disclosers come to like those they have disclosed to (Collins and Miller 1994, meta-analysis, not checked here). Suppressing expression, as a habit and in a new setting, predicted less closeness to others and less social support in students entering college, across self, weekly and peer reports (Srivastava et al. 2009). Suppression within a single conversation lowers the partner's rapport (Butler et al. 2003); that is the others' side and belongs to the scene, not to this card. How the others take up her news (Gable, Reis, Impett and Asher 2004, on responsive uptake in couples) also belongs to the scene, on the interaction card I:Safety->Warmth; a disclosure met badly brakes her fondness there, and where the scene stages that card, play this one small. This card carries her own fondness, raised by having told; E:Safety->Belonging carries her sense of their acceptance. Where one disclosure fires both, play both small. Warmth reads the members as a whole, so scale the rise to how much of the group she has told; telling one friend moves it little. Keep the decrement smaller: masking keeps her from growing closer more than it pushes her away. The rise comes over the minutes of the telling. Forms a loop with E:Warmth->Safety.

forces.name: Passed over for her
forces.increment_logic: When the others turn to me whenever my kind of skill counts, no one is preferred over me in it, and I warm to those who look to me: my fondness for them rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When they turn past me to another member for my kind of skill, I feel the sting; where she plainly earned it, my fondness barely moves, and where she seems not to have earned it the sting turns sour and I resent her and those who turn to her: my fondness for them falls.
forces.explanation: Envy comes in two forms with different experiences and aims: benign envy moves the envier to rise, malicious envy to pull the other down (van de Ven, Zeelenberg and Pieters 2009, three countries); the two are separate dispositions, with hope for success feeding the benign form and fear of failure the malicious (Lange and Crusius 2015). Whether the other's advantage seems deserved is the appraisal that separates them (van de Ven, Zeelenberg and Pieters 2012). The two-type split is itself contested (Cohen-Charash and Larson 2017, not checked here), so lean on the deservingness appraisal more than on the labels. Size the decrement by that appraisal. Where the rival plainly does it better, the envy is benign: I watch how the rival does it and want to match her, and my fondness falls only a little or not at all. Where the rival seems not to have earned it (show, or luck the others mistake for skill), the envy is malicious and the fall is larger, aimed at the rival and those who turn to her. Where the others turn to the rival as a favourite, tilting chances or a hearing towards their own, that is Parity's ground and cools fondness through E:Parity->Warmth; play this card small there. The increment is small: being looked to for her own kind of skill leaves the focal member with no one preferred over her in it and warms her a little to those who look to her, which rests on common sense. A close other's success threatens most when it lies in one's own domain (Tesser 1988), so scale the card to how near the rival is to the focal member and how much the skill is the focal member's own. Warmth is fondness for the members at large, so scale the fall to how much of the group the rival and those who turn to her make up. In a small band where a would-be star is levelled by ribbing, the unearned case also feeds the talk carried by X:Esteem->Repute when the pack is on; this card moves only the focal member's fondness. The card's era rests on prestige-biased copying, deference to those whose skill is worth learning from (Henrich and Gil-White 2001, not checked here); capuchin inequity aversion is contested and does not carry it. Envy is felt within seconds of being passed over; its cooling settles over the gathering.

era.why: Watching and copying skilled or successful models is found in chimpanzees and other primates, and resentment at being passed over has a non-verbal analogue in primate responses to unequal treatment (capuchin inequity aversion). Neither end needs talk, though the wider levelling by ribbing does and is carried by a separate card.

Where she plainly does it better, the envy is benign: I watch how she does it and want to match her, and my fondness falls only a little or not at all. Where she seems not to have earned it (show, or luck the others mistake for skill), the envy is malicious and the fall is larger, aimed at her and those who turn to her. Where the others turn to her as a favourite, tilting chances or a hearing towards their own, that is Parity's ground and cools fondness through E:Levelling->Warmth; play this card small there. The increment is small: being looked to for her own kind of skill leaves no one preferred over her in it and warms her a little to those who look to her, which rests on common sense. A close other's success threatens most when it lies in one's own domain (Tesser 1988), so scale the card to how near she is and how much the skill is the member's own. Warmth is fondness for the members at large, so scale the fall to how much of the group the rival and those who turn to her make up. In a small band where a would-be star is levelled by ribbing, the unearned case also feeds the talk carried by X:Prestige->Repute when the pack is on; this card moves only her fondness. The card's era rests on prestige-biased copying, deference to those whose skill is worth learning from (Henrich and Gil-White 2001, not checked here); capuchin inequity aversion is contested and does not carry it. Envy is felt within seconds of being passed over; its cooling settles over the gathering.

timing.why: The sting of seeing the others turn past her to a rival is an immediate felt reaction, and the explanation puts envy within seconds; the small warming from being looked to arrives just as fast.

forces.subtitle: Being passed over cools fondness
forces.summary: Esteem drives Warmth. Being looked to for her own kind of skill warms her a little to those who look to her. Being passed over for another member stings. How far her fondness falls depends on whether the rival earned it: if plainly so, it barely moves; if not, she resents the rival and those who turn to her, and her Warmth falls further.

evidence.why: Envy studies measure motivation and hostility toward the envied person, not fondness for the group, and none is replicated, so the step from being passed over to lower Warmth is inferred. The deservingness split rests on one lab's studies and their internal meta-analysis.
evidence.boundary: The fall is aimed mainly at the rival and those who turn to her, and benign envy (a plainly earned advantage) leaves fondness near unchanged, as the card already says. forces.name: Going well, glad of them
forces.increment_logic: When I feel surer we can pull the venture off, the work runs light, I laugh more easily with them and am glad to be in their company: my fondness for them rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When the venture starts to look beyond us, the gatherings turn tense and flat and their company weighs on me: my fondness for them falls a little.
forces.explanation: Members of successful groups tend to like one another more than members of unsuccessful ones (Lott and Lott 1965, a review of group cohesiveness as interpersonal attraction), so a lift in the venture's prospects warms her to the members and a sag cools her. That evidence concerns outcomes received; the step from her felt confidence in the venture is by analogy. Affect tracks the rate of progress towards a goal against what was expected (Carver and Scheier 1990, searched). In one lab study, groups exposed to pleasant mood contagion showed more cooperation and less conflict than those exposed to unpleasant contagion (Barsade 2002), a supporting route through shared mood. Performance and cohesion are linked both ways; Mullen and Copper (1994, cited by Model B, not checked here) find commitment to the task the main part, while Beal et al. (2003, not checked here) find interpersonal attraction related to performance too, so the share carried by liking is not settled. Ratings of cohesion after performance feedback may be partly halo. Keep the card small. Boundary: the same review finds that shared failure can also raise liking, especially where it is imposed arbitrarily from outside (Lott and Lott 1965); where the venture sags under an outside blow they all bear, set the decrement nil, and fondness may hold or rise in play. Warmth here reads the members as a whole. Fire it on a change in Team Confidence, not on a steady level: a venture long known to be in reach lifts no one. Distinct from E:Team Confidence->Belonging, which carries the others' ease with her.

forces.name: Pulled up, back in line
forces.increment_logic: When letting a part drop jars me as plainly wrong, whoever does it, and it would show in me, by a word, a mutter or a cold shoulder, I know a part let drop here will not slip by unnoticed, by me at least, and I leave work in their hands with less checking: my confidence that they will do their part rises a little.
forces.decrement_logic: When letting a part drop leaves me unmoved and I would let it pass, I know nothing I do holds anyone to their part, so a part left with them rests more on their goodwill and I start keeping an eye on it: my confidence that they will do their part falls a little.
forces.explanation: The chance to sanction raises and holds contributions (Fehr and Gächter 2000), disapproval that costs the target nothing works too, though less than fines (Masclet et al. 2003), and across 187 effect sizes punishment raised cooperation by about d = 0.7, more in groups that stay together (Balliet, Mulder and Van Lange 2011). Dependability may rest on knowing that a part let drop gets pulled up by the group or its rules. The card carries her own side of that: where a breach jars her, she counts on a dropped part not slipping by; where it leaves her unmoved, her reliance rests more on the others' goodwill. The evidence above makes that expectation a fair one; the step from her own bristle to her confidence in others rests on common sense. A high reading does not by itself mean she will speak up: whether the bristle comes out depends on her power and what she stands to lose (Molho et al. 2020), so scale the increment to whether she could voice or show it; a low member who would bristle and keep quiet gains little. Whether the others then carry their parts belongs to the scene (rulebook 8.5) and moves Dependability through its own plays, so keep both lines small. Where the scene stages the others backing or ignoring her objection, play I:Rule-Keeping->Dependability instead. Where a part has just been dropped in the scene, the dropped part lowers Dependability through its own play; this card only softens that fall for a member whose bristle would show, and never turns a dodge into a net rise. Boundaries. Sanctions do more in high-trust settings (Balliet and Van Lange 2013, not checked here): scale the increment to how far she already trusts the members. Lab punishment effects may not carry over to small egalitarian field groups (Guala 2012, not checked here), which keeps the card small. Where antisocial punishment or counter-punishment is common, pulling up draws retaliation and less cooperation (Herrmann, Thöni and Gächter 2008; Nikiforakis 2008), and she knows her bristle promises little: set the increment small. Where she cannot see who dropped what, her bristle may land on the wrong member and cooperation can fall (Grechenig, Nicklisch and Thöni 2010): set both lines small. Punishment pays on long horizons and can cost on short ones (Gächter, Renner and Sefton 2008, searched): larger in a standing group, small for a one-off task. A standing sanction can lower trust that others act from their own will, and reliance then drops further once the check is gone (Mulder, van Dijk, De Cremer and Wilke 2006); this crowding-out is contested, with a 2023 preregistered replication reported to find no effect (cited by the checker, not checked here), so where she reads the others as carrying parts only because they are watched, set the increment small, and treat the boundary as provisional. Where the others think the breach harmless (H:Rule-Keeping->Belonging, circumstance two), set both small. A lone rebuke she expects no one to take up bites less, so scale the increment to whether she expects others to join. Distinct from E:Parity->Dependability: compliance under one coercer's eye is not this card. With X:Dependability->Rule-Keeping it forms a Reinforce loop: parts carried keep a dodge conspicuous and her bristle keen, and a keen bristle keeps her counting on parts being carried. The loop runs down as readily as up, so keep both small and watch for runs from play to play. Deck X: Rule-Keeping is hierarchical, Dependability egalitarian.

edits_log: Ripple round 1, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): The increment pulls the member back into line with 'a sharp word or a turned shoulder'. Under the revised Rule-Keeping definition a cold shoulder is contempt's form, kept for a breach that repeats or reads as bad character. It lasts and ends in exclusion, not in the member mending their ways and being taken back. The card's mechanism, a part let drop pulled up and then carried through, runs on anger's forms (an objection, a rebuke or mockery), so the increment should name those. The decrement, type, boundaries and literature pass.

Ripple round 2, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Both lines assume the others' response as part of the card: 'and the others take it up' in the increment, 'and no one else says a word' in the decrement. A card is the focal member's reaction from her source Pillar and never assumes another's response (Ben, 6 Nov 2026, 4.37 am); whether others join belongs to the scene, and the explanation already scales the increment to it. The fix removes those clauses. Everything else passes: the source at both levels, Dependability's clause that reliance may rest on a dropped part being pulled up, the boundary with Rule-Keeping, the type (with X:OutResp->NormExp, Inverse, a balancing loop) and the literature as cited.

Ripple round 3, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): (1) Both lines run through the others' response (the next part comes in on time; the member drops the next part and others follow), which the evidence standard (Ben, 6 Nov 2026, 4.37 am) and rulebook 8.5 assign to the scene; the card must be her own reaction from Rule-Keeping. Dependability's definition gives a route that stays with her: reliance may rest on knowing that a part let drop gets pulled up. (2) The explanation calls the loop with X:OutResp->NormExp balancing and says shirking sharpens the bristle; that card is now Reinforce, so the pair forms a reinforcing loop, as X:OutResp->NormExp itself states.

Ripple round 4, 5 Nov 2026 (Ben, 11.22 am: start the ripple process): Source and target readings, type, deck and overlap all pass: the increment draws on Rule-Keeping's high anchor (pulling the member up on the spot, with pulling your weight among the levelling ways) and on Dependability's clause that reliance may rest on a dropped part being pulled up, and the card stays clear of E:Levelling->OutResp and X:OutResp->NormExp. One fault: the decrement line (and the explanation's matching sentence) says that once she would let a dodge pass, a part left with them 'rests on their goodwill alone'. Dependability says reliance may rest on the group or its rules pulling up a dropped part, and her own indifference does not remove those, so 'alone' overreaches. The fix is to say her reliance rests more on their goodwill. The mechanism agrees with the cited literature. One known boundary is missing: a standing sanction can lower trust that others act from their own will, so reliance falls when the check is gone (Mulder, van Dijk, De Cremer and Wilke 2006). That supports the decrement and limits the increment where she sees the others carrying parts only because they are watched. Added as a short boundary; it needs recording in docs/literature.md.

forces.name: Rules we had a say in
forces.increment_logic: When those above hear us out before setting how the work is shared, hold everyone at our rung to the same rules and keep to them themselves, I expect the others to take the rules as their own and carry their parts without being chased: my confidence that they will do their part rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When the rules for the work are set over our heads and bent for favourites, I expect the others to do the least the rules demand and let parts slide once no one is looking: my confidence that they will do their part falls.
forces.explanation: A rule to promote cooperation raised cooperation more when subjects voted for it than when it was imposed, with selection controlled (Dal Bó, Foster and Putterman 2010); Ugandan farmers cooperated more under an elected monitor than a randomly chosen one (Baldassarri and Grossman 2011). Leaders who contribute first shape followers' early beliefs (Gächter and Renner 2018), which bears directly on the clause that those above keep to the rules themselves. Ostrom's principles that members help make the rules and that monitors answer to them are well supported in 91 field studies (Cox, Arnold and Villamayor-Tomás 2010). Apart from the leader clause, the step from the others' behaviour in those findings to her own confidence in them is inferred, resting on what she expects of them and on common sense; keep it moderate. Boundaries: a say in the rules helps only where members adopt them and are bound by them, and choosing institutions is not reliably better than having them imposed (Dannenberg and Gallier 2020, not checked here). The favouritism clause has only small, unreplicated lab support, so play the decrement's bent-rules case small. Reads Parity's hierarchical face; E:Levelling->OutResp reads coercion among equals, so play only the card for the face in play. Deck X: Parity's H face to an egalitarian Pillar.

evidence.boundary: Voice raises others' reliability only where members actually adopt the rules and are bound by them; the advantage of chosen over imposed rules is not guaranteed and depends on adoption and costs (Dannenberg and Gallier 2020). forces.name: Paid apart
forces.increment_logic: When those above hand out pay, credit and chances to us by the same rules, and any gap goes plainly to whoever did more, nothing comes between me and the others at my rung, and I am easy in their company: my fondness for them rises a little.

forces.explanation: In a month-long field experiment, paying co-workers unequally by their productivity rank cut output, attendance and their ability to cooperate for their own benefit, and the effects vanished where the better paid were plainly more productive (Breza, Kaur and Shamdasani 2018). Their measure of cooperation among co-workers is closer to Warmth than to any other Pillar but is not her one-way fondness, so keep the card moderate. The fall comes from members left behind by a gap that is unjustified or opaque; the favoured member is not expected to warm. An earned gap leaves Parity untouched, as Parity's definition already says. The increment is the weakest limb and rests on common sense: the evidence shows equal rules avoiding the harm, not raising fondness, so keep it small. Warmth reads the members as a whole: her coolness to the one favoured counts only as far as that member is part of the group, and the rest of the fall is the gap souring the group's company, the felt side of the lost cooperation in that study. No cooling towards the members passed over with her is assumed. Envy of a peer turned to for skill is E:Esteem->Warmth; where one favoured peer fires both, play only one, this card where the gap was handed out from above. forces.name: Fond, so wanted
forces.increment_logic: When I am fond of them, I take it they are fond of me too, and a nod, a seat kept or a glance my way reads as warmth returned: my sense that they want me among them rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When their company is a duty to me, I take it the coolness runs both ways, and the same nod reads as politeness and a gap beside me as meant: my sense that they want me among them falls a little.
forces.explanation: Assumed reciprocity of liking: a perceiver who likes a target tends to think the target likes her back, and this is among the strongest effects in interpersonal perception; with actual reciprocity of liking it accounts for most of how accurately people know who likes them (Kenny and DePaulo 1993). Her fondness therefore colours how she reads the small, ambiguous signs of acceptance. The card is her projection only; whether they in fact draw her in is the interaction card I:Warmth->Belonging, so on one cue play one. It acts on ambiguous signs; plain welcome or plain exclusion is read as it is. People underestimate how much they are liked early in acquaintance (the liking gap: Boothby et al. 2018), so keep the increment modest for a newcomer. Keep the decrement smaller than the increment: under the E face a reserved member stays one of them. With E:Belonging->Warmth it forms a tight Reinforce loop; the brake is plain exclusion read as it is. Where E:Engagement->Belonging also colours the same cue, play one. Reads generalised assumed reciprocity (Kenny and DePaulo 1993): fondness for the members as a whole colours her sense of being wanted by them as a whole; fondness for one partner belongs to interaction cards. Evidence: provisional; the step from assumed reciprocity to her felt acceptance by the group rests on common sense.

forces.name: Rules worth keeping
forces.increment_logic: When those above hear me out, hold everyone at my rung to the same rules and keep to them themselves, the settled ways read as ours and rightly kept, and a member who breaks them in a way the group would condemn jars me as plainly wrong: my indignation at breaches rises.
forces.decrement_logic: When calls are made over my head and the rules bend for favourites, the settled ways read as theirs, kept for their own benefit, and a member who slips the group's conventions stirs little in me: my indignation at breaches falls.
forces.explanation: Fair procedure from authorities raises the legitimacy members grant them, a path that holds in longitudinal data, and legitimacy raises compliance (Walters and Bolger 2019, meta-analysis); in the group engagement model fair procedure feeds members' identity and through it their rule following (Tyler and Blader 2003). That evidence concerns her own endorsement and compliance. Adjacent evidence links legitimacy to acting against others' breaches: people who judge the police legitimate are readier to report crimes and help bring offenders in (Sunshine and Tyler 2003; Tyler and Fagan 2008; neither checked here). That evidence is behaviour, not felt indignation, so the step to her indignation at another member's breach rests on common sense: one guards ways one holds rightful and shrugs at breaches of ways kept for others' benefit. No direct test found, a gap. Boundaries: where the breach is a refusal of the very rule that serves the favourites, she may side with the breacher (normative conflict, as on H:Engagement->NormExp), so the card does not fire there. The decrement acts on the group's conventions only: a breach that wrongs a member, taking from her, hurting her or leaving her to carry the breacher's share, still jars her however the ways are kept from above, and the card does not soften it. The decrement concerns breaches by members at large; a favourite let off the rules is the tilt itself, read on Parity, and the card does not lower her bristle at it. Fair procedure also raises identification, which reaches Rule-Keeping through H:Engagement->NormExp; where the Engagement update already carries the same treatment, play that card small. Rule-Keeping here is her indignation at others' breaches, not her own conformity. Modest.
